events.title: Kimberly Guilfoyle asked to resign as Greece ambassador
events.summary: The White House has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle , the U.S. ambassador to Greece, to resign after reports of alleged misconduct before and during her diplomatic posting. Why it matters: The potential removal of the president's longtime political ally and former fiancée of his son Donald Trump Jr. follows a series of Wall Street Journal reports alleging she used her political connections to seek financial favors and promote private business interests. Guilfoyle has denied any wrongdoing. White House press secretary Katie Zacharia confirmed the request on Tuesday during her first press briefing. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well," Zacharia said. Guilfoyle's removal isn't entirely surprising, as Trump told reporters yesterday that he was "looking at" firing Guilfoyle following the allegations: "We're not happy," he said. Those comments follow a senior U.S. official telling AP that Trump and Rubio were "extremely pissed off" about the reports and were considering dismissing her. Driving the news: The WSJ's Oct. 8 report said that Guilfoyle allegedly sought $100,000 from a Trump donor to pay a credit card bill before her Senate confirmation hearing, and offered access to Trump administration officials in return. The donor did not make the payment. An earlier investigation alleged she promoted the interests of a Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings. The WSJ also reported that recordings captured Guilfoyle allegedly discussing private jet travel and luxury hospitality provided by wealthy Greek businessmen. For the record: Guilfoyle's lawyer disputed the authenticity of messages the WSJ cited and the U.S. Embassy in Athens said she has followed State Department ethics and gift-reporting guidelines. Zoom in: Secretary of State Marco Rubio publicly defended Guilfoyle during a visit to Athens on Oct. 7, calling her "a strong ambassador." A day later, Rubio declined to address the allegations, saying he didn't know whether they were true. Flashback: Trump nominated Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host and California prosecutor, in December 2024. The Senate confirmed her in September 2025. What we're watching: The State Department's inspector general is reviewing the allegations, AP reported, citing an unnamed U.S. official. It is unclear whether a formal investigation has begun. Congressional Democrats have called for an investigation, with Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, requesting on Oct. 10 that Guilfoyle testify under oath.

events.title: Apple's first smart home device, the HomeView, is here
events.summary: Apple has unveiled HomeView. Apple Apple's first smart home device is here. The Apple HomeView is a new device with a screen and speaker that acts as a control hub for your connected home devices. It's the latest attempt by Apple to make its ecosystem more "sticky," or harder to leave. Apple has officially entered into a new product category: the smart home. The company on Tuesday announced the HomeView, a new AI-powered hub designed to reside in your home and control your connected home accessories. The device consists of a 7-inch Liquid Retina display that sits atop a domed speaker base and works with Siri AI. The device can be placed on a tabletop, and a separate model can be mounted to the wall. "Apple HomeView is designed to be shared by everyone in the home yet feel completely personal to each user," said Greg Joswiak, Apple's senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing, said in a statement. The product, he said, "recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home." HomeView can recognize up to six people and surface personal content for the user in front of it, such as messages, calendar information, and apps. It draws on "personal context from your iPhone to help you find what you need and get more done, all while keeping everyone's information private and secure," Joswiak said. The device is priced at $299, with preorders opening Tuesday ahead of a November 13 launch. HomeView is priced at $299. Apple Part of Apple's new smart home lineup HomeView anchors Apple Home Collection, a new lineup of smart home cameras, thermostats, and a lock that Apple developed in collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. As a smart home dashboard, the device can display camera feeds, adjust thermostats and lights, lock doors, and close blinds using touchscreen or voice commands. Apple said it can livestream up to nine video feeds at once. "With a supported iCloud+ subscription, HomeView works with compatible cameras to deliver intelligent, end-to-end encrypted recognition of people, familiar faces, pets, packages, and vehicles, notifying the household the moment someone arrives at the front door," Apple said. HomeView marks the second major new device announced under new Apple CEO John Ternus, who took over for Tim Cook in September ahead of the company's iPhone event. At that event, Ternus also unveiled the first folding smartphone, the iPhone Duo, which begins preorders later this week. Apple has long supported the smart home ecosystem with its HomeKit standard that third-party device makers could choose to use to help their devices more seamlessly integrate with the iPhone. The HomeView underscores that Apple views the smart home market as one worth competing in with its own hardware. If the new device takes off, a consumer moving outside the Apple ecosystem — or "breaking up with Apple" for Amazon or Samsung or Google or another rival — becomes a harder decision. Apple is famous for deeply integrated software and hardware. This is a developing story… Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: More homebuyers are taking a chance on adjustable-rate mortgages, hoping rates will fall—here’s how to think about that bet
events.summary: Save and Invest Why NFL rookie Barion Brown says he saved ‘every penny’ of his first pro paycheck Become Debt-Free To stop a debt spiral, prioritize these 2 money moves, says Vanguard CFP Save and Invest My 401(k) fully vests this month—why my work anniversary is worth thousands Save and Invest Investing experts: Why 'just buy the market' doesn't necessarily apply to bonds Spend The best deal in housing might be a brand-new home—here's why With 30-year mortgage rates back above 7%, homebuyers are looking for relief wherever they can find it. That increasingly includes adjustable-rate mortgages, or ARMs, which currently offer rates around 1 percentage point lower than a traditional 30-year fixed mortgage. ARMs accounted for 10.3% of mortgage applications in the week ending Oct. 2, up from 5.9% in the week ending Oct. 4, 2024, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. But ARMs also come with a trade-off: The lower rate is typically fixed for only the first five, seven or 10 years, after which the rate — and monthly payment — can reset periodically. If interest rates are higher when that introductory period ends, your monthly payment and interest costs could rise significantly. The thinking among some homebuyers goes something like this: Take the lower rate an ARM offers today and give yourself five or seven years for broader rates to come back down. If they do, you may be able to refinance into a lower fixed rate or see your ARM adjust lower once its fixed period ends. That way, you get a discount now and potentially a lower rate later. "An ARM can be a good choice if it is a strategic decision instead of, 'This is the only way that I can afford a mortgage,'" Hannah Jones, senior economist at Realtor.com , tells CNBC Make It. "If that's already going to be a stretch, then that means that you're going to be quite exposed when that fixed rate period ends." If you're considering an ARM , here's how to weigh the potential savings against the risk — and what to look for before signing. There's a reason most people stick with 30-year fixed mortgages: Your interest rate stays the same, even if rates go up. But if rates fall, you still have the option to refinance later into a new loan with a lower rate. But with the cost of homeownership so high, it's easy to see why more buyers might be willing to consider an ARM. "When the spread between a fixed-rate mortgage and an adjustable-rate mortgage is relatively large, it makes sense that more buyers would be drawn to that adjustable-rate mortgage when they could be saving $100, $200, $300 a month," Jones says. With mortgages above 7%, some buyers may figure five or seven years is plenty of time for rates to come down, allowing them to refinance into a cheaper fixed-rate mortgage or simply pay a lower rate when the ARM adjusts. For many borrowers, rates above 7% may feel unusually high. Before 2022, mortgage rates had spent roughly two decades below that level, according to Mortgage News Daily. There are reasons to think rates could decline from here. Mortgage rates would likely ease if oil prices retreat, inflation continues to cool, tariffs are reduced or the labor market weakens enough to strengthen expectations for Federal Reserve rate cuts, Jones says. But none of those outcomes are guaranteed, and borrowers should consider what would happen if rates move in the opposite direction, Jones says. "The expectation is always that interest rates will cycle, but we've learned a good lesson that they don't necessarily cycle the way you want," says Melissa Cohn, mortgage industry veteran and regional vice president at William Raveis Mortgage. That said, "the chances are still pretty good that we will see lower rates in the next year or two… but never say never, because things change and we have no control over them," she says. That uncertainty matters when weighing the upfront savings of an ARM. "I'd look at the lower rate as guaranteed savings during the fixed period, and a future refinance as potential upside, not the plan you need in order to make the mortgage work," says Arman Javaherian, CEO of homebuying platform Homa AI. Stress-test the ARM before you take it Although ARMs commonly have 30-year terms, the interest rate is typically fixed for only part of that time. A 5/6 ARM, for example, keeps the same rate for five years and can then adjust every six months based on changes in an underlying benchmark rate. A 7/6 ARM gives you seven years before the first adjustment. And if that weren't enough numbers and slashes, ARMs also come with rate caps that limit how quickly and how far the rate can rise. Take the common 2/1/5 cap structure, for example. That means your rate can rise by up to 2 percentage points at the first adjustment, 1 point at each adjustment after that and 5 points in total over the life of the loan. A 5/6 ARM starting at 6.5% with 2/1/5 caps, then, could eventually reach 11.5%. But it wouldn't jump there immediately.

events.title: Centene CEO Sarah London says Medicaid patients are the last to benefit from health care innovation. She wants AI to change that
events.summary: The latest innovations and breakthroughs in health care don’t get routed to the sickest people, they usually go to the deepest pockets.  “Most of the venture money in health care goes into where the money is, and the money isn’t in Medicaid,” Centene CEO Sarah London said on Monday at Fortune’s Most Powerful Women Summit. “That means that underserved communities don’t actually benefit from innovation first. Sometimes they never do.” Centene, a $33 billion company based in Missouri, is built around those very communities. The company runs Medicaid plans in 29 states and sells individual marketplace plans and Medicare Advantage. London, a mainstay of Fortune’s Most Powerful Women and the youngest CEO in the Fortune 500, said Centene’s 26 million members are “among the poorest, sickest members of the communities that we all live in,” she told Fortune senior writer Sheryl Estrada. London, who took the CEO role four years ago at age 41, said she joined Centene because she believed health care and technology had reached an inflection point, and she wanted to lead a company that was part of getting more care to people who are usually last to get it.  According to London, AI offers a massive opportunity to change the way people seek and get medical care, but not in the way it’s mostly used today. Estrada asked London where AI could create the most value, and London said, “everywhere.” But as of the current moment, it’s not happening. “The part that’s really depressing right now is that where AI is being deployed at scale, and where there’s a lot of investment happening right now, is in inflationary use cases,” she said. That means most of the AI effort is going toward driving more revenue in a fee-for-medical-service system, she said. However, just automating the paperwork and the way claims are paid, while valuable in its own right, misses out on a chance to “break the way the system works today” by democratizing care, she said. In rural areas known as medical deserts because they have so few hospitals that are difficult to reach, AI could enable community health workers to potentially be as capable as the first round of triage in an emergency room for non-acute problems, London said.  “That puts community care back in the community,” she said. “It puts individual care back in the hands of patients, and I think that is the thing that is going to fundamentally change how health care works.” AI could also lend patients more agency to make decisions about their own care. ChatGPT is not your doctor, although most people are already using it to find out more information about their ailments, hypothetical or otherwise. (London joked that her ChatGPT is completely confused at this point because she asks it about her whole family, including her “hypochondriac husband.”) But kidding aside, AI used in the right way can make people smarter about their health, more so than most realize. The impact could be significant in terms of medical costs and devoting more funding toward actual care rather than other costs. “If we can create that level of agency and the ability for individuals to make the first couple of decisions themselves, that is actually how you bend the cost curve,” she said.  Getting there is still a work in progress, London said. For now, Centene is using AI in administrative communications with members, she said, but the goal is for interactive tools to eventually help patients take first steps on their own. And the administrative cost savings aren’t to be minimized. “Every dollar that we can save in the administration of health care, we can apply to benefits.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Micron, Seagate, Western Digital sink as chip sell-off deepens
events.summary: Chip stocks tumbled Tuesday, continuing to fall as the sell-off spilled into Asian and European markets. China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, reported progress on a new chip structure, intensifying chip competition. Intel and Broadcom CEOs have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the artificial intelligence boom. Chip stocks fell on Tuesday, extending a sell-off sparked by worries over artificial intelligence financing and intensifying competition. Memory chip giant Micron slipped about 5% while other memory-related names such as SanDisk , Seagate and Western Digital also sank. SanDisk fell 5% while Seagate and Western Digital both dropped 6%. The slide, which followed declines on Wall Street on Monday, comes as investors assessed intensifying competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT . Over the weekend , CXMT announced significant progress in developing a new chip architecture, designed to increase memory density by packing more data into a smaller space. CXMT is China's leading rival to the likes of Micron and South Korean heavyweights SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics . Analysts broadly see CXMT as trailing the U.S. and South Korean memory leaders, which means any advancement from the Chinese firm could add more competition to the market leaders. "Investors are jittery and looking for excuses to take profit on AI-related stocks that have outperformed this year, especially memory stocks," said UBP's senior equity advisor Vey-Sern Ling. "In reality, while the Chinese memory makers can potentially become a threat to global demand-supply balance over time, in the short run they continue to face technology hurdles, especially for more advanced memory like HBM," Ling told CNBC via email. CXMT shares closed 2.8% lower in Shanghai. Phillip Wool, chief market strategist at Rayliant Global Advisors, said CXMT's breakthrough marked a significant milestone for Chinese chipmakers , demonstrating their ability to overcome technology restrictions and potentially challenge established players sooner than expected. But he cautioned that the market reaction appeared disproportionate to the immediate competitive threat, given that CXMT has yet to demonstrate large-scale production and continues to lag Samsung and SK Hynix in market share. "More importantly, we're not even talking about HBM here, and the Korean chipmakers are still unquestionably dominating that space, with very little threat at all from the likes of CXMT or anyone else for the foreseeable future," Wool said. He said the sharp sell-off reflected broader anxiety over the AI trade rather than a fundamental shift in the competitive landscape. "I read that more as a sign of how vulnerable AI sentiment is at this moment," Wool said, warning that volatility could persist as investors reassess chip demand and how long semiconductor manufacturers can sustain their pricing power. The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the AI boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply. Investors are also looking ahead to a busy week of corporate earnings and U.S. inflation data, which could provide fresh clues on the outlook for interest rates that often have an inverse correlation with growth stocks. Adding fuel to the sell-off was a post by Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, who said China has the ability to scale production once it figures out how to manufacture something. "When China figures out how to manufacture a product, their ability to scale is often greater than the rest of the world combined," Musk said on Monday. European chip stocks also sank in early morning trade, with semiconductor equipment maker ASML down 3.3%, and STMicroelectronics and German chip maker Infineon both down 5%. Dutch firms BE Semiconductor and ASM International were both around 4% lower at the open. In Japan, shares of tech-focused investment giant SoftBank Group sank 8.5%. The group, which has significant exposure to the global AI industry through its huge investment in OpenAI, led a broader retreat in Japanese semiconductor and electronics shares. Tokyo Electron , a major supplier of chipmaking equipment, dropped 7.2%, while Advantest , which makes semiconductor testing equipment, declined 2.9%. Other Japanese technology stocks also came under pressure. Lasertec fell over 5%, Disco lost 4.7% and Renesas Electronics shed 5.9%. The declines followed a weak session for technology stocks on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.44% on Monday. events.title: Yemeni government launches air strikes on Houthi positions
events.summary: Yemeni rights group accuses the Houthis of killing five civilians and injuring more than a dozen others. Forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government say they have carried out a series of air strikes on Houthi positions and military equipment in the country’s southwest. A total of nine air strikes were conducted in Taiz governorate on Tuesday, including five in Dhubab district and four in al-Masrakh district, the government said. list 1 of 3 Iran-Saudi talks on Yemen’s Houthis: What’s in it for Tehran? list 2 of 3 Houthi missile attack targets Saudi capital Riyadh for third day in a row list 3 of 3 The escalation in Yemen is a turning point According to the Taiz Military Axis Media Center, affiliated with the Ministry of Defence, fighting is ongoing between government forces and the Houthis in al-Shaqab, south of Taiz. The Yemeni Network for Rights and Freedom said on Tuesday that the Houthis had killed at least five civilians, including a five-year-old girl in Taiz during the previous 24 hours and injured 17 others. The organisation accused the Houthis of shelling residential neighbourhoods, damaging at least seven homes. It also alleged that the group had fired more than 180 projectiles across Taiz during the previous 24 hours. The war in Yemen erupted in 2014 when the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized the capital Sanaa and forced the government to flee. An international military coalition led by Saudi Arabia intervened in support of the internationally recognised government in 2015, leading to years of fighting between the warring sides. A 2022 UN-backed truce halted most fighting, but tensions have been high in Yemen since the Iran-aligned Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabian ports and shipping passing through the Bab al-Mandeb strait in July. In September, the Houthis carried out a lightning ground offensive on Mocha, pushing back forces loyal to Yemen’s government from the strategic port city. The same month, the group’s forces again swept through and seized territory along the western coast and the Bab al-Mandeb strait, including the strategically located Mayyun Island in the strait. As the fighting in Yemen continues to rage, the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross, Mirjana Spoljaric, warned that civilians across the Middle East are bearing the brunt of escalating hostilities and has called for all parties to de-escalate. “Civilians are paying an unacceptable price as a result of military operations in the Middle East,” Spoljaric said in a statement. “In Yemen, the scale of death, displacement and damage to civilian infrastructure, including in Aden and Sanaa, is mounting at an alarming rate. Across the Middle East, civilian infrastructure has repeatedly been hit and lives have been lost,” she said. At least 46 civilians have been killed and more than 130 others injured in Yemen since August, many of them children, according to the United Nations. More than 200,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since September, according to the UN’s migration agency (IOM). As the fighting in Yemen has escalated, the Houthis have carried out a series of attacks on Saudi Arabia’s airports and oil facilities. At least 14 people were killed in separate Houthi missile attacks on King Khalid airport in Riyadh over the weekend, drawing widespread international condemnation. Saudi Arabia’s energy minister promised the kingdom would carry out a “serious response” to the attacks. Several airlines have cancelled flights to Saudi Arabia and neighbouring countries in response to Houthi attacks. These carriers include Qatar Airways and Emirates, the United Arab Emirates’ flagship carrier. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) on Tuesday about regional issues. Merz told MBS that Iran must engage in serious negotiations and accused Tehran of destabilising the region. Meanwhile, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty has met Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed AlBudaiwi. Abdelatty said in a post on X that “Gulf security is integral to Egypt’s national security”. Abdelatty also spoke to his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, and urged an immediate halt to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Although Tehran provides the Houthis with crucial financial and military support, several analysts suggest that Iran holds little sway over the group.

events.title: Fewer Britons plan to ringfence money for holidays abroad next year, says travel industry
events.summary: Spain remains most popular destination as Britons book later in hope of better deals, Abta report finds The UK’s cost of living squeeze means fewer people plan to ringfence money for holidays abroad next year, the travel industry has warned. Despite war, wildfires and EES border checks, the numbers of Britons taking holidays climbed back to pre-pandemic levels this year – but rising costs may mean the numbers have peaked, according to an annual travel industry report on Tuesday. Numbers taking holidays at home and abroad continued to rise, although late bookings and shorter city breaks have been an increasing feature of holidays through 2026. Confidence in travel dropped slightly year on year but rebounded as fears over jet fuel shortages and flight disruption faded since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran in February, according to research from the industry body Abta. Overall, 88% of Brits took a holiday this year, matching the 2019 pre-pandemic peak, with a new high of 74% in the UK and 62% abroad. However, Abta’s report found that almost one in three people were planning to spend less on travelling abroad next year, suggesting that the annual holiday is no longer sacrosanct. Fewer people now say they are willing to reduce spending on phones or other gadgets than the holiday abroad. Abta said the holiday business remained resilient, despite a dip in its travel confidence index to +50 – this measures the net proportion of people who felt secure in going abroad, compared with those who were worried. But it said that score had rebounded since disruption from the Middle East conflict and fears about fuel availability and the EU’s entry/exit system (EES). The Abta chief executive, Mark Tanzer, said it had been a tough year for the travel industry. But he added: “Demand has held up well despite a range of challenges this year, and that looks set to continue, as does the willingness to prioritise spending on travel over other discretionary items.” Speaking at the annual Abta travel convention in Madeira, Tanzer added: “It’s been a stop-start year but the market did come back in the summer. “We saw people switching their holiday plans and booking later, waiting and seeing – maybe hoping for better deals but also managing the uncertainty.” He said the industry would continue to lobby ministers hard to reduce aviation taxes and increase help in the switch to sustainable aviation fuels, to help cut costs and support an industry that contributed £57bn to the UK economy. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Tanzer said the investment in tourism continued but he admitted: “The pressures of the last few months are not going to go away in the next 18 months.” Spain increased its dominance of the British outbound market. The number who said they visited Spain was up four percentage points to 36%, while Portugal moved up to sixth in popularity for holidays. Polling next year’s travel intentions, only 26% said they were planning to visit Spain, with places such as Japan and Norway cited in the top 10. However, previous surveys have underlined that, despite dreams of somewhere more exotic, Britons head resolutely back to Spain. Travel to the convention was provided by Abta

HomeView will act as a voice-controlled smart home hub for Apple devices and was built to showcase new Siri AI abilities. Apple on Tuesday announced a new home hub called HomeView . Apple said the device with a 7-inch screen was designed to be mounted on a wall or placed on a table. It's designed for multiple people in a household, and will recognize the user by their face to display pertinent information. It starts at $299 and ships on Nov. 13. Tuesday's launch event is the second under new CEO John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in September. Last month, Apple announced new models of its most important product, the iPhone, including a foldable model called the Duo that retails for nearly $2,000. Apple also announced new Apple TV and HomePod hardware on Tuesday. The new Apple TV 4K costs $299 and has a redesigned remote that can play a sound if it is lost. Apple's HomePod Mini speaker comes in new colors and costs $149, a slight increase over its previous $129 price. The products announced Tuesday are less critical for Apple than the iPhone, and investors remain focused on iPhone sales, but the accessories were positioned on Tuesday as a showcase for the company's new Siri abilities released last month. Apple said that HomeView features Siri AI, which can answer a broad range of questions. Users will be able to converse with Siri, and their conversations will continue on their iPhone or iPad. It has a built-in speaker for playing music. "It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home," Apple's chief marketer Greg Joswiak said in a statement. Apple said that HomeView will show information from the Messages, Photos, Calendar, and Reminders apps based on who is using the device, powered by Apple Intelligence. It can also be used to make FaceTime calls and as a digital photo frame. It's equipped with an Apple A18 chip. It supports up to six users. Apple TV, HomePods, and HomeView are included in Apple's Wearables, Home, and Accessories category, which reported $7.88 billion in sales in the most recent quarter ended June, which was about 7% of the company's total revenue. The category also includes wireless headphones like AirPods and the Apple Watch. But while Apple has dabbled in home products and platforms in the past, Tuesday's announcement shows Apple is making its home products a higher priority under Ternus. Apple said on Tuesday that its new products, including HomeView, can be used as a smart home hub, coordinating notifications and actions in the home and working with a range of products, including new locks, doorbells, and cameras from LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. Apple's integration with the smart home is not just about sales but also helps further lock customers into its own ecosystem. People who use multiple Apple products and connections are less likely to switch to an Android phone. HomeView can also become a smart home dashboard, Apple said. It can be used to view camera feeds, adjust the thermostat, or lock connected doors around the house. Apple said that setting up a new smart home device takes one tap from the user's iPhone. Tuesday's launch shows Apple's confidence as it launches new product categories. But the broader consumer electronics industry has been dealing with price increases and demand deterioration related to component shortages in memory and storage. It also comes as new boss Ternus has reportedly pushed the company to release products faster. Apple's new Apple TV 4K got a price hike from $199 to $299, and comes after a similar price increase earlier this year, after Cook said that memory costs for Apple were unsustainable. events.title: Martin Shkreli violated lifetime pharma industry ban, FTC and states say in contempt claim
events.summary: The Federal Trade Commission and seven states asked a federal judge on Tuesday to hold notorious "Pharma bro" Martin Shkreli in contempt. The FTC and the states allege that Shkreli "flagrantly and repeatedly violated" a 2022 court order that had banned him for life from the pharmaceutical industry. The civil case that led to the order is unrelated to the criminal case that ended with Shkreli's conviction in 2017 on securities fraud charges related to hedge funds he once operated and another drug company he founded. The Federal Trade Commission and seven states asked a federal judge on Tuesday to hold notorious "Pharma bro" Martin Shkreli in contempt, alleging he "flagrantly and repeatedly violated" a 2022 civil court order that had banned him for life from the pharmaceutical industry. The FTC and the states say Shkreli, since being released from prison in May 2022, violated that court order by publicly trading in at least 60 pharmaceutical industry stocks and "broadcasting his opinions about the business and management of many pharmaceutical industry companies," according to a press release. The contempt filing asks a judge to order Shkreli to "divest any pharmaceutical company stocks he currently owns" and "pay a fine equal to his profits from any pharmaceutical company stock trading (plus prejudgment interest) without the ability to account for offsetting losses." The filing also asks that a judge make Shkreli "face clear and escalating consequences for any future violations, including financial penalties and potential incarceration." FTC Commissioner Mark Meador said in a statement, "A lifetime industry ban is only effective if breaches are met with consequences commensurate with the seriousness of the order." The court order stems from a finding that Shkreli organized an anti-competitive scheme to perpetuate his company's monopoly in the anti-parasitic drug Daraprim. Shkreli had hiked the price of Daraprim from $17.50 per tablet to a whopping $750 per pill. In addition to banning him from the drug industry for life, a judge ordered Shkreli to disgorge more than $64 million. The civil case that led to the order is unrelated to the criminal case that ended with Shkreli's conviction in 2017 on securities fraud charges related to hedge funds he once operated and another drug company he founded. Shkreli was sentenced to seven years in federal prison in 2018, and was released in 2022 with credit for time locked up before he was sentenced and other factors. "When judgment is entered by a court, whether it's a settlement or an order following a trial, defendants must fulfill their obligations," Guarnera said. "Today's action should serve as notice that the FTC will not hesitate to enforce violations of court orders."

events.title: U.S. Treasury yields fall as energy prices pull back
events.summary: Bond yields fell on Tuesday after energy prices moved lower in early trade, as investors look ahead to key economic data releases this week, including the latest U.S. inflation print. The 10-year Treasury note yield — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans, and credit card debt — fell more than 4 basis points to 5.202%. The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasurys — which tend to move on geopolitical events — was down more than 4 basis points at 5.552%. The yield on the 2-year Treasury note , which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve rate decisions, rose less than 1 basis point to 4.80%. One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely. U.S. Treasury markets reopened for trade Tuesday after closing Monday for the Columbus Day holiday. The slide in borrowing costs follows a sharp fall in oil prices Tuesday, as investors continue to gauge the prospect of more Russian diesel entering global energy markets following the U.S.-brokered so-called ' energy ceasefire ' between Russia and Ukraine. West Texas Intermediate futures for November delivery were more than 1% lower at around $92 a barrel. Brent crude futures were down more than 1% to about $105 a barrel. Investors are gearing up for a flurry of domestic economic data releases this week, which will offer clearer insights into the U.S. inflation picture and interest rate trajectory. September's annual inflation rate — due out Wednesday — is expected to come in at 3.7%, according to consensus forecasts, up from August's 3.4% print. Consumer prices, which exclude food and energy, are expected to rise to 2.5% from 2.4% in August on an annualized basis. The inflation data will be followed on Thursday by September's monthly producer price index and retail sales data.

The company on Tuesday showed off its new Apple Home Collection, which includes a new smart deadbolt lock, video doorbell, thermostat, temperature sensor, and a range of security cameras. The new devices are designed to work with HomeView , the company’s new smart home hub which can be used to control connected accessories and interact with Apple’s software. This new range of smart home accessories could help Apple compete better with Amazon Ring and Google Nest, two established players in connected home security. The products will become available in December. Apple says the devices were built in partnership with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric — an interesting move for the company, which has long sought to build and support every smart home accessory itself. The smart lock, priced at $349.95, stands out for its support for ultra-wideband (UWB), a wireless technology that enables more precise proximity detection than traditional Bluetooth. This could allow the lock to recognize when an authorized user approaches and automatically unlock the door, reducing the need to pull out a phone or reach for a physical key. The $249.95 wired video doorbell, meanwhile, will let homeowners see who’s outside, monitor visitors, and receive notifications when someone approaches their property. When someone rings it, a chime will sound through Apple devices like HomeView, HomePod, and HomePod mini. Users will also be notified on their iPhone or iPad. As for the temperature sensor, it can provide insight into conditions in individual rooms, helping users identify temperature differences between areas and make adjustments. For security, Apple is also introducing indoor and outdoor cameras, as well as a floodlight camera ($399.95) that combines exterior lighting with video monitoring. events.title: Paul Tudor Jones says 2027 could be a really challenging year for the stock market
events.summary: Paul Tudor Jones told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Tuesday that next year could be a tough one for the stock market because of increased equity supply from big tech IPOs. "2027 is going to be really, really challenging for the stock market," he said. The founder and chief investment officer of Tudor Investment said that corporate buybacks, along with mergers and acquisitions, that have been a tailwind for the four-year bull market is about to turn. Legendary hedge fund manager Paul Tudor Jones told CNBC that next year could be a tough one for the stock market because of increased equity supply from big tech IPOs coming down the pipe, as well as a potential reckoning from the ballooning U.S. fiscal deficit. "2027 is going to be really, really challenging for the stock market," Jones told "Squawk Box" on Tuesday. "You've probably got the most negative flow picture for the U.S. stock market that we've had, say, since 2002." The founder and chief investment officer of Tudor Investment said that corporate buybacks, along with mergers and acquisitions, have been a tailwind for the stock market for most of this four-year bull market as they decreased the equity supply. That tide is now turning against the market with major offerings ahead in the AI space from Anthropic and OpenAI, along with one just finished in SpaceX. There will also likely be more secondary offerings from companies in order to raise money for the AI buildout, said Jones. It all adds up to an increased equity supply picture that could weight on prices. The billionaire hedge fund manager's comments come as investors worry that a bull market now in its fourth year could start to dwindle and run out of steam as concerns grow around mounting inflation, higher bond yields and a more hawkish Federal Reserve. Jones repeated that the current period in the market is akin to 1999 , just about a year before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000. He noted the bifurcation in the current market between those companies benefitting from the AI boom and those that aren't. He also added that a ballooning fiscal deficit are among the dangers for the current stock market, for which he thinks there could be a reckoning. "We're never going to fix these deficits until the market makes us to. It's going to be just like 2008 and TARP [Troubled Asset Relief Program]. So that's the reality. No politician is going to voluntarily raise taxes or cut spending. They're going to be forced to," he said. "And the only question is, are we now at that tipping point where the market's about to do that? And if you put a gun to my head, I'd say 60-40, we're down that path," he continued. Oil, which he is long, is another headwind for the market, according to the hedge fund manager. He argued that prices could rally another $20 to $25 after the midterms , a scenario that the stock market will "hate" if it comes to pass. "I'll be short the whole year. There just — there's little value," Jones said. "You had all this issuance, all these IPOs in '98 and '99, and really 2000, 2001, 2002. Those were the easiest years to be short because you kept having these unlocks that just kept adding supply to the market."

events.title: I'm a French mom with a child in an American school. I like the school spirit, the shorter days, and the less rigid approach.
events.summary: The author is French, but raising her 9-year-old in America. Courtesy of Virginie Romary My 9-year-old daughter is enrolled in an American public elementary school. The school system here differs significantly from the one in France. I like that it is less rigid, with many extracurricular activities and a strong sense of community. I moved from France to the US 10 years ago. My 9-year-old daughter was born in Florida, and when it was time to enroll her in school, I chose not to enroll her in a French school. I wanted her to experience the American education system to be part of the community. I like the school spirit here What I appreciate most about American schools is that they function as communities, whereas in France, they are primarily places for academic instruction. I admire how school spirit is actively promoted here. My daughter takes great pride in her school, and her favorite T-shirt features its colors. She eagerly participates in spirit weeks, dress-up days, and various entertaining events like the color run that she never wants to miss. I also value the morning rituals in the US, including the morning announcements and the Pledge of Allegiance. Such practices do not exist in France. My daughter feels deeply engaged with her school . She has a sense of belonging that I never experienced as a child, because my schooling focused solely on formal instruction, with no fun activities. Americans' school days are shorter At first, when I realized that my daughter's school finishes at 2 pm, I panicked. How was I supposed to work at the same time? However, once I organized our daily routine, I really appreciated that she had a more compact day and more time in the afternoons to focus on extracurricular activities like swimming or playing music. Typically, in France, school days are longer, running from early morning to late afternoon, with more breaks and a longer lunch period. Wednesdays are half days or off days for the youngest, giving children time to participate in extracurricular activities they may want to take part in. However, there are no school-sponsored extracurriculars, and theater, music, or competitive sports are played in clubs outside the school system. Often in the evening, I hear music and cheering from the football matches at the nearby high school, and I look forward to my daughter having this kind of experience. Until then, I value that her days are more balanced, with afternoons dedicated to non-academic skills, even if it means she has fewer holidays throughout the year. School is less rigid in the US In France, I would never see my daughter's teacher in her sleepwear for Pajama Day or her principal wearing bunny ears for Halloween. The boundaries between school and home are stricter there, and teachers tend to adopt a more authoritarian position. In the US, my daughter has a less formal relationship with her teacher, knowing details about her personal life. Her teacher is easily accessible outside class and puts significant effort into encouraging and praising her students . I'm often surprised when my daughter receives prizes, as this practice is not common in France. Her teacher always finds something positive to express, even if it is as simple as saying, " I like your energy, " for a child who struggles to remain seated. The French approach is different , and teachers are less inclined to compliment. They focus more on correction and improvement, using a 20-point grading scale that makes a perfect score almost impossible. I found the letter grade system here less stressful, with an A being more attainable. Consequently, making the honor roll is easier. This recognition doesn't even exist in France, where children's achievements are not celebrated publicly. However, not everything is perfect. I also have a few concerns about the American school system, such as the culture of standardized testing and the competitive atmosphere. Still, my daughter enjoys her school, which is a great relief. events.title: Oil prices fall as traders assess Russian diesel supply prospects and Saudi-Houthi conflict
events.summary: Oil prices slipped Tuesday after as investors assessed prospects of more Russian diesel entering global markets. President Donald Trump said Russia had agreed to boost diesel supplies to global markets. Oil prices fell Tuesday as investors weighed prospects of more Russian energy entering global markets, while concerns over the Saudi-Houthi conflict limited losses. Brent crude futures declined 1.3% to $105.24 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures fell 0.9% to $92.90. President Donald Trump on Monday defended his administration's decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel supplies, despite bipartisan criticism from U.S. lawmakers who warned the move could undermine sanctions imposed over Moscow's war in Ukraine. In a Truth Social post, Trump said that the European Union had spent billions of dollars on Russian energy imports and insisted he had made the right decision for Americans. The agreement would allow Russia to supply diesel to U.S. and global markets for six months. Goldman Sachs said additional Russian diesel supplies were unlikely to significantly ease pressure on global fuel prices, estimating that an increase of 800,000 metric tons, equivalent to roughly 6 million barrels, would lower wholesale diesel prices in the U.S. Gulf Coast and Europe by just $1 to $2 a barrel. The bank underscored in a note published Monday that Russian refinery outages jumped by 3 million barrels per day from a year earlier, limiting Moscow's ability to ramp up production. Global diesel markets remain under significant strain, with U.S. inventories down 14% from a year earlier and visible stocks in China falling 11%, according to Goldman Sachs. The bank attributed the shortages to seven consecutive months of declining global diesel production, with seaborne exports falling by 1.4 million barrels per day, or 20%, year on year. Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen attacked King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh on Saturday, leaving 12 people dead and more than 300 injured in a major escalation. — CNBC's Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

events.title: Ukraine’s ex-defense minister unveiled a new interceptor built for Russia's fastest drones. He wants AI to help fly it.
events.summary: Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine's former defense minister, has developed a new interceptor drone. Kyodo via Reuters Connect Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine's digital-focused former defense minister, has unveiled a new interceptor. The interceptor is in testing and has already downed Russia's fastest jet-powered drone, the Geran-5. Fedorov told Business Insider this week that he plans to be producing hundreds a month by the end of the year. Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine's former defense minister who pushed for rapid innovation in war technology, has unveiled a new interceptor designed to take down Russia's fastest attack drones. The new interceptor drone is currently flown by a human pilot, but Fedorov said in comments shared with Business Insider that he intends to make it autonomous in flight using artificial intelligence. He aims to be producing hundreds of interceptors a month by the end of the year. Ukraine is increasingly turning to AI-enabled autonomous drones and robots that can continue fighting when electronic warfare severs the connection between systems and operators. The interceptor that Fedorov unveiled is the latest model developed by Ukrainian engineers to combat the rise in Russian jet-powered drones , weapons which are much faster than their propeller-powered predecessors and pose a significant challenge for Kyiv's air defenses. It also reflects a broader shift toward interceptors equipped with artificial intelligence that can fly with less human input. Ukrainian defense firms have developed several new interceptors capable of engaging Russia's fastest drone, the Geran-5 , which is powered by a mini turbojet engine and able to reach speeds of up to 375 mph. It's unclear how fast the interceptor can fly, but in recent combat tests over Kyiv, a specialized unit of Ukraine's National Guard used it to take down two Geran-5 drones. Fedorov said that testing is ongoing. The next steps are to improve the technology and scale up production. In translated remarks, he said the interceptor "will be very affordable." "That was our goal from the outset: to develop a low-cost, mass-producible solution that can be scaled rapidly," he said. A view of a Russian Geran-5 captured by Fedorov's interceptor. Mykhailo Fedorov/Screengrab via X During his six months as Ukraine's defense minister earlier this year, Fedorov pushed for a sweeping modernization of the military , including through a robotic-centric approach to combat. His tenure coincided with a string of battlefield successes for Kyiv, primarily through drone warfare. Following his sudden departure in July, Fedorov launched a defense company focused on developing warfighting technology to strengthen Ukraine and support international partners. He said in early September that the first investor will be Alex Karp, the CEO of Palantir , an American AI, data, and operational intelligence firm. On Monday, Fedorov said he intends to invest more in research and development and the Ukrainian engineering team behind the interceptor, making its intellectual property a "key asset" in his portfolio. He also plans to open investment to other partners; the first funding round is expected soon. The development of the new interceptor drone comes as Moscow has ramped up its use of jet-powered drones this year. Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 350 drones in June, but that number swelled to 2,800 in August. These attacks present a serious challenge for Ukraine. Officials said that the interception rate of Russia's propeller-powered drones , which reach 115 mph, typically sat above 90%. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in late September that Kyiv shot down just 55% of Russia's jet-powered drones that month. Russia has developed several jet-powered drone models. The Geran-5 more closely resembles a cruise missile than its slower delta-wing predecessors, and it is playing a growing role in Russian strike tactics . Zelenskyy warned last month that Moscow plans to invest heavily in these weapons next year. Fedorov said on Monday that he's "confident that Russia can be stopped" and that Ukraine has already demonstrated it can engage the slower drones. "Our next challenge is to do the same with jet-powered versions," he added. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: India delays digital payments fee rollout amid retailer pushback
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Following broad pushback from merchants across the country, India has delayed plans to introduce merchant fees on its digital payments network that aimed to make the business more lucrative for the companies that facilitate the payments service, long dominated by Google and PhonePe. The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), which operates the country’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI), said on Tuesday it was postponing the planned October 15 rollout of a 0.4% fee on eligible merchant transactions exceeding ₹2,000 (about $21), citing the festive shopping season. The fee, announced last month, would mark a significant departure from India’s years-long policy of keeping UPI payments free for merchants. The rollout will now take place after Diwali, one of India’s biggest festivals and shopping periods, though the NPCI did not specify a new date. In September alone, UPI processed 24.07 billion transactions worth ₹29.37 trillion (about $305 billion), per NPCI. The proposed fee drew opposition from retailers and petrol pump operators , some of whom warned they could stop accepting UPI payments if the charge took effect. Over the past several years, UPI has become the backbone of India’s digital payments system, powering payments through apps such as Google Pay, PhonePe, and Paytm. Its growth has been supported by the Indian government keeping UPI payments free for merchants and providing subsidies to banks and payment providers to help them cover some of the costs. UPI was not always free for merchants, however. Banks and payment providers previously charged merchants for transactions, but the Indian government scrapped those fees in January 2020 as it sought to encourage more people to shift away from using cash, long the dominant way people have paid for goods and services in the country. UPI has continued to grow in both transaction volume and value. In recent years, the government has sought to take UPI overseas. In April 2020, NPCI set up its international arm, and the network is currently available in several countries, including Singapore, the United Arab Emirates, and France. NPCI had sought to limit the impact of the new merchant fee by exempting payments of ₹2,000 or less, as well as small merchants that receive less than ₹100,000 (about $1,033) a month through UPI. It also capped the fee at ₹300 (around $3) for larger transactions. The organization said it would share the money collected among participants in the UPI ecosystem to help pay for infrastructure, cybersecurity and fraud prevention. Citing industry estimates, NPCI said last month that the annual cost of running UPI was about ₹200 billion (around $2.1 billion), including spending on server capacity, fraud prevention, and technical support. Banks and payment companies have for years argued that they need a way to recoup those costs as transaction volumes grow. Apple launched a new $299 Apple TV 4K streaming device today, with an upgraded chip, integration with the updated version of Siri AI for content discovery, and mics that allow users to issue voice commands directly without using the remote. The refreshed Apple TV 4K comes with an upgraded A19 chip to enable various AI features. Hardware-wise, the new streaming box comes with three far-field microphones, letting users talk with Siri without a remote or a paired HomePod. The company said that users can now have a four-speaker surround sound experience with Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini 2 or HomePod 2 speakers. The device is not updated as often as other Apple hardware, given this long-pending upgrade comes four years after the launch of Apple TV 4K in 2022. Apple has preloaded the device with several of its apps, including Calendar, Messages, Photos, FaceTime, Notes, Reminders, Music, and Podcasts. That means users won’t need to reach for their iPhone if they want to check a calendar appointment, send a message, play some music, or look at photos. Apple sees the device being particularly useful in places such as the kitchen. Someone cooking dinner, for example, could pull up a recipe, watch a video, check a calendar, or start a FaceTime call without resorting to their phone. It’ll also act as a smart home dashboard, allowing users to ask Siri to view camera feeds, adjust the thermostat, turn on lights, and lock doors. This comes as Apple announced its lineup of smart home accessories today, including a smart deadbolt lock, security cameras, and doorbell. Users will hear a chime from their HomeView when someone is at the door, for example. One of the more interesting aspects of the device is how it works with different members of a household. The hub runs Apple’s updated Siri AI assistant and can recognize individual people in the house. Once it identifies someone, the screen can show information meant for that person, such as their messages, contacts, calendar appointments, notes, and preferred apps. The experience changes automatically when another family member walks up to the device. The company says HomeView can recognize up to six people. HomeView puts Apple in a much more direct fight with Amazon and Google, both of which already have established smart display products: Amazon has its Echo Show line, while Google offers the Nest Hub. Apple has had a mixed history in the smart home space, however, with products such as the HomePod struggling to reach the same level of popularity as competing devices. The new hub is an opportunity for Apple to change that by combining home controls with the company’s wider ecosystem. The device has been rumored for quite some time, with reports pointing to delays caused in part by problems with Siri AI. Those issues have reportedly affected Apple’s broader smart home plans as well. This may only be the first phase of Apple’s smart home plan. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman has previously reported that Apple could eventually take the concept further with a more advanced version that features a robotic arm. Such a device could move its display and interact in a more physical way. Preorders start today, and the device will be available to buy from November 13. events.title: Dating app Bumble swipes right on US$1.3b buyout as users fall out of love
events.summary: Paying users of Bumble fell 16.2% to 3.2 million in the second quarter of 2026. NEW YORK – Bumble has agreed to be taken private by Ithaca Holdings in a deal valued at US$1.3 billion (S$1.6 billion), as the dating app pushes forward with its months-long turnaround amid shifting Gen Z dating habits and declining paying users. Ithaca Holdings will pay US$6.05 per share, according to a statement on Oct 12. The deal price represents a 138% premium over Bumble’s closing share price on Oct 9. After the deal is completed, Bumble will remain based in Austin, Texas, with other major offices in London and New York. Bumble and larger rival Match Group, which owns Tinder and Hinge, have been grappling with weaker user engagement , particularly from younger users tired of endless swiping. Founded in 2014 by CEO Whitney Wolfe Herd , Bumble pioneered the “women-go-first” approach to online dating. Under Herd, who returned as CEO in March 2025 after stepping down in 2023, the company has doubled down on revamping its core product with AI-powered features, group dating and a redesigned member experience in a bid to revive growth. In August, Bumble ditched the women-go-first model, its latest move to boost user engagement. The company also introduced an artificial intelligence-powered assistant designed to act as a personal matchmaker, offering an alternative experience to swiping through user profiles. The efforts follow steep declines in total paying users and revenue. Total paying users fell 16.4% to 3.2 million in the second quarter of 2026, while quarterly revenue has been declining for nearly two years. Herd said she would “remain actively involved with Bumble”. Bumble’s market capitalisation has shrunk to about US$582 million as at Oct 12, a far cry from the US$14 billion valuation when it went public in 2021. REUTERS, BLOOMBERG

events.title: French fridge fright: Why supermarkets have become target for hackers
events.summary: More than 500 shops across France were hit in a major cyberattack targeting freezers, which caused tonnes of food to perish. Hundreds of French supermarkets have suffered unprecedented cyberattacks resulting in tonnes of food perishing and raising fears about the vulnerabilities of food systems to advanced technology. The attacks, which appeared to target internet-linked refrigeration systems manufactured by a Danish company, raised the temperature of fridges and freezers to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122F) at more than 500 shops and supermarkets across the country. Supermarkets confirmed the attacks on Monday. list 1 of 4 Cyberattack on French supermarkets causes fires, millions in losses list 2 of 4 OpenAI ‘reviewing’ report of failed hacking attempt against Canada’s gov’t list 3 of 4 AI could self-replicate on home devices within ‘months’, Anthropic says list 4 of 4 Hundreds of supermarkets in France hit by ‘unprecedented’ cyberattack France’s cybersecurity agency has advised companies operating affected freezer models to immediately disconnect them from the internet – or restrict access to them – and to perform software updates. It is unclear who may have been behind the attacks, but authorities say they have now launched an investigation. Hackers gained internet access to the refrigeration systems and remotely cranked up temperatures in freezers and fridges to 50C during the night when shops were closed. Millions of euros worth of food was spoiled, according to retailers. In some cases, the raised temperatures sparked fires or melted equipment. French supermarket groups E-Leclerc, Intermarche, Carrefour, Monoprix and Cooperative U were all hit. At least 300 of Intermarche’s stores and its Netto brand were affected. Cooperative U said more than 100 of its supermarkets were targeted, while Carrefour said 80 supermarkets were affected and Monoprix reported that about 5 percent of its roughly 490 stores were hit. Officials are still investigating who launched the attack and how it was carried out. French TV channel BFM reported that the attackers appeared to have remotely triggered a forced defrosting option in the refrigeration systems. The systems targeted are built by Danish manufacturer Danfoss, according to France’s government cybersecurity agency. The refrigeration models attacked included the AK-SM800 and AK-SC355. Danfoss told the AFP news agency that most of the affected control systems were “legacy” products that had “outdated firmware”. The company said it had previously advised supermarkets to update them. AFP also reported that officials are liaising with other European countries which may have been affected. It is unclear exactly how much food has been lost. The attacks come after President Emmanuel Macron ordered last month that the country’s critical infrastructure be protected from Russian “hybrid attacks”. Have supermarkets been hit by cyberattacks before? Yes. Attacks like these have been reported in other parts of Europe and in the United States. In April 2025, British retailer and supermarket chain Marks and Spencer suffered a sophisticated ransomware attack that the company said cost it approximately 300 million pounds ($397m) after it was forced to suspend online and app orders. The attack was orchestrated by a hacker group called Scattered Spider, using ransomware from DragonForce, another criminal group. Ransomware attacks involve using malicious software to hide essential data unless a ransom is paid. According to UK media, the same hackers also tried to attack Co-op and the iconic Knightsbridge store, Harrods. Similar reports have also emerged from the US. In June 2025, United Natural Foods, a frozen food company which supplies big supermarket brands such as Whole Foods, said it had discovered a cyberattack that forced it to take its systems offline. The company did not reveal the nature of the attack. In November last year, Ahold Delhaize USA said it was the victim of a cyberattack that disrupted operations at more than 2,000 stores, including Hannaford, Food Lion and Stop and Shop. They are an easy target and the consequences can be widespread. As food and agricultural systems increasingly digitise, analysts say supermarkets selling perishable foods are increasingly vulnerable to attacks due to the nature of their stocks. The rising sophistication of cyberattacks now means that common people and local, third-party companies relying on big chains for business are also falling victim as attacks disrupt supply chains, experts say. Speaking to Al Jazeera, tech and cybersecurity analyst Steven Lachance said smart appliances connected to the internet will always be vulnerable as hackers seize on security lapses to log in to the systems remotely and trigger malicious features. “It’s the new reality of having these connected equipment,” Lachance said, pointing out that attacks could evolve to target medical or energy systems.

events.title: Delta delays first-ever direct US to Saudi Arabia flights after airport missile strikes

Massimo Insabato/Archivio Massimo Insabato/Mondadori Portfolio via Getty Images Delta Air Lines planned to launch a route from Atlanta to Riyadh later this month. The Saudi capital's airport has suffered a number of Houthi missile attacks recently. Delta has postponed the new route until next March. Delta Air Lines  is delaying the launch of its new route to Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, following recent  Houthi missile attacks  on the city's airport. The route, which would have started in Atlanta, was scheduled to begin on October 23 with a week of daily service before moving to three times a week. It was set to be the first non-stop flight between the US and Saudi Arabia. "Saudi Arabia remains an important market for Delta, and we are committed to serving the Kingdom for the long-term," the airline said. Delta said the flights will now start in March 2027, though it did not specify an exact start date. "The safety and security of our customers and employees always come first and continue to guide our operational decisions," Delta said in its announcement. "We remain in close contact with relevant government and aviation partners, including Saudia and Riyadh Air, as we monitor the situation." Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport has suffered a number of attacks in recent weeks. On Saturday, hundreds were wounded, and 13 people were killed by a missile strike. The following day, another strike killed one person and injured about a dozen. The Houthis, who are backed by Iran, have been attacking Saudi Arabia after gaining control of a key strait in the Red Sea. Delta's decision came after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a warning for US airlines on Sunday. "Threats could pose a potential risk to aircraft at all altitudes, including overflight, the arrival, and departure phases of flight," the FAA said. As recently as last Thursday, Delta CEO Ed Bastian said that the airline was weighing whether to postpone the route. "Safety is going to make the call," he told CNBC. events.title: Trump’s diesel deal opens a new rift with Europe over Ukraine
events.summary: Trump calls for Zelenskyy to be replaced, while Europe devotes summit to funding Ukraine. Trump’s Russian diesel deal won’t change US oil markets much: Analysis Russia has claimed it can supply even more diesel to the global market than the quantities agreed with United States President Donald Trump. “By the end of the year, we could reach supply volumes of 3.5 million tonnes per month to global markets, just as was the case before the crisis,” Alexander Novak, Russian deputy prime minister, told the news programme Vesti on Monday. list 1 of 4 Ukraine warns Trump-Putin diesel deal will bankroll Russia’s war list 2 of 4 ‘Energy ceasefire’: What’s behind Trump’s love-hate ties to Russian oil? list 3 of 4 From a ‘dangerous competitor’ to an unknown: Who could replace Zelenskyy? list 4 of 4 Trump insists energy ceasefire holds as Ukraine reports new Russian strikes President Vladimir Putin and Trump spoke on Friday on an agreement expected to bring 300,000 tonnes of diesel to global markets in October, half a million tonnes in November, and a million tonnes in December. “Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” Trump posted. But experts are sceptical, and the move has opened a rift between the US and Europe on the Ukraine war. Kostis Stambolis, executive director of the Institute of Energy for South-East Europe (IENE), described the US move as “purely political” and designed to put Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a corner. Trump wants to signal that the US has “no problem with Russia”, unlike Europe, he said. “Russia produces 5.8 million tonnes of diesel a month. Two million are likely to be available for export,” he added. Europe has reacted to the diesel deal by backing Ukraine, whose war funding will be “front and centre” of this week’s European Council summit, European Commission President Ursula Von Der Leyen said on Sunday. Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen on Monday called on Europeans to ban all tourist visas to Russians. Stambolis believes Trump was leveraging European weakness to shift its position on Ukraine. “About 30 European refineries have closed in the past 15 years for environmental reasons, because they have to pay to emit greenhouse gases,” he said, referring to Europe’s Emissions Trading Scheme, “so now Europe is not self-sufficient in products”. Trump is showing the Europeans “he doesn’t want to deal with Europe and to hell with them … This is opening the rift between the US and the EU further,” said Stambolis. Ukraine says it has destroyed roughly half of Russia’s refining capacity, forcing Moscow to stop exporting lucrative petroleum products which help it to finance its war. It has also bombed Russian tankers carrying crude oil to global markets. Zelenskyy said the strategy was effective, and Trump’s deal, which would suspend sanctions on Russian oil products until April 2027, undermined it. “Gifts to Putin will not lead to peace,” Zelenskyy said Saturday. “Any weakening of sanctions against Russia without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious sign of weakness.” Although Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Sunday, leading Ukraine to suspend its attacks on refineries, Russian strikes pounded Kyiv’s energy grid and killed 12 people in Dnipropetrovsk. “I do not think he has earned a respite,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said of Zelenskyy. Europe supports Ukraine’s economic strategy against Russia’s war machine, but Trump has blamed it for raising petrol prices at the pump for Americans as he heads into Congressional midterm elections in early November. “[Zelenskyy] wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world,” Trump told reporters in the White House after Zelenskyy’s reaction. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president ,” he said. Trump has followed a seemingly self-contradictory policy towards Russia. He cut US military aid to Ukraine when he assumed power in January 2025, but agreed to sell Europe weapons to help Ukraine. He had a public dispute with Zelenskyy in the Oval Office in February 2025, saying “You don’t have the cards,” but at the NATO summit this year said Zelenskyy had “done an amazing job” and “been very effective”. Last month, Trump signed the Lindsey Graham Act, which would allow him to punish countries buying Russian oil. Eleven days later, he reversed policy. “The moment the pendulum comes to one side, Trump tries to balance it with a completely different and opposite tool,” said Victoria Vdovychenko, an expert on European security at Cambridge University’s Centre for Geopolitics. “In this way he sees how he controls the narrative, but also negotiations of any kind,” she told Al Jazeera. “So this pendulum will continue to prevail.

Tehran, Iran – Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has condemned the United Kingdom’s attribution of an alleged plot near a military airbase in the town of Fairford to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which it views as part of a greater Western effort. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Parliament on Monday that the suspected plot last month against the Royal Air Force base was “highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran” and “almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard”. list 1 of 3 Two Latvian men arrested inside UK military base after breach list 2 of 3 At least 81 US aircraft worth up to $3.3bn lost or damaged in Iran war list 3 of 3 UK blames Iran for airbase plot, sanctions two Iranian nationals Burnham promised action against what he described as Iran-linked “criminal networks” and their financing networks. The UK announced sanctions against two Iranian nationals over alleged “hostile activity” at RAF Fairford in southern England. It follows an incident around the base, which hosted US military aircraft, in the early hours of September 27, when five British men in their 20s suspected of “terrorism” and explosives offences were arrested. The men were not charged and were released on police bail. Another two men were also arrested and later released. Information about a suspected security threat to RAF Fairford and the events remains opaque. In a statement late Monday, the Iranian ministry described the UK’s claims of an Iranian role as “an ugly plot” that would also serve to “evade accountability for Britain’s participation” in the ongoing war against Iran on February 28. It said the UK had failed to provide sufficient evidence to back its claims and rejected the accusations of Iranian involvement as a “clumsy false flag operation”. “Britain’s track record of fabricating security claims against other countries, which have in some cases led to damaging tensions and conflicts in West Asia, is well known,” the ministry said, without elaborating. British Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said investigators assessed the coordinator to be a known individual based in Iran, although she did not name that person or disclose the supporting communications, financial records or other intelligence. RAF Fairford is a prominent base for United States aircraft that have participated in the war on Iran, which began on February 28 following US and Israeli strikes that killed several Iranian leaders and officials, including Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. After news of the incident, the US withdrew approximately a dozen B-1 bombers from the Fairford base. US media cited unnamed sources as alleging there was intelligence suggesting the bombers could run the risk of being hit by small drone attacks. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu publicly claimed at the start of October that his administration warned the UK about a plot. “We gave the Brits the intel that there was going to be an attack, and it’s an Iranian-sponsored attack, and pretty much the next day they slapped sanctions on us,” he said during an interview with US broadcaster Fox News. Netanyahu was criticising UK measures in response to the illegal expansion of Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank amid a diplomatic dispute. Earlier this month, Tehran grouped the Fairford incident with allegations surrounding the Flydubai cockpit attack – which authorities in the United Arab Emirates claimed was a “suicide” mission to crash the plane at Israel’s Ben Gurion airport in Tel Aviv. “I think even a schoolchild recognised how amateurishly it was designed,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said about the aircraft incident. He also argued that such incidents were being manufactured to assign blame and justify a war facing public opposition in the US and elsewhere. IRNA, the official news website of the Iranian government, argued in an analysis last week that the Western-led vote at the board of governors of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to refer the case of Iran’s nuclear programme to the United Nations Security Council could be classified as another attempt to pressure Iran to capitulate to US demands. It said increasing reports over recent weeks attributing a major role and responsibility to Tehran for the considerable battlefield advances gained by the Houthis in Yemen pointed to a “plan to identify Iran as the main reason for insecurity” on the regional and global stage. “The series of suspicious incidents recently, which have been attributed to Iran by the US president and senior officials without offering any evidence, appear to be a coordinated wave to smear Iran,” IRNA said. But UK officials have advanced undeterred with measures against Iran in reaction to the Fairford incident.
