events.title: Iran threatens Gulf data centres: How exposed is the region’s internet?
events.summary: Iran has warned that cables and data centres in the region could be attacked, as Houthi allies hold internet chokepoint. Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, has warned that cables, data centres and artificial intelligence (AI) facilities across the region could be attacked if war with the United States erupts again. The warning comes as the capture of Yemeni territory along the Red Sea coastline last month by the Iran-backed Houthis has raised concerns over the safety of internet cables linking Europe and Asia. Fierce fighting is under way between Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Houthis at several locations, including Bab al-Mandeb, through which nearly one-fifth of global internet traffic passes. list 1 of 4 US suspends Microsoft and Adobe from visa programme amid fraud claims list 2 of 4 Trump gives top US science awards to Elon Musk and other tech executives list 3 of 4 Why has Iraq decided to ban online map service Waze? list 4 of 4 Russia’s Yandex says data centre shut down after drone attack Data centres and US business interests were hit in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates during the US-Israel war on Iran. Tehran said these attacks were in response to US attacks on Iranian civilian installations. Active hostilities have largely ended since the June memorandum of understanding between Iran and the US, but attacks on ships passing through the global oil chokepoint – the Strait of Hormuz – have continued. So how exposed is the region’s internet? Here’s what you need to know: Why are data centres and internet cables vulnerable? Because so much data travels through a few narrow routes. More than 90 percent of data capacity between Europe and Asia passes through cables under the Red Sea, according to estimates by the research firm TeleGeography. They enter the sea through Bab al-Mandeb, a strait about 26km (16 miles) wide at its narrowest, one of the busiest maritime routes connecting Europe to Asia. Cables can be cut by anchors or sabotage, and repairs in a war zone need permits and safety guarantees. Data centres, which run banking apps and cloud services, are large, fixed targets. “An attack does not necessarily need to destroy the servers themselves to render an entire facility inoperable,” Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer in security studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera. Data centres depend on uninterrupted electricity, cooling and telecommunications, he said, while undersea cables “are difficult to protect continuously and disruption can affect several countries simultaneously”. Has Iran threatened to attack data centres and cables? Yes, repeatedly since the war began in February. On March 11, the semi-official Tasnim news agency said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has published a list of “Iran’s new targets”, including cloud infrastructure belonging to Google, Microsoft and Oracle in Israel and some Gulf states. That same month, the IRGC named 17 US firms in a Telegram post, including Google, Meta, and Apple, as well as the Emirati AI company G42 as potential targets. Krieg said he would take Rezaei’s threat seriously, but drew a distinction between Iran’s ability to cause significant disruption and its ability “to systematically destroy the Gulf’s digital infrastructure”. “What makes Mohsen Rezaei’s warning particularly significant is that he is not simply threatening another set of targets,” he said. “He is identifying a new category of strategic infrastructure that connects Gulf economic diversification directly to American technological power.” He described the warning as “fundamentally about deterrence”, aimed “as much at Abu Dhabi, Riyadh and Doha as at Washington”, giving Gulf governments a reason to discourage another US offensive. Have tech infrastructure and cables been attacked before? In March, Amazon Web Services (AWS) said two of its facilities in the UAE were “directly struck” by drones, while a strike near one in Bahrain “caused physical impact to our infrastructure”. Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank said its app was unavailable due to a region-wide IT disruption, though it did not directly link this to AWS. In September, AWS said it could not restore several sites in Bahrain and one in the UAE. Under the sea, three cables were damaged in February 2024, most likely by the dragging anchor of the Rubymar, a cargo ship disabled by a Houthi missile, according to the industry consensus reported by Data Center Dynamics, with repairs taking months. In September 2025, two cables were cut near Jeddah, slowing internet access across the Middle East and South Asia. No cause has been confirmed. The March attacks “exposed the limits of treating commercial infrastructure as something that automatically benefits from national air defence”, Krieg said.

events.title: Trump’s Russian energy strategy could backfire
events.summary: Tim’s view The contradictory tangle of energy policy actions taken by US President Donald Trump toward Russia over the weekend risks repeating mistakes that he and his allies often slammed his predecessor for. On Friday, Trump announced the US would waive sanctions on Russian diesel exports until the spring and permit it to release 300,000 metric tons of diesel into the global market, before announcing an energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv. The diesel deal was quickly condemned by a bipartisan group of senators , who argued that the volume was too small to make a difference — equal to less than a day of US consumption — and extended a “financial lifeline” to Russian President Vladimir Putin. This, they said, contradicted both a 2022 US ban on Russian energy imports and the spirit of the new sanctions law Trump signed last month, which seeks to penalize countries like China and India for the very same kinds of purchases the president is now pursuing. The diesel relaxation, former State Department energy diplomat Geoff Pyatt told me, is “enough of a sweetheart deal to encourage [Russian Direct Investment Fund CEO Kirill] Dmitriev and Putin to keep fighting in hopes Trump will deliver Kyiv.” As for the “ceasefire,” Russia seems to have violated it almost instantly . A Ukrainian official told me on Monday that Kyiv was temporarily holding off on further long-range drone strikes against Russian refineries while it assessed Moscow’s behavior and was waiting for a chance, potentially later this week, to clarify details of Trump’s proposal with US officials. Axios reported the deal could apply only to refineries , which would make little sense for Ukraine to participate in given that it has only one barely-functional refinery. Kyiv is more worried about the power sector, which a recently leaked Russian military planning document makes clear is still directly in Moscow’s sights . Dangling a limited ceasefire deal that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy can’t accept sends the same message to the Kremlin as the diesel deal: Ukrainians are the problem in this war, and US resolve in support of Ukraine is barely paper-thin. The past few years have shown repeatedly that accommodating Putin pushes him away from the negotiating table, not toward it . Trump and his energy officials have criticized Biden often and loudly for authorizing, in 2022, a record release of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which they framed as an irresponsible stab at tamping down US fuel prices ahead of an election at the expense of long-term American security interests. They also criticized Biden’s decision in 2021 to relax sanctions on the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline in the interest of repairing relations with Moscow, which helped embolden Putin to undertake the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. With just three weeks until the midterms, Trump is clearly riled about diesel prices and the slow recovery of exports of refined products from the Persian Gulf. But it’s counterproductive to capitulate to Putin: In addition to the uncountable human toll, a longer war in Ukraine means more energy market distortion ahead. Notable A new poll found that even if Trump managed a political feat like ending the Iran war or bringing down gasoline prices by $1 ahead of November’s midterms , a majority of voters would not be more likely to vote Republican.

events.title: ‘The amazement is kind of wearing off a little bit’: Wharton survey reveals managers are learning what Gen Z already figured out
events.summary: Have you talked to a Gen Zer or even a Gen Alpha kid about AI lately? On playgrounds, kids point at each other and say “that’s AI” about behavior they find fake or unconvincing. In high school and college, AI is a cheating tool that turns in easily spotted slop if you’re not careful. In the workforce, it’s a tool for rendering an email inbox almost entirely useless. In short, the AI natives most exposed to this technology have the most intense love/hate feelings about it. It’s not a technological revolution to them; it’s a giant pain. Managers at large U.S. companies are using AI more than ever and increasingly feeling the way their kids and younger colleagues do, according to a new survey from Wharton Human-AI Research and research firm GBK Collective . Among managers and above, 62% reported using AI daily, up from 46% last year . Meanwhile, the share describing themselves as excited fell eight percentage points to 51%. A quarter described themselves as skeptical, and 44% as cautious. The researchers called it the first wave in their four-year study in which usage and excitement moved in opposite directions. “The amazement is kind of wearing off a little bit,” Prasanna “Sonny” Tambe , a professor of operations, information and decisions and co-director of the Wharton Human-AI Research, told Fortune . In its place, he said, is greater caution: “This technology is moving so fast and our organization is not ready to keep up.” This cooling isn’t a backlash. Optimism among managers and above held steady at 59%, and 80% reported positive financial returns from AI, though only 28% called those returns strongly positive. The annual waves are separate samples rather than a panel tracking the same people, so the data describe a shift in mood across the management ranks; the findings suggest that the people responsible for putting AI to work are encountering a distinction younger users have already been expressing. A technology can be useful, even game-changing, without inspiring confidence about everything that comes with it. A Gallup survey conducted with the Walton Family Foundation and GSV, published in April, found that 51% of Americans ages 14 to 29 used generative AI at least weekly, even as excitement fell 14 percentage points from the previous year. Among employed Gen Z respondents, 48% said AI’s workplace risks outweighed its benefits, even as 56% acknowledged that AI tools can help them do their work faster. For Jeremy Korst , a Wharton lecturer, GBK partner and founder of AI consultancy Mindspan Labs, the cooling reflects the move from experimenting with a technology to making it work inside an organization. He said it’s like going from an “Oh, wow” level of excitement to how to make that transition actually work. The work after the output One of the most consequential changes may be what happens after AI produces an answer. Seventy-two percent of managers and above said their focus had shifted from creating outputs to managing AI-generated outputs. Among managers and directors, the figure was 63%; among vice presidents and above, it reached 82%. That shift puts verification at the center of the job. An agent’s ability to carry out a task is not the same as an organization’s ability to determine whether it carried out that task correctly. “I think we have been overindexing a little bit on what agents can do, as opposed to … what is it that we can verify that agents can do,” said Tambe, who is also working on economic research from within OpenAI while he’s on sabbatical. (“It is very interesting,” he said. “This economy, as you know, is evolving so quickly that each of us … are seeing a different piece of this and trying to figure out from all the signals we can get what’s going on here.”) Verification, Tambe said, gets more complicated when an agent’s work crosses organizational functions. Korst pointed to research by Wharton’s Gideon Nave and Steven Shaw on what they call “ cognitive surrender ”: the question of whether reviewers are truly checking AI’s work, or at what point they simply sign off. Organizations haven’t settled who answers for the mistakes that slip through. Tambe offered that as a deceptively simple example of the work ahead: “It’s a simple question, but from an organizational perspective, it’s pretty hard because it involves job roles and complicated things like that that actually take time to resolve.” Asked who is held most responsible when an autonomous AI makes a consequential error, 28% of managers and above named a governance or risk team, 26% named the deploying employee’s manager, and 25% named the employee. Among managers and directors specifically, one in five said nobody was clearly accountable or they did not know. Among VPs and above, 3% said the same. For now, most departments keep a person in the loop. Among managers and above who identified their department’s highest permitted level of AI autonomy, 48% said AI performed the work but a human approved it before execution. Another 35% said AI provided suggestions or drafts while a person made every final call. Only 17% reported autonomous operation with either after-the-fact sampling or real-time monitoring and guardrails. Strain in the middle All of that checking, approving and deciding lands on a layer of the company that was already busy. Korst said it’s “putting a bunch of strain in the middle of the organization,” describing “middle managers and teams who are tasked to lead this transformation and do it right.” That layer, he added, “doesn’t have a lot of capacity.” The technology’s expanding capabilities can make the problem worse, Korst said. Being able to do more does not tell a manager what is worth doing. “How do I prioritize what I should be doing?” he asked rhetorically. “Or else I can very quickly find myself running a new treadmill because of the technology.” The strain runs downhill, too. A third of managers and above reported that their departments had already slowed or frozen hiring because of AI, and 24% expected AI to result in fewer entry-level hires over the next two to five years, compared with 14% who expected fewer executive hires. Bosses and their employees also disagree about how well prepared the workforce is. While 78% of managers and above said employees received adequate AI training, only 56% of entry- and mid-level employees agreed. Those junior employees were added to the survey for the first time this year, and the results do not compare managers and employees matched within the same companies. Who’s getting it right The survey’s answer to Korst’s “how” question is that the companies seeing real returns are the ones redesigning the work around it. events.title: Amex introduces a framework to prevent AI agents from making unauthorized purchases
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Personal AI agents are increasingly making transactions on their users’ behalf, but given the nondeterministic nature of large language models, AI bots are prone to doing what they’re not supposed to. Which, in this case, raises the possibility of AI misfiring and making unauthorized transactions. To get ahead of this problem, American Express is introducing a new framework designed to capture and authenticate a customer’s purchase intent before an AI agent completes the transaction. The idea is that there should be a way to ensure that the customer’s purchase instructions are carried throughout the transaction lifecycle, Amex says, from the purchase to everything that follows. Dubbed the “Intent Intelligence Framework,” the company hopes it will become an industry standard for AI-powered transactions. “These new transactions will have a consumer, a merchant, and an agent,” explained Amex’s VP of Agentic Partnerships and Strategy, Hannah Bozian, in an interview with TechCrunch. She said the company wanted to ensure that agentic transactions are still “seamless, trusted, and secure, the way our card members expect them to be.” This framework’s release follows the company’s April launch of Amex’s Agentic Commerce Experiences, or the ACE Developer Toolkit, which includes a handful of services that now include the intent framework. Amex said it has not yet seen an increase in disputes because of agentic commerce, but it wanted to be proactive in building this technology as this type of commerce scales. In part, that’s because consumers have signaled they’re open to trying agentic commerce. In a recent Amex Trendex report, 66% of surveyed U.S. consumers said they’re likely to use AI agents to research the best price for a product or service, and 61% said they’re likely to use it for a product or service recommendation over the next 12 months, the company told TechCrunch. To start, Amex’s new intent framework begins with a Create Intent API, which will capture the customer’s purchase instructions along with other constraints they may have included in their request, like the merchant’s name, maximum budget, and other product preferences. How this intent is collected may vary depending on the AI model involved, but the plan is to make this framework flexible enough to support all agentic commerce models, Bozian said. The customer then authenticates their identity and signs off on the intent captured by the agent. Then an Intent ID, a unique identifier representing the intent, is created, along with a Proof of Intent Token, which includes the customer’s high-level constraints. This token is used to obtain a secure digital payment credential that the agent will use at checkout instead of the customer’s actual credit card number. In doing so, Amex says, the purchase will remain secure while being aligned with what the customer authorized the agent to do. This Intent ID and token can also be used in different parts of the transaction process, helping companies to manage areas like fraud prevention and dispute resolution, Amex said. “Our approach differs from the implementations of others in that it pulls intent earlier into the transaction flow. And this is important because it helps mitigate some risk before the risk occurs,” said Bozian. She offered the example of a customer asking an agent to buy white Nike sneakers in a size 9, but the agent submits a request to purchase shoes from Adidas. In such a case, Amex could prevent the transaction from going through because the agent made a mistake. Bozian also notes that while many agents today ask for customer consent before making a purchase, Amex foresees a future where agents may act much more autonomously in some cases. For instance, a consumer might allow their agent to re-order household staples, like paper towels or toilet paper — categories in which the only real constraint is the price and size, not merchant or brand. In these scenarios, it makes sense to have technology in the loop performing that extra check, to ensure the transactions match the customer’s intent. Having a log of what was authorized by which agent and when could also help address fraud on behalf of the agent, she noted. Amex is already in discussions with partners across the payments ecosystem for implementing ACE, which includes the agentic tokens that contain Amex’s payment credentials, as well as other parts of the developer kit. The company said it plans to actively develop ACE further as the agentic commerce ecosystem evolves.

events.title: Rwanda to host a Grand Prix in 2030s as Formula One returns to Africa
events.summary: Rwanda has secured a 10-year deal to host F1 races at a purpose-built race track on the outskirts of capital Kigali. Kigali, Rwanda – Formula One will return to Africa after a decades-long absence, with Rwanda scheduled to host a Grand Prix in the early 2030s. Rwandan President Paul Kagame made the announcement during a ceremony attended by Formula One President and CEO Stefano Domenicali and FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem in Kigali on Tuesday. “Rwanda has been working very hard towards hosting the African Grand Prix,” Kagame said. He referred to it a “partnership” that was long overdue but “a milestone for the continent”. The East African nation has secured a 10-year deal to bring Formula One back to the continent for the first time since 1993, with the inaugural race projected for the early 2030s. The Grand Prix will be held near Kigali, with former Austrian motorsport driver Alex Wurz’s racetrack design firm in charge of designing the new circuit. It will be built near the Bugesera international airport, 40 kilometres (24.8 miles) south of Kigali. The circuit will stretch over six kilometres, with 17 corners and an anti-clockwise layout. Designed to follow the natural terrain, it will feature an elevation gain of 197 metres per lap. The track will be developed to FIA Grade 1 standards and is expected to host other motorsport competitions and major events. Kagame emphasised that “Rwanda is happy and excited to be part of a journey that will change how Africa is conceived by the world of sports”. Mohammed Ben Sulayem, president of the sport’s governing body, hailed Formula One’s return to Africa as “a moment of immense pride”, adding that it opened “a new chapter in the history of Formula One”. Formula One chief Domenicali termed Africa “the missing piece” in the championship’s global footprint. In December 2024, the Rwandan president announced the country’s bid to host a Formula One Grand Prix during an address to the FIA General Assembly in Kigali. Lewis Hamilton, Formula One’s most successful driver with seven world titles and 106 Grand Prix wins, has been a leading proponent of the competition’s return to Africa. At last week’s Singapore Grand Prix, Hamilton was asked about the prospects of an F1 race in Africa and reiterated his stance, saying: “We need to have a Grand Prix in Africa.” “It is, for me, the most important continent, to be honest, the most beautiful continent,” the Ferrari driver said. “We’re on all the other continents but that one and there should be no reason for it.” The British driver is known to have advocated for an F1 race in Africa for years and has publicly urged F1’s Domenicali to add a race in Africa. “It is something I’ve been pushing for in the background, and Stefano has been amazing,” Hamilton said last week. “He’s flown to Africa so many times over the last couple of years, speaking to lots and lots of different people, so I hope that he has some news for me soon.” Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, the reigning world champion, also expressed his excitement. “We want to race in a lot of different places in the world, so I really hope that it can be pushed through,” he said. “I’ve been once to Rwanda. We have to wait to see if it’s all going to go through, but I think we’re all very excited if that happens.”

Text of this article October 13, 2026 PRESS RELEASE Meet Apple HomeView, a new way to enjoy entertainment, stay connected, and manage the home Apple HomeView is powered by Apple Intelligence with Siri AI and built with privacy and security at its core CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today introduced Apple HomeView , designed to be central to the home and personal to everyone in it. With a stunning 7-inch Liquid Retina display, HomeView brings entertainment, connection, and smart home management together in one place, from playing music and making FaceTime calls to home monitoring and hands-free automations with voice control — all designed with privacy and security at the core. 1 HomeView recognizes users by their faces, adapting so they can access their personal content in Messages, FaceTime, Calendar, Reminders, and Find My. HomeView features Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri that’s profoundly more capable and conversational, with broad world knowledge that powers richer music discovery and onscreen awareness. When paired with an Apple Intelligence-enabled device, it can also draw on a user’s personal context, such as their Calendar, Messages, and relevant information across their apps, to provide more helpful, personalized responses. 2 Designed to fit in any space, HomeView can be placed on a tabletop as the center of the home or wall-mounted to fit in spaces like the entryway or hallway. Pre-orders start today, with availability beginning November 13. “Apple HomeView is designed to be shared by everyone in the home yet feel completely personal to each user,” said Greg Joswiak, Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing. “It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home. And it’s powered by Apple Intelligence with Siri AI at its core, drawing on personal context from your iPhone to help you find what you need and get more done, all while keeping everyone’s information private and secure.” Elegantly Designed for Any Space HomeView features a beautiful aluminum design with a 7-inch Liquid Retina display connected to a domed speaker base by a stainless steel hinge that provides a smooth tilt for comfortable viewing on tabletops of any height. The perfect addition to a kitchen counter, nightstand, or side table, HomeView comes in four beautiful colors — silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray — each finished with a matching cable. The elegant design and Liquid Retina display seamlessly blend into any space while remaining clearly visible from across the room. It features adaptive display technologies, including True Tone, that react to changing light throughout the day. Automatic brightness adjusts from 500 nits — bright enough to stay vivid and easy to see even in a sunlit room — down to just 0.3 nits, making it ideal for the nightstand. The HomeView interface intelligently adjusts based on the user’s distance, showing simpler information that’s viewable from across the room and richer detail as they step closer. A separate wall-mounted HomeView model — available in space gray and silver — offers the same 7-inch Liquid Retina display, powerful set of features, and rich audio. It can be attached to a wall using three purpose-built mounts from Schneider Home, with options for self-installation or professional installation. A Personalized Experience for Each User in the Home HomeView recognizes up to six people and delivers a personalized experience for each one. Each user gets their own personalized Home Screen with apps and widgets. Personal content stays private from others, while shared photo albums and music can be easily enjoyed by everyone in a household, including guests. Featuring Siri AI, Powered by Apple Intelligence HomeView features Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence and advanced Apple silicon. Siri AI is a profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding and onscreen awareness. With broad world knowledge, anyone in the home can ask Siri about virtually any topic and get an answer.

Text of this article October 13, 2026 PRESS RELEASE Apple unveils the new Apple TV 4K, supercharged by Siri AI A more capable and conversational Siri, faster performance, and an even more immersive home theater setup elevate the entertainment experience CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today announced the next generation of Apple TV 4K , delivering its most immersive home theater experience yet. The new Apple TV 4K features Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence, transforming how users search for, discover, and enjoy their favorite movies and TV shows through a full-screen Siri AI experience. 1 With built-in far-field microphones, Apple TV 4K also lets users talk to Siri completely hands-free. 2 The new Apple TV 4K delivers even faster performance and, when paired with four HomePod mini 2 or HomePod (2nd generation) speakers, unlocks the most immersive home theater surround sound setup Apple has ever offered. As a home hub, Apple TV 4K also makes managing the smart home easier than ever, with Apple Intelligence-generated camera activity descriptions and summarized notifications in the Home app, and control of accessories and scenes. 3 The new Apple TV 4K can be pre-ordered starting today, with availability beginning November 13. “The new Apple TV 4K is our most immersive home theater experience yet,” said Bob Borchers, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Product Marketing. “With Siri AI, finding something to watch becomes a full-screen, conversational experience, and with built-in far-field microphones, it’s completely hands-free. Pair it with HomePod for the best surround sound setup we’ve ever offered, and it makes managing your Apple Home accessories easier than ever. Now, alongside HomeView, HomePod mini 2, and Apple Home Collection, it’s part of the most connected Apple Home we’ve ever built.” An Entirely New Version of Siri Powered by Apple Intelligence Apple TV 4K brings Siri AI to the living room with a rich, full-screen experience. An entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence, Siri AI is a profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding, broad world knowledge, and the ability to take even more systemwide app actions, making it effortless to find entertainment. Users can simply ask Siri “What Apple TV shows won at the Emmy Awards this year?” and see beautiful poster art pulled directly from the Apple TV app, along with relevant suggestions like “More award-winning comedies” to keep exploring. While watching, users can ask Siri AI follow-up questions and tap into Siri AI’s broad world knowledge to go deeper into a show, asking things like “Where was Pluribus filmed?” or “Is this appropriate for a 15-year-old?” Responses appear in a compact, subtle overlay, providing helpful information when viewers ask while keeping them immersed in the action. With an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone, Siri AI on Apple TV 4K can now tap into a user’s personal context to answer requests like “Play the show Alinda recommended.” A Fully Hands-Free Experience with Far-Field Microphones The new Apple TV 4K features three far-field microphones, letting users control what they’re watching and discover new shows completely hands-free. Advanced echo cancellation intelligently isolates a user’s voice from background sound to deliver crystal-clear “Hey Siri” or “Siri” recognition, even while audio is playing. Faster Performance, Smarter Remote The A19 chip in the new Apple TV 4K delivers up to 50 percent faster CPU performance and up to 2x faster GPU performance than the previous generation, for greater responsiveness, faster navigation, and smoother animations. The A19 chip also includes a new, dedicated AV1 decoder, enabling more efficient, high-quality streaming while using less bandwidth. The new Siri Remote keeps its familiar design while adding Find My support with Precision Finding and an option to play a sound on the remote — making it far easier to locate. 4 Apple’s Most Immersive Home Theater Ever Pairing HomePod with Apple TV 4K already offers users an immersive viewing experience that’s easy to set up, and the new Apple TV 4K takes it even further. For the first time, users can create a four-speaker surround sound experience with Apple TV 4K (4th generation) and HomePod mini 2. The four speakers work together with Apple TV 4K to intelligently recognize their position in the room so audio timing and levels are automatically calibrated to the space. HomePod (2nd generation) can also be used in this four-speaker setup for the ultimate audio experience, as long as the front and rear speaker pairs match. 5 An Even Smarter Home Hub The new Apple TV 4K continues to serve as a powerful home hub, giving users control of their smart home accessories from anywhere. 6 With a compatible doorbell, notifications appear directly on the TV so users can see who’s at the door, speak with them, and control other accessories like unlocking the door — all without interrupting what they’re watching. Apple TV 4K supports automations, guest mode, and secure local processing of HomeKit Secure Video, now enhanced with Apple Intelligence-generated camera activity video descriptions and summarized notifications. Users can also use Siri AI to control smart home accessories and turn scenes on or off hands-free. And with built-in Wi-Fi and Thread, Apple TV 4K can seamlessly connect and control a user’s smart home. More Ways to Enjoy the Living Room Apple TV 4K is more than just a way to watch — it’s a home essential that transforms the living room to reflect what users want in the moment.

events.title: Deadly Houthi attacks in Yemen’s Taiz as government forces advance in Marib
events.summary: Government troops launch major offensives across multiple fronts, while Houthi bombardments kill civilians in southwestern Yemen. Yemeni government forces say they have made strategic advances into the Marib governorate in north-central Yemen as they push on with operation “Dawn of Yemen”. The offensive by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, launched just over a week ago, comes after major gains by the Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah or Supporters of God, in September, when it swept along the country’s Red Sea coast, capturing the strategic port city of Mocha and territory around the Bab al-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important shipping routes. Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, said operation Dawn of Yemen aimed to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the group has controlled since 2014, when the war first started. Meanwhile, intense clashes and Houthi shelling on residential neighbourhoods in Taiz in the southwest of the country have caused dozens of civilian casualties. In the northwest of Marib governorate, a military source told Al Jazeera that government troops have successfully taken control of strategic, commanding heights surrounding the strategic Maas camp facility in the Medghal district. The source noted this followed intensive attacks that had breached the Houthi group’s fortifications. On the southern front, forces from the Saba and Bayhan axes announced the capture of the al-Muqailat and Jabal Zajjar positions north of the Harib district. Government forces claimed the fierce clashes resulted in the Houthis retreating and suffering human and material losses. This field progress coincided with continued violent battles along the front lines in the north and south of Marib. Government forces launched concentrated strikes using warplanes, drones, artillery and rocket launchers, targeting Houthi military positions and reinforcements. The armed forces’ media centre published footage it said documented drone attacks on Houthi military barracks and vehicles within the scope of the third military region’s operations, noting the destruction of multiple combat vehicles and equipment. Above: Footage from the battles within the operational theatre of the seventh military region north of Marib: Media centre of armed forces. Military spokesperson Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili announced on Monday that operations have involved 1,879 precise strikes, neutralising 950 Houthi fighters and destroying 380 military vehicles. Meanwhile, Houthi-affiliated media reported that air strikes targeted Kamaran Island and the al-Qanawis district in the coastal Hodeidah governorate along the Red Sea and the Harf Sufyan district in Amran, western-central Yemen. In the southwestern governorate of Taiz, where the Houthis have the city of Taiz under siege , government forces and popular resistance fighters are engaged in fierce battles across multiple major axes amid a wide-scale field escalation. On the western fronts, heavy fighting has flared in al-Dhabab, Hathran and Jabal Han as government troops have sought to thwart infiltration attempts and repel Houthi attacks. Sources within the government forces told Al Jazeera that troops captured 81 Houthi fighters in al-Dhabab on Monday afternoon. In the southern and southwestern countryside, battles have intensified in the al-Shaqb, al-Aqroud and al-Misrakh areas. A field military source told Al Jazeera that government forces are involved in fierce clashes from all directions in the al-Shaqb area of Taiz, with confrontations extending to areas the Houthis seized on Monday in Sabir. Also in the southwest, a field military source from the Southern Giants Brigades told Al Jazeera that Houthi forces had fired a ballistic missile at the highly strategic mountain range of Jabal Kahboub at midnight. The source confirmed there were no human or material casualties, with damage limited to the missile’s distant impact zone. The military escalation has severely affected civilian populations. Al Jazeera correspondent Abdullah Qatran reported seeing Houthi mortar shelling targeting the al-Ikhwa residential neighbourhood in the centre of Taiz, resulting in an undetermined number of deaths, injuries and property damage, causing widespread panic. With Taiz under Houthi siege, civilians there are also suffering severe shortages of fuel and other essential supplies. Yemen’s Ministry of Public Health and Population said on Saturday that medicines, intravenous fluids, medical supplies and fuel at the city’s health facilities were “nearing depletion”. Compounding this, the Yemeni Network for Rights and Freedoms has documented 43 violations by Houthi forces in Taiz over the past 24 hours, which have killed five civilians and wounded 17.

Text of this article October 13, 2026 PRESS RELEASE Apple announces the next generation of HomePod mini with support for Siri AI, beautiful new colors, and rich sound With a profoundly more capable and conversational Siri AI, new ways to enjoy music, and a more immersive home theater experience, HomePod mini does more than ever before CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today announced HomePod mini 2 , featuring Siri AI, gorgeous new colors, and enhanced audio experiences. Siri AI, 1 coming to HomePod mini 2 in a future software update, is a profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding, broad world knowledge that powers tasks like richer music discovery, and the ability to tap into even more apps — bringing a whole new level of capability to HomePod mini. 2 Users can enjoy room-filling audio with a single speaker, in a stereo pair, or using multiroom audio. When paired with the new Apple TV 4K, HomePod mini 2 supports four-speaker surround sound — Apple’s most immersive home theater setup yet. And HomePod mini makes it easy for different users to manage the connected home with just a voice command, securely controlling accessories and running automations. HomePod mini 2 can be pre-ordered starting today in pink, green, blue, white, and midnight, with availability beginning Friday, October 30. “HomePod mini 2 brings together Siri AI, gorgeous new colors, and incredible audio,” said Kaiann Drance, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Home Product Marketing. “With Siri AI, it understands you better than ever, drawing on personal context and broad world knowledge to make music discovery even richer. It fills a room with sound on its own, which gets even bigger in a stereo pair or with multiroom audio, and when paired with the new Apple TV 4K, it delivers our most immersive home theater setup yet. And with just your voice, HomePod mini makes it easy to securely control your accessories and run automations across the connected home.” Siri AI Transforms the HomePod mini Experience Powered by an entirely new architecture built on the latest generation of Apple Foundation Models, Siri AI transforms the HomePod mini experience and helps users get more done than ever before. When paired with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, HomePod mini can tap into a user’s personal context to help them find what they need in the moment. HomePod mini can recognize up to six users in a household by their voice and securely connect to their device across apps like Messages and timers, while playing their favorite music, and more. Siri AI can also privately act on this context across a user’s iPhone and iPad apps to complete tasks like finding a song a friend recommended in a text, setting a reminder tied to a calendar event or location, locating a recipe from an email, or adding ingredients to a grocery list. With broad world knowledge, Siri AI can answer questions on almost any topic by getting up-to-date information from the web. And users can go back and forth with Siri in a conversation like never before. Once Siri AI is enabled on a supported HomePod mini speaker, even users without an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad will benefit from Siri AI’s broad world knowledge; its ability to have rich, natural conversations; and its improved music discovery. Immersive Audio Experiences HomePod mini delivers rich 360-degree sound from its compact footprint, whether it’s used as a single speaker, in a stereo pair, or as part of a multiroom audio setup. Powered by the Apple S10 chip and advanced computational audio, it analyzes music in real time to optimize dynamic range, loudness, and acoustic performance. For the first time, users can create a four-speaker surround sound experience with Apple TV 4K (4th generation) and HomePod mini 2. Together, the four speakers and the new Apple TV 4K intelligently recognize each speaker’s position in the room, so audio timing and levels are automatically calibrated to the space. 3 The new HomePod mini can serve as a speaker for Mac, delivering expansive sound for everything from movies and gaming to FaceTime and video calls. 4 Finished in complementary colors, the new HomePod mini creates a beautifully unified desktop setup with Mac. Introducing Sound Glow With Sound Glow, the top of HomePod mini transforms into a visual canvas that glows and pulses in sync with the music, reacting in real time to bass and treble. 5 The song’s album artwork from Now Playing generates a color-matched light experience that’s unique to every song, and users can pick a soundscape like rain to trigger bespoke animations for a soothing atmosphere. Effortless Smart Home Management HomePod mini makes controlling the connected home easy at an incredible value. With just their voice, users can conduct a series of smart home actions, including locking the front door; closing the garage when leaving the house; and lowering the blinds, adjusting the thermostat, or turning off the lights at bedtime. With the Home app, users can automate their smart home accessories and create scenes to control multiple accessories at the same time. As a home hub, HomePod mini also lets users securely control accessories from the Home app on iPhone, whether they’re at home or away. 6 Sound Recognition gives HomePod mini users peace of mind by listening for a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm and, if one is detected, sending a notification immediately to the user’s iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch. Using the Home app, users can check in via HomePod mini and listen and talk to someone at home to make sure everything is all right. 7 The new HomePod mini also works seamlessly with smart home accessories, including Apple Home Collection 8 video doorbells and cameras, using Face Recognition to announce who is at the door. 9 Private and Secure by Design As with every Apple product, privacy and security are foundational to HomePod mini. Siri AI takes full advantage of the bold new architecture for Apple Intelligence. Siri requests on HomePod mini 2 can use on-device processing or Private Cloud Compute, which extends the privacy of the device to the cloud.

Text of this article October 13, 2026 PRESS RELEASE Introducing Apple :br(s):Home Collection, a new lineup of smart home accessories In collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric, Apple brings the simplicity, reliability, and privacy of iPhone and Apple Home to a new suite of smart cameras, thermostats, and a door lock CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today announced Apple Home Collection, a new lineup of smart home accessories — including indoor and outdoor cameras, thermostats, temperature sensors, and a video doorbell and door lock — designed in collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. 1 These new accessories are simple to set up starting with one tap with iPhone, and everything is managed through the Apple Home app — no separate app or account required. Each accessory is encrypted end-to-end in Apple Home, so only users and the people they choose can access their home data. Building on the thousands of Works with Apple Home and Matter accessories available today, Apple Home Collection offers customers a new array of recommended products to better understand what’s happening inside and outside their home, manage access, and keep the temperature just right throughout the day. Availability for all products begins in December, with select accessories available starting early 2027. “Apple Home Collection makes it easy to choose smart home accessories with confidence,” said Matthew Costello, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering. “Working closely with industry leaders LG Electronics and Schneider Electric, we designed every accessory to work seamlessly with Apple Home, so managing your home is simple, reliable, and private.” A New Kind of Apple Home Works with Apple Home and Matter certification have allowed a wide array of third-party accessories to connect with Apple’s smart home ecosystem for years, and Apple Home Collection takes it even further. Apple worked closely with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric to create an integrated Apple Home experience across the new product lineup. And like all accessories in Apple Home, Apple Home Collection products are designed for privacy, with Home app data encrypted end-to-end, so LG Electronics, Schneider Electric, and Apple can’t read it. These new Apple Home Collection products feature a clean, minimal aesthetic and premium materials, with every detail considered, from how they mount and adjust to how they look and feel alongside Apple products throughout the home. Each product can be set up starting with a single tap with iPhone, controlled entirely from the Home app and using Siri, and work as either standalone accessories or together as a connected system. “LG Electronics has spent decades developing technologies and products designed around the way people live,” said Kihyun Jung, LG Electronics’ executive vice president. “Working closely with Apple, we’ve co-created a more connected, intuitive, and convenient home experience for our customers.” “As a global leader in energy technology, we are proud to bring our experience in innovative and advanced climate control to Apple Home,” said Olivier Blum, Schneider Electric’s CEO.

events.title: A pioneering Jeddah schoolhouse show reaches Frieze Masters in London 58 years later
events.summary: It took 58 years for a pioneering Jeddah schoolhouse show to reach Frieze Masters in London. In 1968, two female artists hung their paintings at a school in Jeddah called Dar Al-Tarbia Al-Hadetha, in one of the first exhibitions women had ever held in Saudi Arabia. One of them, Mounirah Mosly , spent the decades that followed — long before Vision 2030 set off a boom in Saudi art — designing Aramco publications, helping run its children’s art competitions, and working dyes, snakeskin, and rope into collages about war and Palestine, until her death in 2019. This week, her creations go on display at Frieze Masters , Frieze London’s fair for art made before 2000, where a slot reads as a verdict that the work now belongs to history. Jeddah’s Athr Gallery is debuting with Mosly and a second pioneer of Saudi modernism, Abdulrahman Alsulaiman. Her work hangs in the fair’s Feminist Legacies section. — Manal Albarakati

events.title: AI is an inflation problem, Fed’s Goolsbee says
events.summary: The News Inflation tied to the AI boom is “jumping out of its lane” and starting to push up prices in unrelated corners of the economy, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said. “Prices are going up in spaces that are not just components in data centers and the directly adjacent industries,” he said on Semafor’s . “I’m getting increasingly nervous that that’s just straight, old-fashioned overheating demand.” Prices for land, electricity, water, construction, and electrical components used in data centers have surged. Those spikes don’t appear to have yet hit consumer pain points — for example, the cost of groceries or a haircut — but economists are closely watching how AI’s wealth, from paper millionaires in Silicon Valley to higher-paid construction workers, is being spent. Fed Governor Lisa Cook warned last month about “some economy-wide pressure from AI-fueled demand” but said that so far the boom looks like “a shift in demand toward AI-related sectors rather than an increase in economy-wide demand.” Fighting that kind of sector-specific inflation with rate hikes “could be a mistake,” she said. Goolsbee isn’t a member of the Fed committee that sets interest rates, but will join it in 2027. He and other economists have been trying to parse how much of today’s stubborn inflation — 3.4% in August, with September’s numbers due out this week — is from higher oil prices triggered by the war in the Middle East, which the Fed can’t do much about, and how much is coming from hotter demand across the economy for goods and services. “If inflation remains persistent, then I think it’s clear what the Fed has to do,” he said, when asked whether the central bank should raise interest rates again when it meets later this month. Liz’s view The Fed’s problem is that its best tool for fighting inflation doesn’t seem to be denting the demand for AI inputs. Hyperscalers aren’t slaphappy consumers who might be deterred by higher interest rates. They are locked in a must-win battle and don’t seem to mind higher debt costs. Companies like Alphabet and Meta have cash-cow advertising businesses that can support a few extra basis points of interest. It’s a broader problem for the Fed: Big parts of the US economy no longer respond to rising interest rates. There may be a pain point for the hyperscalers, but it’s likely to be intolerable for the rest of us. Room for Disagreement The issuance of new AI-linked debt fell in August, according to Morgan Stanley, which could show investors tapping on the brakes, even if corporate executives don’t want to. Transcript Liz Hoffman: Austan Goolsbee, welcome to the show. Austan Goolsbee: Thank you for having me. Liz: You are a great communicator in a world of wonks, literally a champion talker. Kevin Warsh wants the Fed to talk less and to force investors to look at the numbers and make their own decisions. What do you think? I’m an old friend and fan of Chairman Warsh. I worked with him back in the financial crisis. Before he ever got there, I’m uneasy with people expressing what we’re now calling forward guidance, that is saying, “Here’s what I think will happen at the next meeting. Here’s what I think four months from now the interest rate should change.” Most of the discussion about communication seems to have been about that, and I kind of agree with we should phase out that kind of communication. I’m engaged in a demystification project about the Federal Reserve. Here’s what we do. We’re not the bad guys. We’re the Guardians of the Galaxy. I’m going to stay on that for sure. Liz: Getting to those numbers that you would all like the market to put more stock in and make their own decisions about, even if they were prepared to be weaned off the commentary, does the data that you’re seeing right now lay out a clear picture? I like how you phrased that. I would say no, not a super clear picture because inflation’s still way too high. I have been worrying publicly about the potential for supply shocks like tariffs, like oil prices to shove us into a stagflationary kind of a trade-off. There is one sense in which it hasn’t been ambiguous. It hasn’t been stagflationary. The job market still looks very stable to me. Growth has been solid, consumer spending solid. We’re falling down on the inflation side of the mandate. But the ambiguity comes, is the inflation getting better on its own as it might if a supply shock kind of worked through or if you had a tariff that was just a one-time increase in the level of prices that should fade away and it hasn’t really been fading away. And you’ve seen inflation in services kicking up and that’s not really from tariffs, that’s not really mostly from oil. So that’s where you start to get the ambiguity in it and it’s not totally clear. Rohan Goswami: How much of that is AI, which obviously it’s driving a huge investment boom that’s sending up the price of inputs, power, land up. But at the same time, there is this deflationary promise that it’ll make everything cheaper. How do you think about those two things? This dynamic where there is great promise to come that is factored into massive stock market valuations and massive incentives for companies to engage in business investment. All of those things, the bigger the hype, the greater the chance that you overheat the economy in the short run, that for the day job of the Fed, the more promise there is, the more temptation, the more tendency to spend today based on the promise of what is to come. And that you got to be careful about because that’s just old-fashioned overheating right now. Rohan: What would a financial unwind of that trade, of the AI trade actually look like from where you sit? If it’s a discovery that the fundamentals are not there and it’s a bubble, that we have had bubbles in US history in the past, including in the recent past, and their unwinds can get ugly depending how much leverage is associated with those bubbles. It could be more like the popping of the internet. Now, Rohan, you’re not old enough. You don’t remember it, but if you back up, if you’re older than dirt like me, you’ll remember we had an experience with the internet that they were building out the infrastructure premised on growth rates of 20% per year. events.title: How the Houthis’ Zaydi heritage influences their strikes in Iran
events.summary: The Houthis firing missiles at Riyadh are not just Iranian proxies — they’re heirs to a 1,000-year-old Zaydi imamate that ruled northern Yemen on and off until the modern state was established in 1962. Zaydism holds that power belongs to the Prophet’s descendants, not elected officials. In an explainer video , Baraa Shiban, a RUSI fellow who sat on Yemen’s National Dialogue before being exiled for criticizing the group’s abuses, describes how, after a 1995 trip to Iran, the group’s founder, Hussein al-Houthi, fused the Zaydi branch of Shia Islam with Tehran’s revolutionary doctrine and built a militia in Hezbollah’s image. The group seized Sanaa in 2014, a decade after its founder was killed. Rather than replace the state, the Houthis hollowed it out, Shiban said, assigning a “supervisor” to sit over every ministry and neighborhood, extorting businesses, indoctrinating the public, and recruiting children as soldiers . They now rule most of Yemen’s population and sit on one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes. — Manal Albarakati

The two countries were also responsible for every round of $100 million or more. Regional funding fell 7%, and the number of deals dropped by a third. Take out the big rounds and the picture is bleak. Most of the money went to a handful of fintech and logistics companies that have already proven themselves. Early-stage deals have thinned out, which leaves fewer companies ready for growth rounds in 2027. Gulf money is filling the gap that other investors left: Investors from outside the region want to know they can get their money out, and right now that’s hard, with fewer startups being bought. — Ed Clowes

events.title: The IMF cuts its 2026 growth forecasts across the Gulf
events.summary: The IMF cut its 2026 growth forecasts across the Gulf and now expects the Middle East and North Africa to be the only region in the world to shrink this year. In April, the fund still forecast Saudi Arabia and the UAE would grow. Both will still do better than Kuwait, Bahrain, and Qatar, whose emir said today that government revenue was down 42% in the first half of the year , because they can pipe crude around the Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea and Fujairah. The fund expects a strong rebound next year, but only if the strait gradually reopens from March, a date it has already pushed back. Oman, whose ports sit outside the strait, is the only Gulf economy still expected to grow in 2026, though its growth will roughly halve next year as Qatar and Kuwait rebound by more than 17%. — Ed Clowes

events.title: Why this little known Chinese chipmaker has caused a global stock rout
events.summary: China's leading memory chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, has reportedly made progress on new designs. And until a recent blockbuster IPO the company was little known outside of its home market. Memory chip giants including Micron, SK Hynix and Saumsung all dropped on the news. Tech stocks plummeted on Tuesday after a Chinese memory chipmaker said it had made significant progress in developing new and more efficient designs. ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT , announced over the weekend it had made headway on new architecture which will increase memory density by packing more data into a smaller space. The announcement spooked the market because CXMT is China's leading rival to global memory makers including Micron , SK Hynix and Samsung. And, until a recent blockbuster IPO , it was little known outside of its home market. Micron was down 3.7% in premarket trading, while SK Hynix's South Korean-listed shares closed 10% lower and Samsung Electronics fell 7.4%. Other memory-related stocks, including SanDisk , Seagate and Western Digital , were all lower. CXMT leapt onto the global consciousness with its initial public offering in July. The company soared nearly 466% in its debut on Shanghai's tech-heavy STAR Market, making it the most valuable China-listed company at the time. Headquartered in Hefei, CXMT's listing came roughly a decade on from its founding in 2016. One of the biggest questions for CXMT after its IPO was whether it would be able to narrow the capability gap with Micron, Samsung and SK Hynix, particularly in high-bandwidth memory — a key component of AI chip systems. While huge domestic demand is supporting CXMT, it still faces challenges accessing chipmaking equipment, which has been effectively barred from China by U.S. export controls, including ASML 's extreme ultraviolet, or EUV, lithography machines, which are needed to manufacture the most advanced semiconductors. CXMT reportedly plans to roll out a new server-memory product based on new cell architecture by the end of 2026. The new design allows higher storage density, based on "4F square" tech. 4F square designs are also being pursued by SK Hynix, which in 2025 presented a roadmap for developing the tech. CXMT is often seen by analysts as trailing global competitors at the frontier of memory developments, and any news of breakthroughs can have a significant impact on investor perception of global rivals' market advantages. CXMT has made significant market gains, despite challenges related to export controls. Its share of the global dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM, market has risen to around 10%, up from about 4% a year ago, according to an HSBC note from Thursday. "While US government is unlikely to allow made in China memory sales to US, sales to data centers in other regions like Europe could indirectly impact Micron," Citi analysts said in a note from August. Apple has started testing CXMT's DRAM chips for devices sold within China and was lobbying the U.S. government to permit broader use of the company's products, the Financial Times reported in July, citing people familiar with the matter. Apple has been approached for comment.

events.title: African Union holds Kigali talks as fighting continues in eastern DRC
events.summary: Three former African presidents discussed security commitments, refugee protection and regional cooperation. Kigali, Rwanda – The African Union (AU) has held consultations in Kigali, Rwanda, as part of efforts to advance the peace process in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where fighting continues despite diplomatic initiatives to end the conflict. The consultations, held on October 6, focused on implementing the Washington Peace Agreement, security arrangements, the disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration of fighters, refugee protection and regional economic cooperation, the AU said in a statement. The delegation comprised former Ethiopian President Sahle-Work Zewde, former Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta and former Botswana President Mokgweetsi Masisi. Zewde is the deputy chairperson of the AU Panel of Facilitators for the eastern DRC peace process. The Kigali consultations followed meetings in Goma, eastern DRC, on October 5. According to the AU, the delegation met representatives of the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO), the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), the Expanded Joint Verification Mechanism Plus (EJVM+) and the Alliance Fleuve Congo/March 23 Movement (AFC/M23). Following the Goma meetings, the AU panel called for respect for ceasefire commitments, cooperation with verification mechanisms and restraint from actions that could undermine the peace process. It also stressed the need to protect civilians, ensure safe humanitarian access and prevent sexual and gender-based violence. In Kigali, the facilitators held separate consultations with Rwandan officials and representatives of regional institutions. The AU said the discussions covered security commitments, the protection of refugees and returnees, and regional economic cooperation, including mineral traceability, cross-border trade, energy and infrastructure. The facilitators said they would continue their engagements in Kinshasa as part of efforts to support dialogue and advance the peace process. Two agreements, separate negotiations The consultations come amid parallel diplomatic efforts to address the conflict. The Washington Peace Agreement, signed by the DRC and Rwanda on June 27, 2025, includes security commitments intended to address concerns over armed groups and the presence of forces in eastern DRC. Implementation remains a central issue. At a meeting of the agreement’s Joint Oversight Committee in June 2026, the parties expressed concern over escalating fighting and called for the agreement to be fully implemented, including commitments concerning the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) and the disengagement of forces. The Washington agreement is separate from the Doha Framework for a Comprehensive Peace Agreement, signed on November 15, 2025, by representatives of the Congolese government and AFC/M23 under Qatar’s mediation. The Doha framework provides a basis for negotiations between the two sides on outstanding issues, including security arrangements and ceasefire monitoring. Subsequent discussions have focused on implementing existing commitments and negotiating remaining protocols. The two processes address different aspects of the conflict: the Washington agreement deals with relations and security commitments between the DRC and Rwanda, while the Doha process addresses negotiations between the Congolese government and AFC/M23. Kinshasa accuses Rwanda of supporting AFC/M23, an allegation Kigali denies. Rwanda, in turn, accuses the Congolese government of supporting and arming the FDLR, which it considers a threat to its national security. The Washington agreement includes commitments by the DRC to address the FDLR and by Rwanda concerning the disengagement of its forces and the lifting of defensive measures. The parties have continued to discuss how those commitments will be implemented and verified. The continued diplomatic engagement reflects the challenges facing efforts to resolve the conflict, with security commitments and negotiations involving different parties proceeding on separate tracks. The AU’s consultations in Goma and Kigali form part of its wider mediation efforts. Whether those efforts contribute to improved security will depend on the implementation of commitments by the parties and continued engagement in the respective peace processes.

events.title: Giraffe Bio aims its bespoke biomolecules at the looming copper shortage
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Between the AI data center boom and economywide electrification, the world will need a lot more copper. By 2040, copper supplies could fall 25% short of demand. That’ll be a tall order for the mining industry, which boosts production mostly by opening new mines, which is a costly, luck-driven endeavor. Typically, just 0.3% of prospective mines pan out. A new wave of critical minerals startups have been working on new ways to squeeze more copper out of existing mines using biotechnology, mostly by focusing on heap leaches, where microbes help separate minerals from waste. Endolith has created “Olympic caliber” microbes, Ceibo is working on its own strains, and Transition Metal Solutions has developed prebiotics to boost microbial activity. Giraffe Bio is taking an alternative approach. The startup develops mineral-specific chemicals to help mines recover up to 5% more copper. In mining, that amount “is really very material,” Alejandro Buffo Sempé, co-founder and CEO of Giraffe Bio, told TechCrunch. Most would be happy with an additional 1% to 2%. The startup says it can extract more copper because it’s able to engineer compounds specific to each mine’s mineral content. To bring the technology out of the lab, Giraffe Bio recently raised a $6.4 million seed round led by Orion Industrial Ventures, with participation from BHP Ventures, Twynam, Air Capital, and Baruch Future Ventures, TechCrunch has exclusively learned. Rather than douse ores with bacteria thought to facilitate copper extraction, the company grows engineered microbes in a bioreactor to produce the bespoke compounds. Those chemicals are then inserted into a mine’s existing process. “We can leverage all of the biological machinery without having to deal with keeping alive a microbe, which is very complicated in [mining] environments,” Buffo Sempé said. The startup is beginning with copper, but it says its platform can be tailored to other minerals, too. “The beauty of this is that we can target copper or we can target gold or silver,” he said. The startup’s compounds are used in a mine’s flotation process. In flotation, chemicals help minerals either float or sink in a bath of water, allowing the operators to skim the desirable minerals off the top. The tighter the chemicals bind to the minerals of interest, the more that can be recovered. “We are extremely good at only picking up the copper,” Buffo Sempé said. Mines also use chemicals called depressors, which bind to unwanted compounds like arsenic and sink them out of the mix, leaving more desirable products at the top. Giraffe Bio is using the same biotech platform to develop depressors as well, the CEO said. In addition to improving mine production, Giraffe Bio can supplant toxic chemicals in the flotation process, too. “Instead of pouring chemicals that are usually very harmful for the environment and so forth, we’re replacing the function that they are providing to the flotation process with a biomolecule,” Buffo Sempé said. “We’re minimizing the friction towards maximizing the output.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Five things to watch after Trump's Russian diesel deal
events.summary: President Trump is turning to Vladimir Putin to help ease a global diesel crunch, setting up a clash between Washington's energy priorities and its efforts to pressure Russia over its invasion of Ukraine. Why it matters: The fuel shortage is among the most severe effects of the Iran war and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries. Average U.S. diesel prices remain far above $6 per gallon, adding to GOP headwinds in the midterm elections. Trump says his deal will help bring costs down. Catch up quick: Trump on Friday claimed an agreement to bring escalating Russian exports, and the Treasury Department waived sanctions to help enable it. A few things to watch... The campaign trail. So far a few Republicans in close races — including Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers and Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan — have criticized the agreement. Republicans already saddled with Trump's unpopular policies in the midterms now face another awkward choice: whether to back his diesel deal with a dictator many of them despise, Axios' Andrew Pantazi writes. The market. Diesel futures dipped after the announcement. But analysts expressed doubt that the levels Trump is claiming will meaningfully sway prices in the U.S. and elsewhere — if Russia indeed delivers. Per Trump's claim, Russia will "immediately" provide what amounts to 2.24 million barrels, followed 3.73 million next month (equivalent to around 124,000 barrels per day spread over a month), and then roughly double it thereafter. "In the near-term, it's hard to see the waiver helping global fundamentals for diesel much," writes economics and geopolitics analyst Rachel Ziemba. The global market currently has a deficit of about 1 million barrels per day, per market intel firm Kpler, and "Russia's ability to deliver additional barrels remains uncertain," writes Kpler's Michelle Brouhard. Capitol Hill. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.), one of those lawmakers in a close reelection fight, will try and force a House vote to block Russian oil purchases. The law. It's not clear if any Russian barrels will reach U.S. shores — or whether it's legal if they do. A bipartisan group of seven senators, in a statement , say the decision runs afoul of a 2022 law barring U.S. imports of Russian oil and petroleum products. Treasury's Office of Terrorism and Financial Intelligence said it is acting "in compliance with all applicable laws." Meanwhile, the White House faces an Oct. 18 deadline to begin implementing a more recent law — named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham — that imposes fresh sanctions on Russia and trade penalties on buyers of Russian energy. But the law gives the White House discretion to waive key provisions. Ukraine. Trump is pushing Ukraine and Russia to ease attacks on energy infrastructure. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has criticized Trump's deal, said Russia has continued its barrages even as he maintained Ukraine held back early this week. events.title: Ecuador’s president tried to kill the dollar. Here’s what that means for Venezuela, Argentina and the Rest of Latin America
events.summary: Ecuador’s experience with dollarization matters beyond Quito. The possibility of mothballing local currencies and replacing them with the dollar is a hot topic in Latin America. It’s also on the agenda in Washington, D.C., where there is renewed interest in promoting the use of the greenback. Ecuador is an ideal natural experiment in how a dollarized system holds up against a hostile government. Rafael Correa, who holds a PhD in economics from the University of Illinois, opposed dollarization before it was adopted in Ecuador and before he became president. He led the country for a decade but could not dismantle Ecuador’s dollarized system because it produced excellent results and garnered widespread public support. The collapse In 1999, Ecuador’s sucre began a catastrophic plunge. At the end of 1998, it traded at 6,825 sucres to the U.S. dollar. By the end of 1999, it had plunged to 20,243 sucres to the dollar, losing two-thirds of its value against the greenback in one year. The losses did not stop there. During the first week of 2000, the sucre shed another 27.7% and hit an all-time low of 28,000 to the dollar. Faced with a currency in free fall, a banking crisis, and an imploding economy, President Jamil Mahuad announced on January 9, 2000, that Ecuador would replace the sucre with the dollar at 25,000 sucres to the dollar. President Bill Clinton and Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers had encouraged the move. Dollarization worked. Inflation dropped sharply, deposits flowed back into the banking system, and the economy switched from negative to positive growth with a surge in exports leading the way. With a system immune to currency crises, stability was established in Ecuador, and while stability might not be everything, everything is nothing without stability. A durable regime Today, dollarization enjoys roughly 90% approval. It is the longest-lived Ecuadorian currency regime since independence in May 1830, and it has lasted longer than any constitution. Its resilience is all the more notable because it survived Correa’s presidency (January 2007 to May 2017). Before entering politics, Correa published papers denouncing dollarization and sketched a plan to unwind it. As president, he called it “an immense error” and “monetary suicide.” Yet he knew an open attempt to dedollarize would trigger bank runs, economic collapse, and perhaps his impeachment. So, Correa repeatedly assured voters that abandoning the dollar would be catastrophic and was not on his agenda. What Correa did instead Below the surface, his actions told a different story. In his first year in office, he dismantled one of dollarization’s natural complements, a fiscal anchor. Ecuador had built an oil reserve fund, which, together with the dollar, had delivered the country’s first run of concurrent fiscal surpluses since it began pumping oil. Correa scrapped the fund. That same year, Correa introduced a series of economic policies that cut against dollarization’s logic. He closed the economy to foreign capital, which runs contrary to the principles of a dollarized system. He selectively defaulted on Ecuador’s foreign debt despite record oil revenues. He imposed an exit tax on every dollar leaving the country and sharply raised import tariffs. To exert control over private banks, he forced them to repatriate 45% of their liquidity and park it at the central bank. Correa also introduced a central bank electronic money program. It was billed as a tool for financial inclusion, since it let Ecuadorians pay by mobile phone. But because the central bank, not private banks, issued the balances, the government could have used it to pay its bills in digital credits not fully backed by dollars. The public wanted nothing to do with it, and the program was shut down. Most egregiously, the central bank began lending directly to the treasury. In effect, this allowed Correa to print unbacked “ecuadollars.” Central bank financing of the government peaked at about 10% of GDP, according to the IMF, with the heaviest lending in 2009–2014. The loans were of questionable legality and ran contrary to the tenets of a dollarized system. The legacy Correa was convicted of bribery in the Sobornos case and sentenced to eight years in prison. He lives in Belgium, outside the reach of that sentence. His legacy lingers. The full benefits of dollarization are not realized in Ecuador today because the central bank still sets interest rates and directs bank lending toward favored sectors. In addition, remaining capital controls restrict Ecuador’s access to the world’s deepest pool of international dollar liquidity. For countries weighing dollarization, the lesson is clear: the dollar does its job. For 26 years, Ecuador has remained immune from the plague of a currency crisis and has sustained respectable economic growth, low inflation, and surging exports. events.title: Australia bowl out South Africa to win first cricket Test in Durban
events.summary: Hazlewood’s 6-49 ⁠helped the visitors clean up the South African batting, wrapping up the win before tea on day five. Australia’s pace bowler Josh Hazlewood has bowled his side to a 214-run ⁠⁠victory over South Africa on the last ⁠⁠day of the first cricket Test match at the Kingsmead Stadium in Durban. The hosts’ resistance ended before tea on Tuesday as they were dismissed for 206. Hazlewood took 6-49 ⁠⁠as Australia bagged the six wickets they needed on the last day to go 1-0 up in the three-match series. He struck twice in one over with the new ball after ⁠⁠already having taken two wickets on Monday and then breaking through South Africa’s stoic early fightback. The 35-year-old Hazlewood also removed the last batsman to ensure the victory in the first clash between the teams since South Africa upset Australia in last year’s World Test Championship final at ‌‌Lord’s in London. South Africa held out for the first 110 minutes of Tuesday’s play before a legside delivery from Hazlewood was edged by Wiaan Mulder and snagged by a diving catch from wicketkeeper Alex Carey. Mulder and Aiden Markram resumed at 102-4 overnight, and the pair extended the fifth-wicket partnership to a patient 69 runs off 205 balls before Hazlewood’s breakthrough, with Mulder making 29. Part-time spinner Matt Renshaw, who was the man of the match ⁠⁠for Australia with the bat, then took a second Test wicket ⁠⁠when Kyle Verreynne quickly followed Mulder back to the change room with a reckless shot that saw him caught at slip by Steve Smith without scoring. South Africa were 166-6 at lunch and added 25 runs before the new ⁠⁠ball was taken, but crumbled quickly thereafter. Marco Jansen was bowled by Hazlewood for 35 and three balls later Simon Harmer followed as he brushed ⁠⁠the ball through to Carey with his glove. Markram then ⁠⁠fell after a patient 75 off 237 balls, edging Mitch Starc’s delivery off his pads to be caught behind, but was only given out after a television review. Hazlewood then completed the win as tailender Anrich Nortje popped up the ball ‌‌to short midwicket for Nathan Lyon to catch. Former Australia captain Smith, who did not field in Monday’s late session after a blow to the head while batting, returned to action on ‌‌Tuesday. “Steve ‌‌Smith has undergone a series of clinical assessments over the past 24 hours in accordance with Cricket Australia’s concussion protocols and has been cleared to take the field this morning,” a statement said.
