events.title: Car finance compensation payments delayed until next year
events.summary: Millions of drivers who were mis-sold car finance agreements must wait until at least 2027 to receive compensation, regulators have announced. Average payments of about £829 are expected under the rules published by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). However, legal challenges to the scheme - which will be heard in February 2027 -mean compensation calculations and payments have been delayed. Who could receive car finance compensation? The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest. Compensation could be given to many of those who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024. The decision by the FCA, the financial regulator, applies to about 12 million car loans - just over 40% of the total number during the period. In 2021, the FCA banned deals where car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them. The FCA said this provided an incentive for a buyer to be charged a higher-than-necessary interest rate, leaving them paying too much. Other car buyers were also judged to have signed unfair contracts because the commission paid to the dealer was so high - accounting for at least 35% of the total cost of credit and 10% of the loan. Some customers were not given accurate information about the best finance deal because of exclusive arrangements between car dealers and lenders. How much compensation could victims receive? Under the latest proposals, the FCA expects average payouts of £829 per mis-sold agreement. The total cost of the compensation, including administrative costs, could hit £9.1bn. How much individual consumers receive will depend on the degree of harm suffered. For some customers - especially if their contact details have changed - it could take many months before compensation is paid. What do victims need to do to claim compensation? Complaints have already been made about four million finance agreements. Those people do not need to do anything. The regulator urged anyone who has not yet complained to contact their car loan provider directly, rather than using a third-party claims management company. The regulator's central compensation scheme allows people to complain and potentially receive compensation for mis-sold deals without the need for a lawyer or to go through the courts. Motorists have also been warned to be on the alert for scammers posing as car finance lenders offering fake compensation . The FCA has published this guidance on how to complain , external . lenders will respond to claims, explaining if you are owed compensation and how much – but timing of those letters is now uncertain owing to the legal challenge those who complain before the scheme gets up and running are likely to receive compensation faster people who complained by 30 June and are not owed compensation should be told by 18 November, those who complained by 31 August will be told if they are not owed compensation by 18 January 2027 those who have not complained will be contacted by their lender. People will be asked if they want to opt in to the scheme to have their case reviewed those motor finance borrowers who do not receive a letter - for example because lenders no longer have their details and cannot trace them - can still make a claim Regulators have warned claims management companies and law firms involved in motor finance commission claims to make sure consumers do not have multiple representatives for the same claim and are not charged excessive termination fees. FCA boss Nikhil Rathi told the BBC's Today programme there are "many law firms out there who would like to get 30% of any compensation", stressing that the regulator's scheme was "free to use" for consumers. When will drivers receive compensation and who will pay? Millions of drivers were in line to receive compensation this year, and most of the remainder should have got compensation by the end of 2027. But the FCA has confirmed that no compensation will be paid before 2027 as a result of legal challenges to the scheme. Consumer Voice said the scheme left "too many people short-changed" . The FCA has also received challenges from three lenders: Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services, and Credit Agricole Auto Finance. The UK's Upper Tribunal has agreed to hear legal challenges to the scheme, with a hearing scheduled for 16 to 26 February. It means that lenders will no longer need to calculate or pay compensation to people owed money under its scheme, until the legal process concludes. The FCA said it would need to decide what to do next if the courts decided to overturn the programme.

events.title: Yemeni families’ search for missing loved ones hindered by new fighting
events.summary: Hundreds of people have gone missing in Yemen, with families not knowing if they were killed in fighting or detained. Sanaa, Yemen – In 2020, 18-year-old Munif bid farewell to his family and left his home in Sanaa to fight with the Houthis on the front lines of Yemen’s civil war After six months, all of his comrades went back to their families, but Munif never returned home. list 1 of 3 ‘We no longer eat three meals’: Yemen’s displaced face daily fight for food list 2 of 3 Yemen’s displaced children dream of returning to school list 3 of 3 At least 139 dead, 84 missing as migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti More than six years have passed, and Munif’s family, who asked to use just his first name for security reasons, are still searching for answers about his fate. He is one of hundreds of people who have disappeared in Yemen since war broke out in September 2014, when the Houthis – an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God) – captured the capital and forced the internationally-recognised government to flee south. “Ten other men from our village joined the front line on the Saudi-Yemen border. All of them came back. We asked them about my brother’s whereabouts, but none could tell us where he had gone,” said Mohammed, Munif’s brother. “A definite answer about his status would be a relief for the entire family.” There were hopes that a truce in 2022 between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government and Iran-aligned Houthis could help families begin their search for their missing loved ones. Since July this year, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has received more than 1,800 tracing requests from families looking for missing relatives in Yemen. But the resumption of fighting in July has halted this search for many families, who are trying to find out if loved ones have been detained, injured, killed, or simply lost in records, due to displacement or desertion. After careful consideration, Mohammed believes there are two possible outcomes for his brother, Munif. “He might have been hit by an air strike, leaving no trace of his body, or perhaps he was captured, and he remains in captivity,” Mohammed said. If Munif was killed in an explosion, finding a body part that could be identified would bring the family some relief. But the family is still hoping for the latter scenario, and that Munif is being held captive by government forces. “We would have accepted his death, adjusted to the loss, and forgotten my brother’s possible return. We just need to know what happened to him,” he said. “We have heard about some fighters who were believed to be dead, and their families accepted the news of their deaths and mourned them. However, they emerged alive after years of captivity. So, Munif may still be alive.” Both sides have held many prisoners of war over the decade-long conflict, but the number of captives remains uncertain. In May, Yemen’s internationally-recognised government and the Houthis signed a United Nations-backed agreement in Jordan to exchange more than 1,600 detainees. However, the implementation of the deal was postponed after both sides accused each other of obstructing the agreement. Abdulaziz, 24, has been on the front lines in Marib, an energy-rich region in central Yemen, fighting for the Houthis. Before the recent surge in fighting, he used to call his family once every 10 days. But for the past two months, his family has not heard from him. “We are waiting for a phone call from Abdulaziz, and we do not know if he will ever call us,” said Ahmed, Abdulaziz’s brother. Fighting has intensified on the front lines in Marib and Al-Jawf since the Houthis seized part of the Yemeni coast in September, and Rashid al-Alimi, the head of the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), announced a counteroffensive by government forces. The use of artillery, drones and warplanes to target Houthi positions likely means that many more people will be killed or missing. Ahmed, 26, assumes that his brother may have been killed in attacks by government forces in recent weeks. “We have not received any information from his comrades and field leaders about his injury or death. But my parents state that Abdulaziz’s voice or appearance is the only believable proof that he is alive,” he said. “Abdulaziz is in the battlefield. And people there kill or get killed. So, his [possible] death is not a shock for me. But continued ambiguity is more painful than confirmed news of his death.” With no word on his whereabouts, Abdulaziz’s mother will not know whether to wait for his safe return or begin to mourn his loss. “Whether he continues to be lost or his dead body returns, my mother’s eyes will never stop filling with tears,” Ahmed added. Christine Cipolla, the head of the ICRC’s Yemen delegation, said families of the missing had the right to know about the fate of their loved ones. “Behind every missing person is a family living in anguish.

events.title: Just 5 years in, interactive chatbot platform Character.AI files for bankruptcy
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Only five years into its journey, Character.AI, which lets users create AI characters and have conversations with them, has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, following a slew of lawsuits and struggles to scale its popular platform. In a court document , the company said it had assets and liabilities between $50 million and $100 million. “Over the past year, Character.ai has taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve its business in the face of significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. After a comprehensive review of the available alternatives, the board determined that this court-supervised sale process provides the Company with the best opportunity to maximize value for all stakeholders,” Character.AI CEO Colin Adams said in a statement. The startup has also agreed to sell some of its assets to Disney for $20 million, as well as a non-exclusive perpetual license for its technology. The company said Disney will provide transition services via former Character.AI employees who joined the entertainment giant last month alongside its former CEO Karandeep Singh Anand . Adams said the company would continue operating during the sale process, which is expected to close in late November or early December. However, he did note that there isn’t yet a bid for the company’s assets or a buyer. “We hope that the sale process will yield an actionable proposal that will allow continued operations of the Character.ai platform. If such a bid is unavailable, however, the platform will be wound down,” Adams wrote. Character.AI has had a tumultuous five years. Founded by former Google engineers Noam Shazeer, a co-author of the landmark Transformer paper, and Daniel De Freitas in late 2021, the startup initially focused on training foundation models and developing an AI chatbot platform that lets people create custom characters they could chat with. By September 2022, the startup reached unicorn valuation with a $150 million fundraise on the back of high demand for its platform, with the company saying at the time that its users had exchanged more than 2 billion messages with its bots in five months, and active users were averaging more than two hours on the platform daily. In May 2023, the Character.AI’s apps attracted more than 1.7 million installs in their first week after launch. But about a year later, in August 2024, Google struck a $2.7 billion deal to license the startup’s models, and both Shazeer and De Freitas returned to the search giant . At that time, the startup’s general counsel, Dominic Perella, stepped in as interim CEO, and the company moved away from training foundation models to focus on growth. Character.AI’s traction didn’t slow, however, with its platform recording 20 million monthly active users by October of that year. But things got difficult after the startup was sued following the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida boy whose mother says he became obsessed with a chatbot on its platform. Soon after, Texas launched an investigation to assess if the platform conformed to child privacy and safety laws. The company subsequently settled some of these lawsuits , added more safety features, and banned minors from its platform. In June of last year, the company appointed Anand, a former Brex and Meta executive, as CEO, and expanded its products to add AI video generation, and social feeds. The company has since tried to introduce new ways to spur user engagement via interactive storytelling formats as well as microdramas. But the fact that the company had to file for bankruptcy shows that such changes couldn’t move the needle on sustainability for the startup. It also shows that consumer-facing AI products are really hard to scale and monetize. Character.AI was one of the top apps in terms of time spent, according to analytics firm Sensor Tower. But high engagement can be a double-edged sword; AI costs rise the more people use the app, which consequently also increases the pressure to monetize users. Character.AI has raised over $193 million in funding across multiple rounds from investors including Lightspeed, SV Angel, Greycroft, and a16z, according to PitchBook. events.title: French supermarket fridges get hacked, heating to 122°F and sparking fires
events.summary: Hackers targeted hundreds of French supermarkets, causing refrigerators and freezers to overheat. The attack sparked fires and spoiled food across supermarkets in the region. European Commissioner for Agriculture and Food Christophe Hansen warned that "the weaponization of food has become a reality." Hackers targeted hundreds of French supermarkets in a cyberattack that reportedly caused refrigerators and freezers to overheat, spoiling food and sparking fires. Fridges at French supermarket chains Carrefour, Monoprix, the Les Mousquetaires-owned Intermarché, and Coopérative U, among others, all saw fridges heat up to as much as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) overnight, Reuters reported Monday. Coopérative U's CEO, Dominique Schelcher, confirmed that cyberattacks had affected "refrigeration production facilities of several stores." "Attacking equipment that is essential to the preservation of fresh products and the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and unprecedented. It is unacceptable," Schelcher said in a LinkedIn post . CNBC has reached out to Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarché, Coopérative U and E Leclerc for comment but did not immediately hear back. Felix Aime, a senior cyberthreat intelligence analyst ​at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research, said the attack affected several European countries, including Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium, according to the Reuters article. "I strongly condemn the cyberattack targeting food products at @intermarche @CooperativeU @Leclerc," European Commissioner for Agriculture and Food Christophe Hansen said in a post on X on Monday. "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponization of food has become a reality." Les Mousquetaires said it was expecting the damages, which affected around 180 stores, to reach "several million euros in losses," in an email to CNBC. It said some fresh and frozen food displays have been out of service after the cyberattack affected one of its service providers responsible for managing refrigeration systems inside some stores. "Intermarché and Netto have taken all necessary precautions to remove and dispose of any affected products as quickly as possible, to ensure consumer safety," the Les Mousquetaires spokesperson said. "In some stores, the overheating of equipment resulted in smoke, but no fires have been reported." They're now awaiting findings from a court-appointed bailiff and insurance experts to get more precise figures on damages. Stop & Shop parent Ahold Delhaize , which owns popular Dutch supermarket chain Albert Heijn, said that it was experiencing a "security issue within its network," and that systems had been taken offline. It said its stores are still open. This comes amid a broader wave of cyberattacks and cybercrimes, which experts are warning are being enhanced by artificial intelligence. British online fashion retailer Asos experienced a cybersecurity breach last week which revealed some customers' personal information. Meanwhile, a small power plant in the U.K. was shut down for four days in July after a cyberattack which was suspected to be linked to Iran. Interpol's global chief information security officer, Bjorn R. Watne, recently told CNBC that AI can be used to target multiple victims at once, and is increasing the scale and speed of cyberattacks. "It's an evolution and not a revolution." Correction: Bjorn R. Watne is global chief information security officer at Interpol. An earlier version misspelled his name.

events.title: Americans are stressed about grocery prices, so why do they toss or overlook so much ‘misfit’ food?
events.summary: Shoppers are much more inclined to buy misshapen produce if they can be assured the quality is good. Carly Reeves on Unsplash , CC BY There’s a paradox that drives the shopping decisions of many Americans: Almost three-quarters say they’re feeling stressed out about skyrocketing grocery bills . But they keep discarding large quantities of food that’s safe to eat, from crooked carrots to surplus yogurt to “best before” items pulled from shelves early. Overall, the U.S. government estimates that 30% to 40% of all food – from consumers, retailers and producers – is thrown out. That’s not just a massive missed opportunity for people experiencing food insecurity , but it’s also a significant contribution to global warming. According to the United Nations, 8%-10% of carbon emissions globally result from food waste. In recent years, however, a market to rescue discarded groceries and repurpose food scraps and by-products has grown dramatically. This ranges from marketing “ugly” produce to appeal to more consumers to upcycling food by-products . I study how consumers evaluate product value and quality, and my research suggests that American shoppers are much less fixated on prices or environmental impact. Instead, they care about quality. Even when perfectly good “misfit” produce is deeply discounted, for example, many shoppers assume that the low price reflects poor quality and either walk away or reach for a fruit or vegetable they think looks better. What does this mean for reducing food waste and shedding these purchasing biases? My research has found that smarter and more effective labeling can make a big difference. A discount or promise of lower carbon emissions isn’t enough by itself – people have to believe the food is good first. Making ‘ugly’ food attractive A whole retail sector is now dedicated to marketing misfit food. “Ugly produce” delivery companies like Hungry Harvest and Misfits Market are rescuing and reselling food to shoppers who want to save and reduce their carbon footprint. Misfits Market alone has rescued more than 265 million pounds (about 120 million kilos) of food since 2018 and sells it at an average discount of 35%. Companies that sell ‘misfit’ produce have seen a surge of consumer interest in recent years. Jintao Zhang , CC BY Another example is Too Good To Go , an app that sells “surprise” bags of surplus food at about one-third of the retail price. It estimates that it has saved more than 26 million meals, including through partnerships with more than 530 Whole Foods stores . And the app Flashfood encourages grocers to list meat, dairy and produce nearing their best-before date at around half price and directs shoppers, including those on public food assistance, to those deals. Consumers appear to be responding. Too Good To Go users in the U.S. saved 8.1 million meals in the first seven months of 2025, a 67% jump from the year before , while Misfits Market rescued 27 million pounds of food (about 12 million kilos) in 2025, up from 23 million (about 10 million kilos) in 2019, its first full year of operation. This market is also using smarter labeling to grow its appeal. Shoppers who believe that food appearance is important tend to judge misshapen produce as lower quality. But labeling these offerings as “ugly” actually reduces that bias because it signals that the only flaw is cosmetic. Another study found that in-store messages that raise shoppers’ self-esteem can also make a different: In field tests, a “ Different Outside. Same Inside ” message successfully urged people to overlook external appearance when making judgments, whether on people or food. The upcycling boom This sustainability push is also playing out in the processed and semi-processed foods market, where would-be waste is converted into upcycled products. Examples include flour milled from soybean pulp, snacks that leave the fruit peel on, and “bites” made from rescued bananas . Companies that want to market these goods can get third-party certification through Upcycled Certified if they pass an audit of their supply chain. More than 600 products from over 100 brands now carry it, and sales of certified products grew 17% from 2024 to 2025. Here, too, perceptions of quality matter. In research on consumers’ acceptance of these foods, my co-authors and I found that they made their purchase decision based largely on whether they believed the product was as good as its conventional counterpart. But in this case, in contrast to “ugly” produce, these products tend to be pricier, so they can’t compete through discounting. Rather, they usually sell at a premium – like this small bag of specialty flour going for $7. That means that it’s even more important they signal higher quality so they can appeal to less price-constrained shoppers. Generational attitudes differ on this point, our research found . Gen Z, millennials and baby boomers are more willing to buy foods certified as upcycled if they agree that the quality and environmental appeal are worth it. But Gen Xers – those who were born between 1965 and 1979 – show less enthusiasm, citing a perception of lower quality. That result fits what we generally know about Gen X shoppers. We discovered they are hard to persuade and cost-conscious, and they tend to rely much more on their own judgment. Gen Xers are also least likely to eat out or go shopping for groceries online, preferring instead to cook for themselves. That means they tend to scrutinize foods more closely in the store. A “green” benefit won’t beat these skeptics. They need an assurance of quality from brick-and-mortar retailers they trust, rather than from online platforms. When logos matter The encouraging news from our research is that it sometimes doesn’t take much to change beliefs. In two experiments, my co-authors and I tested whether a simple logo could shift shoppers’ perceptions of foods made from rescued ingredients. We designed one version that was round, green and descriptive, following established design principles: Circular logos signal higher quality , while descriptive ones lift brand evaluations . The other was hexagonal, monochrome and bare. Shoppers respond more favorably to logos that provide information and incentives, research has found. From Jintao Zhang. , CC BY We found that shoppers who saw products with the well-designed logo rated those foods higher in quality and were more willing to buy them than those who saw the same products with no logo. The poorly designed logo, meanwhile, made no difference. It was the increase in perceived quality, in our view, that made people more willing to buy. A logo that looks credible, explains itself and signals care can change what shoppers believe. A forgettable one might as well not be there. Closing this gap in perceptions, in short, doesn’t require shoppers to care more about the planet. It requires them to believe the food is good. events.title: As 'Cockroach' protests grow over alleged voter fraud, Modi defends India as ‘mother of democracy’
events.summary: Protests in India demanding the removal of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, for alleged fraud have intensified. On Monday, thousands of people reportedly joined leaders of Indian opposition parties in their march to the Supreme Court in Delhi to file a petition against the Election Commission. Over the weekend, authorities cracked down on protestors by resorting to mass detentions, which led to the United Nations Human Rights Office flagging concerns. Experts said the scale of the protests does not pose a threat to the stability of India at present, but crackdowns could broaden the unrest. Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday defended India as a " mother of democracy ," as protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter fraud are intensifying. "A wide range of issues are debated openly, and diverse perspectives are discussed by the people," Modi said, speaking at a Bloomberg New Economy event. His comments coincide with a severe crackdown by authorities against protestors demanding electoral reforms. Earlier today, key members of the viral pseudo-political movement, Cockroach Janta Party, were detained for protesting without permission . CJP, whose leaders were detained by authorities over the weekend as well, had sought permission from Delhi Police on Monday to launch fresh protests at the Jantar Mantar grounds in the capital. However, the government then barred the use of the site for protests. On Monday, thousands of people reportedly joined leaders of Indian opposition parties in their march to the Supreme Court in Delhi to file a petition against revisions made to the voter list by the Election Commission. Names of 130 million people have been struck off from the voter list after the commission began conducting "special intensive revisions" (SIR) to update voter lists across the country last year, as per several local media reports. Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the opposition in India, said the huge crowds were a sign that people were not going to be "intimidated" by the government . "There are no parallel protests. It's one protest, and it's a protest where everybody is standing together," Gandhi said, dismissing concerns over the absence of members of the Cockroach Janta Party who had called for protests over the weekend. "Delhi is once again flooded with people standing up to save democracy ," Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the viral pseudo-political movement, CJP, said in a post, reacting to the crowd amassed for the march led by Gandhi. Over the weekend, Indian security forces reportedly clamped down on protests in the capital city, detaining young people, several opposition party politicians, YouTubers, lawyers and a few journalists. The Delhi police, which is under the control of the Indian home ministry, did not respond to an email seeking comments. Experts told CNBC that while the scale of the protests does not pose a threat to the stability of India at present, crackdowns could broaden the unrest. "If security forces keep taking heavy-handed approaches, this will create a more volatile environment that could make protestors angrier and galvanize even larger groups of marchers," Michael Kugelman of the Atlantic Council told CNBC. He added that at present the scale of the protests was not significant enough to impact "capital flow and investor behavior" but warned that "heavy-handed tactics that generate violence and volatility" by the state could change it. The United Nations Human Rights Office on Saturday raised concerns over mass detentions and called on Indian authorities "to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled." On Sunday, India's Ministry of External Affairs responded to the UNHR's comments, calling them "unwarranted" and claiming they constituted an "unacceptable interference in the internal affairs of India." The crackdown during the latest protest has been "significant and massive" compared to earlier reactions to farmers' protests or uniform civil code protests, Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at Teneo, told CNBC. He added that there is a higher chance that the broad-based retaliation to the police crackdown could lead to more demonstrations. The CJP had first called for a nationwide protest on Oct. 2 , seeking the removal of the election chief after an investigative report by the Indian Express showed discrepancies in the functioning of the Election Commission and reports of deletion of millions of voters. On Sept. 26, following reports of the voter deletion, the Election Commission of India launched a special drive across India to enroll voters who have been left out of the rolls . It has downplayed discrepancies as highlighted in the Indian Express report and maintains it is "committed to ensuring that no eligible voter is left out of the voter list .

events.title: BlackRock and Baillie Gifford bet big on Icon 3D printed homes
events.summary: Austin-based Icon, one of the biggest players in 3D printed real estate, is announcing its $200 million Series D financing co-led by Baillie Gifford and funds managed by BlackRock, among others. The new financing brings total funding to $700 million, with the company reporting a $1.4 billion valuation. The funds come on the heels of Icon's latest technology, the Titan multi-story robotic 3D construction system, which launched commercially in March of this year. A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox. Austin-based Icon, one of the biggest players in 3D printed real estate, is announcing its $200 million Series D financing co-led by Baillie Gifford and funds managed by BlackRock, among others. That brings total funding to $700 million, with the company reporting a $1.4 billion valuation. The funds come on the heels of its latest technology, the Titan multi-story robotic 3D construction system, which launched commercially in March of this year. Previous Icon technology could build only single-story structures. The Titan also reduces the average time to build a home by six weeks, reduces the number of workers needed and lowers overall costs by 40%, according to Icon. "We were really looking for an investor group who had helped built-world, physical companies move from early startup proof points to scale," said Jason Ballard, co-founder and CEO of Icon, pointing to Baillie Gifford's experience with the likes of Nvidia, Tesla and SpaceX, as well as BlackRock's massive real estate portfolio. "It really is just kind of a world class outcome for us," he added. Icon is moving ahead at a time when the traditional homebuilding industry is under stress from higher interest rates and higher costs for land, labor and materials. There is also a continuing housing shortage, with some estimating up to four million new homes are still needed to meet current demand. The funding will be used to scale the Titan, as well as advance new technologies. It will also help the company to broaden its current footprint in Texas, Florida and Washington, D.C., as well as bring it to new markets across the U.S. "The construction system that Icon has developed over the last decade is compelling, not just because it brings new technologies to bear, but because it works with, rather than against, the business realities that shape a project's success too," said Luke Ward, private companies investment manager at Baillie Gifford. "As long-term investors, we look for exactly this kind of big opportunity for our clients, paired with patient, compounding execution." Icon previously used its printers on its own projects, like this fully 3D community outside Austin that was a project for Lennar. Now it is selling its new technology to other builders, with the help of special financing from Wells Fargo . The lender is also offering incentives to buyers of the homes. "This is a new motion for us, right? Putting these things into other people's hands, and we have like 10X the demand in terms of actual money down reservations that we actually forecasted needing for next year," said Ballard, adding that the demand has come from both large publicly traded builders as well as smaller private firms. Just eight years old, Icon has already scaled quickly. The company's goals are to build homes faster, more affordably and more sustainably. "We hit all these quality, measurable performance metrics. That's got people excited," said Ballard. "This is an industry that's under a lot of distress right now and is looking for new solutions because the old ways simply aren't working." Icon is on pace to see four times revenue growth this year, according to Ballard, who predicts they will at least double that next year, based on their current pipeline. He also said he sees a potential IPO in the future. Icon has also been working with both the U.S. military and NASA. It is currently deploying robotic construction systems to, "rebuild military readiness, strengthen national security infrastructure, and extend human presence beyond earth," according to the company. For the latter, it was awarded more than $370 million in government contracts to advance Project Olympus, which is developing construction systems to eventually build on the moon. "I think there's going to be some pretty exciting announcements in the back half of this year from NASA about the moon base, and we'll stay in lockstep with them, but that program is feeling really exciting, and we're pretty optimistic about it," said Ballard.

events.title: Poundland in rescue talks as owners seek buyer
events.summary: Published 13 October 2026, 10:42 BST Retail chain Poundland is in talks with potential buyers as it seeks a rescue deal, it has confirmed. Executives are working with an Irish property development group on a management buyout, as first reported by Sky News , external . But a union representing shopworkers warned that the retailer could fall into administration if that deal falls through, putting thousands of jobs at risk. This outcome would be "a disaster for our members", the Usdaw union said. Poundland has about 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, and 12,000 employees. The chain has been struggling for a number of years due to pressures including rising costs and competition. However, it expects sales to have grown more than 3% in 2026 compared with the previous year, which managing director Barry Williams said earlier this month was evidence that its recovery plan "is working". The retailer was sold for £1 last summer by previous owner Pepco to US investment firm Gordon Brothers. The current owners are in the process of seeking buyers, with the Poundland management attempting a buyout, a spokesman said. Mr Williams, along with the firm's leadership team and Andy Bond, a former chairman of Pepco, have been working with Irish real estate firm Martin Property Group on a management buyout. Martin Property Group is the management team's "preferred partner", the spokesman said, but the team will "work with whoever can deliver the best result for the business, colleagues and suppliers and build on the successful recovery that's already taking shape," he added. However, Bally Auluk, a national officer at Usdaw, said there are "deep concerns that the business could go into administration" should this buyout fail. "We are aware that a management buy-out has been attempted and we are told that their offers are being turned down," he added. A Poundland source disputed this, however, saying the Martin Property Group is part of the sale process and remains the management team's preferred partner. Retail analyst Catherine Shuttleworth said there were "tough times" on the High Street for all retailers. She said retailers were struggling with "significantly subdued consumer confidence as prices continue to rise" due to higher fuel costs. Poundland itself faces intense competition from rivals including B&M, Aldi, Lidl and from online retailers including Temu and TikTok Shop. The business "lost its strong £1 identity leaving shoppers to think it was getting too expensive", Shuttleworth said, and a costly expansion into clothing and frozen food under past management had not been successful. However, increased sales this year showed a deal with Mr Williams as boss "would make good sense", she added. Are you a Poundland customer? Do you think it is doing well, or badly? Get in touch here. events.title: Mark Zuckerberg and Alexandr Wang don't seem to like Guinness very much
events.summary: Guinness is a dark Irish stout with a bitter, roasted taste that some drinkers compare to coffee or dark chocolate. Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty Images Mark Zuckerberg and Alexandr Wang's drank Guinness and talked tech with Stripe's John Collison. Neither of the Meta execs really seemed to enjoy drinking the malty Irish beer. A clip of Zuckerberg sipping his pint and looking somewhat uncomfortable went viral on X. Mark Zuckerberg and Alexandr Wang joined Stripe cofounder John Collison for a beer on the latest episode of "Cheeky Pint" — but viewers aren’t convinced the Meta executives were converted to Guinness. Zuckerberg and Wang spent 134 minutes on the podcast discussing Meta’s AI ambitions, including the company’s new Muse product and its massive spending plans. As is customary on Collison’s interview series, the discussion took place over pints of Guinness, an Irish dry stout , known for its rich, malty, and slightly bitter taste. The episode began with a series of cheers between Collison, Zuckerberg, and Wang. Later, Zuckerberg revealed that he brought his host a keg of Guinness from Dublin. The exchange has drawn attention after viewers shared clips of Zuckerberg and Wang drinking the stout. In the footage, Zuckerberg takes a slow sip and swills it around in his mouth, before appearing to wince — a moment that prompted comments about whether he was enjoying it. Social-media users were quick to focus on Zuckerberg’s expression after the sip. One user observed, "Never seen someone try and chew a Guinness." Although for those who do not enjoy the trademark acquired taste that is Guinness, Zuckerberg's reaction seemed somewhat relatable, with one user noting, "That was the most normal thing I've ever seen him do, actually." Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Zuckerberg and Wang's thoughts on the taste of Guinness. Elon Musk outdrank Zuckerberg on 'Cheeky Pint' Tyler Cosgrove, who works on the TBPN podcast, watched the full two-hour show and counted how much Wang, Zuckerberg, and Collison drank. events.title: Hobbs and Whistles owner investigates hack that may have exposed customer data
events.summary: Cyber-attack on TFG London comes less than a week after online fashion seller Asos was hit by hackers The owner of Phase Eight, Hobbs and Whistles has said its websites and IT systems have been hit by a cyber-attack that may have compromised customers’ personal data. The South-African listed TFG London said it identified the “cybersecurity incident” at the three UK-based retail chains on Sunday. Its two other UK brands, Inside Story and White Stuff, are not affected. TFG said its stores had stayed open and trading but some of its IT systems “remain unavailable” and it had paused all online orders as a “precautionary measure”. An “investigation is ongoing, including establishing whether any personal or other sensitive information has been compromised,” the company said. If the investigation establishes that any personal information has been accessed by hackers, TFG said it would “notify affected individuals or organisations”. “Some of our brand’s website capabilities may not be available as the investigation continues. We apologise for any disruption and will provide additional updates to our customers as appropriate,” the company added. In an email to Whistles customers, the company said any orders placed on or after 11 October may be delayed. Orders placed before that date are being processed normally. Returns can only be made via stores at present and Whistles told customers it was “working on a solution for postal returns”. TFG has engaged external cybersecurity specialists to contain the incident, which has been reported to the relevant UK authorities. The group’s operations in Africa or Australia run on separate systems and are not affected. The attack on the three UK fashion brands comes less than a week after a cyber-attack affected the online fashion seller Asos , in which the names, addresses and recent search data of millions of customers was accessed. H&M said on Monday that it was also investigating claims that its systems had been attacked. However, the fast fashion retailer said: “We have not found any indications that our data environment has been compromised.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning On Monday, it emerged that hackers had forced the temperature of many French supermarket fridges up to 50C overnight , in an “unprecedented” cyber-attack affecting several hundred stores. Several other British retailers, including Marks & Spencer , the Co-op and Harrods , were hit by damaging cyber incidents last year. M&S and the Co-op faced stock shortages and the former was forced to shut down its website for several weeks while it ensured its systems were clean. Marijus Briedis, the chief technology officer at the digital security firm NordVPN, said: “Coming so soon after the Asos incident, this latest attack on TFG London is another reminder that the retail sector is firmly in hackers’ sights. These attacks are becoming a recurring nightmare for businesses, and there’s every reason to believe we’ll see more of them. “Retailers are particularly attractive targets because they hold valuable customer information and rely on a sprawling network of payment systems, suppliers and third-party technology providers. Every connection is a potential weak point, and attackers are increasingly adept at exploiting stolen credentials, human error and gaps in security.”

events.title: Steel ships, railroads, and data centers: A VC takes the Industrial Revolution analogy seriously
events.summary: In 2026, Hans Tung and I are talking about 19th-century ships. “The Dutch, the Spanish, the Portuguese—they sailed around the world with beautiful large ships, but they were wooden wind ships,” said Tung, Notable Capital managing partner and early backer of companies like Airbnb , Coinbase, and Anthropic. “The British were the first to scale ships with the steam engine. Adopting steel technology and applying it to the steam engine—that made the British Navy stronger than the rest of the world combined. Without that buildout—steel ships, the steam engine—we wouldn’t even have the American concept of free trade.” Tung loves history (as do I, which anyone subjected to whaling ventures-centric writing knows) , and I came to him with something that had been irking me: I’ve often heard VCs talk about AI as an “Industrial Revolution-level change,” in a way I’ve frequently found hand-wavey. My question to Tung: What if we took the historical analogue seriously? What does it mean to take that parallel to its full conclusion?  And so Tung started with ships, suggesting a throughline from Portuguese spice routes to Britain’s steel ship global dominance (in 1890, 80% of the world’s ships came from British shipyards). To Tung, this is his first mental model for the technological leap we’re living through as our global infrastructure morphs to meet the age of AI. His case: There’s perhaps too much focus on any one app or company, and that major technological change only creates geopolitical dominance if the infrastructure is there to back it up. “Wood ships don’t last as well in the long run,” said Tung. “The need for steel ships with steam engines was important to be able to go around the world. The British end up doing this because they invest in technology that allows them to leverage the benefits of the Industrial Revolution. They end up dominating the world for more than 100 years.” I also asked Tung a question I’ve been asking all sorts of people lately, my own strange version of a Rorschach test perhaps: Are data centers the railroads of the 21st century? His personal answer is, essentially, yes. “If you don’t have enough compute to meet demand, it doesn’t matter if you have a better model,” Tung told Fortune . “The models that win are the ones that are available.” Consider, for example, the Civil War, won partially because the railroad infrastructure of the North was far more developed than the South’s. It wasn’t just about having food or troops; it was about getting around. “It doesn’t matter if you have the resources if you don’t have the [means] to move them,” said Tung. “Most major Civil War battles happened within 24 miles of a railroad… If you don’t have a railroad—or compute—it doesn’t matter if you have better engineers, better politicians, or better thinkers.”  This is, vitally, where geopolitical concerns enter the picture: China has been largely outbuilding the U.S. for decades.  “Over the last almost 20 years, the [amount of] subway and high-speed rail built in China was unprecedented,” said Tung, who’s Taiwanese-American. “Now, China has more high-speed rail than the rest of the world combined, kind of like the North in the Civil War. They executed very, very well. It’s mind-boggling.” This goes beyond modern railroads: Looking at ships, some stats suggest that over 80% of new shipbuilding orders worldwide go through China. For perspective: Each year, one state-owned Chinese conglomerate (the China State Shipbuilding Corporation) builds more commercial ships than the aggregate U.S. shipbuilding industry has built over the 81 years since World War II ended.  In short, China is uniquely adept at building, at a moment when that especially matters.  For the data center buildout, the picture’s more layered: China currently controls about 24 gigawatts of working data center compute capacity, while the U.S. has at minimum 47 gigawatts by conservative estimates. However, the U.S. is staring down the challenge of executing a historic building boom. (A Columbia Business School professor has estimated that the AI infrastructure buildout could account for an average of 3.6% of U.S. GDP every year until 2032. This buildout, of course, comes with all kinds of concerns, from community pushback to questions about the electric grid’s capacities.) Tung’s case, ultimately, is this: The best ideas and talent don’t count, not on their own. Amid a sweeping socioeconomic shift driven by technology, it’s not invention that matters most. It’s having the infrastructure to use the AI that you’ve built, effectively and at scale.  “We’re not going to just win,” said Tung. “We have to work hard and make sure we win.” See you tomorrow, Allie Garfinkle X: @agarfinks Email: alexandra.garfinkle@fortune.com Submit a deal for the Term Sheet newsletter here . Joey Abrams curated the deals section of today’s newsletter . This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Du and etisalat unveil new services boosting UAE push towards 6G
events.summary: UAE telecoms operators du and etisalat have unveiled new services to boost mobile phone communications as the nation accelerates its push towards 6G technology . Du said on Tuesday it has delivered commercial U6GHz connectivity on its 5G+ network, which will serve as a foundation for high-capacity services across homes, businesses and industries . U6GHz – the new spectrum for the next generation of mobile connectivity – is expected to enhance the cloud, artificial intelligence, digital experiences and connected environments. The U6GHz band was identified for international mobile telecoms in the Europe, Middle East and Africa region, several Asian countries, as well as China, Brazil and Mexico, according to global technology advisory Omdia. U6GHz combines a wide contiguous spectrum bandwidth with characteristics closer to that of existing bands than that of other higher candidate bands, making it the “sweet spot” that balances capacity and coverage, the UK-based research firm said. Placing U6GHz “into the hands of customers … [will be] unlocking new opportunities for consumers, businesses and emerging digital applications”, Saleem Alblooshi, chief technology officer of Dubai-based du, said in a statement. Separately, Abu Dhabi's etisalat said it has commercially launched a service that increase upload speeds to smartphones threefold. The company – which recently rebranded back from e& – is using 2x2 Mimo, a wireless technology that allows the transmission of two data streams between mobile devices and cellular base stations. That new capability is exclusive on compatible smartphones on etisalat UAE’s 5.5G network and will be useful in sending high-resolution photos, videos and large files faster, in addition to harnessing the abilities of AI-powered applications, the company said. “Mobile experiences are changing,” said Marwan bin Shakar, chief technology officer of etisalat UAE. “Smartphones are no longer primarily consuming content – they are creating, sharing and increasingly sending richer data to AI and cloud applications in real time. That changes what we need from the network. By bringing this capability … we are increasing upload capacity where it matters.” Last month, etisalat claimed it had launched the world’s first mobile network operating on U6GHz. Mr bin Shakar said this was key to “accelerating the nation's transition to the 6G era”. Sixth-generation technology , or 6G, will offer faster speeds and data transfers for users of smartphones, tablets, laptops and other devices. Though the announcement does not mean 6G cellular technology has officially arrived, the UAE telecoms company's U6GHz mobile network makes use of several innovations that “elevate the 5G-advanced experience” and pave the way for it to become standard. The announcements from du and etisalat are the latest in a series of developments in the UAE related to the eventual adoption of 6G. Last month, du and Khalifa University said they had carried out field trials for the new technology. In 2024, the UAE's Telecommunications and Digital Regulatory Authority announced plans to allocate 600MHz and 6GHz bands, a move that helped accelerate the development of 6G services in the Arab world's second-largest economy. South Korea's Samsung, one of the world's largest manufacturers of smartphones, has predicted widespread adoption of 6G networks by 2030, with “completion of standards and early commercialisation by 2028".

events.title: All Systems Go: Global PC App Ecosystem Ready for NVIDIA RTX Spark
events.summary: NVIDIA RTX Spark is a new beginning for the PC — a reinvention combining the capabilities of a gaming PC, a creative studio and a personal AI supercomputer into a single superchip. With up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of AI compute, RTX Spark delivers the full stack of NVIDIA RTX and CUDA technologies for creators, developers and gamers, while unlocking a new paradigm in personal computing via powerful local AI agents. Last week, NVIDIA and Microsoft announced that RTX Spark laptops will be available on Friday, Oct. 16 . Ahead of the launch, NVIDIA and its ecosystem partners are rolling out new software features and performance optimizations to expand what’s possible with local AI on RTX Spark. New and upcoming RTX Spark updates — among the thousands of apps, games and models available at launch — include: New agent features, models and tools that enhance local agents on RTX Spark: Updates to top agent apps including GitHub Copilot, Hermes, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy streamline setup on RTX Spark, improve security with OpenShell and Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), and enable hybrid local and cloud AI routing. The NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B model, purpose-built for agentic AI on RTX Spark, releases on Thursday, Oct. 15. NVIDIA PAIR moves out of beta and adds llama.cpp support. Top creative apps optimized for RTX Spark: Up to 2x performance is coming soon to Adobe’s top apps. NVIDIA and Adobe have collaborated to rearchitect Photoshop for GPU-accelerated compositing and Premiere for playback, rendering, effects and more. The NVIDIA Broadcast 2.3 release brings new Video Super Resolution, Video Frame Generation, offline file processing and agent Model Context Protocol (MCP) controls to the app. NVIDIA RTX Video Frame Generation and high dynamic range (HDR) capabilities are available now in ComfyUI to accelerate AI generative video workflows. NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction will be available in Blender 5.3 in November to improve interactivity in the viewport. Developer tools are now ready for RTX Spark: Top developer frameworks are now available for RTX Spark, including PyTorch, Python and CUDA, as well as all CUDA libraries. GitHub Copilot, Pi and other coding agents are now optimized for RTX Spark. Llama.cpp adds support for decision models, and releases a Windows app. Hundreds of top games and anti-cheat are supported on RTX Spark, plus: A 2x faster DLSS 5 AI model arrives Friday, Oct. 16, and a new Performance Mode for DLSS Frame Generation is available today via the NVIDIA App beta . Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, the third-generation small language model (SLM) for NVIDIA ACE AI game characters, releases Friday, Oct. 23. The latest RTX Remix update, including DLSS 5 support, releases on Friday, Oct. 23. Advancing Local AI Agents With New Apps, Models and Tools AI is changing the way people interact with PCs. Agent popularity skyrocketed this year, with projects such as OpenClaw and Hermes topping popularity charts on GitHub. Local large language models (LLMs) surpassed the intelligence threshold to power agents, with models like Qwen 3.8-Flash-Next catching up to frontier cloud models released just a few months ago. As a result, local LLM downloads are already 5x higher than all of last year. From models to agent harnesses to security to tools, NVIDIA is partnering closely with the local AI ecosystem to make RTX Spark the ideal hardware to run local agents. Local AI Agents Made Easy On RTX Spark From the first boot of RTX Spark, users will be greeted with a “Getting Started” screen to choose and install their agent app. These agents will come with new, secure sandboxing technology thanks to NVIDIA OpenShell and MXC. MXC delivers operating system-level security, while OpenShell makes it simpler for agents to adopt MXC and adds advanced capabilities such as credential protection and security monitoring. Hermes Agent will integrate granular OpenShell controls and MXC by the end of the month. OpenClaw and GitHub Copilot now support MXC. After installing an agent, setting up local AI is also now seamless in GitHub Copilot, Hermes Agent, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy. The apps will recommend an optimized local model and settings configuration for RTX Spark, and set it all up for users in a few clicks. Many users want the best of both worlds — local models for free iteration, and cloud models for frontier intelligence. NVIDIA Switchyard, an open source model router library, enables agents to intelligently route queries between local and cloud LLMs, allowing the user to minimize cloud usage but still obtain similar results to just running on cloud. Hermes will be adding Switchyard later in October, and other agents like Perplexity Computer and GitHub Copilot have integrated their own routing solutions. Software providers have made it simple for agents to connect to top Windows apps, with easy-to-use MCP libraries and command line interfaces (CLIs). NVIDIA has also now made available MCPs for its applications, including NVIDIA App, Broadcast, PAIR, Omniverse, RTX Remix and a large library of CUDA-X Skills . NVIDIA is also releasing AI playbooks for RTX Spark, available on Friday, Oct 16. Users can set up their first agent, build an AI chief of staff, configure their system for development or design a creative assistant. Meet Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B: Built for Local Agents on RTX Spark NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, available Thursday, Oct. 15, is a new LLM purpose-built for running local agents on RTX Spark. This model is a 74B parameter, 9B-active-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, packed into 24GB using 2-bit quantization with advanced quantization-aware training techniques to retain quality. It aims to achieve the optimal balance between speed and intelligence, being faster than most popular dense models while smarter than most popular MoE models with a similar memory footprint. Users will be able to run Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B at launch through llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth and LM Studio. It will also be directly accessible via agents such as Hermes and OpenClaw. Like other Nemotron models, Bolt 74B is fully open source — including training data, weights and recipes — so developers can fine-tune and customize their own agents. Local AI doesn’t have to run on just one PC. NVIDIA PAIR , a personal AI router, is officially moving out of beta today, making it easier to tap into the total AI compute of compatible PCs on a local network. The free, open source software tool automatically discovers and connects devices, installs AI models and inference engines, and distributes AI workloads across available systems. The official release adds llama.cpp support, direct model downloads from Hugging Face, customizable inference engine settings and RTX Spark support, along with a variety of inference and user experience improvements. PAIR works on Windows, Linux and macOS.

events.title: This Y Combinator startup raised $6.1 million to let product managers and designers ship code. See its pitch deck.
events.summary: Lightsprint raised a $6.1 million seed round to build its coding product and hire more talent. Lightsprint Lightsprint raised $6.1 million to empower non-engineers, such as designers, to edit codebases. Lightsprint's product turns plain English into code and prototypes. Check out the pitch deck that the Y Combinator startup used to secure the funding. The way engineers, product managers, and designers work together is still slow and janky, says one Y Combinator-backed startup . Now, it's raised $6.1 million to help non-engineers directly make changes to a company's existing codebase using AI agents. San Francisco-based Lightsprint said its software can turn a plain English request into a reviewable pull request, which is a proposed code change that engineers inspect before merging it into production. This allows non-technical staffers such as product managers (PMs), designers, and operations workers to get more directly involved in shipping software. "We found that actually there were a lot of PMs like me as well as designers who actually really wanted to shift to production," Benjamin Ong, Lightsprint's cofounder and CEO, told Business Insider. AI has changed the work of designers and product managers. Designers increasingly use generative AI tools to make early concepts and prototypes faster, while product managers are using agents and vibe-coding tools. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics projects a 5% growth in web and digital interface designer employment from 2025 to 2035. Ong said software development has traditionally involved a long chain of handoffs: a product manager writes a requirements document, engineers assess technical feasibility, designers create mockups, and engineers ultimately rebuild the feature in code. That could take up to two to three months. The startup, which Ong, Benedict Chan, and Heng Hong Lee founded earlier this year, is positioning itself against the fragmented tools many companies use to build products — including prototyping software such as Lovable, design software like Figma, and coding assistants such as Anthropic's Claude. Lightsprint says it's a one-stop shop that connects to a company's existing code. Then its agents can write product requirements documents, generate code, and create live previews. After, human engineers can review the code and decide whether to add it to their software. The startup began working with early users in April and now works with over 100 companies. Lightsprint went through Y Combinator's Spring 2026 batch . 645 Ventures led its seed round , along with January Capital, Rebel Fund, and angel investors, including Opendoor CEO Kaz Nejatian. The startup has a six-person team split between San Francisco and Singapore. Ong said the new funding will go toward hiring in business sales, marketing, design, and engineering. "We're seeing product managers, designers, and even business teams build features and submit high-quality code changes themselves, while engineering stays in control," said Ong. events.title: Current price of oil as of October 13, 2026
events.summary: As of 7:45 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil is trading at $107.29 per barrel, based on the Brent benchmark we’ll explain in a bit. That’s 75 cents below yesterday morning’s level and about $44 higher than where it stood a year ago. Oil price per barrel % Change Price of oil yesterday $108.04 -0.69% Price of oil 1 month ago $106.02 +1.19% Price of oil 1 year ago $63.69 +68.45% Will oil prices go up? No one can say for sure where oil prices will go next. Many forces shape the market—but at the core, it’s still about supply and demand. When risks like a potential recession or war ramp up, oil prices can change direction quickly. How oil prices translate to gas pump prices When you buy gas at the pump, you’re covering more than the cost of crude oil. You’re also paying for every step in the process, including refineries, wholesalers, taxes, and the markup your local gas station adds. Even so, crude oil has the biggest influence on what you pay, often making up more than half the cost per gallon. When oil prices jump, gas prices usually climb right along with them. But when oil falls, gas prices often slip much more slowly—a pattern sometimes called “rockets and feathers.” The role of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve If an emergency hits, the U.S. keeps a backup supply of crude oil called the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. It’s mainly there to protect energy security during crises, such as sanctions, catastrophic storm damage, even war. It can also help cushion the blow when supply shocks send prices soaring. It’s not meant to solve long-term problems. Instead, it provides quick relief for consumers and helps keep vital parts of the economy moving, like essential industries, emergency services, and public transit. How oil and natural gas prices are linked Oil and natural gas are two of the world’s primary energy sources. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by extension. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, which which increases demand for natural gas. Historical performance of oil When looking at how oil performs, two main benchmarks stand out: Brent crude oil is the main global oil benchmark. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) is the main benchmark of North America. Of the two, Brent gives a better picture of global oil performance because it prices a large share of the world’s traded crude. It’s also the go-to for tracking oil’s historical trends. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now relies on Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook. If you look at the Brent benchmark over several decades, oil has been far from stable. It has experienced sharp rises tied to wars and supply cuts, along with steep drops linked to global recessions and oversupply (called a “glut”). For example: The early 1970s delivered the first major oil shock when the Middle East slashed exports and placed an embargo on the U.S. and others during the Yom Kippur War. Prices fell in the mid-1980s due to lower demand and an influx of non-OPEC oil producers joining the market. Prices surged again in 2008 as global demand grew, but then crashed alongside the global financial crisis. During the 2020 COVID lockdown, oil demand plummeted like never before—pushing prices below $20 per barrel. To sum up, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s heavily influenced by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, shifting energy policies, and much more. Energy coverage from  Fortune Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage: Delta’s CEO says those higher ticket prices could be here to stay as long as demand holds up Zelenskyy: Russia striking Ukraine’s energy facilities despite Trump’s ceasefire claim The IEA wants to empty its oil reserves faster Frequently asked questions How is the current price of oil per barrel actually determined? The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic. How often does the price of oil change during the day? The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing. How does U.S. shale oil production affect the current price of oil? In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply. How does the current price of oil impact inflation and the broader economy? When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf. events.title: The Download: open model trade-offs and geothermal power’s promise
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks? Anthropic recently released a report arguing that a powerful new model released by the Chinese company Z.ai, poses a major cyberattack risk. Its core concern was that it is freely available for anyone to download and modify. The warning was the latest flashpoint in a debate over whether frontier AI models should be open or kept behind the doors of frontier labs. Safety advocates warn that open models can be misused by bad actors, while supporters argue they could prevent a handful of companies from controlling this powerful technology. Here’s why the debate over open AI is more complicated than it seems . —Grace Huckins This story is part of MIT Technology Review Explains, our series untangling the complex, messy world of technology to help you understand what’s coming next. Read more from the series here .  10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Fervo Energy and its plan to streamline geothermal power Fervo Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026 , available exclusively to subscribers . Fervo Energy wants to expand geothermal power beyond the handful of places where it has traditionally been practical. The company uses horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing to open pathways through underground rock, potentially making geothermal development possible in far more places. Now, Fervo is betting that AI’s power boom will help scale up enhanced geothermal energy. With a $2.2 billion public offering and an expanded agreement with Google, it plans to build larger plants and drive down costs. But can its approach work beyond Utah and Nevada? Read the full story to find out . —Eshan Raul Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch , spanning everything from sustainable cement to shipping containers packed with old EV batteries.  The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 A cyberattack overheated fridges at hundreds of French supermarkets Temperatures rose to 120°F, spoiling food and sparking fires. events.title: Burnham’s Your First Home scheme ‘could boost Bellway’s house output by 10%’
events.summary: Help-to-buy initiative for England could slow market while first-time buyers wait for launch, builder admits The new Your First Home programme for first-time buyers could increase the number of houses British builder Bellway produces each year by 10%, its boss has said. Faced with a chronic shortage of homes, the government has made housing one of its top priorities and Andy Burnham’s surprise announcement of the YFH scheme a fortnight ago sent housebuilders’ shares soaring by more than 10%. Jason Honeyman, who has led Bellway since 2017, welcomed the new programme, which will be more targeted than previous help-to-buy initiatives. It features household income caps to exclude those with big salaries, and price caps to ensure people can only buy modest houses. Full details, including the launch date, are expected be announced by John Healey in his first budget as chancellor on 28 October. YFH applies only to England and is for prospective first-time buyers hoping to buy a new-build flat or house. They will be offered a government-backed equity loan worth 20% of the purchase price and the minimum deposit the buyer will have to put down will be just 2.5%. While the scheme has the potential to “provide significant support for first-time buyers”, it could weigh on the market in the near term, Honeyman said, as some will want to wait for the initiative to be launched. However, he added that it could drive Bellway’s annual completions back to 10,000 homes, in the 12-month period from next September at the earliest. “Based upon our past experience with help to buy, the new scheme has the potential to boost volumes by around 10%, and with a market recovery, provide a path back to at least 10,000 homes a year and a return on equity of 15%,” Honeyman said. Bellway is targeting between ⁠9,000 and 9,400 homes in the current year, ​down from 9,695 ​last year, ‌given a lower order book and “ongoing pressures on customer demand” coupled with higher construction costs, running at between 3% and 4%. It has a forward order book of 4,981 homes worth £1.4bn, compared with 5,285 homes with a value of £1.5bn a year earlier. Bellway also expects the average selling price to be flat over the coming year at about £325,000. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The chief executive’s comments came after the company beat analysts’ expectations with revenue of £3.16bn for the year to 31 August, up 13% from the previous year. This lifted underlying profits before tax by 5.7% to £305.7m. Bellway shares rose 2% on Tuesday but are still down by more than a quarter so far this year. YFH is expected to give a shot in the arm to most big housebuilders, such as Persimmon, MJ Gleeson, Taylor Wimpey and Bellway. However, the upmarket builder Berkeley Group, which is focused on London, where prices are higher, and Vistry Group, which has pivoted towards building affordable and social homes, are not expected to get much help from the initiative.

events.title: Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi shows why artillery still matters in a drone fight
events.summary: Ukraine is using artillery systems like the US-made HIMARS in key roles to take back territory from Russia in a major new operation. Serhii Mykhalchuk/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Artillery is playing a key role in a major operation to push back Russian forces. Drones dominate the battlefield, but artillery is still proving indispensable. A lead combat unit said it used heavy artillery to stop Russia from bringing up reserves, equipment, and ammo. Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi, a major counteroffensive push to retake territory in the east, is showing that even as drones transform the battlefield , artillery remains an important tool for holding gains and keeping the enemy off balance. Unfolding near the city of Lyman, Operation Vivaldi has relied on drones and robotic systems , as well as some new battlefield tactics, to achieve key wins, but artillery has also been important to the operation's success. Ukrainian forces had recaptured 176 square kilometers of territory by the end of September, according to the Third Army Corps, the lead unit. The Institute for the Study of War, a US think tank, wrote on Friday that reports indicate that Ukrainian forces "heavily relied on artillery strikes in order to prevent Russian forces from regaining lost positions during Operation Vivaldi." It said those efforts demonstrated "how artillery remains relevant even in modern, drone-dominated battlefield conditions. " The ISW assessment cited an update from the Third Army Corps that said it had, for the purpose of executing this operation, "assembled one of the largest artillery formations of any corps — deploying so many systems per kilometer of the front that fire could be maintained continuously, even if individual guns were knocked out." The unit said its "artillery turned 'Vivaldi' into a kill zone for the enemy!" Drones worked with artillery to find targets that the artillery then destroyed, the unit said. "The artillery deprived the enemy of the ability to maneuver or return fire, allowing the Third Corps' assault troops to keep pushing forward." It said that the 52nd Separate Artillery Brigade and the rocket artillery units of multiple brigades were able to keep multiple settlements under fire. "Russian forces could not bring up reserves, equipment, or ammunition to try to restore their lost positions." The Third Army Corps said strikes by Ukrainian HIMARS, the US-made High Mobility Artillery Rocket System , destroyed more than 20 artillery guns, two Buk air defense systems, and two transport-loading vehicles, and also struck Russian command posts that were at the battalion level or higher. The beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine was a war of artillery, but drones quickly became a  key weapon , with both militaries using them to launch attacks, gather intelligence, and help direct other weaponry. The Third Army Corps shared footage of what it said were strikes that prevented Russia from bringing in reserves, equipment, and ammunition to retake the positions it was losing. Third Army Corps In July, Mykhailo Fedorov, then-Ukraine's defense minister, said that drones accounted for around 95% of Russia's front-line losses. Drones are taking on new roles, as are other robotics systems, and that's been clear throughout Operation Vivaldi. The Third Army Corps said last month that it was using aerial drones to drop explosive-laden robots behind Russian lines, saying it "was the first in the world to begin air-deploying ground robotic systems." The success of drones has sparked debate in the West over what drones mean for more traditional weaponry like tanks and artillery. The latter appears to still have a part to play. Ukraine is developing multiple new artillery systems, and in June, its commander-in-chief announced plans to modernize the artillery forces, describing artillery as one of the main tools on the modern battlefield. Western analysts say artillery remains vital, especially when employed alongside a growing drone arsenal. Analysis published by RAND last month said that while strike drones "offer unprecedented operational agility, they cannot independently solve every tactical problem." Heavy artillery has remained indispensable against hardened, protected infrastructure, they wrote. Ben Jarvis, the UK's minister of state for security, said in June that "there are some who hold the view that we should trade everything in the locker for drones. I understand the temptation, but there are important distinctions to make." "Even in Ukraine, amid extraordinary advances in technology, it is still a war fought in the trenches where ground is held street by street, and where the reach of artillery and deep precision strike has proven invaluable."
