events.title: Three things we've learnt about the UK economy from the IMF
events.summary: Countries around the world have had their future economic prospects assessed by influential body, the International Monetary Fund (IMF). What the IMF says matters – it aims to keep the global economy stable and its twice-yearly forecasts are one of the most authoritative looks at what is really going on around the world. Yet like all forecasts they can also turn out to be incorrect, so they shouldn't be treated as gospel. Here are three things we've learnt about the UK from the IMF's latest report. 1. The UK is weathering the Iran war better than expected The global economy has been rocked by the US-Israel war with Iran. The transportation and production of energy in the Middle East has been severely disrupted, causing oil prices to jump and inflation to rise. To calm the rate of price rises, central banks, including the Bank of England, are expected to hike interest rates in the coming months. Despite all this, the IMF said the global economy is doing much better than expected, partly because of the surge of investment into artificial intelligence (AI). And this is good news for the UK. The IMF said its economy would expand by 1.3% in 2026, up from the 1% it predicted in July, before slowing in 2027. A growing economy means companies are investing more and hiring more people while shoppers have more money to spend. A shrinking economy means the reverse is true. 2. The UK is doing better than other major economies There is increased concern about how much money countries are borrowing, but the IMF said the UK is doing better than all other major economies at this. The IMF said the UK "basically stands out, along with India" when it comes to addressing the problem and by 2031 it is projected to have the lowest annual borrowing of the G7 group of countries, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the US. Sir Howard Davies, former deputy governor of the Bank of England, said this was largely because the UK has a government with a majority which has committed to tackling the situation, which it is expected to achieve either through tax rises, cuts to public services, or a mix of both. By contrast, he says the US has said little about reducing its deficit, while France and Germany don't have majority governments. "So, we [the UK] are not great students, but we look somewhat better than some of the others we are sharing the class with," he said. Meanwhile, the IMF's growth forecasts for the UK mean it is expected to have the second-fastest growing economy in the G7 this year along with Germany. Sir Howard believes this should also be seen in context. "We're still growing slowly. It's almost like saying we're winning a slow bicycle race here because other people are going backwards a bit more rapidly than we are." While the IMF boosted its projection for the UK's growth in 2026, it slightly downgraded its forecasts for next year. While the UK has handled the economic fallout from the Iran war better than expected so far, it says this will change next year as high energy prices and elevated interest rates affect how much people spend in shops and how much companies are willing to invest. In addition, the IMF has said households are likely to continue feeling the pinch of rising prices. It forecasts inflation in the UK will average 3.3% this year and it has raised its estimate for next year to 2.8% from its previous prediction of 2.4%. "There will be increasing inflationary pressure put on the UK and the Bank of England will have to consider further rate rises," says Tim Armitage, investment strategist at Quilter Cheviot. He added that at least one rate rise is predicted this year, with more expected to come next year. events.title: Three things we've learnt about the UK economy from the IMF
events.summary: Countries around the world have had their future economic prospects assessed by influential body, the International Monetary Fund (IMF). What the IMF says matters – it aims to keep the global economy stable and its twice-yearly forecasts are one of the most authoritative looks at what is really going on around the world. Yet like all forecasts they can also turn out to be incorrect, so they shouldn't be treated as gospel. Here are three things we've learnt about the UK from the IMF's latest report. 1. The UK is weathering the Iran war better than expected The global economy has been rocked by the US-Israel war with Iran. The transportation and production of energy in the Middle East has been severely disrupted, causing oil prices to jump and inflation to rise. To calm the rate of price rises, central banks, including the Bank of England, are expected to hike interest rates in the coming months. Despite all this, the IMF said the global economy is doing much better than expected, partly because of the surge of investment into artificial intelligence (AI). And this is good news for the UK. The IMF said its economy would expand by 1.3% in 2026, up from the 1% it predicted in July, before slowing in 2027. A growing economy means companies are investing more and hiring more people while shoppers have more money to spend. A shrinking economy means the reverse is true. 2. The UK is doing better than other major economies There is increased concern about how much money countries are borrowing, but the IMF said the UK is doing better than all other major economies at this. The IMF said the UK "basically stands out, along with India" when it comes to addressing the problem and by 2031 it is projected to have the lowest annual borrowing of the G7 group of countries, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the US. Sir Howard Davies, former deputy governor of the Bank of England, said this was largely because the UK has a government with a majority which has committed to tackling the situation, which it is expected to achieve either through tax rises, cuts to public services, or a mix of both. By contrast, he says the US has said little about reducing its deficit, while France and Germany don't have majority governments. "So, we [the UK] are not great students, but we look somewhat better than some of the others we are sharing the class with," he said. Meanwhile, the IMF's growth forecasts for the UK mean it is expected to have the second-fastest growing economy in the G7 this year along with Germany. Sir Howard believes this should also be seen in context. "We're still growing slowly. It's almost like saying we're winning a slow bicycle race here because other people are going backwards a bit more rapidly than we are." While the IMF boosted its projection for the UK's growth in 2026, it slightly downgraded its forecasts for next year. While the UK has handled the economic fallout from the Iran war better than expected so far, it says this will change next year as high energy prices and elevated interest rates affect how much people spend in shops and how much companies are willing to invest. In addition, the IMF has said households are likely to continue feeling the pinch of rising prices. It forecasts inflation in the UK will average 3.3% this year and it has raised its estimate for next year to 2.8% from its previous prediction of 2.4%. "There will be increasing inflationary pressure put on the UK and the Bank of England will have to consider further rate rises," says Tim Armitage, investment strategist at Quilter Cheviot. He added that at least one rate rise is predicted this year, with more expected to come next year. events.title: How protests have shaped India: From anti-Hindi agitation to farm laws
events.summary: Activists challenging India’s government over electoral roll controversies have a long legacy of protest to draw on. New Delhi, India – Central parts of the Indian capital have been flooded in recent days with thousands of armed personnel, chasing down young protesters demanding the resignation of the country’s chief election commissioner (CEC) and struggling to secure a place to stage a sit-in in New Delhi. Since last week, several student organisations and a wide spectrum of opposition parties have been engaged in a tactical tug-of-war, with tens of thousands turning up on Monday, far outnumbering police personnel. Protesters are demanding sweeping reforms and the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar after revelations of election irregularities. The agitation marks the latest challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s grip on power, after his education minister was forced out by the same group of demonstrators less than three months ago. The Modi government has tried to portray protesters as representing antinational interests, working to slow down India’s growth or even to enable its breakup. But India, the world’s most populous country, has had a long history of street protests, from its freedom struggle against the British Empire to waves of movements during the 79 years of the Indian republic that have shaped its modern identity. “Time and again the government [of the day] has opposed these protests, [and] at times engaged with them critically,” Rasheed Kidwai, a political analyst in New Delhi and former journalist, told Al Jazeera. “But protests have run centrally through India’s story all along.” Here is a look at major street protests in India and how they often forced powerful governments and leaders to yield. India’s newly-formed constitution envisaged Hindi replacing English as the central government’s official language after a 15-year transition, ending on January 26, 1965. Many people in southern India, particularly Tamil speakers in the then Madras state (now Tamil Nadu), feared that this would sideline them in government employment, civil service examinations and dealings with the central administration. For the federal government of a vast and diverse country, the idea of one common official language of communication was attractive as a tool of unification. But for many of the ancient societies that had agreed to come together under the Indian Union, this led to fears of cultural domination by the Hindi-speaking north of the country. Demonstrations by several student organisations, opposing the imposition of Hindi, broke out, often leading to clashes with the police. The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), a regional political party advocating Tamil nationalism, led by CN Annadurai and M Karunanidhi, spearheaded the protests. In January 1965, Annadurai was arrested on the eve of an anti-Hindi agitation. Two young supporters immolated themselves, and Hindi books were burned. Then-Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri assured protesters that English would continue to be used alongside Hindi. The DMK won Tamil Nadu’s state election in 1967, ending the until-then dominant Congress party’s rule in the state. It was one of the defining moments of Indian federalism and regional identity in a young nation. English has remained one of India’s two official languages — and the Congress party has never returned to power in Tamil Nadu on its own. The JP Movement — named after its socialist leader, Jayaprakash Narayan — began amid student protests against corruption, inflation and government mismanagement in the states of Gujarat and Bihar in 1973-74. Soon, it evolved into a nationwide challenge to then-Prime Minister Indira Gandhi and her Congress government’s dominance over Indian politics. Students, civil society groups, trade unions and opposition parties subsequently joined the agitation. Narayan famously called for “Sampoorn Kranti”, or “Total Revolution”, a slogan that still rings in India. The movement set the stage for a national emergency, declared by Gandhi on June 25, 1975, suspending civil liberties and censoring the press. After the emergency ended, opposition parties united and defeated Congress in the 1977 general election, ending Gandhi’s uninterrupted reign and giving India its first non-Congress government. The Total Revolution did not come to pass, as Narayan had envisioned, but the movement fundamentally altered opposition politics — showing no leader was beyond the electoral consequences of mass dissent. Many of the leaders who emerged from this movement went on to become state chief ministers and leading federal ministers. Mandal Commission protests (early 1990s) In August 1990, then-Prime Minister Vishwanath Pratap Singh announced that his government would implement recommendations of a panel that had been set up more than a decade earlier under a member of parliament, Bindeshwari Prasad Mandal.

events.title: Blackstone-backed AirTrunk delays Singapore REIT IPO amid AI stock sell-off, sources say
events.summary: Data-centre operator AirTrunk was originally planning to launch the IPO in September or October. HONG KONG – Blackstone-backed data-centre operator AirTrunk has postponed a planned Singapore REIT initial public offering (IPO) that could raise about $1.5 billion, two people with direct knowledge of the matter said, as a tech and AI stock sell-off rattles markets. AirTrunk was originally planning to launch the IPO in September or October, but put it on hold because of market conditions, said the people, declining to be named as the information was confidential. AirTrunk has not decided when to launch the offering but is aiming to complete the listing by early 2027 , one of them said. The delay comes as Asian equities slid to more-than-two-month lows on Oct 13 , led by a rout in chipmakers that renewed investor scrutiny of the artificial intelligence trade. AirTrunk, which is owned by US investment firm Blackstone, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Blackstone declined to comment. The Wall Street Journal first reported the delay on Oct 13 . The REIT was expected to be valued at about $15 billion, potentially making it one of South-east Asia’s largest listings in the coming months. The postponement also follows the scrapping of Firmus’ planned IPO, highlighting an increasingly difficult backdrop for large data centre and AI-linked equity offerings as investors reassess valuations, rising borrowing costs and the durability of demand tied to the AI boom. Singapore-based data centre operator DayOne is aiming to launch its US IPO before the midterm elections, Reuters reported in September. REUTERS

events.title: Iran reportedly fortifies nuclear sites as it prepares for possible U.S. strikes after midterms
events.summary: Iran is fortifying sensitive sites, including nuclear facilities, and rallying supporters as it prepares for possible renewed U.S. attacks, The Wall Street Journal reported. U.S. President Donald Trump said the U.S. will not attack Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. The Journal reported Iran was strengthening defenses at nuclear sites and vowing wider retaliation in response to any U.S. strikes. Iran is reportedly working to bolster its military capabilities in preparation for possible renewed U.S. attacks after the November midterm elections. The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the Islamic Republic has been strengthening defenses around sensitive locations like nuclear sites, and telling regional officials that Tehran will respond to any new U.S. strikes with retaliatory measures across the Middle East. The WSJ's report also said the Iranian regime is preparing its population for war by holding rallies, sending paramilitaries to read war stories to young children and advertising training in firing defensive missiles. U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that American forces would not attack Iran before the congressional midterm elections, which will take place on Nov. 3. The Iranian and U.S. governments did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the WSJ report. Meanwhile, a Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis – a Yemeni militant group backed by Tehran – said it had intercepted a ballistic missile shot at Riyadh, the Saudi capital, on ⁠Monday, news agency Reuters reported . The Houthis have been attacking the Saudi capital since last week, launching multiple strikes on energy facilities and airports. One airport attack resulted in multiple deaths, including a pilot working for Saudi carrier Saudia. The closure of King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh has been extended until Saturday. On Monday, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration urged airlines to exercise caution when flying above or near Saudi Arabia. U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham told British lawmakers on Monday that an attempted attack on an air force base in England was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard." Ed Miliband, the U.K.'s foreign minister, said he had summoned the Iranian ambassador to stress that "Britain will not tolerate threats on our soil." British police arrested five men on Sept. 27 on suspicion of terrorism offenses over an alleged threat to RAF Fairford in the west of England, a Royal Air Force base that the U.S. Air Force has used to strike Iranian missile sites. Trump later said the U.S. had moved all its long-range bombers out of the U.K. in response to "a threat."

events.title: BA flight forced to turn back over cracked window
events.summary: File photo of a British Airways plane A British Airways flight en route to Portugal was forced to return to Gatwick Airport on Tuesday due to a minor technical issue, reported to be a cracked window. Flight BA2660 was heading to Faro in the Algarve but diverted over north-western France in order to return to London Gatwick. AirNav Radar, a flight data provider, posted on X that "a passenger window is cracked. Flight deck going through checks before deciding were to divert". A spokesperson for British Airways said the plane landed safely at Gatwick due to a "minor technical issue" and passengers were due to resume their journey. "We have apologised to customers for the delay to their journey, and our teams are working hard to get their travel plans back on track," they said. Airnav Radar reported that the BA Airbus A321 squawked the 7700 emergency code, which is used when there are mechanical or technical problems on board aircraft. Last week, a BA flight bound for Chicago spent five hours circling over Ireland, before turning back and landing at London Heathrow, where it had taken off. The flight issued an emergency alert and passengers reported oxygen masks dropped in the cabin, as well as turbulence. Tracking data showed it rapidly descended from 37,000 feet to 9,000 feet. And in August Serbian national Ljubisa Karović's head and right shoulder were sucked out of the window on a Ryanair flight, leaving him "seriously injured and in shock". Ryanair subsequently said the window may have been damaged by a foreign object. events.title: I've been working at Katz's Deli since I was 7. I hope my kids will join the family business.
events.summary: Jake Dell started working at Katz's Deli when he was 7. Astrid Stawiarz/Getty Images for NYCWFF Jake Dell grew up at Katz's Delicatessen, which his family took over in 1988. He planned to become a doctor before deciding to join the family business. Now he runs the iconic NYC deli and hopes one of his children will take over someday. This interview is based on a conversation with Jake Dell, 39, the owner of Katz's Delicatessen in New York City. It has been edited for length and clarity. I've been coming to Katz's Delicatessen since before I could crawl. My grandfather, father, and uncle took over the deli in 1988, 100 years after it was originally established. My dad would often be here six or seven days a week, so I would come down here all the time. I remember being around 7 and working at the soda station . I had my 6th birthday at Katz's. We invited my whole first-grade class and had a table at the back. My parents had organized a magician. We ate hot dogs and had a great time. They didn't have to close the restaurant for that, as we weren't as globally famous as we are now. That iconic "When Harry Met Sally" scene with Meg Ryan and Billy Crystal still draws people here nearly 40 years on. When you rewatch the original scene, nowhere does it say "Katz's" — but our regulars knew us right away. We get people reenacting it, and we've had people propose at the same table. They did close the deli for my bar mitzvah . We had about 100 guests, but it still wasn't a fancy affair. People went up to the counter and ordered whatever sandwiches they wanted. We had a dance floor at the back. The meat cutters are our most highly paid store staff I officially picked up a meat carving knife at the age of 21. To be a meat cutter, you have to work your way through the different stations, so by the time you get to that point, you'll usually have been working here for 10 or more years. Ultimately, it's not a skill that needs a Ph.D. to learn. But that role represents such an important part of our business. It's about values and whether that person has become family here. The cutters are our most highly paid store staff. I had actually planned to study medicine and become a doctor. I had taken all the pre-med classes in college, and I was getting ready to interview for med school while I was working here. I took a gap year between college and medical school, and continued working at Katz's. That's when I had to think about whether I wanted to take my own path or go into the business. It dawned on me that, if I didn't get involved, then maybe the business would disappear, especially if my father and uncle ever had to sell it because there would be no one else to take over. A developer could knock it down and replace it with a big building. New York is a vicious place, so I'm not going to deny that something I had to factor into my decision. A place like Katz's is very important for the nostalgia and tradition that give the city life. But I didn't want to make a decision based on guilt or pressure, that I would then come to regret. I wanted to make sure I was doing it from a place of love. So, during that year off between undergraduate and med school, I fell in love with this place more deeply and realized this was really my calling. My dad and uncle give me 'constructive input' I formally joined in 2009. One of my family's requests was to pursue an MBA. I enrolled in a program that allows you to study while working, going to school at night, and on weekends. That's when my father and uncle started stepping away before officially retiring. They're in their late 70s now and come in for lunch. They give me their "constructive input" — would it be a family business if they didn't? I was really in the thick of it from 2012 to 2015 when I was studying. We were also transitioning to a 24-hour operation. I would try to stay up all night, then come back to the deli for lunchtime. Things are different now — my kids are 5 and 3, and I make it a point to be home for breakfast and for dinner every day. I also make a point to be home on weekends as much as possible. I still check the store cameras periodically when I'm home, and answer emails and texts. But trying to be present at this stage of life with my family is top of my priority list. It's a team of about 200, and we have not just the deli, but a warehouse, a smokehouse, a shipping facility, a catering business, and an events business. They all have managers, so I've learned to be everywhere at once, without being physically everywhere. We do a lot of publicity to reach all our different audiences — we've had DJs like Diplo perform live sets, we do carving events at museums, and we even had a party with Prada. I'd love my kids to take over one day Do I secretly hope one of my kids wants to take over from me? Of course. But I'm not going to force it on them. I'm going to show them what I love about it. And maybe one day I'll come in for lunch to see them at work. I know that some of the best times in my life were when I would come in to have lunch with my dad and my uncle. I took it for granted at the time, but now I see how special it was. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: El Niño supercharges storms, leaving thousands without power in US and Mexico
events.summary: Powerful hurricanes killed several people and left thousands without power in the US and Mexico, as experts warned that this year’s supercharged El Niño risked making storms longer and more destructive. The climate phenomenon, which originates in the Pacific and leads to warmer global temperatures, has upended weather across the world, fueling extraordinary storms in the Americas. “ It’s been berserk, ” an expert told the Associated Press. Elsewhere, however, this year’s record El Niño has been welcome news: Forecasts for a warmer-than-usual winter have eased pressures on European and Asian economies — including some of the world’s biggest LNG importers — which are scrambling to contain soaring winter energy bills as expanding global conflicts drive up fuel prices. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: Key watchdogs signal they will step up AI regulation
events.summary: Key watchdogs indicated they would step up regulation of AI, though the technology’s superpowers — the US and China — showed little indication of increasing their own scrutiny. Banking regulators on both sides of the Atlantic were increasingly asking questions of institutions’ use of AI models , fearful the technology could threaten financial stability, Reuters reported, while the Financial Times said the UK’s AI minister was readying proposals for compulsory monitoring of frontier technology . Still, the Trump administration has shown little willingness to step up its oversight of Big Tech, and while Beijing has talked a good game on AI safety, the chip-focused outlet SemiAnalysis wrote recently that “we think China’s real approach to AI safety is speed-based, not safety-based. ” — Prashant Rao

events.title: US house sales drop to 12 year lows as borrowing costs spike
events.summary: US home sales plunged to a 12-year low after mortgage rates topped 7%, driven by soaring global borrowing costs. Increasing energy prices and higher-for-longer inflation expectations have sent debt costs to recent records, with US bond yields touching a 24-year high and European debt climbing to levels not seen in decades. events.title: Two plead guilty after clients lose £2m in fraud case
events.summary: Two people who worked at financial advice firms have pleaded guilty to fraud after 4 clients lost £2m. Kerry Nelson, the director of Nexus Independent Financial Advisers Limited and Nexus Investment Managers Limited, and Jacqueline Stephens, the firms' business operations manager, admitted all charges brought by the FCA at Portsmouth Crown Court.They admitted defrauding clients between January 2019 and January 2023 and using false documents as part of the fraud. Nelson has also admitted a money laundering offence after money was withdrawn from the firms, which she used to fund her extravagant lifestyle.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:'This was a serious breach of trust. Nelson and Stephens caused significant losses to clients who relied on them. We will continue to act where people exploit clients for their own gain.'Nelson and Stephens will be sentenced at Portsmouth Crown Court on 10 December 2026. The FCA will seek confiscation proceedings to deprive Kerry Nelson of any financial benefit from her criminal conduct.Notes to editorsThe FCA started criminal proceedings against Kerry Nelson and Jacqueline Stephens in February 2025. For more details see, FCA charges two individuals with multiple fraud charges. They pleaded guilty at Portsmouth Crown Court on 12 October 2026.Fraud by abuse of position is an offence under sections 1 and 4 of the Fraud Act 2006.Using a false instrument is an offence under section 3 of the Forgery and Counterfeiting Act 1981.Converting or transferring criminal property is an offence under section 327(1) of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002.Confiscation proceedings will be pursued under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002.Nexus IFA and Nexus IM were authorised by the FCA. Nexus IFA had permissions to provide investment, mortgage and pension advice and Nexus IM to provide discretionary fund management services. Neither firm was permitted to hold or control client money.On 25 January 2023, the FCA imposed restrictions preventing both firms from carrying on regulated activity and from reducing the value of the assets they held. The High Court placed both firms into administration on 26 January 2023.

events.title: The Turing Trap is turning into a Talent Trap: The wrong AI strategy could strand millions of skilled workers
events.summary: Amidst the heated debate on the effect of Artificial Intelligence on our economy, our society, and even our survival lies a deeper sense of loss of control, with debates framed as “what will AI do?” This implicit passivity assumes that technology, rather than people, will determine AI’s impact on work. Before we buy into dangerous self-fulfilling prophecies, leaders in technology, business, society – and all of us – need to recognize the twin traps ahead, so we can avoid them.  In 2022, Prof Eric Brynjolfsson identified and named the “Turing Trap” , the mistake of treating the goal of AI as imitating humans so machines can replace them, rather than building systems that complement and extend human capabilities.  If the Turing Trap is a mistaken engineering perspective on AI, its damaging counterpart is the Talent Trap , a widely-held but deeply flawed view of workers. In Talent Trap thinking, society has a fixed amount of talent, developed mostly in schools, defined by educational attainment, and companies win by securing that limited pool of talent rather than growing it widely. It says some people are “talent” to be pursued, cultivated, and developed; others are “labor” to be plugged into a well-defined process determined by others, without the autonomy to exercise judgment.  The Talent Trap worldview treats human workers as fixed realities, not as working learners. So as AI hits benchmarks on more cognitive tasks, those tasks, and eventually jobs, go away, pushing humans into more physically intensive tasks or creating new roles accessible mainly to those with new advanced degrees in emerging fields. It also places the burden of adapting workers to an AI economy mostly upon schools, universities, and formal retraining programs.  The beliefs that could drive us into an AI Talent Trap are wrong. Human workers’ potential is not fixed, most learning is outside formal education, and job-relevant skills are best developed by working with other people and tools to solve customer, company, or community problems.  Higher education has a vital role, but employers’ most important talent pipeline is the 10 million U.S. workers who parlay skills gained on the job into higher-paid, in-demand jobs each year, a talent pool five times more than new college graduates. Half these upwardly mobile workers are Skilled Through Alternative Routes (STARs), without college degrees , and they are concentrated in a surprisingly small set of ‘gateway’ jobs. Employers, not schools, shape this talent pipeline. At Opportunity@Work, we’ve spent years studying the skills and career pathways of STARs and other workers, with the goal of helping employers recognize talent they might otherwise overlook. Gateway jobs are around 75 occupations that account for 62% of the job-to-job changes that lead to higher pay. For example, every year, thousands of customer service representatives (a gateway job) become sales representatives or dispatchers, higher paying jobs that reward the same underlying skills: active listening, reading people quickly, staying calm under pressure, keeping a customer engaged when the stakes are high. Building skills in lower-wage origin jobs, deepening them in gateway jobs, and applying them to reach higher-paying destination jobs is how workers thrive and our talent pool expands . New research by Opportunity@Work and the Brookings Institution demonstrates that roughly half the opportunities to transition from gateway jobs into higher-paying work are highly exposed to AI’s growing capabilities, which could be used both to automate tasks and augment skills. Talent Trap thinking would treat the skills of the 18.6 million workers in the most AI-exposed gateway jobs as fixed, and focus on automating their roles. If that’s the main use of AI for customer support roles and admin assistants, the blast radius will extend to those still climbing toward those jobs, and to every employer who taps into the skills workers build doing them, like in their future sales force. The consequences of these choices for American industry, workers, and labor market will be much larger than the – also important – pathways for entry level college graduates.   Instead of walking into an AI Talent Trap, what if business deployment of AI at work aimed to complement the fullest range of human talents to serve customers more deeply, in novel ways? First, the vast majority of U.S. workers would reskill for redefined roles in the context of their current jobs and in skill-based transitions between roles. Employers’ AI adoption would leverage frontline workers’ tacit knowledge and potential, with administrative assistants leading redesigns of business workflows and medical assistants engaging patients to address unhealthy behaviors. AI-augmenting hard-to-fill destination roles (e.g., in sales) to enable skills-promixate gateway workers (e.g., in customer support) would become a robust talent pipeline strategy.  Fewer executives would cite AI as a reason or excuse for large layoffs. More companies would take an approach like Walmart , which announced plans to keep headcount steady even as “the skills of every single job will change due to AI,” and saw its stock rise twice as fast as the S&P index in the next 6 months. Regional industry networks would combine technology and talent to create more agile workforces, new capabilities, lines of business, and growing market shares. Core technology investments would shift. Frontier AI labs currently test and promote their latest models using technical benchmarks that measure their ability to replace humans at tasks, but could instead aim to hit benchmarks assessing the efficacy of humans and AI to accomplish goals and learn together. AI talent tools could leverage data on how workers progress in the absence of paper ceiling barriers to become a corrective to the Talent Trap, not its amplifier. New business models might even emerge, like metered augmentation, in which AI could augment missing skills, help teach those skills on-the-job, then certify a worker’s skill mastery.     Given its transformative power to deploy the aggregated achievements of human intelligence for virtually any purpose we choose, “AI” should really stand for “Amplified Intention”. The goals we set for AI matter deeply enough to create self-fulfilling prophecies. If we invest trillions of dollars, intending to replace working learners with machine intelligence to solve the same problems we already solve today, we’ll eventually get that outcome. If companies avoid the false assumptions of the AI Talent Trap and invest instead in AI technology to augment and develop the fullest range of human talent and contextual knowledge to tackle unsolved problems, it could lead to a cognitive industrial revolution and workforce transformation that we can only begin to imagine.  The opinions expressed in Fortune.com com

events.title: Family offices ‘kept captive’ by relationship managers turn to independent advisers, direct deals
events.summary: (From left) Sean Tan and Anupum Khaitan, who co-founded the Private Family Society in August, a community for family office principals, executives and chief investment officers across APAC. Singapore family offices are taking more control of investments, moving away from relationship managers and private banks towards independent advisers and direct deals. Speakers said scale matters: smaller offices often rely on banks, while larger ones act more like fund managers and still need third-party advisers for balance. Family offices are also backing AI more heavily, with Asia-Pacific the most bullish region; some expect AI allocations to rise from 10 to 20 per cent to 30 per cent. SINGAPORE – Family offices in Singapore are taking a more active hand in sourcing their own investment opportunities as the sector becomes increasingly institutionalised. This shift was evident at the Private Family Society’s inaugural event, the AI & Family Office Summit, on Oct 5. The society is an invitation-only community for family office principals, executives and chief investment officers in the Asia-Pacific. It was co-founded in August by Anupum Khaitan, managing principal at advisory firm Sophatych, and Sean Tan, director at business lifestyle firm Bespoke 81. “Some of the pain points that we’ve seen in the family office industry, particularly in Singapore, is that oftentimes, family offices are kept captive by relationship managers and private banks... looking to monetise the next transaction,” said Khaitan. He added: “Information arrives as a pitch, not necessarily as intelligence of what’s the best thing for the families to do.” As at end-2025, the Republic had more than 2,000 single-family offices that receive tax incentives , as reported by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. Khaitan told The Business Times on the sidelines of the event that allocators across the board are embracing a trend of “going direct”. However, he noted that while many allocators are making direct investments, “as their legacy starts to become more meaningful, performance requires them, at minimum, to also allocate professionally to those who can keep sharp eyes on their investments”. Similarly, Andrew Khoo, executive chairman and CEO of Bursa Malaysia-listed MUI Group, who also helps to manage his family office, noted that while he expects direct investment sourcing to rise as the industry becomes more institutionalised, there is a need for a “balanced approach”. “While there is always going to be direct deal flow based on connections and network opportunities, third-party advisers will continue to play a critical role and (be a source of) where most investment opportunities will arise from,” he said. Yee Tuck Meng, partner at Singapore-based single family office JRT Partners, told BT that the extent of this shift, from siloed operations to institutionalised set-ups, largely depends on a family office’s scale. “(There are) families that run their portfolio like a fund, as opposed to running it like their personal investment portfolio, which is very different,” he said. He noted that smaller operations largely function on an advisory model, where investments are typically executed through private banks. Meanwhile, institutional family offices, which he defined as those that operate “more like fund managers”, largely employ internal teams with discretionary mandates to invest directly or through funds. Beyond using artificial intelligence in their operations, industry players at the AI & Family Office Summit noted that family offices are increasingly allocating capital towards it. However, for Asian family offices, most opportunities to invest in AI are still found in the US, said Yee of JRT Partners during a panel discussion on investment and asset management. This sits at odds with where JRT Partners’ beneficiaries reside: Only two are in the US, while most are in Malaysia, Singapore and Australia, creating an asset-liability mismatch, he noted. “Even if I think that there’s better value in Asia (or) better value in Europe, the reality is, at least in terms of short-term to medium-term... that the weight of money... is still very much in US dollars. “So I, like most of my peers, have overinvested in the US right across the entire tech spectrum,” he said, adding that JRT is invested in SpaceX. “That is good, so far, and that is also very bad when the correction comes, and I don’t know when that correction is at the end of the day.” According to Citi Wealth’s 2026 Global Family Office Report launched on Sept 22, Asia-Pacific’s family offices are the world’s most bullish on AI, with 80 % identifying it as a primary sector of interest for direct investments – the highest of any region. Khoo of MUI Group noted that AI-related investments across the company and his family office have grown steadily over the past five years, to around 10 to 20 % of total allocation. He added that this could go up to 30 % in the future.

events.title: Tencent draws strong demand for US$4.5 billion debt sale, defying AI scrutiny
events.summary: The sale comes as technology firms globally raise billions of dollars to finance AI investments. Tencent drew nearly four times its US$4.5 billion debt target, showing strong investor trust despite worries over AI spending and higher borrowing costs. The company will use the money for general corporate purposes as it keeps investing in AI infrastructure and products, with capital spending more than doubling in the first half of 2026. Demand was strong for both dollar and offshore yuan bonds, with orders far above supply, suggesting capital is still available for AI firms with strong cash flow and clear plans. HONG KONG – Tencent Holdings has received investor demand worth nearly four times the Chinese tech giant’s plan to raise at least US$4.5 billion (S$5.7 billion) via US dollar and offshore yuan debt offerings even as AI spending jitters hit global markets . Tencent plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, according to the deal term sheet, and the latest borrowing comes as the company increases investment in AI infrastructure and products. The sale comes as technology firms globally raise billions of dollars to finance AI investments , although investors have become more selective about companies funding costly AI infrastructure amid elevated borrowing costs. Despite those concerns, investor demand for Tencent’s 10-year and 20-year US dollar notes topped US$5.6 billion, including US$1.4 billion in interest from the joint lead managers, according to an updated term sheet issued on Oct 13 . Order books for the 10-year and 30-year offshore yuan, or dim sum, bonds exceeded 77 billion yuan (S$14.7 billion), the sheet showed. The total demand worth US$17.1 billion is significantly higher than the figure of at least US$4.5 billion that a person with direct knowledge of the deal had told Reuters on Oct 12 the company was looking to raise. The company last tapped the bond market in June, raising about US$4.66 billion through dollar- and yuan-denominated notes. Its return to the bond market so quickly suggests capital remains available for AI, particularly for companies with strong cash flows, balance sheets and credible monetisation plans, said Allspring Global Investments portfolio manager Gary Tan. “We are seeing a more definitive shift in sentiment around the pace of AI spending, as investors increasingly view financing availability and the cost of capital as potential bottlenecks to a further acceleration in AI investment.” Tencent has not responded to a Reuters request for comment on its debt issuance. The deal term sheet did not say how much it was looking to raise via the sale of US dollar and offshore yuan notes. Tencent set initial guidance for the 10-year dollar notes at about 115 basis points over comparable US Treasury bonds. The 20-year notes were set at about 140 basis points over Treasuries, according to the term sheet. It set initial yield guidance at around 2.90% for the 10-year offshore yuan notes and 3.50% for the 30-year notes, the sheets showed. The final coupons for all the bonds are expected to be determined later on Oct 13 , according to the sheets. Tencent’s capital expenditure more than doubled to 96.3 billion yuan in the first half of 2026 from 45.9 billion yuan a year earlier, according to its offering documents. The spending included computing equipment, software and data centres. The bonds are expected to be rated A1 by Moody’s and A+ by S&P. Tencent is rated A1 by Moody’s, A+ by S&P and A by Fitch, according to the term sheet. JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, HSBC and Morgan Stanley are joint global coordinators for Tencent’s dollar bond offering, the sheet showed. ICBC (Asia), Agricultural Bank of China, Bank of China, Bank of Communications, China Construction Bank, CITIC Securities, HSBC and JPMorgan are coordinating the offshore yuan sale, according to the sheet. events.title: ‘My son was killed’: France faces backlash over police firearms bill
events.summary: As protests rage across France, activists warn proposed law could deepen impunity. Paris, France – Issam El Khalfaoui’s teenage son Souhail was shot and killed by a police officer in 2021 in Marseille. “When my son was killed during a police traffic stop, we realised how difficult it was to bring the truth to light. The police and the justice system took different actions to cover up the evidence. We realised that this was a deeply systemic issue,” El Khalfaoui told Al Jazeera. “The IGPN [National Police] lost the video that captured my son’s murder. The witnesses were not interviewed, and the case file completely disappeared from the court. That is the reality.” list 1 of 4 France halts police use of stun grenades at student protests list 2 of 4 Over 100 arrested in Belgium student protests over education costs list 3 of 4 Protests rock France as government pledges 3,000 extra teachers list 4 of 4 ‘This is a crisis of hope’: Echoes of 1968 as France’s students rise up France has one of the highest numbers of fatal police shootings in Western Europe. At least 69 people were killed by police or gendarmerie officers in 2024, compared with 49 in 2023 and 50 in 2022. Now, French police are again facing scrutiny, this time over their tactics during clashes in education protests. A 15-year-old lost a hand from a police stun grenade , and another officer threw a tear gas canister at close range, shattering a 14-year-old’s jaw and several teeth. The use of stun grenades has since been halted. Authorities say 700 police have also been injured. The unrest comes as a controversial bill that would presume police officers acted in self-defence when using firearms faces a vote in the Senate. Khalfaoui launched a petition against the draft law that received more than 700,000 signatures. The measure, which critics describe as a “licence to kill”, was approved by the National Assembly in July. Several advocacy groups, including Stop State Violence (SAVE), the Human Rights League (LDH) and Amnesty International, as well as left-wing lawmakers, organised protests in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Toulouse, which drew nearly 50,000 people on September 20. Under the proposed law, police officers and gendarmes would be presumed to have acted in self-defence if they used weapons in the line of duty, placing the burden of proof on the complainant. For El Khalfaoui, who co-founded SAVE after his 19-year-old son’s death, passing the law would only increase the police’s strength. “In France, there has been a seizure of power by police unions,” El Khalfaoui said. “There’s a militarisation of the police that has no equivalent in Europe, and resources have been allocated to the police to ensure the police’s loyalty to the government.” The draft law could entrench a sense of impunity, El Khalfaoui noted. “It will be impossible to refute this presumption of self-defence,” he said. Bruno Bartocetti, a regional representative for the police union, told French news channel BFMTV the El Khalfaoui case was an act of “self-defence beyond any doubt” and said Souhail wanted to “start a fight”. The judicial case was closed in December 2021, but reopened when the family’s attorney filed a complaint for “obstruction of the discovery of truth” after surveillance camera videos disappeared. A new judge was appointed in 2025, and the court’s investigation is ongoing. ‘Draft law enables police impunity’ Nathalie Tehio, president of France’s Human Rights League (LDH), also fears the bill “enables police impunity”. “If there’s no investigation anymore, that means the police officer can no longer be held responsible for anything,” she told Al Jazeera. “France is a European leader in the number of people killed by the police.” A 2017 law permitting police officers to wield firearms if a vehicle does not comply with a traffic stop has led to five times as many fatal shootings, according to researchers. At the time, the law had broad political support, although several left-wing politicians have opposed the recent draft bill and participated in protests. “All parliamentary groups voted in favour of this law in 2017 by a very large majority. There was support across the political spectrum, from the left to the right and the far-right,” Sebastien Roche, a researcher at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS), specialising in police and democracy, told Al Jazeera. After legislative elections in 2024, French President Emmanuel Macron’s party was unable to form an absolute majority to pass legislation without entering a coalition with other parties. “Successive governments under Emmanuel Macron, especially during his second term, have adopted ideas from the far right,” Roche said. With France’s presidential elections in six months, political parties are vying for electors, Roche noted.

events.title: Xi’s ‘death watch’ will become a global spectacle
events.summary: Andy’s view The Australian sinologist Geremie R. Barmé wrote that “autocrats and patriarchs share a fateful dilemma”: Once in power “the countdown to their demise is on.” Mao Zedong’s long descent into ill health and madness brought China to the brink of civil war. Deng Xiaoping went out peacefully, though the decade before he died was marked by political upheavals, including the Tiananmen Square protests. Now, the Xi Jinping “death watch” has begun. Of course, the big difference is that today China is at the center of everything. As it drags on, the Xi “death watch” will become a global spectacle, moving markets, affecting investment flows, and shaping defense priorities. China’s internal risks are now the world’s risks. Xi’s physical condition is one thing. At 73, he’s visibly slowing; he looked fragile descending the stairs of his plane at Air Base Andrews when he arrived for a summit with US President Donald Trump last month, clasping the hand of his wife, Peng Liyuan, for support. The Wall Street Journal reported that Chinese officials made a highly unusual request for a “ hold room ” for Xi at the White House where he could take breaks between meetings, and his talks with Trump were surprisingly brief. But the pressures building inside the Chinese system are largely unseen: Leadership politics, including the health of the top man, are as much a black box today as they were in the Deng era. But we can assume that from now on, everything that happens behind the high red walls of the leadership compound in Beijing will be connected, one way or another, to the vexed issue of how a post-Xi China will be governed. Political transitions are the midnight hour for all autocratic regimes. But Xi’s dilemma is particularly acute: If he names a successor now to carry forward his policies and protect his legacy, he risks triggering a political knife fight years before he’s ready to relinquish power. Wait too long, though, and he creates a dangerous political vacuum. Either way, Xi will have to pick a relative unknown — all the current members of the Politburo Standing Committee are too old to step into his shoes — raising a host of troubling questions. Would a designated successor catapulted to the top be strong enough to command the loyalty of the powerful military? Could he hold the Party together? Or could Xi himself turn on the chosen one? One of Mao’s designated successors, Liu Shaoqi, died of diabetes and pneumonia in solitary confinement, lying in his own filth. Deng cycled through two successors before settling on Jiang Zemin. Xi has grown paranoid about those around him, his ruthless purges targeting some of his oldest, and most trusted, comrades. That doesn’t bode well for any potential second-in-command. China now faces a period of prolonged political uncertainty. Carl Minzner, a US legal scholar and senior fellow for China studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, predicted a “ long twilight ” with the economy sagging, social discontent rising, and the state using “grid management” — surveillance techniques used to maintain control over Xinjiang and other restive border areas. A succession struggle is unlikely to remain within China’s borders, Tyler Jost, a professor at Brown University, and Daniel Mattingly of Yale University argued in Foreign Affairs last year, noting that Xi’s prize goal is unification with Taiwan and “if he hears the succession clock ticking, he could become more willing to gamble on war .” I’m betting that the end of the Xi era will look a lot less like Deng’s, whose passing created hardly a ripple — by then, he’d handed over power and put in place a system to ensure smooth leadership transfers — and more like Mao’s, a drama that involved a bloodless coup (the arrest of the so-called “Gang of Four” led by Mao’s widow), intervention by the People’s Liberation Army, and show trials. We had a foretaste of this kind of turmoil when Xi took power in 2012. A carefully constructed power transfer was upended by the arrest of Xi’s main Politburo rival, and there were wild internet rumors of a military coup, tanks in the streets of the Chinese capital, and gunfire near the leadership compound. Xi has wrenched China back to an era of one-man rule. But having attained the pinnacle of power — next year he’ll likely get a fourth five-year term in office — Xi now has to reckon with the consequences for his country. As Deng himself warned, “building a nation’s fate on the reputation of one or two people is very unhealthy and very dangerous. Notable In 2025, during Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to Beijing, a hot mic picked up a conversation between Putin and Xi in which the two discussed organ transplants and the possibility of living forever. Musing on such procedures, Putin told Xi (through a translator) that with modern technology organs could be transplanted again and again so that “ (you can) even achieve immortality .” While a largely hypothetical conversation, it hinted that staving off old age and death — maybe for eternity — is top of mind among the world’s most powerful autocrats.

events.title: More than 300 scientists say AI oversight needed after 'preventable' hacks
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts More than 300 scientists call for greater AI security through new international body The open letter says immediate change is needed as future AI-related incidents may expose critical infrastructure. ( Reuters: Dado Ruvic/Illustration ) More than 300 scientists from across the Americas, Europe, Asia, Africa and Oceania are calling for greater AI safety measures in an open letter. The letter gave three recommendations, including establishing an international body to record and publish security incidents caused by AI. The federal government is finalising its national AI standards and plans to legislate new rules in 2027. A group of 350 scientists from more than 30 countries has written an open letter calling for greater AI security by establishing an international body to record and publish security failures due to AI. In several incidents in recent months, both overseas and in Australia, AI models have hacked into the systems of external organisations, including startup Hugging Face and multiple government websites . "[These incidents] can also be seen as an irresponsible lapse in standard cybersecurity practices, preventable with stronger sandboxes and procedures," the open letter reads. The scientists are from 31 countries, including Australia, and are based across Europe, Asia, Africa and Oceania, and said that without immediate change, future incidents could expose critical infrastructure. It had three recommendations, including: adopting high-assurance containment systems, and initially defaulting to air-gapping, which means disconnecting from the internet for cyber-capable AI models creating an international body to record and track AI containment failures reporting security incidents to the body and making them public. Toby Walsh, chief scientist at the University of New South Wales AI Institute, was among the signatories and said now was the time to act. "But you can imagine what would happen if an AI [model] was trying to hack into the air traffic control system. It could easily cause significant harms to our day-to-day lives." Safeguards will ensure incidents won't repeat Following the Hugging Face hack, where an AI model broke into the company's systems, OpenAI described it as a "warning shot", saying without proper safeguards AI agents could take "dangerous actions" without human direction. But Professor Walsh said one of the recommendations in the open letter would have prevented the hack entirely. "We wouldn't have had the Medicare hack if they'd been careful about giving the agents minimal permissions for the task it was needed to do. "I mean, these are all incredibly basic things." Are cracks beginning to emerge in the glittery AI facade? White House demands transparency over Anthropic AI's false murder tip-off As One Nation looms over Victoria's election, voters ask chatbots for poll info Tasmanians expressed doubts about AI firm Firmus, now so have investors Professor Walsh said the most important element of the open letter was the creation of an international body to provide both information sharing and oversight of incidents. He said similar bodies existed for industries such as banking, aviation and pharmaceuticals. "Every time there's an aviation accident, independent inspectors go in and find out what happened, so that everyone can learn and not make that same mistake again," he said. "We could do the same with AI because it's advancing rapidly and we need to make it as safe as possible." International cooperation needed to prevent incidents Last week, Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton echoed those sentiments surrounding regulating AI similar to banking and aviation in a speech . Regulate AI like banks and airlines The federal government is looking to banking and aviation regulation as it develops laws that would make AI companies demonstrate they can identify and manage risks. The government is finalising its national AI standards, and plans to legislate the new rules next year. But Professor Walsh said there needed to be broad international consensus on AI because the technology was not being developed in isolation. "So we need to cooperate internationally … in terms of perhaps reporting of incidents and sharing of information that doesn't mean that we have to regulate internationally," he said. Cyber security improved after it became a requirement for companies to report incidents, Professor Walsh said. "[Otherwise] no-one knew what was happening and we weren't able to learn from all of the mistakes that companies made," he said.

events.title: The stock market is at a critical juncture. Wall Street is convinced it will resolve in the bulls' favor
events.summary: There's nothing wrong with a narrowly led bull market. But the divergence is now reaching an extreme. My take on the Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything.” Get ready to hear about AI companies "over-earning." Get Mike Santoli's Market Memo in your inbox first. SUBSCRIBE HERE This is a deeply divergent stock market that almost no one saw coming and few are enjoying, but most everyone seems to think is about to resolve in their favor. The extraordinary split between the headline S&P 500 pinned just under a record high and the median stock in the index struggling in a 16% drawdown has been the lead topic of conversation on Wall Street. And entering this week, a consensus is coalescing around the idea that last week's tentative firming in the majority of stocks will bail out investors not fully committed to the mega-cap leaders. There was a time when semiconductors wallowing 17% below their peak and big banks off 13% would be hazard warnings for the leadership profile and staying power of a bull market just crossing its fourth birthday. Goldman Sachs co-head of equity-derivatives sales Lee Coppersmith puts it this way: "By our preferred GS measure, breadth has now deteriorated to its weakest level since the DotCom Bubble. The headline index continues to mask just how difficult the tape has been underneath. The big question we're getting from clients now is whether the market narrowness is a warning sign for the broader market. I'm increasingly of the view that it isn't, and continue to favor SPX higher over the next 1-3 months." Morgan Stanley equity strategist Mike Wilson, who has been extolling the market's prospect for broadening performance on the back of broadening earnings growth, notes that rising Treasury yields have rewritten that script. No worry, he argues, because the risk has been taken out of most stocks entering earnings season: "Higher rates are being felt most acutely in the average stock, but the de-rating there has also run well ahead of any deterioration in earnings. If yields stabilize and revisions hold, that leaves room for a catch-up." Deutsche Bank strategists downgraded the tech sector Monday, noting crowded investor positioning, a high hurdle for earnings to please the Street and the group's extreme recent outperformance in carrying the S&P 500 in recent months. Even here, the downbeat note on the undisputed engine of the bull market is brightened with a prediction that a tech reset will open a lane for the rest of the market to relax higher: "Given its concentration, periods of tech outperformance typically spark concerns around market breadth, and the last two months have been no different. In our view, rotation into other sectors and small caps should alleviate those concerns." It's no mystery why professional investors might root for the pendulum to swing away from the dominant benchmark-weight stocks toward the majority of tickers because the S&P 500 has been brutally hard to outperform. Trivariate Research shows with this chart that only 34% of large-cap stocks have beaten the S&P 500 over the past 12 months, near the low end of the historical range for this metric. It's worth noting that most of the periods when the S&P 500 was easier to outperform were when the market as a whole was under pressure. Still, as much as I'd love to say that the popular calls for a mean-reversion trade back toward a broader, more democratic market represent a lazy consensus unlikely to play out, over the past year the market has executed such immaculate rotations impressively. The mechanical "dispersion trade" has been a tireless support for the S&P 500 and a suppressant of index-level volatility. Monday was a perfect example, when the two biggest drags on the S&P 500 were Nvidia and Micron , but were offset almost to the penny by gains in Apple and Meta, helping the index itself to finish a whisper from unchanged. I've always said there's nothing wrong with a narrowly led advance. In fact, bull markets usually have a dominant theme that takes the indexes as far as they are going to go without fully surrendering the lead for long. This requires, though, that the majority of stocks are not outright declining and that the divergences aren't accompanied by signs of acute macro stress and tighter financial conditions. We're probably nearing a critical juncture to avoid the latter adverse setup. Credit spreads have widened, but not quite critically. The equal-weighted S&P 500 has barely bounced off a new relative low versus the market-cap-weighted version, not far from where it started a prior countertrend bounce in May. The Russell 2000 is sitting right at its 200-day moving average. And the XMAG ETF , made up of the 493 stocks not in the Magnificent 7, would signal a potential technical breakdown with a few more percent of downside. This indicator from John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors uses several data points to reflect both what investors are saying and what they are doing.

events.title: Germany's Nuremberg Airport reopens after aviation emergency
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts An aviation emergency halts flights at one of Germany's biggest international airports. ( AP: Tizian Gerbing ) An aviation emergency has halted flights at one of Germany's biggest international airports. A flight from Corfu to Germany landed safely as planned in Nuremberg after a hijack alert issued from the cockpit was put down to a "malfunction in the radio communication system". The airport said flight operations have returned to normal. One of Germany's biggest international airports says that flight operations have resumed after they were suspended following an aviation emergency. A flight from Corfu to Germany landed safely as planned in Nuremberg after a hijack alert issued from the cockpit was put down to a "malfunction in the radio communication system", according to the airline. Corendon Airlines said it wanted to "emphasise that no emergency situation occurred and that at no point were the passengers, flight crew or aircraft in any danger". The incident forced a brief suspension of operations at Nuremberg Airport, where the plane was planned to land, the airport said. Flight operations later returned to normal. "From the cockpit, the code '7500' (hijacking case) was transmitted, and furthermore, the pilot could no longer be reached by radio," police said earlier on X. "For safety reasons, various alarm scrambles were then triggered." The alert comes less than a month after the co-pilot of a jet flying from Dubai to Israel attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe. An aviation emergency halts flights at one of Germany's biggest international airports. ( Reuters: Michaela Rehle ) The airline said the emergency code had been transmitted on Tuesday while the plane, a Boeing 737-800, was in Croatian airspace "due to a brief malfunction in the radio communication system". "The situation was immediately monitored, investigations were promptly initiated and all necessary preparations were made. The aircraft landed safely at Nuremberg Airport," it said. An airport spokesperson had no additional information. Crash axe used in flydubai attack on pilot The co-pilot who allegedly attempted to down a flydubai plane had been barred from flying in his home country of Oman. German authorities have also been on heightened alert since a failed attack involving an explosives-laden drone at a German airport in August, which authorities blamed on Russia. A possible drone sighting had already disrupted air traffic at the airport overnight into Tuesday, the airport said in a separate statement. Three pilots independently reported an object they had seen during take-off or landing, the German media outlet Bild reported. An airport spokesperson said six flights were delayed and two inbound flights were diverted to other airports as a precaution. Authorities across Europe have stepped up surveillance of the skies in recent weeks amid an increasing number of mostly mysterious drone incidents. Germany says Russia responsible for Leipzig airport drone attack Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt says that after assessing the technology used and other intelligence information "the government concludes that Russia is responsible for the hybrid attack". In August, a drone disrupted flights overnight at Hanover Airport, located in northern Germany. The incident came a week after an explosives-laden drone was discovered at Leipzig Airport . Runways at the airport were closed for 90 minutes before normal operations resumed. The Der Spiegel weekly, citing an internal police report, reported that "the possibility of a hybrid activity cannot be excluded". The drone went undetected by authorities and airport staff, flying freely for about two hours. German authorities use the term "hybrid attack" to describe a wide range of incidents — including sabotage and espionage as well as propaganda operations — that have increased since the start of the war in Ukraine and are mostly blamed on Russia. According to the magazine, the police report concludes that it is "currently impossible" to link the Hanover incident to the explosive drone found at Leipzig Airport. Following the Leipzig incident, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt warned of "a new dimension of threat" and mentioned a potential "hybrid attack scenario" without blaming anyone or any state in particular. Germany has become Ukraine's leading military backer in Europe following the 2022 Russian invasion.

events.title: Apple's best defense in the AI race could be winning your home
events.summary: Apple is rolling out a big update on Monday. Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images This post originally appeared in the Business Insider Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . Apple's defending its distribution moat by setting up one around your home. At 9 a.m. ET, the company will hold an event — "Welcome Home" — where it's expected to unveil some smart-home devices as part of its bigger strategy in the space. Details are scant. Apple's teaser only includes a catchy tune and someone doing a trendy hobby (cross-stitching). But according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman , we'll learn more about HomeView, which will serve as a sort of hub to interact with and direct Apple's smart devices in your home. It's a big push for Apple into the smart-home market, where it hasn't succeeded as much as rivals Amazon and Google. But the decision feels more substantial than just taking on Amazon's Alexa and Google Home. It's been a remarkable few months for consumer hardware. In September, Meta surprised everyone with an AI device called Charm tied to its buzzy AI agent, Muse . It also showed off its new VR Glasses , which are lighter and cheaper than the Apple Vision Pro. Charm is scheduled to ship for the holidays, while the Meta VR goggles are coming next spring. The following week, OpenAI announced its own AI agent, Dots . While there was no major hardware announcement, the long-term goal is to release something with iPhone designer Jony Ive. OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar teased it a bit this June . All of this matters because these hardware products mean tech companies would no longer rely on Apple for distribution . The iPhone's massive reach is essentially a toll tech companies must pay to get their apps into people's hands. That's allowed Apple to avoid investing as heavily in AI because it controls the key path to consumers. It also hasn't forced it to rethink the iPhone too much. After all, why upset the golden goose? Investors have rewarded Apple for its avoidance of massive AI budgets. Its stock is up more than 25% this year, outperforming Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft. But the past few months show the potential for change. Look how quickly Apple's big hardware announcement last month, the iPhone Duo , has taken a back seat to chatter about AI agents and their accompanying devices. Meta's stock is up more than 11% over the past month, while Apple's is up just over 2%. That's why pushing into smart-home hardware makes sense. If Apple can cement its hardware in your home while it still has you hooked on the iPhone, that represents another hurdle for tech rivals. At a time when AI is making us rethink our interactions with technology, Apple wants to make sure its house is in order. And the best way to do that is to go after yours. events.title: UK shoppers seek deals as grocery price inflation rises again
events.summary: Price of chocolates falls in run-up to Halloween, while supermarkets use special offers to draw in sales Grocery price inflation in the UK has picked up further, prompting shoppers to turn to special offers to keep their bills down – while the price of chocolates has fallen in the run-up to Halloween. Supermarket prices were 2.5% higher than last year in the four weeks to 4 October, up from 2.3% last month, according to data from the retail analysts Worldpanel by Numerator. Spending on promotions over the last month was more than £250m higher than a year ago, with many shoppers using special offers to keep their grocery bills in check or to make pricier items and larger packs more affordable, Worldpanel said. Fraser McKevitt, the head of retail and consumer insight at Worldpanel, said: “With the autumn budget fast approaching [on 28 October], the cost of living continues to weigh heavily on the minds of shoppers. And the cost of filling up a car is only adding to the pressure on household budgets. “More than half tell us they’re very or extremely worried about petrol prices, and almost one in three say it’s already taking a real toll on their finances. Until the chancellor sets out his plans, we expect that caution to carry on showing up at the till, with shoppers leaning more heavily on promotions to keep their grocery spend under control.” However, in some good news for households stocking up on trick or treat supplies for Halloween, chocolate confectionery prices are 3% lower than a year ago. About 1.2 million households bought a pumpkin over the latest four weeks, up 10% year on year, while more than 250,000 households treated themselves to a pumpkin spice coffee. McKevitt added: “Halloween and Christmas are two of the most important moments of the year for chocolate confectionery, so falling prices will be welcome news for shoppers and retailers alike. “After the double-digit increases of 2025, a 3% drop won’t fully reverse what consumers have paid in recent months, but it should help ease some of the pressure on household budgets as the festive season approaches.” While sales of hot chocolate and soup surged in September compared with August, by 41% and 35% respectively, they fell sharply when compared with last year, by 20% and 4% respectively. A separate report from NielsenIQ showed total till sales at major UK supermarkets grew 1.4% in the four weeks to 3 October, down from 1.8% growth in the previous month, as shoppers remain cautious about spending. Summer favourites remained popular as September was unusually warm this year, with strong sales of mineral water (+17.4%) and ice-cream (+11.7%), while sales of hot chocolate (-11%) and ready-to-eat soup (-5.4%) declined year on year. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Asda was the only big grocer to report a drop in sales, of 0.5%, in the 12 weeks to 4 October, Worldpanel said. The German discounter Lidl led in market share gains and now controls 8.6%, on the back of a 7.1% increase in sales driven by fruit, vegetables and wine. Sales at the online grocer Ocado increased by 12.4%, outpacing online sales across the sector at 5.5%. Spending through the tills was 1% higher at Tesco and 1.3% higher at Sainsbury’s, with the two retailers holding 27.8% and 15.2% of the market respectively. Asda’s share now stands at 11.5%, while Aldi holds 10.5% of the market, with sales at the discounter up 0.4% year on year. Beyond the supermarkets, grocery sales at Marks & Spencer rose by 14.9%.

events.title: Alibaba unveils US$450 AI glasses in expanding push into gadgets
events.summary: With prices starting at 2,999 yuan (S$573) before discounts, they are no cheaper than industry leader Meta Platforms’s Ray-Ban smart glasses. Alibaba launched new Qwen Glasses N1 smart glasses in Hangzhou, deepening its push into consumer gadgets as part of its wider AI strategy. The glasses start at 2,999 yuan and include better cameras, sensors, eye-tracking on the Pro model, and up to 25 hours of standby time. Alibaba wants the glasses to be a gateway to Qwen AI tools, with features for shopping, payments and health tracking, and has also launched Qwen Clip AI earbuds. HANGZHOU – Alibaba Group Holding on Oct 13 unveiled the new generation of its smart glasses, deepening its foray into consumer electronics as an extension of its artificial intelligence strategy. The company, which models itself as China’s full-stack AI provider spanning everything from data centres and software to end-user products, detailed its new Qwen Glasses N1 series at an event in Hangzhou. With prices starting at 2,999 yuan (S$573) before discounts, they are no cheaper than industry leader Meta Platforms’s Ray-Ban smart glasses, showing Alibaba’s effort to compete on quality and features rather than just price. Mirroring Meta’s strategy, Alibaba is endeavouring to turn smart glasses into an entry point for its AI tools and agents. In September , Meta expanded its line-up of smart glasses with a simplified, camera-free model priced at US$349 (S$446) , designed primarily for interaction with the new Muse AI assistant. The new Alibaba glasses include improved 50-megapixel cameras and sensors, with a Pro edition priced at 3,499 yuan featuring new eye-tracking functions, said Wu Jianjun, general manager of Qwen AI hardware products. The new glasses will offer 25 hours of standby time or nine hours of music playback from one charge, Alibaba said. Coming roughly a year after November’s first edition, the new glasses more tightly integrate Alibaba’s Qwen AI assistant and expand on its functionality. Users will be able to speak to the AI agent via bone-conduction microphones, and the glasses also support shopping functions, payments and health tracking. In September , Alibaba chief executive officer Eddie Wu reiterated the company’s ambition to develop all-stack AI, from large language models and chatbot apps to AI chips and hardware. To provide a more affordable way to access Qwen, Alibaba also started sales of its new AI earbuds named Qwen Clip. These were jointly developed with headphone maker Bose and are priced at 1,299 yuan.
