events.title: IMF warns UK of risk of inflation ahead of government’s first budget
events.summary: The debt-laden UK economy needs to stay the course on deficit reduction and use cost-of-living relief sparingly or risk reigniting inflation, the International Monetary Fund warned on Tuesday. The warning comes just over two weeks before UK Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey, presents his first annual budget. It is important there is no slippage in the face of higher debt interest costs and pressure to spend more on ⁠defence and energy subsidies , said the new IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro, who served as a Bank of England policymaker from ⁠2017 to 2023. “The UK has already started the [fiscal] consolidation path … It is on that trajectory, and the message for the UK is simply stay the course and continue on that trajectory,” Ms Tenreyro said at press conference in Bangkok, Reuters reported. Mr Healey is preparing to announce a series of time-limited giveaways to help voters with the cost of living in the budget on October 28, Bloomberg reported. The Institute for Fiscal Studies on Monday also urged the Chancellor to address a £35 billion ($46 billion) hole in the spending plans or risk delivering a “work of fiction”, the Financial Times reported. The UK government ran a budget deficit of 4.4 per cent of gross domestic product last year and aims to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenue by the 2029-30 fiscal year. Previous governments have failed to achieve the same goal. Energy crisis Britain is facing a prolonged energy squeeze after the price of European gas surged more than 150 per cent this year. Dwindling gas reserves threaten to keep British consumers' costs high through winter. The price increase brings the prospect of higher household bills, renewed inflation and further pressure on the UK's fragile economy. Underground gas storage in Britain was just 48 per cent full at the start of October, compared with 94 per cent in Portugal and 99 per cent in Poland, according to figures reported alongside the latest winter outlook from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas. Britain has historically relied on imported gas rather than extensive domestic storage, which leave it vulnerable supply disruptions and global market price volatility. Inflation impact In its latest World Economic Outlook published on Tuesday, the Washington-based IMF said debt-burdened economies such as the UK should restrict any public relief to “targeted and temporary” measures so they can still be able to pull inflation back. The multilateral lender expects UK inflation to climb to 3.3 per cent this year and ease to 2.8 per cent next year. The UK aims to bring inflation back to its 2 per cent target and the market expects the Bank of England to start raising rates from next month. Rebuilding the fiscal space is “urgent”, given elevated debt as well as higher borrowing costs and increasing demands on public budgets, against an ever-worsening global geopolitical backdrop, the latest IMF report warned. “Support measures should be used sparingly, designed in a way not to complicate the task of monetary policy, and unwound rapidly as the shock dissipates,” the report advised economies supporting elevated debt levels. The fund expects the UK economy to grow 1.3 per cent this year, an upward revision of 0.5 percentage points from the fund’s projections in April. Growth, however, is estimated to edge lower to 1.2 per cent next year as “higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”, the IMF added. “The IMF projections draw attention to both the resilience and the fragility of Britain’s economic prospects,” said Valentin Boboc, chief economist at Institute of Economic Affairs. “Despite stronger-than-expected growth this year, the longer-term outlook remains disappointing due to high taxes, expensive energy and other impediments to investment.” Before the budget, the Chancellor needs to focus on “removing obstacles to growth” and should restrain spending, Mr Boboc said. The country must restore business confidence and “recognise that Britain cannot tax its way to prosperity”, he added.

events.title: Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’ Has a Unique Perspective on Daddy Issues
events.summary: Alex Gibney’s Musk Has a Unique Perspective on Daddy Issues Only one person agreed to be Alex Gibney’s new Elon Musk documentary immediately: Musk’s father. “We had Errol Musk at ‘hello,’” Gibney says. Eventually, the director would speak with scores of Musk’s associates for his film. His first wife, Justine Musk, appears, as does his ex-girlfriend Ashley St. Claire. Journalist Kara Swisher, LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman, myself, and WIRED global editorial director Katie Drummond also spoke to Gibney for Musk , which hits theaters nationwide on Friday. But landing Errol Musk, with whom the Tesla and SpaceX CEO has a complicated relationship, was a watershed. “Everybody else took a lot of persuasion,” Gibney says. “It was very difficult to get people to appear because the risk profile for talking about Musk in a way that was honest was high.” Once Gibney interviewed all of his subjects, he had enough material to make a documentary that runs nearly four hours, including a 10-minute intermission. It’s a damning portrait of the trillionaire CEO, detailing how much of his genius is based on his formidable ability to promote his own mythology—and the stock price of his public companies. Musk never agreed to an interview with Gibney. Instead, the director’s team researched every public comment Musk ever made and created a simulated Elon Musk who appears throughout the film. I spoke with Gibney earlier this month about his experience making the film, why he decided to make his simulated Elon attractive, and what material he had to leave on the cutting room floor. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. ZOË SCHIFFER: Alex Gibney, thank you so much for being with us today. This shouldn’t spoil anything, but in the four years that you spent making Musk , Elon Musk never agreed to sit down with you for an interview. Instead, your team looked back through the archives of everything he has said publicly, and you put together a sort of simulated interview, which appears throughout the film as a through line. Basically, it plays into Musk’s idea that we are all, in fact, living in a simulation. How did you decide on this approach for the film? Well, what were we gonna do? He’s the main character. I actually thought because he’d been so outspoken about this idea of a simulation, that cinematically we should lean into that. We should play in Elon’s sandbox and have a simulated interview. As we began to develop that idea, by using his real words, his actual audio recordings, but placing them in a kind of avatar which we would design, I think there became all sorts of thematic reasons to do it. One was because he himself had said we’re living in a simulation. But two was the importance of this notion in the Elon Musk story of the shifting sands between what is real and what is unreal. Then also, because a lot of the film deals with his issues of AI, that discomfiting relationship that we’re beginning to explore, all of us on planet Earth, with these AI LLMs and how we begin to project things on these computer interfaces, it felt like this might be something interesting to do. By the way, you’ll notice that when Elon is talking to people in a normal interview situation, he rarely looks at the interviewer or at the camera. He’s always looking this way or that way. So we designed this in a very different way, where he’s looking right down the barrel of the lens directly at the viewer, and we thought that that would be OK. We’re gonna give Elon a break, and actually, I thought our avatar made him look pretty good compared to some of the recent images of him. I have a question about that because your simulated Elon Musk—I think it’s fair to say—looks a lot hunkier than present day Elon Musk. He’s kind of chiseled and tan, and … It is kind of a two-day growth of beard. Exactly. Was that an intentional choice? And if so, can you just talk about why that was? It was. I joke about this, but he’s the star of my movie, I want my star to look good. But I think also it would’ve been a mistake to go into slop AI territory, like some of the images that Elon’s fans are posting about me right now, to sort of denigrate him visually. Also, to some extent, the story is also about image building, too. So I thought, “OK, let’s have some fun with that as well.” Because we had a lot of choices. I mean, we started out with the design firm, like how should he look? What should he be dressed in? You know, we put him in a gamer chair, a leather jacket. There were conscious choices. That extends to some of the comments he makes, where I don’t find like the most bumbling comments that Elon ever made. When we have somebody speaking about something, I want a rejoinder from Elon. We looked for the best rejoinders, like how can he come back at us? Now, later on in the film, his statements become more and more fantastical, but that also is part of what happens. I think it really worked for the film.

events.title: Beauty World Plaza up for collective sale once more for $165m
events.summary: This is Beauty World Plaza’s third attempt at a collective sale, all at the same price. Beauty World Plaza is on sale again for $165 million, or $2,231 per sq ft, in a public tender that closes at 3pm on Nov 19. The eight-storey mixed-use site in Singapore has commercial shops, homes and an open terrace, with 999-year leasehold and approval for serviced apartments. It is the third collective sale attempt after failed bids in 2018 and 2019, though ETC says its location near schools could support hospitality and co-living uses. SINGAPORE – Mixed-used development Beauty World Plaza is up for sale again at $165 million, or $2,231 per sq ft of gross floor area, said real estate advisory firm ETC on Oct 13. The eight-storey property stands on a 24,817 sq ft site, with commercial shops on the first three floors, flats above and an open terrace on the fourth floor. It was built in the early 1980s and has 61 retail and 30 residential units. The 999-year leasehold development site is zoned for commercial and residential use, and has a gross plot ratio of 3 under the Urban Redevelopment Authority Master Plan 2025 . Preliminary approval has been granted for serviced apartments to be developed in the residential component of the development, which could accommodate about 108 keys, based on a minimum unit size of 35 sq m, said ETC. “Beyond a conventional redevelopment play, the buyer can also consider asset enhancement for the existing development,” said Swee Shou Fern, head of investment advisory at ETC. “The property’s proximity to educational institutions enhances its potential for hospitality, serviced apartment, co-living and other accommodation concepts catering to academia.” ETC, the sole marketing agent, is conducting the sale through a public tender exercise, which closes at 3pm on Nov 19. The development’s second attempt at a sale en bloc in mid-2019 at an unchanged reserve price of $165 million failed to draw any takers. Its first bid was in November 2018. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: Chatbot startup Character.AI files for bankruptcy, and Disney is first in line for key assets
events.summary: Character.AI filed for bankruptcy and is putting its chatbot platform up for sale. Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images Character.AI has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy as it pursues a court-supervised sale. Disney has offered $20 million for a license to certain assets, though other bids could prevail. The chatbot platform, which has faced lawsuits over child safety, could be wound down if a sale fails. Character.AI, the chatbot startup founded by former Google researchers, has filed for bankruptcy. The California-based company said it had initiated a voluntary Chapter 11 process in Delaware to pursue a court-supervised sale of all or substantially all of its assets. Character.AI, which lets users create personalized AI bots, said its platform would remain online during the sale process , which it expects to finish by late November or early December. The company has agreed to let Disney Worldwide Services, an affiliate of the Walt Disney Company, act as the opening bidder for a non-exclusive, perpetual license to certain Character.AI intellectual property and claims. Disney said it would pay $20 million and provide transition services using former Character.AI employees it has hired. Other potential buyers can still make higher bids under the bankruptcy process. Last month, Disney hired former Character.AI CEO Karandeep Anand as its CTO. Character.AI's CEO Colin Adams said in a Monday statement that it had taken steps to "sustain and improve" its business amid "significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds." "After a comprehensive review of our available alternatives, our board determined that this court-supervised sale process provides us with the best opportunity to maximize value for all of our stakeholders," the company said in a blog post on Monday. The startup said paid subscriptions remain active and billing is unchanged for now. But it warned that if the sale does not produce a bid sufficient to keep the platform running, it will wind down the service. Character.AI hit with lawsuits Character.AI did not spell out the legal, regulatory, and operational pressures that led to the filing. But the company has faced growing scrutiny over the potential effect of its AI companions on young users. It announced last year that it would ban under-18s from having open-ended conversations with its chatbots, following concerns about AI's impact on children and teenagers. Prior to that, Character.AI had faced lawsuits from families who alleged its chatbots contributed to teenagers' mental-health crises. Earlier this year, Character.AI and Google agreed in principle to settle several of those cases , including claims brought by families of teenagers who died by suicide or experienced self-harm after using the chatbots. One Texas lawsuit alleged that a Character.AI chatbot encouraged a teenager to kill his parents over limits on his screen time. That case was among those the companies agreed in principle to settle. The terms were not disclosed. The startup was founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas. Google rehired the pair in 2024 and paid for non-exclusive rights to use Character.AI's technology, while the startup continued as a separate company. Character.AI said its privacy and security practices remain unchanged during the bankruptcy process. It said users can continue to access its services and export their data or delete their accounts through its app or website. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: We moved into a 3-bedroom duplex and furnished it almost entirely from Facebook Marketplace and thrift shops
events.summary: The author says purchasing secondhand was cheaper and made her house feel like a home. Courtesy of Melissa Noble My family of five recently moved into a new three-bedroom duplex. We needed to decorate, and decided to buy almost entirely secondhand. It was cheaper, helped us avoid indecision, and made the house feel like home. In August, my family of five moved into a new home on the Gold Coast, Australia. We'd been living in my parents' house since January, following an interstate move from country Victoria. When we left Victoria, we put all our  belongings in storage  because we weren't sure how long we'd be staying on the Gold Coast. So, when it came time to move into our new digs, we literally only had a handful of items. We did a quick online search, asking how much we would likely have to spend to furnish a three-bedroom duplex in that area of the world. The AI-generated estimate was anywhere from $8,000 to $16,000 AUD (about $5,580 to $11,150 USD). We're a family of five on a tight budget, and that kind of outlay seemed pretty steep. And so, we decided to furnish it with secondhand items . We purchased almost everything on Facebook Marketplace or in op shops, aside from our bedding and some kitchen staples like a cutlery set. Buying secondhand proved to be a fun experience with all kinds of perks. It's saved us thousands Saving money was a biggie for us. All up, it cost roughly $5,200 AUD to furnish the property , which meant we could put the money we would have spent on buying new items to other use. As we found items online, I'd often check the recommended retail price for comparison. For example, we purchased a king-sized bed, mattress, and two side tables for $650 AUD. The same exact package would have cost $2828 AUD new (without the mattress). We scored a barely used cream couch for $800 AUD, which would have retailed for around $2800 AUD. In general, buying secondhand meant we were only paying a fraction of the price compared to buying new. This has saved us thousands of dollars overall. They got a great price on a secondhand bedroom set. Courtesy of Melissa Noble It removed indecision and time-wasting When my husband and I were furnishing our first home together in Melbourne, we shopped around and visited multiple furniture stores before purchasing our furniture. This was time-consuming and frankly, quite torturous with a 2-year-old trailing along. But buying everything secondhand this time made the process easier and more streamlined. There was no agonizing over which type of fridge or table was right. If it looked reasonable, fit the space, and was affordable, then we took it. Items like this handmade lamp inject personality into the home decor. Courtesy of Melissa Noble It's injected more personality into our home I don't have much of an eye for decor , but buying on Marketplace has helped add flair to our home. When I came across a lady selling a bunch of plants and different styles of stands in a bundle, for example, I snapped it up. It's now one of my favorite areas of our home. The thrill of the hunt was fun As the weeks passed, I found myself getting addicted to shopping for secondhand items, both online and in stores. There's something about finding a beautiful piece for a fraction of its original price that gives you a real buzz. One of my favorite op shop finds was a beautiful oversize white fruit bowl. Underneath, it says, "Made in Italy," and whenever I look at it, I find myself wondering about the journey of where that bowl began, who it once belonged to, and how it made its way to me. This large mirror was purchased for $275 AUD. Courtesy of Melissa Noble I enjoyed the bargaining process We've traveled through many countries where bartering is part of the culture, and I secretly loved dusting off those dormant bargaining skills . When we turned up to buy a fridge only to discover a dent on the front, I negotiated the seller down $50 AUD. A small win, perhaps, but one that helped our hip pocket. The sustainability factor appealed to us Giving perfectly good secondhand furniture a new lease on life, rather than contributing to landfill, has made us feel good about our choices. Along the way, we've discovered so many beautiful pieces, and many of them have their own stories. There's the beautiful oak dining table whose owner was genuinely sad to part with it, as he and his late wife had shared countless meals around it. A stunning king bed and bedside tables purchased from a Scottish man living in a high-rise overlooking the ocean. A repurposed lamp, handmade by a grandma and given new life. Of course, buying secondhand requires patience. Sometimes you show up only to discover that the seller's version of "good condition" is different from yours. But for us, the trade-off has been 100% worth it. We've saved thousands of dollars, rehomed perfectly good furniture, and ended up with a home that feels more interesting than a cookie-cutter style setup ever could. events.title: UnitedHealth Group tops estimates, hikes profit outlook as insurer manages high medical costs
events.summary: UnitedHealth Group posted third-quarter earnings that blew past estimates and raised its full-year profit outlook. The nation's largest private insurer continues to manage high medical costs and is seeing investments in value-based care and artificial intelligence take hold, CFO Wayne DeVeydt said in an interview. The company said it expects fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings of at least $20.50 per share, up from a previous outlook of $19.50 to $20 per share. UnitedHealth Group on Tuesday posted third-quarter earnings that blew past estimates and raised its full-year profit outlook, as the company continues to manage high medical costs and sees investments in value-based care and artificial intelligence take hold. The nation's largest private insurer said it expects fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings of at least $20.50 per share, up from a previous outlook of $19.50 to $20 per share. The healthcare giant's turnaround plan is gaining momentum after three consecutive strong quarters this year. UnitedHealth is working to stabilize margins by shrinking membership, exiting unprofitable contracts and ramping up investments in artificial intelligence and value-based care, which tie doctor and facility compensation to patient health outcomes, quality of care and cost effectiveness rather than the volume of medical services provided. "You'll see in the quarter that we continue to execute not only on the financial aspects of our business, but really doing them with a simpler approach and an approach that's really focused on investing heavily in value-based care," CFO Wayne DeVeydt said in an interview. Here's what the company reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $4.69 adjusted vs. $4.14 expected Revenue: $112.69 billion vs. $111.40 billion expected The company posted third-quarter net income of $4.11 billion, or $4.56 per share, compared with $2.35 billion, or $2.59 per share, in the same period a year ago. Excluding items like business divestitures, restructuring and the expected reduction of reserves for unprofitable contracts, UnitedHealth earned $4.69 per share. Revenue fell to $112.69 billion from $113.16 billion in the prior-year quarter. The company's insurer, UnitedHealthcare, and its Optum healthcare unit both topped analysts' operating earnings estimates for the quarter, according to StreetAccount. Notably, UnitedHealth's medical cost ratio — a measure of total medical expenses paid relative to premiums collected — came in at 88.4% for the third quarter. Analysts were expecting a ratio of 89.9% for the quarter, according to StreetAccount. A lower ratio typically indicates that the company collected more in premiums than it paid out in benefits, resulting in higher profitability. Still, DeVeydt told CNBC that medical costs in the quarter "continue to be elevated versus historical norms" – an issue that has plagued insurers, particularly those operating privately run Medicare Advantage plans, for more than two years. "I think it's something we should keep an eye on. I think you'll see that our medical care ratio has improved quite a bit, but I don't want that to be misleading in terms of [medical cost trends]," DeVeydt said. He said the independent dispute resolution (IDR) process under the No Surprises Act is adding at least 100 basis points, or 1 percentage point, to total medical costs. That federal law, which took effect in 2022, aims to protect consumers from unexpected medical bills The IDR process allows providers and insurers to resolve disputes over out-of-network payments. DeVeydt said those changes are driving up the company's claims costs, which can ultimately be passed on to consumers through higher premiums. DeVeydt added that costs for inpatient services and pharmacy, particularly costly specialty pharmacy drugs for cancer and rare diseases, remain elevated. Still, he highlighted the company's value-based care efforts, which are helping control medical costs by steering patients toward the right providers and emphasizing preventive care, DeVeydt added. He said acute hospital admissions among UnitedHealth members fell 15% year over year through the third quarter, while home health admissions rose 10%, suggesting more patients are receiving care in lower-cost settings. "You're finding more members are actually getting into a lower-cost care environment, but more importantly, they're getting into the care environment they actually want to be in," he told CNBC. "So we think we're really balancing both the quality and the cost." UnitedHealth is also rolling out AI-powered ambient listening tools to reduce physicians' administrative burden and free up time for patient visits. Appointment scheduling done by patients rather than with the assistance of a provider increased 27% year over year, DeVeydt said.

events.title: Trump census plan to cut noncitizens from 2030 count spurs critics toward legal fight
events.summary: A Trump administration proposal to exclude some noncitizens from the 2030 U.S. census could dramatically alter congressional district maps and cause funding for federal assistance to be slashed. Opponents of the change are bracing for a legal fight over the rule, a comment period for which closes Nov. 2. President Donald Trump has in the past attempted to bar noncitizens from being counted in the census, a move that critics argue is unconstitutional. Congressional Democrats and civil rights groups are concerned about a proposed Trump administration change to the U.S. census that would exclude noncitizens without permanent resident status, altering congressional representation and potentially how federal funding is distributed. Opponents warn the rule, which was posted in September, could have negative effects, potentially shifting congressional power to parts of the country where fewer immigrants live and underfunding education, healthcare, food assistance and emergency management programs. The public can comment on the rule until Nov. 2, the day before Election Day. " The greatest likelihood is that this is going to end up in litigation," said Meeta Anand, senior director of census and data equity at the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights . "I'm under no delusion that we will see everything remedied because I do know that it's been a project of the administration to exclude noncitizens from the count." The proposed census change is the latest volley in the Trump administration's push to reduce illegal immigration. If certain categories of immigrants living in the U.S. are not counted, areas where they are concentrated could get less federal money. The rule's supporters say counting all immigrants living legally in the U.S. encourages illegal immigration. Trump census plan to cut noncitizens from 2030 count spurs potential legal fight Elon Musk becomes biggest known donor of 2026 midterm election Trump defends Russia diesel deal: 'I made the right choice' The rule would exclude from the census millions of noncitizens without a green card, including people in the country on student visas, people with temporary protected status, refugees and asylum seekers. It would also bar the collection of demographic information on race and ethnicity from the census's short-form questionnaire. That information can be used for civil rights enforcement and to assess compliance with federal laws that bar racial discrimination. The White House referred CNBC to the Commerce Department, which oversees the census, when asked for comment on the proposed rule. The Commerce Department and the Census Bureau did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Critics argue the proposal flies in the face of the 14th Amendment , which states, in part, that "representatives shall be apportioned among the several States according to their respective numbers, counting the whole number of persons in each State." "This rule is yet another attack on democracy by Donald Trump," Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said in a statement after the rule was announced last month. "An accurate census count is at the very foundation of ensuring equal representation across our country and delivering federal funds where they're needed most. The Census is enshrined in our Constitution and not up for political debate." Census has counted noncitizens since U.S. founding Proponents, including some congressional Republicans who have introduced legislation to end the counting of noncitizens, argue the census practice of counting all U.S. residents — which dates back to the nation's founding — encourages illegal immigration and makes some voters more powerful than others . "Republicans have long warned that Democrats' intentional illegal invasion and sanctuary policies are rooted in a desire to boost blue states' power," Rep. Andrew Clyde, R-Ga., said in a statement in September announcing legislation that would call for reapportioning congressional seats before the 2028 election while excluding noncitizens and adding a citizenship question the 2030 census. The proposal has 42 Republican co-sponsors. Normally, seats are reapportioned every 10 years using new census data. "Amid high stakes and slim margins, Congress must act before the 2028 elections to ensure only American citizens decide how congressional maps are drawn and who resides in the White House," Clyde added. Sen. Bill Hagerty, R-Tenn., introduced similar legislation last year that would require the Census Bureau to include a citizenship status question on any future census, arguing noncitizens heavily skew the congressional map. "While people continue to flee Democrat-run cities, desperate Democrats have back-filled the mass exodus with illegal immigrants so that they do not lose their seats in Congress or their electoral votes, hence artificially boosting their political power and in turn diluting the power of other Americans' votes," Hagerty said in a statement .

events.title: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
events.summary: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here . Late last month, Anthropic released a report arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk. The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company Z.ai, is freely available for anyone to download and modify. Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs.  These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach. But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models. “I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information. Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely. There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly. But any approach that a government or a society might take still involves trade-offs between safety and democratization. Deciding whether to support or limit the production of open models requires understanding those risks and benefits in depth. What are the benefits of open models? Let’s start with the basics. A closed model, like the models that power ChatGPT and Claude, can only be accessed through a website, app, or API. An open model, on the other hand, can be directly downloaded: The details about its internal structure, encoded in a long series of numbers known as the model weights, are publicly available. Such models are sometimes called “open-weight models,” to distinguish them from models for which even more information, such as details about the training procedure, is available.  Right now, closed models are more capable than open models—as of publication, the top eight models on the Artificial Analysis LLM leaderboard are all closed, though open models are only a handful of months behind in development. But there are several reasons why someone might opt to use an open model rather than a closed one. Because open models are downloadable, people can run them on their own computers or hard drives. They can even retrain them to behave differently, if they have the expertise and resources to do so. If you’re an academic researcher working to understand and improve AI systems, you almost certainly need to work with open models in your research. When working with closed models, researchers can’t do much more than send prompts and observe the responses. But researchers can observe the inner workings of open models, as well as the “chain of thought” that the models use to think through a problem before answering. They can also combine multiple open models to build new systems, compress them to make them more efficient, and fine-tune them for new applications. Businesses, too, have reasons to prefer open models. Even if you depend on an external provider to run them for you, open models still typically cost less than closed models, according to a recent report from Mozilla . And if businesses want to use AI to process sensitive data or proprietary information, running a local model on their own hardware may be the best way to keep their operations secure. But perhaps the most important quality of open models is that they challenge the tight control the frontier labs have over how most of us use AI. “The clearest, biggest argument [for open models] is around preventing mass concentration of power—it is about making sure that this foundational technology is a public good,” says Elizabeth Seger, senior policy advisor at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. “I think we’re at this juncture where the question of who controls the infrastructure that allows AI to operate is as big of a question as who gets to control information on the internet.” Seger sees the future of AI playing out in different ways, depending on the role that open models have. In one possible future, frontier AI systems are controlled entirely by select people, companies, or governments, and as those systems grow more powerful, those groups have increasing control over what our world looks like. The world’s most sophisticated hacking models, for example, are currently all made in the United States, so it’s entirely up to US companies and the US government whether other countries can use them to shore up their own cyber defenses. If those companies remain in the lead, we could in principle wind up in a world in which the United States is capable of hacking any other country, but no one is capable of hacking it. Frontier open models could change that balance. “If every individual had a loyal-to-them AI system that was safe [and secure], I think that would be a much less concerning world than one in which they have to just rely on a government that says, ‘Yeah, we’ve got a super intelligent AI system, it’s got this plan, it’s inscrutable to all of you, just trust us,’” says Hamish Hobbs, director of AI policy at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience. But open models are not a geopolitical panacea. Paul Azunre, who cofounded Ghana NLP, an organization that builds open-source AI tools for low-resource Ghanaian languages, notes that open models can also function as a way for companies to benefit from the labor and expertise of less-privileged nations and consolidate more power in their own hands. He identifies a pattern in which AI companies release models openly, observe how the community uses and modifies them, and then integrate those same improvements into their own products—without any credit or compensation for the people who originated those innovations. Mark Zuckerberg himself has said that the ability to integrate community improvements into Meta’s stack is a key benefit of releasing open models. “I think the ideal of open source is a very noble one, and there’s a lot of value that it brings,” Azunre says. “But the way it’s actually implemented in practice, it tends to be a very extractive approach.” Are open models riskier than closed ones? events.title: The UAE embraces AI for kindergartners
events.summary: The country’s approach offers a glimpse of what education could look like if AI literacy becomes as fundamental as reading and writing. In September, Henry Price observed a classroom of 7- to 8-year-olds learn about the Stone Age. They discussed and wrote about cave paintings, then put on virtual reality headsets to explore them. The founding principal of Rugby School Dubai hopes his students will soon study ancient Egypt the same way — reading about it, creating artwork, and then stepping inside a virtual pyramid, or using artificial intelligence to “interview” a pharaoh. “AI does not replace reading, writing, discussion, or creativity. It enhances them and opens new doors,” Price told Rest of World . “We want our students to be excited by AI, but never [be] passive users. We want children who use AI to ask better questions, not children who rely on it to give them all the answers.” The United Arab Emirates recently became the first country to make AI a required K-12 subject. Our goal remains to ensure that any integration of technology is developmentally appropriate and supports meaningful learning.” Saeed Kharbash, CEO of policies, research and programmes at Dubai’s Knowledge and Human Development Authority That puts the country on one side of a growing global debate over what children should learn about AI and when they should encounter it. While the UAE and China are treating early AI literacy as a national priority, some Western governments are moving in the opposite direction. New York City introduced a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI in public schools from preschool through grade eight, citing concerns about children’s mental health. Norway has also enacted a similar near-ban for primary school children. “On one side is the wish to protect childhood, to guard against the addictive pull of some technology, and to raise happy, well-rounded children,” Prince said. “On the other is the fear that those same children could be left behind in a world changing at extraordinary speed.” The UAE’s approach is not to give young children unrestricted access to AI. Instead, schools teach them how the technology works, where it fails, and when humans should use it. At Dubai Schools Al Khawaneej, a joint initiative between the Dubai government and K-12 education provider Taaleem Education , students in grades one through three are not expected to use generative AI independently, elementary principal James Efford told Rest of World . Instead, teachers use discussions, stories, and role-play to teach them about AI. In one activity, a teacher might show children something an AI system got wrong, and ask them to identify what is incorrect or unfair. In another, the teacher pretends to be a robot and asks children to give increasingly precise instructions, teaching them how machines respond to the information they receive. Most UAE schools are treating AI as a form of literacy rather than technical training. Dubai’s Knowledge and Human Development Authority is developing a broader policy framework for digital technology and AI in education. It has a 10-year roadmap to prepare students for rapid technological change with personalized learning. “Our goal remains to ensure that any integration of technology is developmentally appropriate and supports meaningful learning without replacing the essential non-digital experiences that contribute to children’s growth, well-being and development,” Saeed Kharbash, CEO of policies, research and programmes at KHDA, told Rest of World . Abu Dhabi’s Department of Education and Knowledge, which is developing the AI education framework for more than 170 private schools in the emirate, did not respond to Rest of World ’s request for comment. AI is also being used to make classrooms more accessible. Jayda Keer, an inclusion and neurodiversity consultant and former head of inclusion at Dubai International Academy, said schools have used AI to simplify texts for students who struggle with complex vocabulary, translate material for students learning English, and create word banks. The UAE’s embrace of AI does not mean children are being handed ChatGPT and left alone. Schools monitor apps and use firewalls. Younger children rarely use AI directly, while older students have restricted access to school-approved apps such as Padlet, Toddle, Canva, Mathletics, Times Tables Rock Stars, ClassDojo, Edmentum, and Epic. At least two schools told Rest of World they use MagicSchool for teacher-directed activities, while one uses Microsoft Copilot. “We do not currently allow students to use public ChatGPT etc. accounts in school. Nor do we define the programme around a particular AI model or specialist hardware platform,” Efford said. The government plans to train 22,000 teachers to use AI for teaching, assessment, curriculum analysis, and lesson planning.

events.title: Scammers Are Stealing Millions From Food Stamp Recipients. Congress Could Fix It — but Won’t.
events.summary: Jovelle Tamayo/ProPublica. Source images: Zaydee Sanchez/ProPublica, Tina Russell for ProPublica, MPfoto71/Alamy. It wasn’t the kind of call a grocery store gets every day. A customer with a thick Eastern European accent was on the phone saying he wanted to buy several thousand cans of Red Bull. Could the store have them in stock in a few days? Also, did they have equipment to move all those stacks of energy drinks into the parking lot, where two minivans would be waiting? When the day came, Oct. 19, 2022, employees at the Smart & Final store in San Diego sold 3,960 cans of Red Bull and 720 of Monster Energy to two men and two women, all with the same accent, and helped them wheel the pallets out back. To pay for it all — the bill came to $10,747.05 — the group pulled out piles of plastic. These weren’t credit or debit cards; they looked more like hotel-room keys. There were 25 cards in all, each with a different amount loaded onto it, and the four people took turns swiping one after another. Then, the payment complete, they drove off. In the days that followed, people as far away as New York and Florida made panicked calls to the store. They wanted to know why their food-stamp accounts (containing their Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, benefits) had been drained at this seemingly random location in San Diego. It would turn out that what became known as the Red Bull Crew had gotten ahold of their SNAP data and used the funds to buy the energy drinks, which they then sold online or to smaller stores. It was hardly an isolated event. From September through November of that year, the same crew, part of a criminal syndicate based in Romania, bought at least $305,274.52 in energy drinks, using SNAP account information and PINs stolen from at least 174 victims nationwide, according to court documents and federal investigators. To hear the Trump administration tell it, the SNAP program is under siege by well-heeled recipients of food stamps. Vice President JD Vance, upon being named “Fraud Czar” this spring, said : “There are people who have Lamborghinis who currently receive SNAP benefits.” Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, whose agency oversees the program, regularly goes on TV and social media to allege that masses of SNAP recipients are scamming the system, driving Bentleys, Ferraris, Maseratis and, yes, Lamborghinis. The federal government’s own statistics tell a different story. Confirmed cases of intentional program violations — fraud — committed by SNAP recipients account for $64 million a year, or about 0.08% of all benefits issued annually, according to the most recent 50-state reports compiled by the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Meanwhile a far bigger fraud wave has exploded over the past five years: organized theft from SNAP recipients. In 2025, $470 million was stolen electronically from beneficiaries — and thus from the U.S. taxpayer — according to data supplied to ProPublica by Propel , a company that provides a mobile app for SNAP recipients to check their account balances and transaction histories. More than 990,000 households that received food assistance last year had benefits stolen. (The reason it’s necessary to use data from a private company: The federal government has stopped tracking rates of this crime.) ProPublica interviewed nearly 100 victims of SNAP theft, federal prosecutors, Secret Service agents, USDA officials, caseworkers and other experts to understand what’s behind this phenomenon and why more isn’t being done to stop it. The victims are almost all working people with families, or retirees, who have struggled to afford groceries in the current economy. Most didn’t learn about the crime until they were in a checkout line, only to have their benefit card declined. Jared Chesnut, a laid-off software developer in Hoover, Alabama, had $893 in SNAP benefits stolen from him in December: “I ate rice and grits the rest of the month.” Rita Harper for ProPublica Upon reporting the disappearance of their food assistance, victims are informed that nothing can be done under current federal law. “The only thing they said was that [my benefits] cannot be refunded unless they were lost due to a natural disaster,” said one SNAP theft victim in Ohio. “They told me they’d add my name to the list,” said another in rural Oregon. “They advised if I feel the place is sketchy, don’t run my card there,” a victim in Philadelphia said. Still another, in Virginia, added, “They even charged me $2 for a replacement card.” Perhaps the most vexing aspect of all: The federal government knows how to prevent the vast majority of this crime in a single step. Congress just hasn’t been willing to take it. SNAP theft is an old scheme applied to a new target. For years, scammers would surreptitiously install skimming devices on card readers at ATMs, gas pumps and corner stores. These devices could read the data on people’s cards as they swiped — while a pinhole camera or overlay keypad captured their PINs — all of which could be picked up later or sent via Bluetooth to someone sitting in a nearby cafe or parking lot. This pilfered data, in turn, was used to make online purchases, or it was loaded onto cloned cards to withdraw cash. Skimming became exponentially more difficult when credit and debit card companies installed digital microchips in the 2010s and then introduced tap-to-pay. But one kind of card did not get the new chips: Electronic Benefits Transfer, or EBT, cards, which people use to access SNAP and other public assistance. These still rely on the 1960s-era magnetic-stripe technology that skimmers can easily read. EBT cards are not a particularly high-value target compared with bank cards. (The average monthly SNAP benefit is about $350 per household.) But funding boosts to SNAP during the pandemic temporarily increased benefit amounts, and profits could be considerable if you skimmed hundreds of people’s card information every month. Skimming teams, often run by Romanian gangs, pivoted. With cloned magnetic-stripe cards, they started buying up huge quantities of SNAP-eligible products like energy drinks and baby formula that are easy to store and resell. “We’ve started many, many briefings saying that one of the biggest ways we’re going to fight this is to just get chips in the cards,” said Michael Peck, assistant special agent in charge of the Secret Service’s Criminal Investigative Division. Among the Secret Service’s lesser-known functions is investigating many financial crimes, and Peck leads its efforts against benefit theft. He said he and his team have delivered this message on Capitol Hill both at committee meetings and to individual members of Congress. Yet congressional leadership has continually blocked legislation that would fund chip EBT cards nationally, despite universal support for the measure among Democrats and significant support among the Republican rank and file. events.title: Activist Greta Thunberg joins French student protests
events.summary: Thunberg arrives at Paul Eluard high school in the heart of the movement in the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis. Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg has joined the French student protests as more demonstrations calling for better conditions at education facilities are expected nationwide. Thunberg arrived at Paul Eluard high school in the heart of the movement in the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis on Tuesday morning and stood among the students demonstrating. list 1 of 3 Thousands rally for anti-austerity protest in Brussels amid clashes list 2 of 3 Stolen Renoir paintings found behind wall in France following arrests list 3 of 3 Hundreds of supermarkets in France hit by ‘unprecedented’ cyberattack “Young people are not being included in the conversation. Our future is being robbed away from us,” Thunberg told the AFP news agency. Lawyers in robes had also formed a human chain to protect teens following numerous allegations of police brutality at demonstrations. The protests started late last month as students demanded improvements on a range of issues, including the state of school buildings, a lack of teachers, crowded class schedules and other problems in the education system. Students have piled up bins and erected security barriers outside hundreds of schools across the country. Last Thursday, more than 70,000 people took to the streets in the latest major protest event. Tuesday’s demonstration, backed by unions and a left-wing opposition party, France Unbowed, included a march through Paris and marches in other cities. Pupils clustered outside the doors of several schools in the morning hours, brandishing placards and megaphones and chanting slogans, and marches were planned later in the day. The university student union, l’Union, said on X: “They’re not listening to us, so we’re going to them.” Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on France Inter on Tuesday morning that about 200 schools were closed, which was “fewer than last week”, adding that some near protest routes were closing to avoid damage. The Ministry of National Education also said eight members of teaching staff were injured on Monday, mostly in the Paris region and cities of Bordeaux and Lyon, due to the protests. On Monday, a 19-year-old graphic design student in Paris, Leo, told AFP that “Students aren’t being heard enough … not their proposals to authorities and elected officials.” He added that the protesters, many being minors, were “disturbed by the level of repression never before seen for a student movement”. Tuesday’s demonstrations supporting the students are expected to be followed on Saturday by wider public rallies against the rising cost of living. On Monday, French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters at a car show that he urged protesters to exercise restraint. “These are issues that deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect,” Macron said. According to the Ministry of Justice, more than 6,800 people, mainly minors, have been taken into police custody over the course of the protests. Police have also opened investigations into 24 allegations of brutality against demonstrators.

events.title: One killed, several injured in Georgia rollercoaster ‘incident’
events.summary: Six Flags temporarily closes nine similar coasters after a fatal accident at its Georgia amusement park. A person has died and several others have been injured in an incident involving a rollercoaster at an amusement park in the state of Georgia in the United States. The incident happened on Monday at the Six Flags amusement park, about 15 miles (24km) northwest of Atlanta. list 1 of 3 Why the Cornell gang rape case has raised concerns about fraternity culture list 2 of 3 Two deaths reported as Hurricane Simon, storm Rachel batter Mexico’s coast list 3 of 3 Man dies after fall from Six Flags rollercoaster in Georgia Officials are investigating the death but have yet to confirm its nature or how the others were injured. Images and videos have been circulating online that appear to show a man who seems to have been ejected from his seat and landed on the ground. Al Jazeera has not independently verified the footage. Six Flags has since closed nine rollercoasters at six of its parks “out of an abundance of caution”, a spokesperson said, adding that they are similar to the one involved in the incident. Police and the company did not name the ride, but local TV footage showed passengers being escorted off the Goliath rollercoaster, which stopped halfway through the ride. Witnesses also told local station 11Alive that they saw a man land on the roof of a haunted house attraction; those accounts have also not been verified. Six Flags said it was “deeply saddened by the guest incident” and that it was supporting guests and staff affected. Lisa Cupid, chairwoman of the Cobb County board of commissioners, said she “cannot imagine the horror the patrons and employees witnessed today”. The Goliath rollercoaster opened in 2006 and reaches 70mph (113km/h) at a height of 200 feet (61 metres), according to the company’s website. This marks at least the seventh death at the park, according to the Doan Law Firm, which tracks amusement park accidents. Earlier, one occurred on Goliath in 2006, after a man likely had a heart attack on the ride. About two weeks ago, Six Flags Magic Mountain in California announced it would retire its X2 rollercoaster after more than 100 people reportedly sustained brain injuries while riding it. The company said the ride had passed safety tests, but it was closing it regardless because it’s just the “right thing to do”.

events.title: In charts: How one of the world's biggest economies got trapped by debt
events.summary: France's National Assembly begins debate on the revenue side of the 2027 budget on Oct. 13 as lawmakers confront a difficult fiscal outlook. France posted a 5.1% budget deficit and debt of 115.6% of GDP in 2025, leaving the country under pressure to consolidate its public finances. Student protests over education resources are adding pressure as lawmakers weigh spending choices ahead of the 2027 presidential election. France's parliament begins debate on the 2027 budget Tuesday as high deficits, rising debt and student protests sharpen the political cost of fiscal consolidation. The euro zone's second-biggest economy is barreling toward a debt crisis, and risks dragging the continent down with it, unless it sustainably brings down its national deficit, according to many market watchers. Even as thousands take to the streets to protest years of underfunding in public services, particularly education, France has run one of Europe's highest deficit-to-GDP ratios for nearly a decade under President Emmanuel Macron. Government spending remains well above its peers in the politically sensitive realm of social protections, particularly pensions and healthcare, while tepid economic growth has failed to compensate. With presidential elections looming next year and parliamentarians proving reluctant to compromise, France's economic and political uncertainty is weighing on the euro . French government borrowing costs have soared to their highest level in nearly a quarter of a century as jittery bond markets have responded to the country's failure to impose fiscal consolidation. The widening gap in French bond yields over their German equivalents has raised questions over whether the European Central Bank would have to take the expensive and politically controversial step of intervening to stabilize the market. While this could halt a panic that fragments the currency union, the legacy of the Sovereign Debt Crisis — which hammered countries such as Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Italy — means it would require drastic action from France. "The ECB will not step in just to 'bail out' France. If there was a European crisis they will intervene in some form but they will not save a country that cannot save itself," Antonio Fatas, professor of Economics at INSEAD Business School, said by email. events.summary: Asian markets fall and Samsung shares tumble after its Chinese rival CXMT claims strong progress South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index tumbled 6.25% as investors dumped chip stocks, while other Asian markets were also lower. Japan’s Nikkei fell 1.8% and the Taiwan exchange lost almost 2%, with the country’s chip maker TSMC down by a similar amount. Samsung Electronics shares dropped 7.4% on the South Korean exchange, while the memory chip maker SK Hynix was down 10%. In Japan, the chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron fell 7.15% while SoftBank Group, an OpenAI investor, lost 8.5%. US stock futures point to a mixed open on Wall Street after the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite slipped 0.4% on Monday. The US chipmaker Micron Technology slid 3.9% while Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom also fell. Crude oil prices dropped amid escalating tensions in the Middle East. AI shares have been on a rollercoaster in recent months amid concerns that companies are spending eye-watering amounts on AI infrastructure, funded by debt. The latest sell-off came after the South China Morning Post reported on Monday that CXMT had made good progress on new Dram architecture that would boost memory density. Investors are worried that it could challenge Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron, the world’s biggest memory chip makers. CXMT, which had an impressive debut on the Shanghai stock market in late July, makes Dram chips , which store the data that other AI chips draw on for their calculations. “The rout in chip stocks seems set to continue thanks once again to news from China,” said Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG. “CXMT’s new developments remind investors of the huge competition in the sector. While great for customers who can enjoy the white heat of technological improvement and get falling margins into the bargain, it is dangerous for high-flying tech stocks who have promised so much, and on whom the entire stock market rally seems to rest.” Hock Tan, the chief executive of the US chipmaker Broadcom, said the AI boom had attracted investors who did not really understand what they were betting on. events.title: The simple habit that can make you more magnetic at work
events.summary: Business Insider's Ana Altchek shares how to become more magnetic at work. Cadie Thompson/ Business Insider Today's tip to get better at work: Get better at commanding a room by practicing being present. Showing a genuine interest in others without distraction makes people feel drawn to you. Pamela Meyer, author of "How to Read the Room," recommends an exercise dubbed "PAM" to help be more present. Get better at: Being magnetic Today's move The people who command a room aren't just interesting, they're fully present. That allows them to notice how people are reacting and to make those around them feel they have their full attention. To be present during important interactions, you need to first get focused before you arrive. That means you can't be thinking about your to-do list, your last meeting, or what comes after. Why it works Pamela Meyer, author of "How to Read the Room," said taking time to reduce "cognitive load" before a meeting can help you stay focused and engaged during the interaction. A study of more than 1,600 people involving five listening experiments, published in "Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin," found that when people were genuinely listened to, they felt closer and more connected to the listener. That's what being magnetic is about: Making others feel seen by giving them your full attention. Try it today Meyer recommends a quick pre-arrival exercise to help you better prepare for an interaction where you need to be fully present called PAM: Purpose. Attention. Modulate. First, purpose: Decide on one thing you want to accomplish. Second, attention: Put away your phone and clear the mental and digital distractions competing for your attention. Finally, modulate: Take three breaths and think about the energy you want to bring into the room. The bottom line People will feel drawn to you when they feel like way you're paying attention to them. events.title: Nestlé's CEO shares the feedback he got that changed how he leads
events.summary: Philipp Navratil said he used to struggle with giving people feedback. Nespresso Philipp Navratil changed his leadership style after being told he needed to provide honest feedback. He said he now embraces giving direct feedback and feels like it's his responsibility to do so. He said when he has tough conversations, he focuses mostly on finding a solution. No one likes to be told they're doing something wrong — but it's not easy to be the messenger either. Philipp Navratil has spent more than two decades at Nestlé. Early in his leadership career, he received one piece of advice that reshaped how he manages people: Give honest feedback . The CEO of the company behind more than 30 billion-dollar brands, including Nespresso and DiGiorno, said he when he first stepped into leadership, he struggled to tell employees when their performance fell short. "It's easy to tell someone 'Great job, well done,'" Navratil told Business Insider. This is part of a series of stories from Business Insider's conversation with Nestlé CEO Philipp Navratil. To be alerted when the next piece publishes, follow reporter Ana Altchek here. Nestlé's CEO says these 3 qualities will get you promoted Nestlé's CEO says this is the most important skill for workers in the AI era The hard part is speaking up when things aren't going well, he said. The CEO said that he tries to be "as direct as possible," because if you beat around the bush, people may miss the point. "It's much more valuable for them to receive it that way because it's clear," Navratil said. Today, Navratil said, he sees feedback as one of a leader's most important responsibilities — not just because it helps the company overall, but because it helps employees grow, too. Direct doesn't mean harsh, though. Navratil said he gives the criticism, but then he spends more time talking about how to improve the situation. That may mean asking the person how he can help, or suggesting a solution that they can work through together. While those conversations may seem awkward or uncomfortable, it could end up bringing you closer to that individual. Navratil said that feedback discussions lead to stronger personal relationships because they include follow-up conversations. "I feel that I owe it to the person," Navratil said. events.title: UK growth forecast upgraded but higher energy prices to hit economy next year
events.summary: Published 13 October 2026, 03:00 BST The UK economy is forecast to grow by more than previously expected this year before higher energy prices and interest rates hit the economy in 2027, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said. The organisation's latest report, which is closely watched by the government, said the UK economy would expand by 1.3% in 2026, up from the 1% it predicted in July, before slowing in 2027. Economies across the world have proved more resilient to the energy price shock caused by the US-Iran war, the IMF said, but it warned the economic fallout from the conflict remained "highly uncertain". Chancellor John Healey said the government would look to "provide some breathing space" for households in the Budget. Healey is making the final preparations to Andy Burnham's new-look government's tax and spending plans, which will be announced on 28 October. Government borrowing costs have surged, placing pressure on the chancellor to ensure his plans are credible in the eyes of financial markets, which the UK relies on to borrow money. But IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro told BBC News on Tuesday that the UK's process of managing its debts is now leading the major G7 economies. "As you know, the UK has already started the consolidation process and it is the country that basically stands out, along with India", she said. The organisation said the UK is one of the only major economies on course to stabilise levels of national debt. The UK is also projected to have the lowest annual borrowing in the G7 in 2031. Asked if the UK was one of the countries the IMF was telling to reduce borrowing, Tenreyro said that the country had begun the process already and should "stay the course". The head of the IMF has previously called on the world's advanced economies to cut borrowing and reduce debt levels. While the IMF's forecasts are closely watched, the figures are only a prediction, a best estimate, of what will happen in the future. Forecasts often turn out to be incorrect due to world events. Also, the chancellor's spending decisions at the Budget will be based on predictions from the UK's official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility, not the IMF. The predictions in the IMF's latest World Economic Outlook suggest: the UK is expected to have the second-fastest growing economy in the G7 this year along with Germany UK growth is set to slow next year to 1.2% as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates hit household spending and business investment UK inflation is expected to average 3.3% this year, and the IMF has increased its forecast for inflation next year to 2.8%. the IMF said the global economy was "proving resilient" despite the ongoing war in the Middle East, helped by the investment surge in AI. Healey acknowledged that wars in the Middle East and Europe were "hitting people in the UK and around the world", but added that "Britain's economy is showing strong international resilience". When the economy is growing, businesses tend to invest more, more jobs are created and people, on average, tend to feel better off. The opposite can occur if the economy stagnates or shrinks. Sir Howard Davies, former deputy governor of the Bank of England, told the BBC the IMF's growth forecast was "better than it might have been", but noted that for 2027 it remained "more pessimistic". "We're still growing slowly. It's almost like saying we're winning a slow bicycle race here because other people are going backwards a bit more rapidly than we are," he added. Sir Howard said the UK was "a bit of a sideshow" when it comes to the global economy and the IMF was more focused on how much the US is adding to its debt pile. "That is what is putting pressure on interest rates all over the world and that is what is affecting us as well. Unless the US does something about its deficit, we can expect interest rates to be higher, which of course increases our debt interest costs," he said. He added that the IMF was giving the UK credit in its forecast for tax rises which it might not end up actually putting through. Economists have suggested Healey faces having to find £35bn to avoid cuts to public spending while meeting defence promises in his first Budget. On Tuesday, the Resolution Foundation called on the chancellor to "make repairs" to the public finances, but said well-targeted support was needed for those "struggling to heat their homes". Andrew Griffith, Conservative shadow chancellor, said if Healey "reaches for more tax rises" in his Budget, "he is choosing slower growth and working people will pay for it". events.title: Phase Eight and Hobbs owner hit by cyber-attack, as H&M probes separate hack claim
events.summary: The owner of high-end fashion brands Hobbs, Whistles and Phase Eight says it is investigating a cyber-security incident. According to TFG London - the UK arm of retail conglomerate The Foschini Group - it identified an incident on Sunday affecting some IT systems and "specifically impacting our Phase Eight, Hobbs, and Whistles brands". "We are actively investigating and working with external cyber security specialists," the company told BBC News in a statement. Meanwhile, H&M is investigating a separate claim that it was attacked by a notorious hacking group. TFG said its brands' stores are operating as normal but some website capabilities may be unavailable, adding "we apologise for any disruption and will provide additional updates to our customers as appropriate". The retail group reportedly told customers in an email that it did not believe customers' payment information had been affected by the incident. "As our investigation continues, we will be working to identify if any sensitive information related to our customers was impacted," it said. The email, seen by news service PA, also said that those whose personal information had been impacted would be informed directly. "We do not believe it is necessary to change your account login information at this time," it added. Beverley Griffiths, senior lecturer in security and resilience at Bucks New University told PA that this was "a clear sign that major brands are firmly in the crosshairs of cyber attackers". Fashion giants ranging from Adidas to Alexander McQueen have been targeted by cyber-criminals seeking to extort money by threatening to release customer data unless they are paid a ransom. "No organisation is immune, so the real test of resilience is how quickly a business can detect an incident, respond and recover while keeping its customers informed," Griffiths said - adding customers should stay "vigilant" and wary of suspicious messages. Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at cyber-security firm Check Point, said attacks targeting retailers were "starting to look rather like buses... you wait for one, and suddenly three come along at once". She told the BBC that while it was too soon to ascertain how the incident affecting TFG London's systems occurred, or whether it was related to other recent hacks, "the retail industry has some serious questions to answer about how exposed its systems have become". On Monday, it was also reported that fashion giant H&M was investigating a claim of a hack by a cyber-criminal group called ShinyHunters. The hackers have been previously linked to high-profile attacks including targeting the FBI , Rockstar Games and Ticketmaster. "We are aware of information circulating online regarding a potential cyber security incident and are currently investigating the claims," H&M told BBC News in a statement. "At this time, we have not found any indications that our data environment has been compromised." It also comes only a week after Asos customers were informed the online fashion and beauty retailer had been hacked by another group, via a push notification appearing on their phone screens . Cyber-security experts told the BBC it was an unprecedented move for hackers to effectively transform an app notification system into a "ransom note". It later emerged that hackers had obtained more detailed personal information belonging to Asos customers than the retailer initially suggested . An update was issued to customers after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said the breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed. events.title: Eileen Gu says she sees herself and her mom as ‘cofounders’
events.summary: Eileen Gu says her mom set her up for success by letting her choose her own path. Noam Galai/Getty Images For Apex For Youth Olympic skier Eileen Gu said people often mistake her mom for a “tiger mom.” But the opposite is true: Her mom fiercely protected her freedom to make her own decisions. Today, Gu said, she and her mom are more like "cofounders" in everyday life. Eileen Gu credits her mom with giving her the freedom to find her own path. Speaking at the Karim Family Foundation's Inspiring Women Leadership Series in Singapore on Monday, Gu spoke about her upbringing and how her mom set her up for success from a young age. "I think she really optimized for play, and she optimized for optionality. She put me into everything," Gu said, adding that she tried ballet, piano, archery, basketball, soccer, and cross-country skiing. She also attended math and science camps and went for singing lessons. "There were lots of things, right?" Gu said. "And so, the point being that when I was younger, she really gave me the full spread so that when I was older — when I knew myself better and when I was responsible to make those decisions — I could make an informed one having tried all the options." The Olympic freestyle skier said that being entrusted with that agency and responsibility at a relatively young age was critical to her becoming independent . Gu said people often wrongly assume her mother was a "tiger mom," a label she described as a controlling, helicopter-style parent who forces their child down a particular path. "She was in many ways the opposite of that, where she just vigorously provided me with freedom and agency, and enforced my freedom really intensely," Gu said. "That was the effect of her tiger mom." Now, Gu said, they still do almost everything together. "As I got older, I kept calling us cofounders because I really think that's the best way to encapsulate our partnership," Gu said. "We travel together every day. We live together. We work together. We develop together. We change together. We evolve." Gu said neither she nor her mother has all the answers, and they are both figuring life out as they go. They often start with different views before talking them through, finding common ground, and sometimes even landing on each other's original sides, she said. "We come in with unique perspectives and, most importantly, a respect for one another. We have dialogue that is respectful, that is critical, that is conducive, that is productive," she said. events.title: IMF raises its forecast for world growth this year but warns of risks from AI boom and debt
events.summary: The International Monetary Fund has slightly upgraded its outlook for the world economy for this year, but it's forecasting growth at a still sluggish 3.1% BANGKOK -- The International Monetary Fund on Tuesday slightly upgraded its outlook for the world economy for this year, while warning of growing risks from rising debt, including the financial frenzy around artificial intelligence. The IMF says it expects the global economy to grow at a 3.1% pace this year. That's up from its July forecast for 3.0% growth and well below the 3.5% expansion in 2025. Growth in 2027 should rebound to 3.4%, it said in its latest Economic Outlook. The report, released as world economic and financial leaders gathered in Bangkok for the fall meetings of the IMF and World Bank, predicts that growth in the United States will remain steady at 2.3% in 2026 and 2027. Collectively, advanced economies will grow 2.1% this year, up from 2.0% in 2025, and then slow to 1.9% growth next year, it said. The forecasts are based on a nearly 41% increase in oil prices this year, at an average of $96 a barrel. Global inflation is foreseen at 4.7% in 2026, falling to 4.1% next year. They also are based on the assumption that shipments of oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz will resume by March, and that the boom in AI demand will moderate. The boom in artificial intelligence is offsetting damage from sharply higher prices for oil and gas, IMF economists say, but it also carries risks. Its benefits are not shared equally: the U.S. and China account for more than three-quarters of net demand for imports of computer chips and other AI-related equipment, the report said. “The outlook is highly uneven,” Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF's director of research, told reporters in Bangkok. Growth is increasingly concentrated, with 32 countries accounting for 95% of global growth, the report said. That compares with 54 countries as of April. “The global economy is not simply slowing or accelerating; rather, growth is being reallocated across countries according to their exposure to the war-induced supply shock and AI-related demand strength,” it says. Athanasios Vamvakidis, deputy director at the IMF's Monetary and Capital Markets Department, said an AI-related correction in stock markets is just one of the risks. Rising bond yields are another evolving problem, along with cyberthreats that could disrupt financial systems, he said. Underscoring such concerns, sell-offs of AI-related shares swept through Asia on Tuesday, with South Korea's Kospi sinking as much as 7% before it closed 5.5% lower. AI's effects on employment are another worry, “a slow moving tsunami, but a tsunami nonetheless,” IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said. And we are already seeing some of this impact,” she said. The IMF chief is urging countries to do a better job of improving their national finances and taming mounting levels of debt. That's especially crucial at a time of high borrowing costs, Tenreyro said. Countries that are somewhat insulated from the energy shocks of the Iran war and that are benefiting from rapid adoption of AI are managing to keep growth on track. But developing economies and emerging markets more vulnerable to higher costs for oil and gas will see growth slow to 3.7% this year from 4.5% in 2025, the report says. It forecasts they will regain momentum next year, expanding at a 4.4% annual pace. The situation is much worse in the Middle East and Central Asia, where those regions' economies are expected to contract this year before recovering to a 6.3% rate of growth in 2027. The 21 European countries that share the euro currency are expected to grow by a meager 1.1% this year and 1.2% in 2027. China , the world’s No. 2 economy, is expected to expand 4.5% this year, down from 5% in 2025, in line with the government's official target. India is once again forecast to be the world’s fastest-growing major economy, advancing at a 7% clip, down from a sizzling 7.7% last year. The IMF is a 191-nation lending organization that works to promote economic growth and financial stability and to reduce global poverty. At the meetings in Bangkok, finance ministers and central bank governors will assess the state of the world economy and discuss strategies to support financial stability and sustained growth.
