events.title: Axios-Ipsos poll: "Medicare for All" support surges
events.summary: Supporters of "Medicare for All" now outnumber opponents by nearly 2-to-1, according to a new survey of U.S. adults from the Axios-Ipsos American Health Index . The big picture: Two-thirds of all survey respondents — and half of Republicans — said the federal government should be willing to spend more tax dollars to lower health care costs for Americans. Why it matters: With three weeks to go before the midterm elections, and private health insurance premiums and prescription prices crushing voters, these findings suggest a path for swing-state candidates who embrace socialized medicine. But the public's openness is driven more by desperation than by confidence in government. Affordability is foremost on most Americans' minds, and health care brings almost daily reminders of economic pressure. Between the lines: Survey respondents say they want more government intervention — but they trust those leaders less than ever. Trust in President Trump for health-related information fell to a survey low of 20%. Trust in Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. fell to a survey low of 25%. Trust in congressional Republicans (20%) and Democrats (25%) also were at lows. By the numbers: 43% of Americans said they support the idea of establishing a "Medicare for All" program to provide government-run health insurance to all, largely replacing private health insurance; 24% oppose the idea and 32% say they aren't sure. Nearly half of independents (47%) support it, as do 62% of Democrats. 21% of Republicans support Medicare for All, and 27% are undecided, compared with 52% who oppose the idea. The other side: Opponents said their top reason is they fear Medicare for All would have a worse quality of care than private insurance. Other reasons were feeling it would become too expensive for taxpayers; that government should not be providing health care; or that it would expand the size of government too much. But resistance to the idea has changed markedly from recent campaign cycles, when centrist Democrats were likelier to embrace a public health insurance option or a version of Medicare for All with a role for private insurance. What we're watching: Respondents said they'd be more likely to support congressional candidates this year if those candidates favored expanding government subsidies of health care costs, reinstating enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits that expired at the beginning of this year and expanding prescription drug discount platforms. Republicans are less supportive than Democrats and independents. But the GOP is divided over expanding government subsidies for health care costs, with 31% more likely to back a candidate who supports the idea, 29% less likely and 31% saying it would make no difference. Half of respondents said they'd be less likely to support a candidate backed by pharmaceutical and drug companies, compared with 7% saying they'd be more likely. What they're saying: "Health care is one of the significant ways that people experience economic pressure every day," said Mallory Newall, Ipsos vice president for U.S. public affairs. "'Medicare for All' is still something that many Americans have questions on" and "the amount of Americans answering 'not sure' tells me people's sentiments aren't fully formed," Newall said. Still, the current level of support is "noteworthy — and it is not solely driven by members of the Democratic Party," she added. Depending on the candidate's party affiliation or the makeup of their district, "Maybe they don't call it 'Medicare for All,'" Newall said. But expanding federal programs to cover more Americans' health costs "is a message that can connect with voters during this cycle." Methodology: This Axios-Ipsos Poll was conducted Sept. 25 – 28, 2026, by Ipsos' KnowledgePanel®. This poll is based on a nationally representative probability sample of 1,122 general population adults age 18 or older. The margin of sampling error is +/-3.0 percentage points at the 95% confidence level, for results based on the entire sample of adults.

events.title: AI labs are fueling a wild market for your Slack DMs
events.summary: Tyler Le/BI As they race to automate white-collar work, AI labs have found the perfect source of training data: your Slack DMs. Business owners are getting six-figure "exploding offers" that expire in 48 hours to sell their data. Instagram is flooded with ads declaring that "AI needs your data" and promising millions. The data is priced by the terabyte, anonymized, and sold to AI giants desperate for an edge. Tech giants have moved to harvest their employees' data for AI training. And, once focused on dead startups, brokers now pay for live data from active companies. "Right now, the demand is just astronomical," said Dan Novaes, the CEO of Mode.Inc , a startup that sells data to AI model developers. Mundane workplace data is more valuable than ever as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and others build AI agents for businesses. Annual spending on data for AI is projected to explode from less than $1 billion last year to almost $6.5 billion in 2027, Gartner estimates. The boom has a darker side. Employees rarely profit from — or know about — their Slacks, PowerPoints, and Google Docs being sold to the highest bidder. Suspected hackers have shopped around a large company's stolen codebase for millions of dollars. Meta's attempt to harvest its own employees' data for its AI models sparked a revolt . This story is part of a series called The AI Data Grab , an inside look at how tech giants are increasingly turning to workers, users, and the physical world to get data to train AI. Read more stories in this series here . Some CEOs are getting blindsided. Doug Kreuzkamp, who runs airline operations company Springshot, was sitting in his office on a Zoom call in August when he found out that Google had bought his data. Springshot, a longtime vendor for the now-bankrupt Spirit Airlines , helped flights coordinate with workers such as gate agents and cleaners. Bankrupt Spirit Airlines is selling off its data. The Dallas Morning News/ Getty Images "I had less than 48 hours' notice — from the media — that the intellectual property we had spent 15 years building could be given away," Kreuzkamp told Business Insider. The surging market is pushing into uncharted waters, and the industry risks a reckoning with workers and regulators, said Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University. The lack of federal privacy laws leaves few legal barriers to companies collecting data from their employees for AI training, she added. "The question is, does the consent of the employees from whom they collected that data actually extend to the sale of the data? I think it's an ethically gray area," Ajunwa said. Business data has become the new oil The boom has created a thriving group of go-betweens who hunt for small businesses rich in data and low on cash. After scrubbing sensitive information like Social Security numbers and home addresses, they resell it to AI giants. Although the industry is new, it's become highly competitive. Ryan Lock, cofounder of AI broker Polyshares, compares it to the oil boom that hit Texas in the early 1900s, when prospectors snapped up cheap land from farmers who didn't realize the true value of the oil underneath it. Small-business owners sitting on troves of internal records may not realize the seemingly mundane files could be worth big money. Tactics like 48-hour deadlines have become common, Lock said. "The offers being made look almost identical to those early oil offers," he said from his home base in Dallas. "They'll say, 'I'm offering you double market. I need an answer by Friday.'" Pumpjacks operating in the Permian Basin in Texas. Bloomberg/Getty Images Lock and his cofounders went through the data-licensing process themselves with their other companies, sometimes laughing out loud at the lowball offers they got. Their firm tries to bridge that information gap by giving business owners more transparency about what their data is worth. "There's still plenty of money for everyone, but business owners should receive more of the benefit," he said. Wanted: data from companies, dead or alive Data that demonstrates how work is actually done is highly valuable, said William Almeida, the chief revenue officer of AI training startup Micro1 , because it provides critical context on how decisions are made and products are built. That information can help train agents , the autonomous computer-using AI tools that have become a major focus for companies like Meta and SpaceXAI. As AI companies build new models, the real-world data guides the AI on how best to handle specific tasks. Micro1 announced a program earlier this year that pays midsize companies $100,000 to $2 million for access to anonymized data. Almeida said AI developers increasingly want "long-horizon" data that can provide a full picture of how work gets done. If a company won't sell its Slack, customer relationship management, or email records, the rest of the corpus is less valuable. The data is priced based on a multitude of factors, with volume being a critical one. The more white-collar employees a company has, the more valuable its data corpus is, said Novaes, the Mode.Inc CEO. Mode.Inc CEO Dan Novaes and tech chief Kiran Panesar. Mode.Inc Other factors, like exclusivity, matter — there's lower demand for a codebase that a rival lab already has its hands on. Fields that AI giants are trying the hardest to automate, like law and accounting, see especially high demand. Generally, though, any company — dead or alive, big or small — can sell its data, as long as it has enough. "People need to wake up to it and take this opportunity," Novaes said. Grant Gooley decided to license his company's data to an AI training company. His agency, MyPortal Marketing, has sold Micro1 everything from Figma and Canva files to checklists for onboarding clients to Google ads. He said it didn't sell client-specific material. "If AI is going to be trained, why not be part of that, and do it responsibly?" Gooley said. A new breed of security and privacy concerns While the market creates wealth for some, it's breeding new kinds of cybersecurity and privacy risks for others. Nick Heiner helps improve AI agents by building office-like digital environments at AI training startup Surge AI . Heiner said that earlier this year, he was approached by a group offering a large company's codebase for millions of dollars. "It became apparent that this group did not have the rights to sell this data," Heiner told Business Insider. "They had illicitly obtained a copy of the codebase and were just going around to all the data vendors saying, 'Can I get a few million bucks for this?'" Security and consent concerns aren't limited to hackers. Google's bid to buy Spirit Airlines' old data for $10 million has been held up, in part, by flight attendants worried about how their records will be used. Last week, Sen. events.title: Raising financially capable children begins before their first dollar
events.summary: As children grow up, parents eventually face a longer-term question: How can we make sure our children become financially capable themselves? SINGAPORE – It takes a village to raise a child , as the popular proverb goes. Most parents would agree. Recognising this, Singapore’s Government recently announced additional measures for families, ranging from more childcare leave and lower pre-school fees to housing assistance and increased direct funding of nearly $70,000 for every Singaporean child from birth to age 17, up from around $56,500 previously. But financial support for new families is only one part of the story. As children grow up, parents face a longer-term question: How can we make sure our children become financially capable themselves? The answer is not simply to teach them more about money. Rather, it is to help them develop the judgment to use it well. And that happens through conversation, observation and age-appropriate practices – a process sometimes described as financial parenting. Children begin learning about money well before they can count it. Those who see their parents compare prices learn that money involves choices. A child who is told that something is too expensive may learn restraint. And one who sees adults panic whenever markets are volatile may conclude that uncertainty is something to fear. These early experiences shape financial habits, behaviours and confidence, which over time influence financial well-being. In effect, parents are teaching their children about money even when they are not trying to. The apple does not fall far from the financial tree That also means parents should think about what they themselves learnt about money when growing up. Many of us carry powerful money stories from childhood. Money may have represented security, freedom or opportunity, or perhaps secrecy, scarcity, status or anxiety. These stories, or “money scripts”, can often shape how we parent around money. It’s worth asking ourselves: What do we want to pass on to the next generation from our own upbringing? What are we teaching through our words and actions? And importantly, what are we actually allowing them to practise? These tough questions help clarify which lessons are worth preserving, which may need updating, and which are better left behind altogether. This distinction matters because financial knowledge and financial behaviour are not the same thing. Knowing the importance of saving money is financial awareness. Regularly setting aside part of an allowance is behaviour. Similarly, understanding why diversification matters is part of financial capability. Remaining calm rather than selling impulsively during a market decline is behaviour. This is why financial education cannot stop at knowledge alone. Children need opportunities to make choices themselves. That can start simply by making money visible without making it overwhelming. Explain choices and trade-offs, and involve children in appropriate family decisions. Give them some responsibility for a small budget, a saving goal or defined spending categories. It is equally important to let them see how we behave when things do not go according to plan. How do we respond during market volatility, when an unexpected expense arises or when we realise we have made a poor financial decision? And children should be allowed to make some mistakes, manage consequences and reflect on what could be done differently next time. For affluent families, there is an added challenge. Wealth can give children tremendous advantages – education, networks, access to good advice and, later in life, the ability to take entrepreneurial risks. But there is a paradox here. The same resources that create opportunities can also remove some of the everyday experiences through which financial judgment is formed. Waiting for something you want. Choosing one purchase over another. Living within a budget. Making a mistake and having to live with the consequences. If their every overspent budget is topped up and every financial mistake quietly fixed, children may grow up enjoying the benefits of family resources without seeing the effort, planning and trade-offs behind them. This does not mean wealthy parents should manufacture hardship. Nor should children be made to feel guilty about being fortunate. A better approach is to give them responsibility while keeping sensible guardrails in place and raising the stakes gradually as judgment improves. When should investment education begin? Investment education is a natural extension of this process. A young child does not need a complex lesson on asset allocation. But as children become teenagers and young adults, investing provides a useful way to bring together many of the lessons they have already learnt about saving, patience, risk and choice. Research on younger investors also suggests that parents matter.

events.title: Qatar's government revenue fell 42% in first half due to Iran war, Emir says
events.summary: Qatar's revenue fell 42 per cent in the first half of this year, as exports of liquefied natural gas (LNG) dropped due to the impact of the Iran war, Emir Sheikh Tamim said during a Shura Council meeting. LNG exports from Qatar, the world’s second-largest supplier before the conflict, has fallen sharply due to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz as well attacks on its Ras Laffan complex . “The crisis naturally had an adverse impact on public finances, with total revenues falling by 42 per cent during the first half of the year, while public expenditures decreased by 14 per cent – all without compromising essential services or development priorities,” Sheikh Tamim said. “We decided against curtailing essential services and chose not to alter development priorities, aiming to sustain the economic momentum Qatar is experiencing.” Measures taken before the crisis, such as strengthening reserves, reducing public debt, adopting conservative oil-price assumptions in the budget and developing non-oil revenue, helped Qatar absorb the economic fallout, he said. About 17 per cent of Qatar’s LNG capacity is offline after Iranian strikes damaged two of its 14 export trains, removing 12.8 million tonnes a year from the market. QatarEnergy has said repairs will take three to five years, meaning even a safe reopening of Hormuz would restore access to only part of Qatar’s prewar supply. Gas prices have soared globally due to the disruption. Disruption to Qatar's energy sector affects markets and consumers worldwide, the Emir said on Tuesday. “The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, along with direct damage to some energy facilities in Ras Laffan Industrial City, has disrupted a significant portion of the country's exports,” he said. However, the economic fallout is concentrated mainly in the energy sector, while non-hydrocarbon industries continue to grow, accounting for about 80 per cent of real gross domestic product, he added. “This reflects the national economy's ability to withstand and continue growing under exceptional and complex circumstances,” Sheikh Tamim said. Economies across the Gulf are projected to contract by an average of 4.3 per cent for 2026, down 5.7 percentage points from April, driven by lower export volumes due to the Strait of Hormuz's closure, leading to significant losses in output and government revenue, the World Bank said last week. Qatar's economy is estimated to be hit the hardest among all countries in the region, facing a 20.9 per cent contraction this year, compared to 1.8 per cent growth in 2025, the World Bank said. The estimate would represent the country's weakest economic performance in five decades, after its average monthly gas production fell by about 67 per cent between March and July due to damage sustained at its sites. Meanwhile, the International Monetary Fund in its update this week said it expects Qatar's economy to contract by 15.6 per cent this year, before rebounding to growth of 18.8 per cent in 2027. Investments of $60.7 billion However, Qatar will emerge from the regional crisis more resilient and better adapted to global changes, Sheikh Tamim said. “We have a portfolio of projects and investment opportunities valued at approximately 221 billion riyals [$60.7 billion] over the next five years,” he said. Planned investments will cover infrastructure, public-private partnerships and private-sector projects in real estate and hospitality, he added. Sheikh Tamim said Qatar had faced three simultaneous responsibilities during the crisis: protecting its sovereignty, fulfilling its role in global energy and economic security, and keeping diplomatic channels open. “Our strategy for shouldering these responsibilities consisted of four main elements: first, firmly defending the homeland without being drawn into war; second, maintaining services, supply chains and economic activity; third, contributing to efforts to secure a ceasefire and open waterways; and fourth, encouraging negotiations and seeking opportunities to return to talks to reach peaceful solutions to the conflict,” he said. Sheikh Tamim said the goal is “not merely to return to the pre-crisis status quo, but to use recovery as a springboard to accelerate economic diversification and strengthen national capabilities”. “God willing, Qatar will emerge from this crisis more resilient and better adapted to global changes,” he added.

events.title: A golden age of corporate profits
events.summary: Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips; Note: After-tax profit data includes inventory and capital depreciation adjustments. Corporate America is raking in record profits, luxuriating in luscious margins and capturing the largest chunk of the country's income on record. Why it matters: The corporate bonanza is bolstering the stock market, but it may also be playing a role in the persistently sour sentiment among the American electorate. The latest: Tuesday is the unofficial start of third-quarter earnings season as JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs and others report results. Zoom in: Wall Street expects the members of the blue-chip S&P 500 index to continue to make it rain. Third-quarter earnings per share are expected to grow roughly 29% for the index, compared with the quarter in 2025, according to estimate data collected by FactSet. That's after a massive 50% annual increase in second-quarter earnings that was supercharged by the giant, non-operating gains on valuations of tech investments reported by Amazon and Alphabet. (Amazon, for example, penciled in its stake in Anthropic as boosting its profit by more than $50 billion.) But even without those enormous gains, the numbers were quite strong, thanks to the AI boom that analysts expect to keep powering giant profits. What they're saying: The market is still all about AI, but the gains are extremely concentrated . "At the stock level, AI infrastructure stocks are expected to drive more than half of S&P 500 EPS growth in Q3," wrote Ben Snider, chief U.S. equity analyst with Goldman Sachs. Snider noted that more than two-thirds of the total growth in S&P 500 earnings for the quarter is expected to come from just 10 stocks. What's more, Micron Technology and Nvidia alone are expected to generate more than one-third of the growth in earnings for the blue chips, Snider wrote. The big picture: Broader measures of U.S. corporate profitability captured by economic — rather than stock market — data also seem to show remarkable strength. For the economy as a whole, after-tax corporate profits in Q2 jumped 18.2% compared with the same quarter of 2025. And key measures of corporate profit margins across the entire U.S. economy are some of the fattest on record. Data: FactSet, U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips; Note: After-tax U.S. corporate profits, including inventory and capital consumption adjustments as a share of gross value added of U.S. corporate business. Reflects profits made within the U.S.; does not include profits produced overseas. The other side: Boom times for corporate America have a flip side, however, with the so-called labor share of national income collapsing to some of the lowest levels on record. The labor share tells you what percentage of the giant paycheck produced by the U.S. economy goes to workers in the form of wages and benefits, rather than to corporate profits, dividends, rents and interest paid to other economic actors, commonly summarized as "capital." The bottom line: That decline helps explain the persistently sour mood of the American public toward the economy and its deep skepticism toward the AI boom that's producing this bonanza for American corporations.

events.title: Trump AI directive sparks questions
events.summary: The newly minted Super Intelligence Task Force is telling AI companies to report and immediately remediate any instances of rogue behavior involving their products, a rare effort by the Trump administration to exert more power over the firms developing the advanced technology. An Anthropic incident in which a testing model submitted visa applications, according to a State Department spokesman, spurred the task force’s first “action,” which it’s referring to as a “notification and remediation process.” Frontier AI labs largely do this sort of disclosure and incident reporting already, and Trump’s task force has not laid out exactly what will count as an “incident” that must be reported going forward. Still, the administration’s decision to make an example of Anthropic is likely to trigger more disclosures than before. “Our message to all SI companies is clear: delayed notification, inadequate corrective action, and a failure to take responsibility will not be tolerated,” task force leaders Jay Clayton, Andrew Ferguson, Scott Kupor, and Emil Michael said in a statement. The effectiveness and scope of the new requirements will depend in part on how the task force defines an “incident,” how quickly it must be disclosed, who it must be reported to, and the consequences for not doing so. Officials have yet to lay out these details, and companies are seeking more clarity. Anthropic contacted the task force to disclose the latest incident and has a history of reporting security episodes publicly and tweaking models to prevent more harm. — Ashley Gold

events.title: I'm the CEO of Midi Health. Walking all day and my daily Diet Coke keeps me sane.
events.summary: Joanna Strober runs Midi Health, a virtual care platform for women in perimenopause and menopause. Ian Tuttle for BI This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Joanna Strober, the 58-year-old cofounder and CEO of Midi Health , a virtual care platform dedicated to modernizing women's healthcare. She is based in Los Altos Hills, California. This story has been edited for length and clarity. I'm the founder and CEO of Midi Health . We started the company to bridge the gap in healthcare by providing specialized, insurance-covered care for women in their 30s, 40s, 50s, and 60s. For many years, I didn't have time to take care of myself. Taking care of three kids and working was not easy. It was all-encompassing. I had a big wake-up call when I was 44 years old and had a small fall and fractured my shoulder. I discovered that I had osteopenia, or low bone density, at a very young age. That was a good indicator that I needed to focus more on prevention and taking care of myself. Now I'm making up for the lost time. Strober doesn't like to use trackers. Instead, she said she focuses on healthy behaviors. Ian Tuttle for BI I wake up at 6:30 a.m., and I walk I wake up and have two Nespresso pods and two pieces of Levain bread from a bakery called Manresa Bread. It's a very dense multigrain loaf that fills you up. For the past 10 years, I've had this bread every single morning for breakfast, or as soon as the bakery opens. Strober walks for an hour every morning. Ian Tuttle for BI Then I walk for about an hour. That is the most important part of my routine. I listen to podcasts about politics or AI. I like "Hard Fork," "The Daily," "The Ezra Klein Show," and "Call Me Back." I'm in the office by 8:15 a.m. The goal is to lift weights after my walk, but it doesn't always happen. I go to the office after, and then I have lots of Zoom calls and product meetings. I try to schedule another 45-minute walk around lunchtime. I take a lot of phone calls and have been told I talk loudly when I walk. It's actually a joke in my neighborhood. I allow myself one Diet Coke a day I mostly drink chamomile tea in the afternoon, but I also let myself have one Diet Coke per day . Keeping my bones strong is a big focus I take Midi's Omega-3+, which also has vitamin D and K in it, and that's for my bones because I have osteopenia . I also take creatine and fiber. I either take the Midi fiber gummies or I just make sure I get enough fiber. I also use hormone replacement therapy to help prevent bone deterioration. Strober takes an Omega-3 supplement, as well as creatine and fiber. Ian Tuttle for BI I'm not neurotic about my meals I have a salad or a sandwich for lunch, or sometimes I walk somewhere to get lunch. For many years, my life was structured around getting my kids breakfast or dinner. Now they're no longer home, and it's actually very liberating. It means I can work much later and have fewer guardrails. I usually get dinner between 6:30 and 7 p.m. Sometimes I'll pick up a random dinner on the way home or make pasta. Or, I'll eat ice cream for dinner. I watch TV every evening and eat ice cream I don't drink or do drugs. I love British detective TV shows. I find it very relaxing to watch TV and eat ice cream. I buy low-sugar blackberry jam from the farmers market and eat it with chocolate ice cream every night. I'm asleep by 9:30 p.m. Walking keeps me sane Strober walks The Dish, which is a roughly three-and-a-half-mile uphill hike, at least twice every weekend. Ian Tuttle for BI In general, I've been trying different meditation apps . I can't say it's working, but I am trying. Walking is my best route to sanity. I walk over 10,000 steps every day, but it's less about step count and more about making sure my body moves for multiple hours. My morning walk is in the hills, but when I walk flat, I try to wear a weighted vest. Every weekend, I walk The Dish at least twice, and sometimes three or four times. It's our local hike in Palo Alto. It's about three-and-a-half miles, and it's uphill. I also schedule at least one or two walks a day with different friends for social activity. On weekends, I also go to the farmers market and cook. My 81-year-old mom makes me dinner every Friday When I was younger and had children, my mom and I made a deal that she would cook dinner for my family every Friday night. Now the kids are gone, and she still cooks dinner for my husband and me every Friday. It's the one night a week I know I'm going to get good food, and someone is going to take care of me. I feel really lucky. I think a lot about prevention Strober said she thinks a lot about prevention and that she prioritizes "sleeping enough, eating the right foods, and getting the right exercise." Ian Tuttle for BI I don't want to be crippled as an older lady. I've also watched what it's like to have someone with Alzheimer's in my family, and I'm scared of that. I think a lot about what I can do to stay healthy and prevent heart disease, Alzheimer's, and bone disease. I don't track macros or anything like that, but I am very neurotic about my cancer screenings and the behaviors that are easy to do to make sure that I stay healthy as long as I can — like sleeping enough, eating the right foods, and getting the right exercise. I think about what I can do to make sure I can eventually run after my grandkids. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Why would anyone want this job?
events.summary: Ben’s view On May 13, 2022, then-White House Middle East envoy Brett McGurk asked his boss how he liked his job. Joe Biden, he’d noticed, had been a chatty, expressive vice president, but had grown quieter in a way that wasn’t just about his age. “There’s no joy in it,” Biden responded. “That’s the difference. No joy in this job.” McGurk’s new memoir cataloguing two grim years of trying to negotiate between American and regional officials is, among other things, a set of portraits of miserable world leaders: There’s the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who “seemed annoyed to be there” when the Americans showed up to ask for help with oil prices. Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, pressed by Biden to negotiate, “seemed lost, used to meetings that started nowhere and ended there.” Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi “looked down at his shoes shuffling on the carpet” as “something was weighing on him.” Biden took out his own irritation on the short-lived Israeli Prime Minister Yair Lapid, telling him, “Don’t be a phony, man.” Lapid, in turn, “recoiled.” And so on. In McGurk’s account, only the “smug” and inscrutable Benjamin Netanyahu isn’t obviously unhappy. This narrative of the woes of leadership could serve as a cautionary tale for the few dozen men and women in both of America’s political parties currently searching their souls and consulting their spouses about whether to run for president. Journalists typically treat these deliberations as theater. But even the people most obviously preparing to run take them more seriously than you’d imagine. Win or lose, a candidate’s campaign will consume their life and their loved ones’; a victory guarantees their life will change forever. So while Vice President JD Vance’s aides right now appear quite confident he’ll run, they also sincerely believe that he hasn’t yet — totally — decided. Vice presidents are special: They have already paid the price of national office, getting far less in return than their bosses. But one Republican elder who likes Vance is advising against it: He suggests Vance return to Ohio, get to work reinventing trade education or some other worthy task, and run for president as the guy, rather than Donald Trump’s shadow. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s supporters, meanwhile, swear he hasn’t taken any steps toward running, much less decided on it. They also caution people against saying he’s not running, however: He hasn’t decided anything. On the Democratic side, we assume they’re all running — California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Sens. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., and Cory Booker, D-N.J., and the rest. But they might want to read McGurk’s book and think about whether they really want the job. Because oddly, of all the distinguishing qualities of successful presidential candidates, ambition turns out to be perhaps the most salient. One former Biden administration official recently quipped that their money was on Maryland Gov. Wes Moore for the Democratic nomination, because he has the single quality you most need to become president: really, really wanting to be president. Room for Disagreement The potential candidates will also hear more cynical arguments in favor of running no matter what. ABC News observed in 2024 : “there are also a lot of benefits, even if you lose: better job opportunities, increased public profiles and the chance to build up a war chest for the next run.”

events.title: Swing-district Democrats keep focus on high prices
events.summary: The News New controversies concerning the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement and foreign lobbying aren’t steering Democrats away from their focus on affordability in the final three weeks before the midterms. “Billionaires are better off, but certainly the average people living here in Bucks County are not, and so people are tired of it,” said Bob Harvie, a Bucks County commissioner running to unseat Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., in one of the swingiest districts in the country. Harvie is trying to link Fitzpatrick to Trump and national Republicans, though the incumbent has maintained an independent streak in Congress, including by voting against Republicans’ domestic policy megabill. Following last week’s ICE shooting in New York, Harvie said, “what people see is a government that really is run through chaos, which is what Donald Trump specializes in, and Brian Fitzpatrick sits and watches it happen.” Fitzpatrick’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment. Know More Democrats have previously come up short in trying to defeat Fitzpatrick, who is one of the few House Republicans representing a district won by Kamala Harris in 2024. But Democrats hope national headwinds against Republicans will flip the seat; they also see Harvie as having a key advantage, given he’s better funded than previous challengers and can draft off support for Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro. “I think there are definitely people who are tired of Fitzpatrick’s act. They realize that you know he’s not independent,” said Harvie. “He basically does what Donald Trump needs him to do.” In a show of support from party leadership, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries appeared with Harvie over the weekend. Harvie said he’d support Jeffries for speaker next year: “I’m looking forward to having somebody in the leadership role for this party who’s going to move us forward and focus on the issues that matter to people.”

events.title: Every major Nvidia customer is now a competitor as Microsoft reveals new Maia chip
events.summary: The trillion-dollar AI race is moving from software to silicon, as Microsoft's massive bet on its proprietary Maia chips proves Big Tech wants to wean itself off Nvidia's dominance. Why it matters: Microsoft's plan to power its AI products with custom silicon shows how every major Nvidia customer is now a competitor, seeking lower costs, improved performance and more control. The shift is particularly significant for inference — the computing needed to generate AI responses — as more sophisticated AI models and agents drive demand for computing power. Driving the news: Microsoft unveiled Maia 300, its latest custom AI accelerator, saying it will begin deploying the chip in 2027 and it will become the primary inference system for its own products and services. The company says Maia 300 will deliver 40% more AI tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems. It's also designed to minimize unnecessary data movement between chips and memory, a growing bottleneck as AI models become more complex. The big picture: Microsoft's plan is part of a much broader shift, with nearly all major AI players seeking Nvidia alternatives. Google has been developing its own Tensor Processing Units for years, with its latest generation including separate versions optimized for training AI models and running inference. OpenAI is developing its Jalapeño chip with Broadcom, initially focusing on inference workloads. The company said in August that its first chip was outperforming Nvidia hardware on certain workloads and that it was already developing subsequent generations. Amazon has its own ⁠ Trainium family of AI chips, which are being used by customers including Anthropic. OpenAI has also committed to using Amazon's custom silicon as part of a massive infrastructure agreement. Anthropic confirmed in August that it is exploring its own chip designs, even as it continues to rely on chips from Nvidia, Amazon and other suppliers. Meta also has an internal chip development program, while continuing to buy substantial computing capacity from Nvidia and other suppliers. Between the lines: Nvidia isn't necessarily losing business just because its customers are developing competing chips. Nvidia's revenue more than doubled to $96 billion in the second quarter, a reminder that overall demand for AI computing leaves room for Nvidia chips and new offerings from Microsoft and others. Like Microsoft, most Nvidia competitors are focused on inference, where margins are highest, while Nvidia remains dominant for training. Still, Nvidia has begun to leverage its balance sheet to bankroll the AI buildout , so any competition that even slightly reduces its strength is noteworthy because it could weaken its centrality to continued growth. What they're saying: Building competitive AI hardware requires designing entire systems, optimizing everything from memory and networking to software and power consumption, Rani Borkar, Microsoft's president of Azure Hardware Systems and Innovation, told Axios. "We prioritize Maia for inference," Borkar said, describing it as the largest and fastest-growing opportunity for AI computing and an area where Microsoft can distinguish itself on cost and efficiency. "For us, it's not an either-or strategy," she said. "We want a broad ecosystem while investing deeply in our first-party silicon." Yes, but: Microsoft's plans to make Maia its primary inference platform apply specifically to Microsoft's own services, not necessarily to third-party Azure customers, including OpenAI. Borkar also cautioned that the shift won't happen overnight. Maia 300 deployments will begin in 2027, but reaching multi-gigawatt scale will take time, extending beyond next year. The catch: As Axios ⁠ previously reported , companies developing their own chips remain dependent on the same limited manufacturing capacity, advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory that Nvidia relies on. That means even if custom chips can reduce dependence on Nvidia, they don't eliminate broader supply-chain constraints. The bottom line: Nvidia remains central to the AI boom, but its biggest customers increasingly want to control more of the technology powering their own services — and capture more of the economic benefits for themselves.

events.title: Dems' red-state showings raise prospect of a bigger 2028 map
events.summary: Data: RealClearPolitics , American Presidency Project ; Note: Nebraska's Senate race is between a Republican and an independent; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Move over Wisconsin and Arizona. With Democrats making Republicans sweat in a host of red-state Senate races , a new batch of swing states may be emerging. Why it matters: Some of the closest Senate races are in Nebraska, Ohio, Texas, Iowa and even Kansas. Sure, this could be a blip — or a reminder that it's a 50-50 moody nation, even in a bunch of red states. The conditions that helped Barack Obama carry conservative states like Indiana and North Carolina in 2008 — an unpopular war, a bruising economy, an electorate hungry for change — could resonate again in 2028. State of play: Democratic and Republican Senate candidates are running margin-of-error races in red states that not long ago were thought to be forbidding, or even a wasted effort, to many Democrats. The Senate races in Kansas and Ohio are tied. So is Nebraska, where independent Dan Osborn is trying to knock off Sen. Pete Ricketts. Democrat James Talarico has consistently led polls in Texas, though that race appears to be tightening as money pours into the state on behalf of Republican Ken Paxton. Alaska is also a toss-up. President Trump won all these states by double digits in 2024. Zoom in: Republican operatives told Axios they're far from convinced that what's happening now will create a new slate of swing states in the 2028 race for the White House. They see the current campaign as more of a one-off — a combination of dismay with Trump, high prices and uninspiring candidates. "None of those states will be targeted [by Democrats] in the 2028 presidential. I will bet big money on that. But … all are in danger this year," one GOP consultant told Axios. "It's a function of the atmosphere that we're playing defense in R+15 states. There's lethargy on our side," a Republican pollster said. "I don't think they're the new swing states per se." But Democrats say better-than-expected performances by their candidates in several red states would at least open the door to an expanded map — with a big "if." "An opening, yes," Obama's former chief strategist, David Axelrod, told Axios. "A guarantee, hardly." Obama, he said, spent an enormous amount of time in rural communities and got to know voters. The Democrats who are faring well in those places this year have made a point of speaking with, not at, conservatives. Yes, but: There's no certainty that Democrats will prevail in red states this year, much less set a path for 2028. Polls are narrowing in several other Senate battlegrounds besides Texas, and the polling industry has had enough misses and challenges in recent elections to raise questions about whether we're getting an accurate picture of the political landscape at this time. Either way, it's safe to say Democrats have made things interesting for the Nov. 3 election. The big picture: The backlash against Trump has set the tone in many of these surprisingly competitive Senate surprise states, but Democrats also have also benefited from factors specific to each race. In Ohio, former three-term Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) is better known than the incumbent, Sen. Jon Husted (R). In Texas, Democrats have a seminarian candidate in James Talarico who's emphasized the Bible's teachings as Republicans have tried to tag him as a radical leftist. His opponent, Ken Paxton, has been dogged by corruption allegations throughout the race. In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton is the pastor of the largest United Methodist church in the country. His opponent, GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, has been hurt by reports that his former medical practice sued patients for even small unpaid bills, and that his 2020 campaign stiffed a bakery on a $700 bill. What we're watching: To build on any openings Democrats might realize this year, the party will need a 2028 candidate who can appeal to center-right voters the way Democrats in red states have this year, Axelrod said. "Part of the long-term problem for Democrats has been that it's still a party of working people, but it often approaches working people — especially in small towns in rural areas, in the spirit of missionaries and anthropologists," Axelrod said. Like, "we're here to help you become more like us." So in 2028, he added,"it depends on who the candidate is, and what kind of bonds of trust that candidate can build."

events.title: SpaceX agrees to testify to NYC Council about AI safety after receiving subpoena
events.summary: SpaceX has agreed to testify before the New York City Council as part of an investigation into artificial intelligence safety risks. The city council subpoenaed SpaceX CEO Elon Musk ordering that he or another representative testify at a hearing last week. SpaceX skipped that hearing, while representatives from Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and Google all testified. SpaceX has agreed to testify before the New York City Council this week as part of a legislative investigation concerning artificial intelligence safety risks, the council announced on Tuesday. The council said in a press release that the hearing will take place on Friday at 10 a.m. ET in front of its tech committee. Julie Menin, council speaker, and Nwamaka Ejebe, general counsel, issued a subpoena to Elon Musk and SpaceX's AI unit on Sept. 28, compelling testimony for a hearing that took place last week. Representatives from Anthropic , OpenAI , Google and Meta all testified at the hearing on Oct. 5, but SpaceX did not appear. Menin said in Tuesday's statement that SpaceX agreed two days later to testify after the council said it intended to have its subpoena enforced by a judge. "Last Monday, we held a major, hours-long hearing with whistleblowers, the world's largest tech companies, and the nation's foremost experts in AI," Menin said in Tuesday's release. "Conspicuously absent was SpaceXAI, which is unacceptable." Musk folded his AI venture, xAI, into SpaceX in February, creating a conglomerate that includes its Grok models, which are used by some federal agencies, including the Pentagon . SpaceX went public in June and is now valued at over $2 trillion. In August, SpaceX also completed a $60 billion acquisition of AI coding startup Cursor. SpaceX competes with Anthropic and OpenAI in the AI market, though Grok trails far behind models from top rivals. The NYC council opened its investigation following a month of intense debate surrounding the risks posed by advanced AI models. In its original letter ordering testimony from Musk or another SpaceX leader, the council said its investigation would help, "assess whether fast-emerging risks to public safety, cybersecurity, economic stability, privacy, consumers and businesses warrant immediate legislative action to protect New Yorkers." SpaceX's "failure to comply" with the subpoena, the council warned, could subject the company to penalties or other punishment under New York City laws and regulations. Carmen De La Rosa, chair of the tech committee, told CNBC in a statement that the council expects answers from SpaceX. "With the proliferation of Elon Musk's technology at the federal level, it is even more important they come to the discussion with robust context about data privacy, safeguards, and whistleblower protections," she said. Lawsuits are piling up against SpaceX after Grok's image generator enabled mass production and distribution of deepfake porn based on images of real people who did consent. SpaceX didn't respond to a request for comment. — CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed reporting. WATCH: Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and Google execs testify at NYC Council meeting

events.title: What Flock Actually Costs Cities Across the Country
events.summary: In 2020, the police department of picturesque Covington, Georgia, paid Flock Safety , the surveillance technology company, $40,000 to maintain 20 cameras around the city. The next year, it paid the same amount. In 2022, that cost went up to $81,250. Fifteen new “Falcon” cameras, which Flock says have more sophisticated technology for reading license plates, accounted for $37,500. Another $3,750 went toward installing the new cameras, and the rest was spent maintaining the initial fleet. WIRED has made this article free for all to read because it is primarily based on reporting from public records requests. Please consider subscribing to support our journalism . Then, in 2024, the department paid Flock $113,225. Of that, $87,500 was to maintain its existing 35 cameras, a rate it agreed to pay for the next five years, and the remainder went toward eight new Falcon cameras. The next year, Covington paid Flock $159,000 for a combination of camera maintenance and enrollment in its Drone as First Responder program, which uses drones to fly to emergency scenes and stream footage back to the police station. It’s unclear how much Covington will wind up paying Flock in 2026, but through August, it has paid $201,000—$100,000 to maintain its existing cameras, $800 to replace one, and another $100,200 for new software products. The Covington Police Department did not respond to a request for comment. Overall, Flock is a small fraction of the Covington police department’s $12,488,733 budget for June 2025 to July 2026. But amid fierce blowback about Flock’s surveillance practices, contracts with the company are now being scrutinized in cities across the country. Flock did not provide a comment for this story. WIRED obtained documents via public record request from a dozen Flock customers across the country and compared them to publicly available information from more than a dozen others. The documents shed light on how much Flock can actually cost communities, the way many of those deals are structured, and how the deals can expand over several years—leaving taxpayers on the hook year after year, with no end in sight. “Once you let police officers try a tool,” says Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, “it becomes really hard to get the political will and motivation to take that tool away from them.” When Flock was founded in 2017, it originally sold its license plate readers to private homeowner associations (HOAs). By the time the company decided to sell to police departments in 2019, it had an in: Rather than starting a camera network from scratch, police could start by accessing the cameras that HOAs were already using. A version of this story played out in Alpharetta, Georgia . In 2020, the city’s police department paid Flock $17,680 for five Falcon cameras and logins for Flock software called Wing, which can extract vehicle and license plate data from off-brand camera footage. The next year, when Alpharetta bought a few more Flock cameras, a payment justification noted that “several” local private homeowner associations had already purchased Flock and granted them camera access. “We are looking to add more city cameras into the Flock system,” the justification read. According to the city, “other vendors” would “not integrate with our existing Flock system.” Over the next several years, Alpharetta expanded its work with the company significantly. By 2025, the city’s annual Flock bill had ballooned to $381,000. As in other industries, companies that sell technology to police often use financial incentives to get customers in the door. Clearview AI , Ring , and Taser have all ponied up enticing offers to agencies around the country. “A lot of these police surveillance vendors have learned the lessons of general old salesmanship,” Guariglia tells WIRED. In other words, deals and discounts work. In some cases, this looks like new and increasingly expansive Flock products. In 2025, for instance, Alpharetta paid for an upgrade to the Elite Package of FlockOS, which Flock describes as a real-time crime-center platform. Other products are first offered with a free trial; Alpharetta took advantage of one 90-day window last year to try a new product dubbed Nova. Flock also expands its contracts by offering discounts if departments sign a multiyear contract. In 2024, Alpharetta locked into a five-year contract with Flock that would cost $254,250 the first year and $238,000 for each successive year. The agreement was $232,500 less than five one-year agreements, which could be subject to higher rates. The Alpharetta Police Department declined to comment. Five-year agreements are common among Flock customers, which the company has sometimes marketed as a “price-lock promotion.” In a November 2023 email, Flock customer success manager Gwen Saltal used this framing to offer a five-year deal to New York’s Albany County Sheriff’s Office.

events.title: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
events.summary: When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old. But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money. He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says. The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups. Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going ­belly-up—has emerged. Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs. SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April. Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents. Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models. Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026. CEO Dori Yona has seen these transactions, once rare and “somewhat taboo,” become increasingly routine, with 47% of SimpleClosure deals now including code or data sales. And it’s got company. Industry rival Sunset also has a rapidly growing data resale business. Founder and CEO Brendan Mahony says Sunset values a dying client’s assets by head count, years in operation, volume of data, and how the team used its tools. Particle board, he says, is a good analogy: “This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.”  Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets. Surge AI, for example, buys data to build “reinforcement-learning gyms” where clients’ AI agents practice tasks—think debugging a complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs. Nick Heiner, who leads the company’s work on these environments, says he seeks data archives reflecting a range of situations, from disagreements to tricky judgment calls. Heiner explains that one company’s Slack history, if it captures conversations with variety and depth, can be worth more than another’s Slack, email, and calendars combined. Real archives avoid common errors in synthetic worlds, such as references to dates that don’t exist, but the extent of performance gains remains unclear. No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives. Pricing reflects this uncertainty: Buyers quote wildly different numbers, Heiner says, because valuations are based on “research theses” estimating how many useful tasks come from, say, 100,000 lines of code. That hasn’t stopped bigger deals from happening. This past August, as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data , including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and 176,000 employee records. The price tag: $10 million. And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups. Legally, this all could get iffy. Spirit’s flight attendants’ union objected to the sale on privacy grounds, and Greg Ewing, an attorney who advises AI startups, has called such data “legally radioactive.” Suppliers employ data scientists to scrub personally identifiable information and exclude HR records, and buyers say they scrub too. But Ewing points out some of the private details that lurk in emails and calendars: doctor appointments, school pickup arrangements, date-night plans. He describes a “Wild West of AI training” that is only starting to give way to proper licensing agreements and vetted use. There’s also the question of who profits from these windfalls. The proceeds typically flow to senior creditors and investors—not employees. To Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University and author of The Quantified Worker , this represents a form of “captured capital.” Legal precedent allows for monitoring to help workers do their jobs, but once a firm is out of business, that justification vanishes. “Employers should have express consent before selling workers’ data,” says Ajunwa, but she adds that there’s no federal law banning such sales. While many see this new market as a chance for failing businesses to recover some value, these wind-down sales also have limitations. Founders have little to no visibility into who is buying the data and what they plan to do with it. Plus, there’s little assurance they’re getting a fair offer. Data prices will likely stabilize in the coming year, though, unless an AI bubble pops first. Either way, tech’s new undertakers will be there to appraise what’s left.  Matthew King is a technology and environmental journalist based in Baltimore.

events.title: He Waited Nine Years in Prison for His Lawyer to File a Single Brief. In This State, There’s No Rule Against It.
events.summary: Mark Harris for ProPublica. Source images: Alejandro A. Alvarez/The Philadelphia Inquirer, courtesy of Patrick Hickson, court records. In 2020, seven years after he was appointed to represent a client who claimed he was wrongly convicted, attorney Scott Galloway told the judge that he was still looking into the case and needed more time.   “I am still in the process of interviewing individuals,” the lawyer wrote to the judge in Delaware County, outside Philadelphia, who had already granted him 32 extensions.  His client, Nolan O’Neal, had been a 20-year-old high school student when he was arrested for murder by Chester police, who had four eyewitnesses identifying him. At his 2005 trial, those witnesses all recanted, saying police had pressured them to accuse O’Neal.  By the time Galloway joined the case, in 2013, O’Neal had already spent eight years in prison insisting he was innocent. The lawyer’s job was to help him file a petition under Pennsylvania’s Post Conviction Relief Act. That law provided a narrow path to freedom if Galloway could find crucial new evidence or prove that previous lawyers had mishandled the case. But court records do not show that the attorney did much other than ask for more time.  In 2022, after nine years, one unsuccessful request to access evidence and 41 extensions, Galloway filed a two-page petition addressing just one of the many issues O’Neal had wanted him to raise. It would not be enough to get O’Neal his day in court.  Nolan O’Neal visits with his sister, Erin O’Neal, earlier this year at the State Correctional Institution Chester, where he is incarcerated. Courtesy of Erin O’Neal For more than half a century, Pennsylvania has promised people who claim they didn’t get a fair trial the right to “effective” post-conviction legal representation, regardless of their ability to pay. That’s more than most states promise people after they have been convicted and lost their appeals.   Yet Pennsylvania has done little to fulfill that promise. The Philadelphia Inquirer and ProPublica previously reported that Pennsylvania lets lawyers resolve cases quickly using a practice that is discouraged in several states: filing “no-merit” letters, also known as Finley letters, urging judges to reject their clients’ handwritten or typed claims. In Philadelphia, dozens who had received such letters later had their convictions or sentences overturned based on issues their lawyers had rejected or overlooked .  But the problems go deeper than that: The state’s loose rules and its failure to fund post-conviction work have made the type of breakdown O’Neal encountered a recurring feature of this system.  By filing public records requests with courts serving all 67 Pennsylvania counties and analyzing a decade of court dockets, an Inquirer and ProPublica investigation found that the system Pennsylvania set up to protect the right to counsel instead allows, or even encourages, shoddy representation. The news organizations found that: Unlike in other types of appeals, attorneys handling post-conviction cases work under no particular timeline and are allowed numerous extensions. The state also has no standards regarding how many cases lawyers should be assigned, and many counties ask lawyers to sign contracts that set no limit on the number of cases courts can assign them. At least 250 people have languished in prison for five years or longer while waiting for their lawyers to act. Unlike some other states , such as North Carolina and New York, Pennsylvania requires no specific training, experience or qualifications for appointed post-trial lawyers, and it holds them to few standards. Lawyers are not required to speak to their clients or take other basic investigative steps before withdrawing from cases by writing no-merit letters. Pennsylvania, which lags behind almost every other state in funding legal defense for poor people, known as indigent defense, dedicates no money for post-trial work. Instead, it leaves it up to each individual county to set pay rates. A majority of county court systems use flat-rate fee structures that some other states ban. While almost every county in the state has a public defender office, most post-conviction cases are handled by private lawyers who are paid hourly, by the case or by the year and work with little to no supervision. Our review of court records found pay as low as $500 per case and delays as long as 19 years without a single court filing.  In some counties, contracted lawyers’ backlogs spanned dozens of cases. In Chester County, an affluent region west of Philadelphia, a lawyer left cases untouched for as long as two years before the county ended his contract last fall.   Delaware County, where O’Neal was convicted, relies on a group of part-time lawyers to handle most of its post-trial matters. One is Galloway, who has handled 20 or 30 post-trial cases per year for the county in addition to running his own law practice and, for a time, holding local elected office. Galloway said that his ethical obligation to confidentiality prevented him from commenting on O’Neal’s case. Judge George A. Pagano, who granted him 41 extensions on O’Neal’s case, declined to comment. In the years Galloway was on the case, O’Neal wrote him dozens of letters from state prison, proposing legal arguments and sending leads to investigate.  “It is a daunting and exhausting task to navigate this legal process and be heard,” O’Neal said in an interview. “We at times even have to fight the attorneys who are supposed to represent us.”  In 2020, he received a letter from the brother of the murder victim, admitting that his testimony against O’Neal was a lie. “I want to fix it. I know my brother would want me to. It’s been long enough,” he wrote. O’Neal said he pleaded with Galloway to track down the man.  In 2022, Galloway attached the brother’s signed statement to a sparse two-page brief, which mentioned none of the other issues O’Neal had raised nine years earlier or the other witnesses who’d come forward over the years. The judge started the process of dismissing the claim. One reason: The filing had been made too late. O’Neal is still fighting his case, now with a new court-appointed lawyer. Dear Judge Pagano: I am writing to your attention as I have grave and urgent concerns about my current appointed attorney Scott D. Galloway, who you have appointed to represent me on my PCRA petition pending in your court. This is the best I can do to bring matters to your attention as my filings are going unanswered. Delays and Extensions Before they are assigned a lawyer, Pennsylvania prisoners must write the first draft of their post-conviction filing on their own within a strict one-year deadline. events.title: More anti-Trump billboards hit the heartland
events.summary: Drivers in three key swing states are about to see even more billboards blaming President Donald Trump for rising prices, according to details shared first with Semafor. Home of the Brave is nearly doubling its billboard campaign in Michigan, Ohio, and Iowa, adding $1 million in new billboards on top of the $1.25 million the group already spent. The new plans bring the group’s total billboards across those three states to more than 350. The billboards hit Trump for higher grocery prices, ding Republicans for supporting Trump’s tariffs, and link gas prices to the unpopular Iran war. They’re intended to help Democratic Senate and House candidates that will determine congressional control. “Job number one is winning back Congress. Once we do that, we can start finally holding this administration accountable,” said Home of the Brave advisory board member Sarah Longwell.

events.title: Dubai inflation eases even as fuel costs rise
events.summary: Dubai's inflation rate eased slightly in September from the previous month, even as rising oil prices pushed up the cost of petrol. Inflation on an annual basis stood at 5.03 per cent, down from the 5.54 per cent recorded in August and the 5.7 per cent peak for this year reached in June. . The figures were released by the Dubai Data and Statistics Establishment on Tuesday. Meanwhile, Dubai’s General Monthly Consumer Price Index decreased by 0.05 per cent month-on-month in September on falling airfares and cheaper holiday packages. Airfares on a monthly basis fell by 23.44 per cent and holiday packages dropped 12.47 per cent from the August level. However, on an annual basis, the transport division was the biggest contributor to the rise in consumer prices in September, climbing 14.7 per cent. The increase in transport charges was driven by a 37.52 per cent rise in the cost of fuels and lubricants for personal transport, as well as a 13.48 per cent rise in passenger transport by air, according to the latest government data. Biggest contributor The transport segment, which accounts for 9 per cent of Dubai’s Consumer Price Index basket, has been the main driver of inflation in the emirate over the past several months amid a rise in prices petrol prices . The UAE lifted fuel subsidies in 2015 and prices are evaluated on a monthly basis, based on movements in global markets. Petrol prices in the Emirates rose for a third consecutive month for October as prices in global oil markets remain elevated amid escalating geopolitical concerns in the Middle East. Global crude prices, which surged by nearly 109 per cent during the peak of the war, now in its eighth month, are still more than 70 per cent higher on concerns of a possible resumption in fighting between the US and Iran . Brent crude, which hovered around the $110 per barrel mark in September, has largely remained above $100 over the past few weeks. The West Texas Intermediate benchmark passed $105 a barrel in September as the Strait of Hormuz remained a flashpoint. Increasing attacks on Saudi infrastructure in the Red Sea by the Houthi rebels in Yemen have added another layer of risk to energy supplies from the region. Rebound Despite economic headwinds, Dubai's economy has largely skirted the deeper slump experienced by some neighbours. Non-oil private sector business activity in the emirate, which is one of the largest business and tourism centres in the Middle East, also maintained a sharp growth trajectory. The Purchasing Managers' Index stood at 54.5 in September, up from 54.1 in August, indicating a “solid improvement” in Dubai, as the pace of growth was fastest in 2026, S&P Global Markets Intelligence said earlier this month. The boost to the emirate’s non-oil economic activity was largely driven by a “sharp and accelerated increase in output” as new orders also rose markedly and employment in the emirate rose, according to the PMI survey data. The tourism and retail sectors in the emirate have also bounced back from the initial shock of the war. Property, among the top contributors to the emirate’s economy, has also held up relatively well. The food and drinks category increased by an annualised 8.05 per cent last month, while housing, water, electricity, gas and domestic fuel rose by almost 6.23 per cent, “as a result of the growth of the average residential rental prices in most areas of the emirate during September”, the latest government data shows.

events.title: Germany's China calculation shifts as import pressures eclipse export benefits
events.summary: Why Germany is backing tougher EU trade defenses against China Germany has long resisted tougher action against China, fearing retaliation. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect its industrial base. Germany's cautious approach toward Beijing is cracking. For years, Berlin blocked a harder line on what the European Union describes as China's unfair trade practices. In the last few months, that caution — a fear of Chinese retaliation that could hurt German exporters — has given way to a willingness to escalate. Last week, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron wrote jointly to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen seeking a new tool to cut a trading partner off from the EU's single market if unfair practices continue. Clearly aimed at Beijing, the letter warned the measure was necessary against countries that "deliberately seek to undermine ... fair market conditions by political or economic means." China's Commerce Ministry warned Europe would "suffer the consequences" if it adopted such a "kill-switch" plan, which was timed to coincide with crucial EU-China trade talks in Beijing last week. Noah Barkin, a senior adviser with research consultancy Rhodium Group's China practice, told DW that the threats to Germany's export powerhouse "have convinced Merz and his closest advisers that the benefits of action outweigh the costs of inaction." Before the COVID pandemic , the two economies rose in tandem and German industry benefited from China's ascent . Since 2021, however, China has fallen from Germany's second-largest export market to its ninth, according to data from Germany Trade & Invest for the first half of 2026. Chinese competitors have quickly closed the technology gap and benefit from much lower costs and state subsidies. That pressure is being felt especially in Germany's automaking , precision engineering and chemicals industries. Why Berlin's China policy is changing German vehicle makers have suffered a large sales drop in China, which was once their second-largest market. According to data from Rhodium Group, German car exports to China plummeted by 66% between 2022 and 2025. Big German brands now face heavy rivalry from a new wave of Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufactures in other major markets, including Europe, which is forcing a wave of layoffs and possible factory closures . In Germany alone, imports of new Chinese-made cars rose 121% in the first seven months of the year, according to Destatis, the federal statistics agency. Overall, Chinese-made vehicles accounted for nearly 14% of total vehicle imports. "After continuously losing market share in China ... it [the rivalry] seems to be hitting their business within the European automotive market," Andreas Mischer, an associate fellow at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW. Mischer said pressure from Germany's powerful automotive lobby was key to Berlin's "shifting attitude toward trade defense instruments." Industry pressure grows for trade defenses Among the many German business leaders who have demanded a more hard-line approach in recent months, Oliver Richtberg, head of foreign trade at VDMA, Germany's mechanical engineering association, was perhaps the most blunt: "We are currently being deindustrialized through unfair measures — and most companies are no longer willing to accept this," Richtberg told Welt am Sonntag newspaper in August. According to Eurostat, the wider EU's goods deficit with China was around €360 billion ($402 billion) last year — effectively €1 billion per day — and widened again in the first half of 2026. While Brussels has been pushing back against the dumping of cheap Chinese goods, a separate industrial protection law and other anti-coercion measures are running into trouble from Beijing and at home. Business groups question industrial policy proposals The EU's Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed in March, aims to pull manufacturing investment back to Europe by favoring EU-based firms in public contracts and subsidies. Foreign investments in key sectors would only be approved if European partners keep majority control, which Beijing has framed as discriminatory. How to dismantle China's stranglehold on raw materials? The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) warned last month that the draft act does little to counter the threat from cheaper Chinese rivals. In a position paper, it said the incentive to produce within the bloc has to be large enough to "cancel out the extra cost of producing locally." Berlin's chief concern was that China could place new export curbs on rare earth minerals and the magnets made from them. China has a stranglehold on these elements, which are essential for German automotive, renewables and defense manufacturing.
