events.title: Books Insider: A conversation on the death of conversations
events.summary: Jessica Pons for BI Books Insider is a regular feature from Dan Slater about the latest and best books in business and self improvement. Each month, through essays and interviews, Dan will introduce you to today's most fascinating authors. America is in the throes of a "silent epidemic: a connection crisis," writes best-selling author Vanessa Van Edwards. We're hanging out less . We're talking to chatbots and agents more than we talk to people. The share of US adults who say they have no close friends rose from 3% in 1990 to 12% in 2023. We've lost the subtle art of conversation. Van Edwards, who has more than a million followers on Instagram and runs an Austin-based behavioral research lab called Science of People, wants to help us reconnect. In her new book , "Conversation: How to Connect with Anyone and Make Every Interaction Count," she writes: "'I like you' might be the three most powerful words you can gift someone else. Why? Because we're terrified of being unlikable. And research shows that we grossly underestimate how much people like us." If venturing an "I like you" feels weird, that's okay. Exposure to social risk decreases our sensitivity to rejection and strengthens our confidence in connection. Confidence "is not the absence of discomfort — it's feeling awkward and doing it anyway," writes Van Edwards. We all have "conversational power," she argues, and in "Conversation," Van Edwards' third book, she offers a blueprint for building it. The chapters are short, clear, and propulsive. The book's central aim is to guide the reader through three ascending levels of conversation. Some of her advice may sound woo-woo, but Van Edwards, a world class talker, swears by it. "We grossly underestimate how much people like us," says Van Edwards. Jessica Pons for BI At Level 1, putting people at ease, Van Edwards instructs us to banish small-talk and awkward silences by turning conversation into a treasure hunt. Don't ask: What do you do? Ask: What do you like to do? Lead with stories, not facts. And don't be afraid to add flair, or what Van Edwards calls conversational confetti: Can I tell you something really weird? To be more likeable in conversation , look for moments where you can authentically say, "Tell me more." To listen well, tilt your head slightly to one side, exposing neck and ear. To sound smart, ask for advice, or ask your conversation partner: What have you always wanted to learn? Have an upcoming business book that Dan can't miss? Get in touch: bydanslater@gmail.com At Level 2, connecting deeply, we share and build one another's dreams. Avoid being quick to tarnish someone's aspirations with skepticism; get excited with them, and bring ideas. And if you don't love their dream, be curious rather than doubtful. Ask for more details. Who will this dream help? It's our dreams, after all, that give our lives meaning, which is what Level 3 is all about. "When done well," Van Edwards writes, "Level 3 creates the rarest of relationships — the kind built on mutual insight, not just mutual interests." I recently caught up with Van Edwards for a conversation about " Conversation . " DS: I used to consider myself a conversationalist. Reading "Conversation " made me realize how superficial many of my conversations are. VVE: I was having conversations that, even though I was trying, were more like surface-level updates. How's the family? How are the kids? Very fact finding. And I wondered why I didn't look forward to socializing, why I was always so drained by my interactions. DS: You begin the book with a painfully funny anecdote about how you once lost out on a big career opportunity when nerves got in the way. You were trying to perform rather than be present. Now, when you're working with students, whether at Google or Harvard, how do you move them away from old conversational habits that kill connection? VVE: I ask a simple question: "How exhausting is it to make small talk?" And everyone agrees that it's totally exhausting. And I say, "It's because you're trying to be impressive." Oddly, now that we have fewer conversations, we feel like the conversations we do have matter more. Some people only see their boss once a year, at the off-site, and think, I better be impressive ! But it's tiring, and never works. DS: While I was reading, I suffered a Level 1 conversation defeat. My son had a friend over. When the friend's dad came to pick up his kid, I asked him what he was up to for the rest of the day. He was like, "I'm going home to do the quarterly taxes for my business, and then my wife is making dinner." And that was it. VVE: Always ask for stories, not facts. And respond with stories, not facts. A fact is a dead-end. A story is a doorway. DS: Your story about trying to find friends for your husband made me laugh. Why do men struggle to connect? VVE: I don't know. I'm not a man. But what I have seen is that if a man is happy — in his home life, his routine, his business — he thinks he doesn't need friends. It's a lot of work. "Some people only see their boss once a year, at the off-site, and think, I better be impressive! But it's tiring, and never works," says Van Edwards. Jessica Pons for BI DS: You note that it takes about 50 hours of interaction to go from acquaintance to casual friend, and 200+ hours to develop a close friendship. VVE: That's what the research says. I was pretty shocked by that. Who's got 200 hours? DS: Are there any shortcuts? VVE: Going sequentially, through nine power questions, can speed things up. For each of the three levels, I propose three questions. At Level 1, the questions are geared toward general traits: "Working on anything exciting these days?" At Level 2, you're trying to find out about personal concerns: "What do you love to talk about?" Level 3 questions elicit the other person's self-narrative. One of the most powerful questions you can ask is: "What would you do if you weren't afraid?" You can honor someone's hidden fears by asking, "What did you fail at this week?" DS: You point out that our fate is determined by the story we tell about ourselves. You list five different narratives: The Ambitious Hero, The Contented Pragmatist, The Selfless Helper, The Creative Disruptor, and the Unlucky Struggler. The first four are desirable. But the Unlucky Struggler is that stuck person whose life is full of obstacles and regret. Their self-knowledge tends to be low, and they often ignore solutions offered to them. About how many of us are Unlucky Strugglers? VVE: Maybe between 15 and 20%. But it's not evenly distributed. At a company, if you have 100 people, it's not like 15 to 20 will be Unlucky Strugglers. It depends on the hiring manager. If the hiring manager is an Ambitious Hero , then you might have 100 Ambitious Heroes. events.title: Market turns cold on luxury after LVMH’s China letdown
events.summary: LVMH on Oct 12 posted a 5% drop in organic sales at its fashion and leather goods division, which generates nearly half of group revenue. LVMH’s weaker-than-expected quarterly fashion and leather goods sales, hit by a deterioration in Chinese consumer demand for its flagship Louis Vuitton brand, have raised fresh doubts about the luxury industry’s recovery prospects. Four sell-side analysts have cut their target price on LVMH shares by an average 9% following the results, the first quarterly report by a major sector player, expecting the miss to also signal weak performance at some of its competitors. LVMH shares were down 1.5% by 7.30am GMT ( 3.30pm Singapore time) . Its peers Hermes, Kering and Richemont were down by a similar degree. Europe’s leading luxury groups, mired in a three-year slowdown, have lost around €330 billion ( S$472.79 billion ) in market value since the start of 2026 , with LVMH alone shedding roughly 40%. “Despite the recent share price weakness, we expect some further pressure on the space as a whole today, with confirmation that the Chinese cluster seems to have taken a material (and bigger than feared) step down”, JPMorgan analysts said in a note to clients. LVMH on Oct 12 posted a 5% drop in organic sales at its fashion and leather goods division, which generates nearly half of group revenue, missing expectations in a Visible Alpha consensus for a 1.8% decline. The group said a “less buoyant environment” in China impacted its revenues, contributing to 1% organic sales growth overall, excluding currency swings, to €18.5 billion, below expectations for 1.3% growth. Asked about Louis Vuitton’s recovery prospects in a call with analysts, the group’s Chief Financial Officer Cecile Cabanis said: “It takes a bit of time, but I don’t think there are a lot of shortcuts here”. Adding to investor concerns, growth in LVMH’s watches and jewellery division, home to brands including Bulgari and Tiffany, slowed to 6% from 9% in the first half of 2026 , marking a changing trend in one of luxury’s few bright spots. events.title: IMF raises UK growth forecast as economist says Healey should ‘stay the course’
events.summary: Fund upgrades UK’s GDP growth forecast for 2026 to 1.3%, but says it is likely to edge down next year IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’ John Healey should “stay the course” and continue repairing the UK’s public finances, the International Monetary Fund’s top economist has said, after the fund lifted its growth forecast for Britain. Little more than a fortnight before Healey’s first budget, Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s economic counsellor, said the UK “stands out” among G7 countries in having a plan to narrow its deficit. “The UK has already started a consolidation process,” she said. “The message for the UK is simply, stay the course.” Tenreyro, a former member of the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee, was speaking at the launch of the IMF’s twice-yearly World Economic Outlook (WEO) at the fund’s annual meetings in Bangkok. Healey is under pressure to announce a generous energy support package in the budget, before the sharp rise in energy bills expected in January . But in its WEO report, the IMF advises member governments against across-the-board subsidies, saying any support should be “temporary, targeted and non-distortionary”. In a fillip for the chancellor, who is due to arrive in Bangkok later this week, the IMF has upgraded its growth forecast for the UK this year, but it expects a modest slowdown in 2027 as higher energy prices take their toll. Responding, Healey said: “Conflict in the Middle East and Europe is hitting people in the UK and around the world. But Britain’s economy is showing strong international resilience in the face of these challenges.” The IMF predicted GDP growth of 1.3% for the UK this year, up 0.3 percentage points from its most recent update in July . UK GDP growth has been stronger than expected in early 2026, at 0.6% in the first quarter and 0.5% in the second quarter. The Office for National Statistics has pointed to the strong expansion of AI-related businesses as one factor behind the upside surprise. However, the IMF warned that prolonged high oil prices and rising interest rates meant growth was likely to “edge down” in 2027 “as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”. It cut its UK growth forecast for next year modestly to 1.2%, from 1.3%. Markets have been revising up their expectations of future inflation and interest rates across big economies since the Middle East conflict re-escalated in the summer. The Bank of England’s nine-member monetary policy committee is now widely expected to raise the policy rate at its November meeting, echoing similar moves by the Federal Reserve , European Central Bank and Bank of Japan. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Mortgage rates in the UK have already been rising in response to higher funding costs for banks in financial markets. The BoE policymaker Megan Greene argued on Tuesday morning that the IMF’s growth upgrade was proof that UK interest rates should be higher. Speaking to the Atlantic Council at the IMF meetings in Bangkok, Greene argued that interest rates were currently not very restrictive. “There’s more recently been some labour market data that has also suggested that maybe slack in the labour market has peaked, so the labour market is loose,” Greene said. The IMF singled out the UK as among the countries – also including Japan – where core inflation, which excludes volatile commodities such as energy, was not expected to return to the 2% target until late next year. It expects average inflation in the UK to be 3.3% this year and to remain at 2.8% in 2027 – a challenge for Healey and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who are promising to offer voters a “breathing space” from rising costs. Healey will spend little more than 24 hours in the Thai capital before flying home to put the finishing touches to his 28 October budget. He is expected to focus on plans to devolve more tax revenues to mayoralties, alongside measures to help households cope with higher energy bills before the winter. A string of other challenging decisions, including when the UK should be aiming to spend 3% of GDP on defence, is expected to be delayed until a big spending review at some point next year. The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) warned this week that the budget would be a “work of fiction” unless Healey explained how he would deal with what it said were £35bn of future spending pressures.

events.title: Hong Kong watchdog freezes US$590m of assets over alleged IPO fraud schemes
events.summary: The SFC has also suspended 65 listing applications so far this year, as regulator looks to strengthen market quality in the city Hong Kong’s securities watchdog has moved against two syndicates suspected of being involved in three alleged initial public offering fraud schemes involving assets worth HK$4.6 billion (US$590 million), according to a statement released on Tuesday. The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) also announced on the same day that it had suspended 65 listing applications in the first nine months of this year due to the poor quality of their listing sponsors’ work, in what analysts viewed as an effort to strengthen the city’s market quality. The SFC has frozen the HK$4.6 billion of assets related to the three alleged IPO fraud cases, according to the statement. The cases involved listed companies allegedly signing agreements with the syndicates to divert part of their IPO proceeds away from the companies under the guise of “financial product investments”, the regulator said.

events.title: Russia is copying cruise missile tech onto its $50,000 drones to deal with Ukraine's jamming
events.summary: Ukraine's intelligence directorate is seeking information about a new optical system found on Russia's latest Gerans. Screenshots via Telegram/GUR Ukraine is warning about a new navigation system on Russian Gerans called the Susanin. It uses a camera and a pre-saved library of images of Ukraine's terrain to fly independently. The capability, similar to a tech on cruise missiles, could help Gerans completely bypass jamming. Last week, Ukraine's defense intelligence directorate put out a call for information on a device newly found in Russia's latest killer drones. The "Susanin," a small cylinder with a camera lens, is an optical system that enables Russia's long-range drones to navigate Ukraine's skies without relying on satellite or radio signals. Should Moscow deploy them at scale, the modules would introduce a major new challenge for Kyiv, allowing Russian one-way drones to bypass jamming — a key pillar of Ukraine's air defense network. Per the intelligence directorate, or GUR, the Kremlin has been fitting them onto the turbojet Geran-4 and Geran-5 K5 , which fly at 280 mph or faster and are seeing growing use by Russia this year. These drones are already significantly harder for Ukraine to destroy by force, since they outpace typical Ukrainian interceptor drones . The Susanin works by storing images of Ukraine's terrain on the drone, then, while in flight, using a downward-facing camera to observe the ground and compare the live feed to the pre-saved imagery. Using these comparisons, the drone can independently determine its position and how to reach its target. "Even Google Earth imagery is sufficient for basic orientation," wrote Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, a prominent drone analyst connected with Ukraine's military, on Sunday. Beskrestnov warned that Russia would likely continue actively developing Susanin systems for its drones by next year. "Our enemy already uses such systems on small Molniya, V2U, and Lancet drones," he added. Cruise missile tech on a drone The technology is similar to what some cruise missiles use to reach their targets in jammed environments. The Tomahawk , for example, features what analysts call Digital Scene Matching Area Correlation to snap photos of landmarks under the missile and compare them to satellite imagery stored onboard. Higher-end Russian cruise missiles, such as the Kh-101, use a Russian version of this tech called Otblesk-U. But the Kh-101 is estimated to cost $2.4 million each, while its long-range drones cost just a fraction of that: The delta-wing Geran-4 is priced at an estimated $50,000 to $70,000 apiece, while the Geran-5 is believed to cost about $100,000 to $115,000 each. Debris of a drone lies on the ground near the Epicenter retail center following a Russian Geran-4 strike in Kharkiv. Polina Kulish/Gwara Media/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Russia has been producing these drones at a much faster pace, launching over 3,500 jet attack drones at Ukraine in September alone. Kyrylo Liukov, who leads the uncrewed technologies department at the Serhiy Prytula Charity Foundation, told Business Insider that it's "quite possible" Russia could scale up its use of navigation systems like the Susanin. "Russia is already using this navigation system for medium- and deep-strike operations," said Liukov, adding that its deployment on Geran-4s and Geran-5s has been increasing recently. Still, Liukov said these systems have their limits. The Susanin is only useful for pre-programmed drone attacks by itself, and wouldn't be able to help the drone find a moving Ukrainian armored vehicle or mobile missile launcher. "In other words, these are predominantly planned, static targets," said Liukov, whose organization raises funds for Ukraine's military and drone manufacturers. But pre-arranged flights fit well into Moscow's strategy with Gerans, which are launched in large numbers to overwhelm Ukrainian air defenses and wreak havoc on its cities. Fighting the Susanin If a Russian turbojet drone is using a Susanin system, Ukraine's only way to counter it, for now, is to use physical force, Liukov said. Ukraine's options in this area remain limited, with its military still in the early stages of introducing advanced interceptor drones capable of catching turbojet Gerans. Another way is to launch rare and expensive anti-air missiles, which are typically reserved for Russia's more powerful cruise or ballistic missiles. One possible solution Ukraine could eventually explore, Liukov said, is to blind the Susanin's camera. The camera's view of Ukrainian terrain could also be obscured by clouds, rain, or fog, he said. "For high-quality route recognition using Susanin, a flight altitude relative to speed is required that will allow for accurate orientation using the captured images, as well as favorable weather conditions," Liukov said. events.title: What to know about the Nord Stream pipeline explosions trial opening in Germany this week
events.summary: A former Ukrainian army officer is going on trial in Germany over undersea explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany four years ago BERLIN -- A former Ukrainian army officer is going on trial in Germany this week over undersea explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany four years ago in one of the biggest acts of sabotage in Europe since the Second World War. The suspect faces charges of causing an explosion, damaging property, disrupting public service and being an “accomplice to war crimes” by attacking civilian infrastructure, according to prosecutors . The attack laid bare Europe's dependence on Russian energy but also raised sensitive questions about Ukraine and its Western allies. While international observers initially blamed Moscow, there are now increasing suggestions that Ukrainian state security agencies may have been involved — even though Ukraine counts Germany as one of its closest allies. According to German privacy rules, the suspect will be identified in court only as Serhii K., although he was publicly named as Serhii Kuznietsov in extradition proceedings in Italy . Here's what we know about the alleged ringleader of the attack and one of the most politically charged court cases of wartime sabotage that will be heard at the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court in Hamburg starting this Wednesday. The explosions on Sept. 26, 2022, damaged pipelines that were built to carry Russian natural gas to Germany under the Baltic Sea. At the time, European countries were moving to wean themselves off Russian energy sources, following the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 . Prosecutors say the aim of the plot was to permanently disrupt gas deliveries and prevent Russia from using the revenues to finance its military operations. The defendant and others allegedly used a yacht that set off from the German port of Rostock. It had been hired from a German company using forged IDs and with the help of intermediaries. The explosions ruptured the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, which was Russia’s main natural gas supply route to Germany until Moscow cut off supplies in August 2022. They also damaged Nord Stream 2, which never entered service because Germany suspended its certification process shortly before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The suspect allegedly organized and carried out the detonation of at least four bombs between 14 and 27 kilograms (around 31 to 62 pounds) at a depth of 70 to 80 meters (230 feet to 263 feet) near the Danish island of Bornholm. He was detained in August in an Italian village, where officers raided a bungalow where he was staying with his family. Police said he surrendered without resistance. He was extradited to Germany in November. A second suspect was arrested on a European warrant in the northern Croatian town of Pula in August. He has applied for asylum in Croatia to fight his extradition to Germany. The pipelines were long a target of criticism by the U.S. and some of its allies, which warned that they increased dependence on Russian gas. Russian officials, however, have claimed that U.S. and British intelligence agencies were involved in staging the explosions, which Moscow declared “an act of international terrorism,” and have launched their own investigation. Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Russia has also accused NATO of involvement in the attack, while several Western countries initially blamed Russia. More recently, the Kremlin has expressed hope that those who orchestrated the explosions will be held accountable. Asked what Moscow expects from the trial, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Monday that “we expect objectivity.” “We expect … that both the perpetrators and those who ordered it will be named. That would be very important. I think no one doubts who it really is,” Peskov said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has denied allegations that his country was involved in the pipeline blasts. He also told reporters in August that Ukraine’s prosecutors and Foreign Ministry were already cooperating with partners and that Kyiv was “absolutely open to joint steps on the investigation,” stressing the importance of keeping Europe’s trust. Nonetheless, “all the evidence points very clearly to the fact that Ukraine blew up the Nord Stream pipelines, not the Russians, whom they initially tried to pin the blame on,” says Joachim Weber, a security expert at the Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies at the University of Bonn. “This is, of course, highly explosive politically, because, as is well known, Germany is one of Ukraine’s closest allies, supporting the country on a massive scale with huge sums of money and also by taking on considerable political risks,” Weber said.

events.title: BT charged me for more than a year despite landline being dead
events.summary: It is billing £32.99 a month but I have had no functioning phone line since it switched me to Digital Voice I’ve had no landline since May 2025 when BT switched it to Digital Voice. Weeks passed, and each call to BT involved at least an hour waiting on hold and answering security questions before being passed between departments. Eventually, last December, two engineers were sent and discovered that a wire had been severed during the upgrade. They said they needed a cherry picker to reconnect it to its original location and would return. They did not. Since then, I’ve called BT to no avail, and all the while I’ve been paying for a landline that doesn’t work. I am on the priority register due to serious illness and am reduced to tears of helplessness. You have been paying £32.99 a month for a dead landline and broadband, which was unaffected. BT claims it was unaware of the problem until you complained last December. You insist you had reported it before then, but do not have records of when. It turns out the case was closed in December after the engineers’ abortive visit. You next complained in January, but BT admits it again closed the case because, by then, your landline had been removed from your account, though you were still being charged. It says it did not hear from you again until I intervened in July. You said that you had believed promises that a fix was under way. A complaints manager rang you after my contact, and you were offered an extraordinary £6.46 to “make up” for its failings. Your line was eventually activated in September. The telecoms regulator Ofcom requires providers to pay £10.34 compensation a day if a reported fault is not corrected within two working days, which means you are, in theory, entitled to more than £4,600. I’ve put this to BT, but it is digging in because, it claims, you waited months to report the problems. Since you can’t provide proof to contradict it, I can’t argue the toss. You have the option of a complaint to the Communications Ombudsman but have now accepted £689 for the 60 days without service which BT acknowledges fall within the compensation rules, and for its mishandling of the two complaints it has on record. Always keep a timeline of interactions with a company and follow up unaddressed complaints promptly and in writing. We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. events.title: ‘People sell their best stuff on Vinted’ – how charity shops became a dumping ground for unsellable clothes
events.summary: Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more . Swamped with ‘daily avalanches’ of soiled items and poor-quality fast fashion, secondhand stores are in crisis. What went wrong with people’s good intentions? And is it possible to donate more effectively? The small stockroom of St Raphael’s Hospice charity shop in Cheam, south London, is rammed with donations. “On average, we get 30 to 50 bags a day,” says Caroline Worley, the commercial manager, “but it’s not unusual to receive over 100.” This might sound like a good problem to have, but the sheer volume of stuff is the shop’s biggest challenge. “Sometimes, there’s only [enough] floor space to tiptoe,” says 48-year-old store manager, Colin French. Rummaging through the donations, it’s clear that much is unsaleable: a smelly, soiled bathrobe, tatty trainers, heavily bobbled jumpers, old socks, an empty Swarovski jewellery case. “Absolutely typical,” says Worley. They’re also overwhelmed with deluges of low-quality fashion – a shift in donation habits that accelerated during Covid, because, says Worley, all that time at home enabled people to sell their best stuff on Vinted. The experience here echoes that of author Tansy Hoskins, whose latest book, Charity Shop World , paints a picture of a charity retail sector in crisis. She spent 16 months working in a London charity shop, sorting through “daily avalanches” of clothing, which swamped “all the other categories put together”. Everyone Hoskins interviewed said similar: “quality is the big change marker – it’s gone through the floor. You’re just fighting against the waste.” The problem is nationwide. Since the book came out, she’s “been contacted by managers of charity shops around the country – for example, Nottingham, Accrington, Newcastle – all saying that most of what they’re getting is waste.” It is, of course, our waste. According to Jose Baladron of Traid, which has 12 shops across London, shopping for new clothes is “through the roof – the UK is the highest consumer of clothing in Europe by far ”. “That obviously translates to more donations, which is far too much to process in small shops.” Hoskins routinely found that ultra-fast-fashion donations would “still have tags on – it was clear people had received their online purchases and gone, ‘What the hell is this?’ It wasn’t even wearable so they’d just donate it.” On average, charity shops only manage to sell about 25% of clothing donations, according to Baladron (a figure replicated by a University of Southampton study ). “So they rely heavily on the ragman” to shift the rest. Yet the price of rag has “plummeted”, according to Merryn Haines-Gadd of the environmental action charity Wrap, “due to the saturation of low-quality fast fashion”. Ten years ago, a charity might have been paid 50-60p per kilo. “Now you’re lucky to get 10p,” says Baladron. Plus there’s only so much the ragman can take. For anything they can’t take, charity shops have to pay to have it collected as waste. At St Raphael’s, some of that has included, according to Worley, saucepans with food still in the bottom, babies’ soiled sleep-suits and used sanitary products. “[Staff] can get a bit worn down when people are donating stuff that isn’t saleable,” says Libby Gordon, CEO of Fara, which has 39 charity shops in London. “Plus there’s a time cost for us to process it all.” Factor in rising utility costs and national insurance payments, and “charity shops are in a perfect storm”, says Hoskins. In June, the British Heart Foundation announced plans to close 150 of its 651 stores; its latest accounts indicate that its retail arm lost £3.3m last year. Cancer Research is part-way through a 190-shop closure programme, and rumours are swirling that up to 100 Oxfam shops might close (which the charity has denied ). Some are fighting back. Fara’s new in-store poster campaign advises would-be donators: “If you’d be happy to give it to a friend, we’d be delighted to receive it.” Items should be “clean, complete, and in good condition” , states their online guide . But just as people “wish cycle” by chucking unrecyclables into the recycling, so do people “wish give”. I certainly struggle to accept that something with life left in it, however worn, can’t be useful to someone. This mentality, however, creates unpleasant work and costs for charities – even more so when people leave donations outside a closed charity shop (technically, it’s fly-tipping, and charity shops do often check their CCTV, record numberplates and report such crimes). These bags are often soiled by foxes or dogs, ripped open and/or rained on. At St Raphael’s, staff have found soiled mattresses, ripped sofas and even an old toilet dumped outside: “It leaves us with a big problem,” says Worley. Disposal at scale is an expensive business.

events.title: Visa approved to prepare domestic payments business in China
events.summary: Visa’s clearance of the regulatory hurdle will allow it to operate in China’s US$144 trillion payments market and marks the end to its years-long pursuit. Visa won approval from the People’s Bank of China to prepare a domestic bank card clearing business, after seeking entry since 2017. The firm must finish preparatory work within one year before applying for a licence, joining Mastercard and American Express in China’s huge payments market. The move ends a long trade dispute issue, but Visa faces a market now dominated by Alipay and WeChat Pay, with 10.2 billion bank cards in circulation in 2025. BEIJING – Visa received approval to begin preparations to establish a domestic bank card clearing business in China, as the firm follows rivals Mastercard and American Express in serving the country’s massive payments market. “We greatly appreciate the important role of the leaders of the United States and China in pursuing a constructive and strategically stable relationship between the world’s largest economies,” Visa chief executive Ryan McInerney said in the statement. The company’s Beijing unit won the green-light from the People’s Bank of China, the official Xinhua News Agency reported on Oct 13. It must complete preparatory work within one year before applying to commence operations and obtaining the clearing business licence, Xinhua added. Visa’s clearance of the regulatory hurdle will allow it to operate in China’s US$144 trillion (S$184 trillion) payments market and marks the end to its years-long pursuit. Visa applied for the licence in 2017, local media reported. Competitor Mastercard received approval to establish its bank card clearing business in 2020, and Amex’s joint venture in the country was approved to start bank card clearing services several months after that. For years, the battle for entry into China’s massive domestic clearing market was a primary friction point in the broader trade dispute between the world’s two largest economies. Earlier in 2026, US President Donald Trump said he brought up Visa’s request for access to China’s market during a meeting with Xi Jinping in Beijing . Visa’s CEO McInerney accompanied Trump on that May trip to China. Xi later met his counterpart in Washington in late September, with both agreeing on a trade truce extension . The two are scheduled to talk again in person on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen in November. China first signalled an opening in the sector in June 2015, announcing that foreign bank card clearing providers could apply for licences by establishing local units or through acquisitions. The move was designed to dismantle the longstanding monopoly held by state-run China UnionPay. While the approval marks a significant milestone, Visa is entering a market that looks very different from the one it first sought to enter. China’s payments ecosystem is now dominated by domestic mobile platforms Alipay and WeChat Pay, which have largely bypassed traditional card networks and become the primary channels for everyday transactions. China had 10.2 billion bank cards in circulation at the end of 2025, with transaction value totalling 963.6 trillion yuan (S$184 trillion) in 2025, according to the People’s Bank of China. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Cost of living struggles inspire 'social supermarket'
events.summary: Thomas Cliffe and Laura Steele welcomed customers into the store for the first time on Monday "Instead of going to a food bank, being handed a bag and getting back home then finding out that they won't use all those items, at least here they can buy the tokens and shop around for the items they would choose to buy." Founder Thomas Cliffe hopes the first "social supermarket" in Newcastle-under-Lyme, designed to help people struggling with the cost of living, will offer the "freedom to shop with dignity". Set up by Community Cupboard NUL CIC, the store allows members to buy groceries at cost price or below, with more choice than other outlets. Customers can sign up for a membership costing £1 for 12 months. They are then able to purchase tokens to spend on items throughout the store. Newcastle's first 'social supermarket' Cliffe said the idea was inspired by his own experience after leaving work because of anxiety. Although his wife was still employed, he said the couple struggled financially and found they were unable to access some forms of support. "It was horrible because you start to panic and think: 'What am I supposed to do? Where am I going to get the next food from?'" "We either had to choose a meal or choose the bills." Cheryl Peeper found that the store was helpful to keep her ticking over to the next big shop without spending to much. The supermarket opened for the first time on Monday. Such stores aim to cut food waste while helping people facing food insecurity by selling surplus goods at lower prices. "It was exciting to have everyone come through the doors for the first time and give them that freedom to shop with dignity," Cliffe said. Voluntary co-director Laura Steele said the level of need in the area often went unnoticed. "One in four children experience poverty from what we have found, and the average income is £29,000." "There was nothing really for the people of Newcastle and it was crying out for it really," she said. Cheryl Pepper, a carer who visited after finishing a night shift, described the supermarket as "absolutely brilliant". "The food's cheap. If you go to Tesco you spend £100, but you come in here, I've put £20 on and I still have some tokens left," she said. Fiona Morris was one of the first to purchase items from the store. Recent research on the growth of social supermarkets , external backed the idea that they were less off-putting than food banks and large commercial stores for those facing food insecurity. But lead researcher, Dr Claire O'Malley from Teesside University, said: "While social supermarkets can improve access to affordable food and reduce waste in the short term, they should not be viewed as a complete solution to food insecurity." The report called for them to supplement, rather than replace, government support for those struggling to put good food on the table. Fiona Morris, who has ADHD, said she had often found large supermarkets overwhelming. After visiting the new store, she said she immediately felt understood by staff. "It feels like Supermarket Sweep - I feel like I'm robbing the place," she said. events.title: Singapore firm eyes hub in Japan for start-up talent in Asia
events.summary: Insignia Ventures Partners’ Yinglan Tan said the academy will train young people from South-east Asia and Japan to bridge the two regions. Insignia Ventures Partners and Iwate Prefecture plan a start-up academy in north-eastern Japan to train talent from South-east Asia and Japan and link the two regions. Yinglan Tan and Governor Takuya Tasso are due to sign an agreement in Morioka, but the opening date has not yet been decided. Iwate hopes the project will boost regional revival and offset ageing, while the site in Hanamaki may need housing, transport and renovation support. SINGAPORE – A Singaporean venture capital firm is planning to launch an academy in north-eastern Japan in partnership with a local Japanese government to develop start-up talent in and around Asia, according to sources familiar with the project. Insignia Ventures Partners and the Iwate prefectural government are crafting a plan to create a start-up hub in Iwate Prefecture by drawing international talent into the broader Tohoku region – a development the two sides hope will lead to increased investment in Japan by fast-growing South-east Asian economies. Yinglan Tan, founding managing partner of Insignia Ventures Partners, and Iwate Governor Takuya Tasso are scheduled to sign an agreement for the project on the sidelines of the Iwate International Convention, set to take place from Oct 29 to Oct 30 in Morioka, the prefectural capital. However, the two sides have yet to decide on a date to open the hub. Founded in 2017, Insignia Ventures Partners has invested in more than 90 companies in Indonesia, Vietnam, Singapore and Taiwan, among other markets, and manages $1 billion in assets. The firm and the Iwate government started talks on the project after Tan and Tasso met during the Summer Davos forum in Dalian, north-eastern China, in 2024. Tan said the academy aims to train young people from South-east Asia and Japan to serve as a bridge between the two regions by combining knowledge of Japanese business culture with an understanding of the diversity of South-east Asian markets. According to prefectural officials, Iwate hopes the project will spur regional revitalisation and ease the impact of its ageing population. The facility will serve as the Iwate campus of the Insignia Ventures Academy, which is based in Singapore. According to the plan, the Iwate campus would offer in-person programmes. Insignia Ventures Partners reports that the Singapore academy has produced more than 250 graduates through its 12-week core programme on venture investment fundamentals. Graduates have joined portfolio companies or launched businesses, and the Iwate campus would be its first base outside Singapore. According to Iwate officials, the planned site of the academy is in Hanamaki, which is south of Morioka. The Iwate government plans to sell the 41,900 sq m Towa High School property, which closed in 2010, to the Singaporean firm. The Iwate government is considering earmarking renovation subsidies for the project, the officials said. Serving as a transportation hub in the Tohoku region, Hanamaki features Iwate Hanamaki Airport, Shin-Hanamaki Station on the Tohoku Shinkansen Line and the Tohoku Expressway. Tomokazu Sugawara, the executive director of the Management Support Division of the Iwate prefectural government, addressed the host prefecture’s need to develop accommodation and transportation for prospective students and faculty. “We recognise the need for such infrastructure so that instructors and students can travel from Singapore and other parts of the world to stay at the school,” Sugawara said. events.title: AI worms and 'digital slime mold': Welcome to the next AI nightmare fuel
events.summary: Anthropic researchers said small AI models might be able to self-replicate on cheap devices such as smart ovens or lawn mowers. Vitalii Petrushenko/Getty Images Small AI models might soon be capable of worming their way into smart ovens and refrigerators. Anthropic researchers wrote that self-replicating systems might latch onto everyday devices for compute. Forget AI slop . We might soon have "AI worms" and AI "slime mold." In this latest instalment of AI nightmare fuel, Anthropic's researchers have discovered that small rogue AI models might — as soon as the end of 2026 — start worming their way into home devices like smart ovens, smart refrigerators, automatic vacuum cleaners, and lawn mowers. These internet-connected devices typically have "minimal security measures in place," allowing small models to feed off of their computing power and self-replicate, Anthropic's AI capabilities research team wrote in a report on Monday. This could take the form of "a slow, distributed 'digital slime mold,' living on relatively insecure compute," the researchers wrote. The team studied the behavior of small Chinese models, such as Z.ai's GLM-5.2 and Alibaba's Qwen, as well as others like Google DeepMind's Gemma4-26B-A4B. They gave a prompt to the Gemma model while running inference on 15 cheap off-brand Android TV boxes, each costing $55, and found it worked. Worms aren't new in the software world. Traditionally, they're a type of malware that can copy itself and spread across networks. Anthropic said an AI worm takes that idea a step further: it can reproduce itself on another device while carrying its AI model with it. This finding showed them that AI models can use the hardware in domestic smart appliances as an alternative to data center compute. These will be challenging to shut down, they said. "As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren't under human control," the researchers wrote. They added that while we should "harden our systems" to prevent such hacks, we should "also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay." The research comes as rogue AI systems are becoming an increasing topic of concern in the tech sphere. Last month, there was an outpouring of criticism directed at frontier AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI after former and current employees warned of the risk of an AI catastrophe within the next 10 years. events.title: From Earth to Orbit, France’s Ecosystem Delivers Agentic Computing at Scale With NVIDIA
events.summary: Companies in France are deploying agentic computing across industries spanning space, financial services, the public sector and scientific research, demonstrating how the country’s ecosystem has moved from ambition to application. France’s progress sits on deliberate groundwork. The AI Action Summit in February 2025 and Choose France Summits in 2025 and 2026 anchored major compute commitments on French soil. What the ecosystem has built since then spans the full stack. France-based companies are expanding agentic infrastructure on NVIDIA technology. Bull is extending its European AI server production to NVIDIA Vera Rubin Ultra NVL72 systems, planned for 2028, with trays produced in Europe and rack integration at its Angers factory — inaugurated Friday, Oct. 2. Altair-1, the first satellite in a $1 billion, 50-satellite constellation with on-board autonomous capabilities, launched this month and has successfully reached orbit. Integrated by Loft Orbital and built in Abu Dhabi by Orbitworks , a joint venture between Loft Orbital and Marlan Space , the satellite is flying NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin edge modules, running Mistral’s models, for real-time Earth observation and autonomous operations in orbit. NVIDIA Nemotron open models are in production across French organizations that require sovereign, trustworthy data. LINAGORA and Docaposte have secured the CANUT framework agreement , making Twake.ai, built on NVIDIA Nemotron, the sole referenced sovereign digital workplace for more than 2,500 French public organizations. In financial services, SBS is launching a sovereign platform enabling banks to deploy governed generative and agentic services within their own environments, in collaboration with NVIDIA. Last week, Mistral introduced under private preview Mistral Large 4 open model, with state-of-the-art, open weight performance in cyber defense, manufacturing, finance and multimodal tasks, and a solid foundation for customizing models across key industries. Fondation Inria , with NVIDIA’s support, is launching a working group on open source advanced modeling and tool adoption, with findings to come in the spring of next year. Across retail, public services, telecommunications and science, the pattern is consistent: open models and NVIDIA infrastructure are driving results in France. L’Oréal is integrating NVIDIA ALCHEMI into its research workflows so scientists can explore formulation possibilities in silico and better help guide laboratory research. Combining computational predictions with hands-on experimentation can make the discovery process up to 100x faster than traditional methods and maximize the potential of the group’s proprietary active ingredients. Mirakl has onboarded more than 70 million products with fine-tuned and open models running on NVIDIA GPUs and inference software, cutting seller catalog onboarding to under two hours. Photoroom and Vestiaire Collective a re demonstrating the measurable business impact of advanced visual modeling on marketplace performance. Omi helps brands bring accurate products into AI-generated marketing visuals at scale, combining its approved 3D digital twins with open models optimized on NVIDIA for 4x faster inference. In Côte-d’Or, ThinkDeep and Akila built a digital-twin agent — powered by NVIDIA Cosmos open world models, Nemotron and Omniverse libraries — managing nearly 5,800 kilometers of roads and buildings, cutting total operating costs by 10% and targeting 30% as deployment progresses. Port Sud de France runs goods processing and port security on ThinkDeep’s DeepBrain platform powered by Nemotron and Cosmos. Enchanted Tools, a robotics company headquartered in Paris, is deploying social robots to support patients in healthcare settings including pediatric cancer care. In telecom, Bouygues Telecom and Prisme.ai have launched AI Studio V2, powered by NVIDIA full-stack infrastructure, to offer all of its employees the ability to build their own agents, securely and in a controlled environment In quantum, Alice & Bob has integrated the NVIDIA NVQLink platform for its superconducting cat qubits, showing how GPUs can make quantum error correction more efficient, including for faster qubit modalities. Quandela has also been using NVQLink to build an integration between a DGX Spark system and its photonic qubits — advancing QPU-GPU supercomputing and exploring hybrid quantum-classical applications. events.title: Lobbying, lawyers and a media blitz: the fight to kill the Church of England’s £100m slavery compensation fund
events.summary: Some of Britain’s wealthiest financiers, including Sir Paul Marshall, have given a platform to critical coverage or are linked to its leading opponent “This is virtue signalling,” said Nigel Biggar. “These are elites who are trying to demonstrate that they are being progressive.” The target of his scorn was one that has obsessed him for years: the movement to pay reparations for the slave trade, and specifically the Church of England’s plan to spend £100m atoning for its involvement. “I’ve got north of 100 parish churches in my constituency, many of them crumbling,” added Katie Lam, an up-and-coming Conservative MP and immigration hardliner . Lord Biggar, a retired professor, Conservative peer and Anglican priest, was speaking alongside Lam last September on a Spectator podcast named after his latest book, Reparations: Slavery and the Tyranny of Imaginary Guilt . Since the church’s commissioners – who manage the church’s endowment – announced in 2023 that they would set up the Fund for Healing, Repair and Justice to make amends for the church’s involvement in the transatlantic slave trade, Biggar has led the backlash. In doing so he has gone from fringe voice to one of the most widely published proponents of revisionist theories about colonialism and the British empire. Dozens of articles have been published against Project Spire, as the fund is known in the church, many by Biggar and people who share similar views, in publications including the Spectator, the Daily Telegraph, the Daily Mail and the Times. Lam has led opposition in the House of Commons, asking questions of ministers and in December coordinating a letter from 27 MPs and peers to the incoming archbishop of Canterbury, Sarah Mullally , accusing the church of “legally dubious vanity projects”. The media blitz has paid off so far, paralysing the church and stalling the fund well beyond its planned launch date of 2024. The church admitted in July it also faces a legal challenge – which could add years more delay. Yet little attention has been paid to the lobbying campaign against Project Spire – and how it has become a cause célèbre within the broader rightwing ecosystem. The Guardian can reveal how some of Britain’s wealthiest financiers, including Sir Paul Marshall, are linked to the man at the heart of the campaign to kill the church’s fund. The multimillionaire co-founder of the hedge fund Marshall Wace has given Biggar and his movement a powerful platform via his stable of media outlets, which spans the Spectator magazine, the broadcaster GB News and the comment website UnHerd. A devout Christian, Marshall also funded several rightwing lobbying groups and organisations linked to Biggar to the tune of hundreds of thousands of pounds. It all appears part of the libertarian financier’s significant efforts to reshape the Church of England – and wider society – in line with his own worldview. In 2007 Dr Rowan Williams, the then archbishop of Canterbury, set in train a reckoning for one of Britain’s most venerable and staid institutions when he said the church should consider slavery reparations for its historical role in the slave trade. It signalled Lambeth Palace’s determination to atone for those failings – from its distant past to the present day. His successor, Justin Welby, reaffirmed that commitment. “I’m ashamed of our history and I’m ashamed of our failure,” said Welby, a former oil executive turned priest, in 2020. “There is no doubt when we look at our own church that we are still deeply institutionally racist.” In 2019, the church commissioners ordered research into the endowment fund’s origins and links to the slave trade. Its initial findings, published in 2022, revealed the funds partly originated in Queen Anne’s Bounty. Queen Anne’s Bounty, which was founded in 1704, invested significant sums in the South Sea Company, which traded in enslaved people – trafficking about 34,000 enslaved Africans. The South Sea Company also received numerous benefactions from individuals such as the slave trader Edward Colston, who were linked to, or who profited from, transatlantic chattel slavery and the plantation economy. Subsequent work by historians on the newly digitised Register of British Slave Traders has revealed how C of E clergymen financed the Royal African Company (RAC) , which trafficked more African men, women and children than any other single organisation in the history of the slave trade. In January 2023 the commissioners published a 25-page report on the endowment fund’s links to the slave trade, employing forensic accountants at Grant Thornton. It declared its intent to set up a £100m fund to invest and generate returns to support communities most affected by African chattel enslavement. Money would come from the church’s endowment, now valued at £11.6bn.

events.title: NutryFarm shareholders demand CEO’s immediate suspension, CFO to take over in interim
events.summary: The High Court discharged NutryFarm from judicial management on Feb 2, but its shares have remained suspended on the SGX since April 11, 2022. On Oct 9, shareholders holding at least 10% of paid-up capital asked to remove Niu from the board and all group roles, and to consider Charlie In as CEO. NutryFarm is reviewing the allegations and seeking legal advice. The row comes as the company stays suspended from trading, despite leaving judicial management in February. SINGAPORE – Shareholders seeking to oust NutryFarm International chief executive Niu Liming have stepped up their demands, calling for his immediate suspension and the appointment of the company’s chief financial officer as interim CEO. The former durian distributor said in an Oct 12 stock exchange filing that it had received an urgent demand notice from shareholders identifying themselves as acting on behalf of the group seeking a special general meeting. Their demands included suspending Niu as CEO and executive director, and appointing the current CFO to temporarily lead the company. NutryFarm’s notice did not name the CFO, but filings on the exchange show that Derek Ong Chee Beng, 60, was appointed group financial controller on June 8. NutryFarm said it was reviewing the notice and seeking legal advice. It also did not detail the grounds for suspension or announce any management changes. The Oct 12 demand follows several letters concerning Niu’s position at the firm and his right to vote on behalf of a major shareholder. On Oct 9, shareholders identifying themselves as holding at least 10% of NutryFarm’s paid-up capital requested a special general meeting to remove Niu from the board as well as his appointments across the group. They also sought to elect shareholder Charlie In as a director, and asked the board to consider appointing In as CEO. In another Oct 9 letter, the shareholders demanded Niu’s immediate removal from executive positions and his recusal from board discussions and voting on the matter. Niu Liming’s involvement in NutryFarm began before he became its executive director and CEO. NutryFarm said it was reviewing the allegations, which its announcement did not detail. The company subsequently received an objection to Niu’s proxy voting rights granted by shareholder Jia Lijie, including any conflict of interest arising from the arrangement, on Oct 11. Under a share pledge arrangement, Niu has a deemed interest in NutryFarm through Jia’s 21.7 million shares and another 13.3 million belonging to Cheng Meng, according to the company’s 2024 annual report. Including his own 360,000 shares, his direct and deemed interest in the company is 25.72%. Niu also has an ownership interest in Corpbond IV, the creditor that applied to place NutryFarm under judicial management in June 2022 . He became executive director and CEO in December that year. The High Court discharged NutryFarm from judicial management on Feb 2, but its shares have remained suspended since April 11, 2022 .

events.title: Jardine Matheson raises 2026 earnings guidance as high as US$5.65 per share
events.summary: Jardine Matheson raised its 2026 EPS guidance to US$5.50-US$5.65, above its earlier US$5.33 estimate, as portfolio performance improved. It bought Balfour Beatty’s 50% stake in Gammon Construction for £250 million, becoming sole owner. The deal should be “modestly accretive” from year one. Gammon will strengthen Jardine Engineering & Infrastructure, which aims to grow through targeted M&A. CEO Lincoln Pan wants to double JE&I earnings across Asia. SINGAPORE – Jardine Matheson expects its 2026 earnings per share (EPS) to come in between US$5.50 and US$5.65, reflecting stronger than previously expected portfolio performance , it said on Oct 13. The company, which previously expected EPS of about US$5.33, said the new range will be a 3% to 6% increase over its 2025 EPS when adjusted for disposals and reclassifications that year. Jardine Matheson on Oct 13 also said that it has acquired a 50% stake in Gammon Construction from Balfour Beatty, making it the sole owner, for £250 million (S$423.2 million). The cash will be paid in three tranches: at completion on Oct 13 , on Dec 31, 2027, and on Dec 29, 2028. The transaction is expected to be “modestly accretive” from its first year, said Jardine Matheson, adding that pricing is not subject to post-closing adjustments. The company will also acquire the Gammon Construction business inclusive of all future dividend entitlements and cash on balance sheet. Gammon Construction, an Asian construction and engineering company operating primarily in Hong Kong and Singapore, “enhances growth and scale for Jardine Engineering & Infrastructure (JE&I)”, said Jardine Matheson, which has been a Gammon investor since 1969. JE&I combines the wholly owned Jardine Engineering Corporation and Gammon Construction with two joint venture assets, Jardine Schindler and Hactl, into a new platform. It is led by Kevin O’Brien, former chief executive of Gammon Construction and Jardine Engineering Corporation, and has plans for growth supported by “targeted” mergers and acquisitions – starting with Gammon Construction. O’Brien said he expects a “significant opportunity” for Gammon to continue its growth trajectory through capturing broader regional growth trends, including demand from artificial intelligence for supporting infrastructure, energy and sustainable solutions and accelerating industrialisation across Asia. Lincoln Pan, CEO of Jardine Matheson, said: “Our goal remains doubling the earnings of JE&I in the coming years by focusing on strategic investments that expand controlled earnings and capabilities across Asia.”

Participants who failed to report and inspect clients’ programme trading, also known as quantitative trading, in compliance with the rules would be subject to disciplinary action, according to separate statements on the websites of China’s five futures bourses including the China Financial Futures Exchange and the Shanghai Futures Exchange. The announcements came just days after the China Securities Regulatory Commission convened a meeting with market participants, signalling possible stabilisation measures if stocks fell further. Top policymakers have placed great emphasis on financial stability this year, as the capital markets are a critical part of Beijing’s tech self-reliance drive, given their ability to generate funding for home-grown companies.

events.title: ACCC takes egg 'cartel' to court
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ACCC takes civil action against egg companies for alleged cartel behaviour Topic: Food and Beverage Processing Industry Sunny Queen is alleged to have breached competition laws. ( Facebook: Sunny Queen Farms ) The ACCC has launched legal action against 12 egg producers and suppliers, alleging they coordinated on production and supply decisions. The consumer watchdog alleges "widespread anti-competitive conduct" has affected egg supply in Australia since at least 2020. A spokesperson for Sunny Queen, Australia's largest egg supplier, has denied all allegations. Australia's competition regulator has launched legal action against some of the country's biggest egg producers, alleging "cartel conduct" and other anti-competitive behaviour. Sunny Queen, the largest egg supplier in Australia, and 11 other producers and suppliers are alleged to have breached competition laws by coordinating on the production and supply of eggs since 2020. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) filed civil proceedings in the Federal Court today, alleging the companies had coordinated on a range of decisions. The ACCC alleges that since at least October 2020, the egg suppliers and producers coordinated on a range of business decisions, including buying a property in Queensland to stop a rival supplier acquiring it. The legal filing comes more than a year since the ACCC launched court action against several large vegetable producers, alleging they formed a price-fixing cartel in supplying supermarket Aldi. The ACCC alleges the egg suppliers and producers coordinated on decisions about production volumes, distribution, expansion plans and culling to manage perceived oversupply in a way that likely "substantially reduced competition for many years". ACCC chair Gina Cass-Gottlieb said eggs were an important household staple, and the alleged behaviour could result in less competitive prices for consumers. "When you have good functioning competition then you have more choice, you also have price competition, so lower prices," she told Victorian Country Hour. "Our concern is that when parties are not competing and they start working together … consumers can ultimately miss out. Gina Cass-Gottlieb says the ACCC is concerned consumers could miss out on lower prices. ( Four Corners: Rob Hill ) Sunny Queen is Australia's largest wholesale egg supplier, holding about one-third of the market for supply of eggs to retailers such as Woolworths, Coles, Metcash, Aldi and Costco. The company has warehouse and distribution facilities in Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia and Western Australia. The proceedings involve allegations against entities including Sunny Queen, Doug Hall Poultry Pty Ltd, Alpair Pty Ltd trading as McLean Farms, Ellerslie Free Range Farms Pty Ltd and Kinross Farm Pty Ltd along with seven other companies. The ACCC alleges Sunny Queen, Hall and McLean Farms's coordination extended to purchasing a property in Pittsworth, Queensland, to prevent rival egg suppliers acquiring it. "We also allege this had the effect of substantially lessening competition," Ms Cass-Gottlieb said. The competition regulator also alleged Sunny Queen restricted how many eggs its rival Kinross could sell to customers, and prevented Kinross from selling its eggs to Coles, Woolworths, Aldi, Metcash or Costco. A spokesperson for Sunny Queen denied all allegations. "Sunny Queen has cooperated fully with the ACCC throughout the course of its investigation," the spokesperson said. The company said the allegations related to the terms of its agreements with its shareholders and main egg suppliers in Queensland and Victoria. It said it would remain "business as usual" while the matter was before the courts. Doug Hall Poultry, McLean Farms, Kinross Farm, Yallamundi Farms and Ellerslie have been contacted for comment. Sunny Queen is one of 12 egg producers named in the Federal Court matter. ( Supplied ) It is the first case the ACCC has brought involving concerted practice allegations since the prohibition was introduced in 2017. A concerted practice involves cooperation between businesses that goes beyond them acting independently in response to market conditions. "It can involve competitors coordinating their behaviour in ways that harm competition, even if there's no formal agreement," Ms Cass-Gottlieb said. "It can involve communication between competitors, as we allege here, a regular exchange of information … in ways that reduce independent decision-making.

events.title: IMF cuts 2026 growth forecasts for Gulf economies due to prolonged Hormuz closure
events.summary: The International Monetary Fund has significantly lowered its 2026 projections for economies across the Gulf due to the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz , and pushed back its forecast on the waterway's reopening. In its latest World Economic Outlook , released on Tuesday, the IMF also slashed its forecasts for the broader region. The Middle East and North Africa economy is estimated to contract by 2 per cent this year, a downward revision of 3.1 percentage points from its April projections. It is the only region expected to record an economic contraction this year. The IMF maintained its 2026 forecast for global growth at 3.1 per cent and lifted its projection for 2027 from to 3.4 per cent. “This is the net result of two main forces that are shaping the outlook,” IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro told reporters, referring to the negative supply shock from the Iran war and the positive demand shock from the AI infrastructure boom. The fund said the global economy had so far been able to withstand the impact from the Iran war energy shock due to a combination of factors including supply adjustment, a drawdown of inventories, lower energy intensity, and households and companies adapting to higher prices. The latest forecasts come as Saudi Arabia vowed to press on with bringing its oil supplies to market despite escalating attacks on the kingdom in recent days by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The number of vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz have declined in recent days after tanker attacks reached their highest weekly count this year on October 9. One tanker crossed the waterway on Saturday, down from eight the day before, data from analytics firm Kpler showed. Confirmed total Hormuz clearance stands at roughly 11.9 million barrels per day, or about 30 per cent below its pre-war baseline, Kpler data showed, although daily readings have swung wildly. Energy supply disruptions from the Iran war are the latest in a round of shocks the global economy has weathered in recent years. These have included the 2025 tariffs row, Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Covid-19 pandemic and the global tightening cycle that followed. “The economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits,” Ms Tenreyro said. “The task ahead is to move from coping to rebuilding, restoring fiscal space and rebuilding supply-side resilience.” The economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits Silvana Tenreyro, IMF chief economist The fund said the economic outlook is highly uneven across countries, reflecting differences in their exposure to commodities, AI-related activity and borrowing costs. Overall GDP growth in the US is forecast to be 2.3 per cent, compared to 1.1 per cent for the euro area, 1.3 per cent for the UK, 0.7 per cent in Japan and 1.1 per cent in Canada. Growth in China, which is classified as an emerging economy, is forecast to slow to 4.5 per cent growth in 2026, compared to 7 per cent for India and 3.6 per cent for Pakistan. Gulf outlook The IMF projects the UAE 's economy to contract by 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding at a 7.7 per cent growth rate in 2027, conditional on the normalisation of shipping routes and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. The new projections for the Middle East 's second-largest economy reflect a downgrade of 7 percentage points for 2026 and an upgrade of 2.4 percentage points for 2027 compared to the fund's April forecast. Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar are forecast to see double-digit contractions of 11.3, 16.7 and 15.6 per cent, respectively, in 2026. The fund also lowered its forecasts for Saudi Arabia , but expects the decline to be less sharp compared to Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar because of its diversified export routes. The fund expects Saudi Arabia to slow from a positive growth rate of 4.6 per cent last year to a 3.3 per cent contraction this year. Oman is the only GCC member to see positive economic growth in 2026 at 4.1 per cent. The latest forecast assumes the gradual reopening of the Strait of Hormuz will resume in March 2027, with a return to prewar conditions by October. It also notes that uncertainty is assumed to remain elevated throughout next year. Under these conditions, oil exporters are expected to see economic activity rebound next year, similar to the UAE. Overall GDP growth in Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar would expand by 13.9, 17.1 and 18.8, respectively, the fund said. Saudi Arabia's economic activity would accelerate at a 7.9 per cent pace. The kingdom's ministry of finance last week said its economy was forecast to grow by 12.8 per cent next year. Other oil exporters also faced downgrades for 2026 including Iraq at minus 16 per cent and Iran at minus 7.6 per cent, with the latter also impacted by enhanced sanctions and a US naval blockade. Meanwhile, the fund said importers in the region were expected to remain relatively resilient. Egypt's economy is forecast to expand by a 5.1 per cent pace in 2026, more than 8 percentage points lower than the IMF's April forecast. Morocco's economy is set grow by 4.5 per cent and Jordan's by 2.7 per cent. The fund did not submit projections for Lebanon. Conflict and AI boom lift inflation The fund said that while the Iran war and AI buildout were driving growth in opposite directions, both were adding to inflationary pressures. Global headline inflation is set to increase to 4.7 per cent in 2026 before easing to 4.1 per cent in 2027, a cumulative upwards projection of 0.7 percentage points. Ms Tenreyro said this was driving up borrowing costs in advanced economies at a time when public debt was already high. The US Federal Reserve and other central banks in advanced economies have already begun raising interest rates or are expected to this quarter. “This interaction of high debt and high financing costs, in turn, has heightened fiscal concerns and risks,” Ms Tenreyro said. Global bonds have been under significant pressure in recent weeks over fears of higher energy prices, higher-for-longer interest rates and concerns over unchecked government spending. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury , a benchmark for global borrowing costs, has recently traded at its highest level since 2002. Bonds in Japan, France, Germany and the UK have also recently hit multi-decade highs. Pimco, a global investment management firm, warned last week the yield on the 10-Year Treasury could hit 6 per cent for the first time since 2000.

events.title: Dating app Bumble in $1bn takeover talks, say reports
events.summary: Published 13 October 2026, 02:36 BST Ithaca Holdings, a technology investment firm, could announce a deal to buy the Texas-based company as early as this week, according to the Wall Street Journal. The jump in Bumble's shares pushed its stock market valuation to over $580m but that is still far below a peak of more than $14bn it reached after listing on the Nasdaq in 2021 . Bumble is one of the world's most downloaded dating apps, operating in a crowded market where growth has slowed. The BBC has contacted Bumble and Ithaca for comment. Bumble was launched in 2014 by Whitney Wolfe Herd, who was also a co-founder of dating app giant Tinder. Wolfe Herd built Bumble's brand around a distinctive feature that only allowed women to initiate conversations with matches. It recently abandoned that rule , prompting debate among users over whether the app had lost what set it apart from rivals. "Today, our community is asking for more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to create real, meaningful connections and that is what this new experience provides," Wolfe Herd said in August. Dating apps like Bumble have come under pressure in recent years as some younger users have grown disillusioned with browsing for dates. Bumble said in 2025 that it would cut almost a third of its workforce as the industry grappled with what Wolfe Herd described as an "inflection point" in online dating. Investments in other dating companies have also soured as apps have struggled to convince users to pay for their services. Match Group - which owns apps including Tinder, OkCupid and Hinge - has also seen its shares fall sharply from their peak in 2021. According a report by media watchdog Ofcom in 2025, adults in the UK were spending less time on dating apps compared to three years earlier. Some single people are instead turning to board game get-togethers , book clubs and other group activities in the hope of finding a partner. events.title: Malaysian King buys stake in miner expanding into rare earths
events.summary: Malaysia’s king, Sultan Ibrahim Sultan Iskandar, bought 2.25% of the firm’s issued shares from its managing director Pek Kok Sam at 42.5 cents per share. Malaysia’s King bought a stake in local miner Southern Alliance Mining, which is expanding into rare earths, including through a project in his home state of Johor. Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar bought 2.25% of Singapore-listed Southern Alliance Mining, an iron ore miner, for $6.1 million , the company said in a statement. He acquired the shares from the firm’s managing director Pek Kok Sam at 42.5 cents each, almost a 12% premium to the Oct 12 closing price, the company said in the statement on the same day. Shares of Southern Alliance Mining rose 10.5% to 42 cents in Singapore early on Oct 13. Sultan Ibrahim has wide business interests spanning real estate, telecommunications an infrastructure, mainly through his shareholdings in various enterprises. He is serving a five-year term as Malaysia’s king under the country’s unique rotating monarchy, in which nine hereditary rulers take turns holding the throne. A representative of Malaysia’s national palace did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Oct 13. In September 2025, Southern Alliance Mining acquired 40% of MCRE Resources, which partnered China Rare Earth Corp. for a rare earth mining operation in Perak state. Southern Alliance Mining is also pursuing a proposed acquisition of Paramount Synergy for a rare earth project in Johor as it positions itself at the forefront of the emerging sector. It has maintained a mining presence in the southern Malaysian state for many years through its flagship Chaah Mine and continues to pursue mineral resources development opportunities in the country. Malaysia has stated ambitions to become a globally competitive player in the rare earths industry, drawing significant interest from foreign miners and refiners. The country hosts Australia’s Lynas Rare Earths, one of only two major producers outside China, with local conglomerates such as Berjaya Corp also exploring projects. France’s Carester SAS plans to build a rare earths separation plant ​in the northern state of Perak as part of a venture with Malaysia’s ‌Malaco Mining Group. Southern Alliance’s Pek remains the company’s controlling shareholder, with a direct interest of 55.74%. The firm said it was not a party to the transaction and did not receive any proceeds. The share transfer will not result in any changes to the company’s management, operations or strategic direction, it said. BLOOMBERG
