events.title: What colleges and universities need from donors to thrive
events.summary: Graduates pass the John Harvard Statue during Harvard University's commencement on May 29, 2025. Harvard was the school's first big donor. Craig F. Walker/The Boston Globe via Getty Images In 1638, John Harvard , an English-born Puritan minister and teacher in the Massachusetts Bay Colony, bequeathed 400 books and half his £779 estate, today equivalent to roughly US$2 million, to the college that would be renamed in his honor after his death. In addition to launching America’s oldest university, Harvard’s donation began a tradition of philanthropy for U.S. colleges and universities that has continued ever since. Today, philanthropy is an important source of higher education funding that covers an average of 10% of college and university budgets . Based on our decades of experience as scholars , academic administrators and school fundraisers , we believe that donors – and not just big ones – are especially important to colleges and universities in tough times. In the crosshairs Since January 2025, the Trump administration has targeted colleges and universities with research funding cuts , student financial aid caps and new restrictions on how long international students can stay in the United States . University endowments have been in the crosshairs since the first Trump administration’s 2017 tax reform package . The big 2025 tax-and-spending package Trump signed raised the taxes on some schools’ endowments . A rule the Trump administration proposed in September 2026 would threaten private schools’ tax-exempt status if any of their programs use race-based criteria. There are demographic problems too. Fewer students are choosing to go to college, and the number of high school graduates who could attend is falling due to a declining birthrate . Although colleges and universities are providing more financial aid than ever , students and their families are still struggling to pay for college . Some schools are being forced to close their doors. Sixteen colleges shut down in 2025 alone , including Indiana’s only predominantly Black college, Martin University, and ecologically focused Sterling College in Vermont. And at least 40 colleges have been acquired by other schools since 2020, including Marymount Manhattan College and Mills College , which are now part of Northeastern University’s global network. A sticky note spotted at Hampshire College’s Harold F. Johnson Library on May 16, 2026, months before the school was slated to be closed for good, assured students that alumni would support them. Finn Gomez/The Boston Globe via Getty Images Higher education giving Donors contributed $79 billion to colleges and universities in 2025, up 4% in constant dollars from the year before. The richest Americans dominate giving to higher education: 89% of the funds raised came from only 2% of donors in 2025. Also in 2025, Phil and Penny Knight, the Nike co-founder and his wife, made what was then the largest single gift to a university in history when they gave the Oregon Health & Science University $2 billion for cancer research . On Sept. 30, 2026, investor Ken Griffin broke that record by giving Carnegie Mellon University more than $3 billion to build a new campus in Miami and meet some other priorities. It’s hardly the only megagift a university has received in 2026: Michael and Susan Dell, whose fortune comes from his computer hardware company, gave the University of Texas at Austin $750 million for its medical center. The Knights gave $1 billion to the University of Oregon for a new engineering college. Software billionaire David Duffield pledged $371 million to Cornell University . And many other schools have drawn gifts in excess of $100 million . The vast majority of these huge gifts are reserved for specific purposes . The share of totally unrestricted gifts to colleges and universities , those given with no strings attached, has been dwindling for decades . In 2024 it slipped below 7% . Unrestricted giving did pick up somewhat in 2025 . Perhaps that was a sign that some donors were responding to federal funding cuts with their gifts. Michael Dell, CEO of Dell Computer, and his wife Susan have given more than $1 billion to the University of Texas at Austin, with much of that funding reserved for specific purposes. Robert Daemmrich Photography Inc/Corbis via Getty Images How donors can help In an article in Change: The Magazine of Higher Learning in September 2026, we listed ideas for college and university fundraising efforts. These tie to three recommendations for donors – and not only those making multimillion-dollar gifts. 1. Pooling donations Donations to colleges and universities don’t have to end in lots of zeros to make a big difference. In 2015, the grassroots Saving Sweet Briar campaign kept the small women’s college operating even after its trustees had voted to close it. The largest gift the rural Virginia school received was $2 million, and the smallest was $1.50 from a graduate’s grandchild. This is the exception rather than the rule. Financial pressures were too much for Hampshire College, a New England private college that is slated to close after the fall semester of 2026, to withstand – even with a fundraising campaign and $5 million gift from alum and documentary filmmaker Ken Burns. Giving Days are high-profile fundraising campaigns through which many alumni and other supporters raise millions. For example, Oregon State University Dam Proud Day 2026 drew 12,400 gifts and raised over $4.1 million. Purdue University’s annual “day of giving” has generated nearly $500 million over the past decade. In 2024, it garnered $76 million from 32,000 donors. Sweet Briar College alumni take a selfie in 2015 at a pop-up fundraiser to save the womens’ college in Virginia. Evelyn Hockstein/For The Washington Post via Getty Images 2. Donating with few or no strings attached Donations with few restrictions or none at all help colleges and universities meet their greatest needs. Even if they’re mostly intended for a new building or to fund a particular program, large gifts can also include unrestricted portions to help cover costs as needs arise and priorities change. Brandeis University , Indiana University , Princeton University and other schools encourage unrestricted annual gifts. These flexible funds are helping to cover research funding shortfalls at Cornell University, undergraduate scholarships at Georgetown University and general operations at the College of the Atlantic. Novelist and philanthropist MacKenzie Scott, the former wife of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, has given more than $26 billion in unrestricted donations to nonprofits, including to colleges and universities. Historically Black colleges and universities as well as other schools with diverse student bodies , such as Robeson Community College in rural North Carolina, Oklahoma’s Carl Albert State College and Wisconsin’s Fond du Lac Tribal and Community College, have received Scott’s big gifts. events.title: Meet the Anthropic Engineer Keeping Its AI Agent Trustworthy
events.summary: If you’ve ever wondered how Claude and similar AI agents can answer complex questions in seconds and where they get the information, you’re not alone. Gurmeet Saran works to find that answer every day as an engineer at Anthropic in San Francisco, the AI research company behind Claude. The IEEE senior member is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind the chatbot’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs. Gurmeet Saran Employer Anthropic in San Francisco Title Member of technical staff Member grade IEEE senior member Alma maters University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India “My job is to make sure the data is accurate, structured, and trustworthy, and that private data stays private,” he says. “As I learned earlier in my career, privacy can’t be a layer you bolt on—it has to be part of the architecture from the start.” If you can’t trust the logic, he adds, you can’t make reliable claims about the behavior, and that has real safety implications. Safety is a priority for Anthropic, he says. According to Claude’s mission statement , the company wants the AI agent to be “genuinely helpful to the people it works with or on behalf of, as well as to society, while avoiding actions that are unsafe, unethical, or deceptive.” Crucial to the mission is ensuring that researchers can observe and understand how AI models behave, a challenge that is especially acute for large language models , Saran says. “We have decent tools to monitor databases and web services,” he says, “but for LLMs, we’re still figuring it out.” Solving data quality problems at Yahoo, Intuit, and Meta Saran’s interest in computing systems dates back to his childhood in Kolkata, where he logged as much time as he could in the school computer lab. “I remember the first time I used one of the computers,” he says. “What struck me was that you could write instructions, and the machine would follow them exactly. No ambiguity. “That felt magical to me.” After graduating from high school in 1999, he stayed in India to pursue advanced degrees. He earned a bachelor’s degree in electronics and telecommunication engineering in 2004 at the University of Kalyani . In 2010, he earned a master’s degree in software engineering from the Birla Institute of Technology and Science in Pilani. While a graduate student, he began his career in 2007 at Yahoo as a technical lead of the data team in Bengaluru, India. While there, he encountered the project that shaped his career trajectory: working on web analytics and business intelligence reporting solutions. “We kept running into a frustrating problem,” he recalls. “Different teams would calculate the same website metric—something like daily active site users—using slightly different logic, and end up with conflicting answers. It sounds like a small issue, but when leadership is making decisions about resource allocation and product development using that data, not knowing which number is correct becomes a problem.” The team built a central data repository with defined metrics, essentially serving as a single source of truth. Saran created a model that defined what “daily active site users” means, breaking down which events counted, how to handle edge cases (or when standard code fails), and more. With the new model, data teams across the company could rely on a standard method to determine the number of daily active users for the projects and sites they were responsible for and obtain comparable results using the same logic. From there, Saran and his team built Yahoo! Digits , an internal web analytics tool used for all the company’s products. Saran left Yahoo in 2010 to join Intuit as a staff engineer in Mountain View, Calif. He helped build the analytics infrastructure that unified data across the company’s products, including TurboTax and QuickBooks accounting software. During his tenure, Intuit developed a feature that detected fraudulent tax filings in real time. It required Saran and other engineers to build a system to protect taxpayer data while adhering to strict U.S. Internal Revenue Service policies. “IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations.” “This taught me that privacy and governance can’t be layers you bolt onto software after the fact,” he says. “They have to be part of the architecture from the start.” Saran joined Meta (known as Facebook at the time) in 2016 as a lead software engineer in Menlo Park, Calif. The company was facing controversy over its video metrics: Meta publicly acknowledged an error that caused it to overstate the number of views for posted videos . “This wasn’t a coding bug; it was an architectural problem,” Saran says. He built a system that worked similarly to what he had developed at Intuit, whereby one single truth was defined to govern all video view metrics across the site. That system, Metric360 , eventually became part of the site’s architecture. By the time he left Meta in 2021, he says, Metric360 was being used across the company to calculate video metrics. He left the company to become a principal software engineer at Wealthfront , a financial services company in Palo Alto, Calif. He helped build the company’s data infrastructure. Building trustworthy AI systems at Anthropic Saran joined Anthropic in 2025 as a member of the technical staff. To describe the implications of his work, he uses a medical analogy: “Imagine a doctor is monitoring a patient’s vital signs and making treatment decisions based on those numbers. What if one or a few of the medical devices used were slightly miscalibrated? Even if most readings are fine, it’s a serious problem because the difficult decisions happen in the margins. “It’s the same with AI systems. My job is essentially to make sure the instruments are giving accurate readings—that the data means what it says it means.” His job comes with high stakes and complex problems to solve. “ AI agents are especially tricky to observe,” he says. “When a system is taking sequences of actions [generating conversational responses with different users], you need a way to capture what it did, what information it was working from, and whether outcomes matched what the end user expected. And you have to do all of that without exposing anyone’s private information—the systems are designed to recognize sensitive data and keep it protected as it flows through. events.title: Cosmetic surgery event cancelled after questions over doctors' registration
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts South Korean company cancels cosmetic surgery event after ABC raises questions A South Korean cosmetic surgery company has cancelled a Sydney event where prospective patients were due to meet Korean doctors. The company had been questioned about promotions featuring doctors who were not registered to practise in Australia. Women who travel to South Korea for procedures are documenting the process online. A South Korean cosmetic surgery company has cancelled a Sydney event where prospective patients were due to meet Korean doctors, after questions were raised by the ABC. The two-day, appointment-only event was advertised by South Korean company Restory Plastic Surgery, featuring two doctors who were not registered to practise in Australia. Examples of some of the advertisements promoting the now cancelled Korean surgeons' visit. ( Supplied: Restory Plastic Surgery ) National laws prohibit doctors who are not registered in Australia from providing medical consultations or services in the country. Previous advertising stated both doctors would attend the event. ( Supplied ) In response to questions about the event and the legalities of foreign doctors providing medical consultations in Australia, the South Korean company pulled down its advertising. "Dr I Yung Moon and Dr Myung Joon Lee will not be travelling to Australia and will not be attending the Sydney event," the company told the ABC. "We acknowledge that the presentation of the promotional material may have created the impression that the doctors themselves would be travelling to Sydney, and we would like to clarify that this is not the case." Pia Marshall documented her procedure on social media. ( Supplied/ABC News: Pete Mullins ) The ABC understands similar medical expo events are held regularly, prompting warnings from Australia's peak plastic surgery body about the risks of overseas procedures and the rules governing medical advertising. Sunshine Coast woman Pia Marshall met a different Korean cosmetic surgery company in Melbourne last year at an expo similar to the one that was due to be held in Sydney. She said meeting patients at events like these appeared to be common practice, but after doing her own research, she decided to undergo the procedure with a different surgeon. The marketing specialist travelled to South Korea with her mother, Marion, for matching face lifts and documented their experiences online. The women, aged 41 and 69, travelled to Incheon, a city bordering Seoul, in June to undergo deep-plane face lifts, neck lifts and lower mid-face lifts. The procedures, performed under general anaesthetic, typically take several hours and involve repositioning the skin and underlying tissues to restore facial contours. The Australian Society of Plastic Surgeons (ASPS) confirmed wound infection and haematoma, when blood collects under the skin, were the most common face lift complications requiring operative intervention. The mother and daughter said South Korea's reputation for skin care, known as K-beauty, and the growing number of social media testimonials made it an "obvious choice", even though the face lifts themselves were not significantly different from procedures available in Australia. Pia Marshall spent 14 days in South Korea for the procedures. ( ABC News: Mark Leonardi ) Australia is now the second-highest-spending K-beauty market per capita globally , behind only South Korea, according to data from Future Market Insights. Pia was quoted $36,000 for the procedures, including accommodation and 14 days in South Korea. However, she negotiated a social media agreement with the company but could not disclose the details of the arrangement. Testimonial-style advertising for cosmetic surgery is prohibited when promoting a health service provided by an Australian-registered practitioner, but the same restrictions do not apply to overseas practitioners. A face lift in Australia typically starts at around $25,000, according to the ASPS, with the cost increasing depending on the surgeon, procedure and complexity. Pia said she found overseas cosmetic surgery options more accessible than those in Australia, due to Australia's strict advertising rules. Influencers are advertising the surgery. ( Graphic: ABC News ) While Pia said she did extensive research before her surgery, other influencers documenting their experiences have taken a more casual approach to discussing the risks. Ruby Tuesday Matthews is a 33-year-old Byron Bay content creator who specialises in lifestyle and luxury content and recently documented her own face lift.

Meta’s Superintelligence Lab released a pair of new state-of-the-art models on Monday, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, representing the company’s first attempt at a frontier model. Where Muse Spark aimed to be a lightweight model that could perform at low latency, the Wonder models are larger and said to be more capable, with higher benchmark scores and better results on complex tasks like coding. According to Meta’s testing (presented in the model card ), Wonder and Wonder Full achieve comparable benchmark scores to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra. “Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” Meta’s blog post about the models reads. That scale is reflected in the pricing: Accessed through the Meta Model API, Wonder will cost $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, making it roughly equivalent in cost to GPT-6 Sol or Opus 5.5. Notably, Wonder Full will only be available to Muse Code subscribers and will not be served through the API. Both models will also be used to power the Muse agent. In keeping with Meta’s interest in developing personal assistants that can perform tasks over a long period, the company placed particular emphasis on the new models’ ability to retain and synthesize information given by the user, a property Meta calls “active memory.” To achieve better recall, Meta highlighted the MemoryBench benchmark , which challenges continual learning and memory construction frameworks. The new models are the first frontier model release since Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang restructured Meta’s AI efforts in August of last year . Since then, Meta has released its lightweight Muse Spark model and Muse agent but has avoided the kind of state-of-the-art model releases OpenAI and Anthropic are known for. According to the post, the models were trained at Meta’s Prometheus data center in central Ohio , which came online earlier this year. events.title: Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring
events.summary: By Ke Yang , PhD Student Chenglong Wang , Senior Researcher Michel Galley , Senior Principal Research Manager Chandan Singh , Senior Researcher Jeevana Priya Inala , Senior Researcher ChengXiang Zhai , Professor, University of Illinois Department of Computer Science Jianfeng Gao , Technical Fellow & Corporate Vice President StudentSim is a research system for evaluating and improving AI tutors before they are tested with real learners; it is not a product, is not deployed in classrooms, and is not intended to replace teachers AI tutoring tools need feedback from students to improve, but collecting that feedback through human studies is slow, costly, and difficult to scale StudentSim trains personalized AI student simulators from publicly available, de-identified learner records, with one simulator adapted to each student The work evaluates simulators along two education-grounded dimensions: whether they respond like a specific student, and whether they update after tutor guidance Across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics, StudentSim outperforms leading baselines and provides a useful feedback signal for training an AI tutor In research settings, teams are exploring how AI-powered tutoring systems can help explain a math problem, suggest an edit to a writing assignment, or guide a learner through a chess position. Yet the quality of teaching cannot be measured only from the tutor’s answer. A tutor needs to know what happens after the guidance reaches a student. Did the student correct the original mistake? Did the hint help them reason toward the answer, or did it give away too much? Would a different student need a different kind of support? In today’s AI tutor research, answering these questions often requires real learner studies. Those studies are valuable, but they are slow and costly to run, which makes it hard to use student feedback during fast model iteration. StudentSim is an AI system that creates personalized simulators of individual students, modeling how they answer questions and how their answers change after receiving a tutor’s guidance. The goal is to make student feedback more available during AI tutor development. This research also introduces StudentSimEval, a benchmark and evaluation protocol spanning chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics. Importantly, the goal is not to replace teachers or classroom learning. Instead, StudentSim helps researchers evaluate and improve AI tutoring systems during the research and development process before testing them with real learners. The research uses only publicly available learner datasets released for research use with de-identified records; no personally identifying information is used at any stage. Measuring what a student simulator needs to do A simple way to build a student simulator is to ask a large language model to role-play a learner. For example, a prompt might say, “You are an elementary-school student who struggles with math.” The model can change its tone and express uncertainty. The harder part is preserving the learner’s actual ability boundary. A model may speak in a young student’s voice while still relying on knowledge and reasoning far beyond that student’s level. For training an AI tutor, this can produce misleading feedback: the tutor may appear effective because the simulated student is too capable. Traditional student modeling approaches face a different limitation. Knowledge tracing and behavior prediction models are grounded in real learning records and can estimate a student’s current knowledge, skills, and learning habits. Many of these models, however, were not designed to take natural-language tutor guidance as input. They can help describe what a student has done, but they do not always tell us how a student would respond to a particular explanation, hint, or Socratic question. StudentSim defines the target through two dimensions inspired by education research. Educators often distinguish what a learner can do independently from what they can do with support. Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development captures this gap between current independent performance and performance with guidance. StudentSim turns this idea into two evaluation goals. Behavioral fidelity measures whether a simulator matches a specific student’s recorded responses on held-out problems. Guidance responsiveness measures whether the simulator updates its response after reading tutor guidance. These two goals are complementary. A simulator that only matches past student behavior may be useful for prediction, but it does not show whether a teaching intervention helped. A simulator that always follows the tutor may respond fluently, but it may fail to represent a particular student’s strengths, weaknesses, and likely mistakes. AI tutor training needs both signals: the learner’s starting point and how guidance affects the learner’s performance. Training personalized simulators from sparse student records StudentSimEval is built entirely from publicly available learner datasets that are released for research use with de-identified records. The records carry no personally identifying information, and each personalized simulator is trained only on the de-identified records of the student it represents. Real student data is often sparse at the individual level. A learner may contribute only a small number of essays, answers, or interactions. Training a separate simulator from scratch for each student would risk overfitting and would require each model to relearn common patterns in the domain. StudentSim uses a two-stage training pipeline. In the first stage, the model trains on records pooled across many students in the same domain. This stage learns common response formats, common errors, and common ways students revise after guidance. In the second stage, the model is specialized on one student’s own records, producing a personalized simulator for that student. The evaluation covers three domains with different response types. In chess, the simulator predicts a player’s next move and how that player may revise after coaching. In second-language English writing, it generates essays with error patterns matching a learner and predicts corrections after teacher feedback. In mathematics, it predicts a student’s multiple-choice answer and whether the student updates after an explanation. Across these domains, StudentSimEval uses the same principle: compare all methods on the same per-student training records and the same held-out evaluation records. StudentSim outperforms leading baselines across the three domains. In chess, for example, StudentSim reaches behavioral fidelity of 0.5150 and guidance responsiveness of 0.9067. GPT-5.4 reaches 0.2316 and 0.7186, respectively. Maia2, a chess-specific human move prediction model, reaches 0.4535 and 0.2721.

events.title: U.K. prime minister attributes plot against U.S. bomber base to Iran
events.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the U.K. House of Commons Monday that Iran's Revolutionary Guard was "almost certainly" behind the suspected plot to attack the RAF Fairford base where U.S. bombers were stationed. Why it matters: This was the first time the U.K. officially blamed Iran for the alleged planned attack . What he's saying: "I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by the IRGC. We will not tolerate these threats on our soil," Burnham said. Driving the news: 10 days ago, the U.S. evacuated a dozen B-1 strategic bombers from RAF Fairford in response to intelligence indicating an Iranian drone attack. It would have been an unprecedented and brazen move by Iran against a U.S. base in Europe — with the potential to dramatically escalate the war in the Middle East. The decision to move the bombers came several days after British security forces arrested several dual British-Iranian citizens suspected of planning an attack on the base. It was unclear whether the people who were arrested were connected to the alleged planned drone attack or if they were planning a different attack. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel provided the U.K. with intelligence that pointed to a threat of an Iranian attack. State of play: British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Monday that the Iranian ambassador was summoned to the foreign office in London to denounce the alleged Iranian plot. The other side: The Iranian ambassador to the UK, Seyed Ali Mousavi, told IRNA that Iran "categorically rejects" the allegations. After his meeting with the UK minister for the Middle East, Stephen Doty, Mousavi said Iran had no involvement in the incident and asked the British government to provide evidence to support its claims. He added that Iran is ready to cooperate with the British authorities in investigating the issue. What they're saying: The U.S., U.K. and 27 other western countries published a joint statement on Monday condemning Iran for "use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners." The group said the threat against RAF Fairford "demonstrates the IRGC's continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors."

events.title: When AI is subject to less regulation than your fridge, something is startlingly wrong | Richard Hermer
events.summary: When AI is subject to less regulation than your fridge, something is startlingly wrong Let’s be clear: the risk to humanity is unprecedented. Without an urgent public debate and robust use of international law, we will lose control of the future I n my two years as attorney general, I spent more time working on national security than any other issue. The range and gravity of the threats posed to our nation are multifold, from terrorism, armed conflicts and nuclear proliferation, to the impacts of financial insecurity and the climate crisis. All profound challenges, yet ones our superb intelligence and defence communities are well placed to counter. The risk from AI is of an altogether different magnitude, not only in scale, but also because there is a limited time window to address it. The risk is difficult to overestimate: it poses an existential risk to humanity. The lights are flashing red and we must act now before it’s too late. Although the extraordinary threats posed by AI have long been flagged by those closely involved in its creation, it was not until very recently, after the disclosure of the Hugging Face hack and the resignation of Jacob Coxon from Anthropic , that the issue at last started to gain traction in the public discourse. This moment is an opportunity, and to capitalise on it we desperately need increased urgency in international coordination to regulate frontier AI. There must also be meaningful public engagement with how AI should be shaped to benefit humanity, rather than entrench the power of a few. We cannot leave this to China, the US and big tech – we must all demand a voice in the debate. AI has enormous potential benefits for us all. It will be the source of mind-blowing advances in science and medicine, and offers hope for empowerment of some of the world’s most dispossessed people. Yet the risks we are now facing are truly staggering. I would put them in two very broad categories. The first is existential risk: quite literally the possibility that AI could kill billions, either because it enables terrible people to do terrible things – such as design and deploy biological weapons – or because AI itself determines it is more efficient to dispense with humans. The second category is existential challenge – that, left unchecked, the development of AI will deprive billions of us of meaningful agency over our lives, with utterly profound consequences for economies, national security and human happiness. As Bill Gates recently wrote , the AI era will herald “one of the most turbulent times in human history”, noting that it will either be the greatest equaliser ever invented or the worst source of injustice. He is right. On its current trajectory, it risks simultaneously revolutionising the meaning and availability of productive work, while placing unimaginable power in the hands of not only two states (the US and China) but also a small number of individuals who control the tech giants. The plain fact is that we really don’t know what the precise degree of risk is, or the full panorama of the challenge. Part of the problem is that AI is rapidly developing to a level that humans simply do not understand and will reach a point at which – even if they do – they will no longer have the means to control it. Recall that the 2008 financial crash was caused in part because no humans really understood the web of financial transactions that were leading inexorably to disaster. What we face today, though, is on a different scale in terms of the complexity of the systems and the human agency over them, as well as the level of devastation that might be wrought. The startling levels of risk we are discussing should be completely unacceptable to all of us. In today’s age it is unthinkable that the manufacturer of a toaster would be allowed to market a product with a 10% chance of electrocuting you. The case for slowing down frontier AI before we are clear that the risks can be managed is blindingly obvious. AI needs rigorous regulation now. There is more regulation governing the safety of your fridge than the work being undertaken by frontier AI labs that threaten to wipe out your family. It is ludicrous to suggest the industry can be left to regulate itself. The AI companies and the financial markets underpinning them are incentivised to develop new iterations as quickly as possible, all of this fuelled by the geopolitics of the race between China and the US for dominance. The sight of President Trump and Elon Musk on the White House Lawn brandishing a “ voluntary code ” provided little in the way of reassurance. It will be international law that matters. While the UK has shown sterling leadership (started by Rishi Sunak, embraced by Keir Starmer and now reflected in Andy Burnham’s promotion of Kanishka Narayan to cabinet ), the scale of the challenge requires international cooperation to have any effect.

events.title: Stellantis and Renault back UK to get EU car industry protection
events.summary: Bosses of Citroën owner and French carmaker also urge UK government to consider limiting imports from China Stellantis and Renault have backed the UK car industry for inclusion in proposed rules to protect EU industry, but urged the British government to consider limiting imports of Chinese cars. Emanuele Cappellano, who leads Stellantis’s European brands including Fiat, Citroën, Opel and Vauxhall, and François Provost, the chief executive of France’s Renault, said the UK should effectively be counted as one of the EU’s 27 member states for the purposes of the proposed “Made in Europe” legislation . The new rules aim to ensure EU subsidies and government procurement benefits Europe’s industry, rather than helping manufacturers from other countries. The executives were speaking at the Paris motor show, which was attended on Monday by the French president, Emmanuel Macron. Brands including Li Auto, GAC and Chery were among a host of Chinese manufacturers exhibiting in Paris with ambitious European expansion plans. Europe’s car industry is under enormous pressure as it copes with lower demand than before the coronavirus pandemic, while also investing tens of billions of euros in shifting production to electric vehicles (EVs). At the same time, Chinese carmakers’ market share has soared as the transition to EVs opens the door to new entrants. The EU confirmed on Monday it would limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year. The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share, which now stands at 6% in a landmark four-year agreement made in Beijing last week. The Made in Europe rules are another plank of the EU’s response to the rise of China in key manufacturing industries such as carmaking and chemicals. Under the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), cars will have to be “made in Europe”, and contain enough European parts and materials, to continue to qualify for EV grants and to be bought by public bodies in the EU. However, automotive manufacturers and politicians are haggling over the details. If Brussels sticks to a strict definition of “European” as being only EU countries, Britain risks being left out – prompting intense lobbying from UK car industry and government to be included. Stellantis is among the manufacturers that still has a British factory, its facility in Ellesmere Port, Merseyside, which produces small vans. “I think that UK somehow needs to be equalised to the EU 27,” said Cappellano, referring to the bloc’s 27 member states. “We have a lot of relationship, we have footprint. Historically UK has been very close to the European market.” Europe’s main automotive lobby groups ACEA and Clepa have also put their weight behind the UK to be included. Some parts of European manufacturing, including France’s industry minister , had argued that the UK should be left out given Brexit. Provost said there was “no other choice” but a deal between the UK and EU. However, he said the UK would also have to stop allowing Chinese cars in without limits. “On your side, you have also to take decisions,” he said. “If the UK is willing to join the European ecosystem, this is to have an industrial ambition … to keep a strong automotive industry.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning He said this would be an industry that “is not closed to Chinese competitors, but … if you want to operate in Europe, you have to deeply invest in the whole value chain, final manufacturing, suppliers, R&D, technologies.” Provost added: “I’m not here to demand whatsoever, but I think if UK is willing to join this ecosystem of IAA, there is some open question about the level of imports.” London has so far rejected pressure to impose its own tariffs on Chinese imports, but the UK business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, this month said that decision was under review . Cappellano also said the UK should consider imposing tariffs on Chinese imports. “It’s very important that the UK defines what is the priority,” he said. “It’s very difficult to defend industrial footprint and at the same time let the market completely open to import. Either one or the other.” He expressed scepticism over whether other countries beyond the EU such as Japan, Turkey and Morocco should be included in the rules. “We don’t necessarily need to have a larger definition of European scope,” he said, pointing to proposals that carmakers be allowed to source 30% of their materials from outside the EU. He also argued for more time until 2030 for manufacturers to source batteries from within Europe. China is dominant in the global supply of batteries and Cappellano said it would take longer to build up the European industry.

events.title: Microsoft to expand Maia chip for the AI era
events.summary: Microsoft to expand Azure Maia system to multi-gigawatt deployments Oct 12, 2026 | Scott Guthrie - Executive Vice President, Cloud + AI Azure Maia 200 now in production; Azure Maia 300 coming in 2027 As we move into the era of Super Intelligence, Microsoft is entering a new phase of infrastructure. We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary inference system for Microsoft products and services. The multigenerational Azure Maia program has become a foundational element of Microsoft’s AI infrastructure strategy. Maia 200 is now serving Microsoft production workloads, including Microsoft Copilot , and supporting the MAI team as they develop next-generation models, with GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry to follow by end of year. Across these workloads, Maia 200 runs OpenAI models , Microsoft’s own MAI models and leading open-source model families. Insights from the scale of Microsoft’s AI services allow for unique co-design between hardware systems and software applications to optimize real-world use cases across enterprise applications and industry scenarios. Maia 300 is a complete intelligent system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks. By improving efficiency across the system, we expect Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems. And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200. Maia 200: Driving the workloads that Microsoft runs at scale The Azure Maia system is designed around the real-world workloads Microsoft runs at scale and the models we expect to build in the years ahead. Because silicon development takes years, our software and hardware teams collaborate early to anticipate architectures, scale and capabilities, translating those requirements into greater memory capacity, higher bandwidth and more accelerators operating as a single system. That co-engineering is already delivering measurable efficiency gains. Maia 200 is deploying across the United States, Europe and Australia and delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt for built-in AI capabilities in Microsoft Teams, Copilot and Cowork experiences compared with leading GPU infrastructure. Experience running our AI models and services on Maia 200 directly informed the design of Maia 300. Together, the two generations are designed to support a broad set of additional Microsoft’s AI services: multi-step agentic work that will help GitHub deliver coding experiences more efficiently; cloud-scale model serving that will help Microsoft Foundry support diverse architectures and deployment environments; inference and data generation for the MAI team; and latency-sensitive interactions that will help Dragon Copilot scale workflows and reduce clinicians’ administrative burden. Maia 300: Scaling more useful AI within every megawatt AI is becoming a foundational layer of every application, workflow and business process. As enterprises move beyond chat experiences to systems of agents that can reason, act and collaborate, AI infrastructure must deliver intelligence securely and efficiently at scale while continuously adapting as models and workloads evolve. As the third generation of our Azure Maia program, Maia 300 is designed with an inference-first architecture optimized for long-context, memory-intensive and decode-heavy AI workloads. This involves balancing compute, memory bandwidth, networking and power efficiency at cloud scale. Key capabilities of the Maia 300 system include: Less data movement, more useful compute: Moving data efficiently, rather than raw compute power, is increasingly the bottleneck in large inference systems. Maia 300’s software-defined dataflow architecture and AI-assisted kernel optimization work together to maximize locality, reduce data movement and improve utilization across compute, memory and networking resources. By treating dataflow as a first-class design principle, Maia 300 delivers a significant performance-per-watt advantage over traditional GPU architectures. Higher memory bandwidth within every watt: As AI workloads become increasingly context and memory-bound, Maia 300 delivers industry-leading HBM bandwidth per watt. Eight HBM4 stacks provide 18.0 TB/s of peak memory bandwidth within a 950-watt TDP, enabling efficient execution of large models and long-context workloads. Specialized kernel support uses on-die SRAM as a software-managed scratchpad, reducing pressure on HBM. Chiplet architecture for enhanced efficiency: A new multi-chiplet architecture separates compute, memory-controller and I/O functions, improving efficiency, scalability and cost structure. Compute chiplets are built on TSMC’s N2P process node to maximize performance-per-watt. Larger context, richer intelligence: By designing for advanced low-precision formats, including enhanced MXFP4, Maia 300 reduces memory and bandwidth requirements for both computation and KV-cache storage. The result is larger context windows, higher throughput and improved model efficiency within the same power envelope. Scale-up networking at datacenter scale: Maia 300 treats networking as a seamless extension of the software-defined dataflow architecture. Rather than moving data through separate communication layers, dataflow operations span compute, memory and network resources as a single system. High-bandwidth interconnects between Maia accelerators are optimized for tensor parallelism, while a custom AI transport delivers performant and reliable scale-up communication across accelerators and racks. The AI-optimized transport leverages Ethernet-based networking infrastructure to enable a unified topology that scales efficiently from a single rack to datacenter-scale deployments. Higher AI throughput from every rack: Maia 300 rack systems bring together 96 accelerators within a 167-kilowatt power envelope, delivering 27.6 TB of HBM capacity and 1.7 PB/s of aggregate HBM bandwidth across a high-speed scale-up domain. That density allows Microsoft to serve more simultaneous AI interactions and larger workloads from each rack, improving datacenter capacity and the economics of expanding AI services. Maia 300 will begin production deployments in 2027. For more information on Maia 300 architectural details, read our technical paper . Azure Maia is at the heart of our Frontier Transformation The future will not be defined by a single model or a single piece of silicon or a single innovation. Model and silicon choice are inherent in our vision for Frontier Transformation. Our focus is on developing responsible, affordable and scalable platforms that will help everyone amplify their intelligence to drive breakthrough outcomes that matter for them.

The U.S. Air Force will buy data collected by WindBorne Systems ‘ fleet of autonomous weather balloons under a new contract that could be worth nearly $50 million to the startup. WindBorne currently has about 700 weather balloons flying around the globe, collecting atmospheric sensor readings that the company sells to customers and also feeds into its own AI weather forecasting model. WindBorne, founded in 2015 and based in Redwood City, California, is one of the first organizations to directly feed empirical data into a deep-learning weather model. The company has worked closely with the U.S. government, particularly the National Weather Service and the U.S. Air Force and Navy, but this is the single-largest contract the company has participated in. The contract is worth up to $49 million, but the Air Force pays only as it needs data. It can place orders for specific regions at specific times. So far, it has ordered $1.7 million worth, and executives expect more orders to follow. “This is largely a vehicle through which continued growth of the constellation can be supported, as well as some work on research and development to continue to improve the hardware and performance of the balloons,” WindBorne co-founder and CTO Andrey Sushko told TechCrunch. He added that the contract, which was awarded without competitive bidding, is “a determination by the government that for this capability of collecting global data, we were the only company able to provide it in the way that met their needs for these operations.” WindBorne CEO John Dean told TechCrunch in August that the company had raised a $37 million Series B round to continue scaling its business. Earlier this summer, the company released the latest version of its forecasting model, WeatherMesh 6, which it says provides more accurate forecasts than the traditional model run by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), which simulates the atmosphere using the laws of physics. Since the arrival of transformer model architectures and the ECMWF’s release of a massive weather dataset a few years ago, AI weather forecasting has become one of the more productive uses of deep-learning technology. Meteorologists previously relied on expensive supercomputers running detailed equations that approximate how the atmosphere behaves. Now, end-to-end learning can ingest decades of weather data and issue predictions more quickly. Models built by frontier labs and government agencies are proving more accurate than traditional forecasts, although it is still a jagged frontier, with both types of forecasts required to enable useful understanding of the weather. Google DeepMind’s latest weather model offers important new capabilities, and its cyclone forecasting tools are becoming increasingly central to how the U.S. government responds to hurricane season. In August WindBorne became the first organization to send an unpowered flight system — one with no engine — to collect data in the eye of a typhoon . The company maneuvers its balloons by adjusting their altitude, bleeding air, or dropping sand carried as ballast, to send the vehicles into winds that take them where they need to go. “That’s a pretty novel step, and the two ingredients for that are one, having good wind and weather models, and knowing how to navigate them; and two, having a large enough constellation that you have balloons in the right places,” Sushko said. “It’s one of the first times that a deep-learning model was used for actual operational decisions.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Trump's Russia deal leaves GOP candidates with a Putin problem
events.summary: Republicans already saddled with Trump's unpopular policies in the midterms now face another awkward choice: whether to back his diesel deal with a dictator many of them despise. Why it matters: The agreement President Trump struck with Russian President Vladimir Putin Friday is designed to ease the cost of living for U.S. consumers. But Republicans who pleaded for help with fuel prices now face a fresh dispute over Russia, with energy analysts questioning whether the deal will deliver the relief Trump is promising. The big picture: With three weeks until Election Day, Republicans are trying to answer voter anger while keeping up with a president whose proposed fixes keep becoming political liabilities of their own. Trump's decision to lock arms with Putin adds another complication. Driving the news: Weeks after signing a sweeping Russia sanctions law, Trump announced Friday that Russia would supply diesel to U.S. and global markets. The next day, Trump blamed Ukraine for soaring diesel prices and called for President Volodymyr Zelensky to be replaced, even as Russia continued attacking Ukrainian cities. Republicans who just supported squeezing Moscow have three options in the final sprint for control of Congress: defend Trump's reversal, break with him or stay quiet. Zoom out: The diesel deal packs some of the GOP's biggest liabilities into one decision: the Iran war's economic fallout, the party's split over Russia and a president determined to make the election about himself. The deal also reverses Trump's own pressure campaign. Last year, he slapped an extra 25% tariff on India for buying Russian oil. On Oct. 2, he and other G7 leaders pledged to keep sanctions on Russia. Energy analysts also doubt the deal will do much for diesel prices, which averaged $6.28 a gallon Oct. 11, up 71% from a year earlier. What they're saying: The White House pushed back on criticism of Trump's record: "President Trump has consistently proven his doubters wrong," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said. A senior administration official said Trump is "laser-focused on bringing down costs, whether it's diesel with the Russians or importing Argentine beef. Some people might not like it, but he's thinking of what Americans are paying and what he can do about it." Friction point: The internal pushback has been swift. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) vowed to force a House vote blocking the oil purchases. Reps. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) and Michael McCaul (R-Texas), along with Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), Susan Collins (R-Maine), Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) and John Curtis (R-Utah), already criticized the deal by Sunday. Tillis told NBC News' "Meet the Press" that Trump's deal may violate a law that requires the White House to notify Congress before lifting sanctions. Even MAGA ally Laura Loomer denounced the deal as not only funding Russia but indirectly helping Iran by putting "money back into the coffers of the Islamic regime of Iran." Yes, but: Some Republicans, like Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (Fla.) and Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso , backed the deal. How we got here: Farm-state Republicans have pleaded with the White House to deliver diesel relief. Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and others urged Trump to ban diesel exports, something the president embraced before the White House abruptly reversed and ruled out a ban. GOP candidates in key Senate races, like Iowa's Ashley Hinson and Michigan's Mike Rogers , have called for ending the Iran war after previously supporting it. Instead, Trump has defended it in vivid terms, saying Iran might have attacked Los Angeles and San Diego if not for his war. Between the lines: Trump's unpopular positions collide with voter sentiment as he touts the war with Iran, the rise of data centers and his own popularity. His efforts to give Republicans something to campaign on leave candidates exposed through big promises, about-faces and proposals that won't materialize before voters cast their ballots. Data centers: Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) has faced Democratic attacks over data centers, an issue the National Republican Senatorial Committee has identified as a vulnerability. Yet Trump used a Husted rally last week to defend the projects: "Look, there's so much money to be made for Ohio. You can't just turn them off. They'll go to China." Dividend checks: Voters have also rejected Trump's proposed $5,000 dividend checks that analysts say would cost $1.3 trillion . A September Reuters/Ipsos poll found 63% of Americans disapproved. Trump: Trump has insisted the midterms should be a referendum on his presidency, telling Republicans at last month's convention to "pretend that I'm on the ballot." But a Pew Research Centerpoll released Thursday found 44% of registered voters view their congressional vote as a vote against Trump, compared with 19% who see it as a vote for him. Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton privately blamed oil prices, the Iran war and the midterm convention for falling poll numbers. The bottom line: For Republican candidates, the challenge isn't just selling Trump's record. It's keeping up with a president who continues to give them new decisions to defend.

events.title: Muse Wonder Puts Meta Back at the AI Frontier
events.summary: When Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg rebooted his company’s artificial intelligence efforts last year, it seemed to be a very expensive gamble. Meta’s latest AI models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, seem to show that the bet is finally paying off by putting the company back at the frontier of AI development. Muse Wonder Full boasts frontier capabilities, Meta says, meaning that it is among the most capable AI models in the world. “Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” the company said in a blog post today. The Muse Wonder models will be available through an API and through Muse Code, a tool for writing software with AI. Meta says the best version of the model will power features across its platforms, including its Muse personal agent . Zuckerberg overhauled his company’s AI research last year by sinking billions into the recently formed Meta Superintelligence Labs, and hiring the former Scale AI CEO Alexandr Wang to lead it. This effort has sometimes been rocky , with some researchers not sticking around for long. Meta was once a trailblazer in AI. Its Llama series of models were the first frontier open-weight offerings from a big lab. Llama, which could be downloaded and run on one’s own hardware, was widely adopted by researchers and startups. But the company fell behind after delivering several disappointing versions of the model, and as Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google rapidly introduced more capable models. Meta announced the first model from its new lab, Muse Spark , in April of this year. The company has also released a small open-weight model called Muse Glimmer , and says it plans to release larger open-weight models in the future. It did not disclose details of how new Muse Wonder models were built or trained. Muse Wonder was built to compete with the very best, however. Meta says the largest version of the new model outperforms Anthropic’s second-best model, Claude Fable 5.1, and ranks just below its best, Claude Opus 5.5, on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , a widely used aggregated score of model capabilities. Meta says the model outperforms OpenAI’s best model, GPT-6 Astra, and both Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 on some specialized benchmarks, including ones that measure a model’s ability to work with legal documents and to build software. Benchmarks are not always a reliable measure of real-world performance, but this is still a significant step forward for Meta’s models. Muse Wonder also includes two novel features designed to help make agents more effective and less inclined to misbehave. The new features, called Active Memory and Active Focus, are designed to keep the model locked into a stated goal and prevent it from becoming confused. This can be a challenge when AI performs complex research or builds a large software project, for example, and can lead to expensive mistakes or compounded errors. Meta says it has put significant effort into training Muse Wonder to refuse to generate dangerous outputs, such as recipes for building bioweapons or help with hacking. It says the company scores well on several benchmarks designed to measure how resilient models are to those prompts. A series of recent incidents involving rogue AI agents from Anthropic, OpenAI, and others also shows how easily powerful AI models can stray when given open-ended commands. Meta did not disclose whether it has seen agents powered by Muse Wonder misbehave in testing or what it has done to mitigate this issue specifically. Zuckerberg said in a post on X last month that the company had delayed the release of its Muse models to work on safety. Meta also revealed a framework designed to ensure that it scales its models’ capabilities safely in a blog post earlier this month. Muse Wonder may add more fuel to an already furious race to develop more capable AI, however. It certainly suggests that Meta is once again competitive in the increasingly high-stakes AI race. events.title: Honeyjar offers AI tools to improve PR and comms at every company
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Journalists, entrepreneurs, and even some public relations professionals will tell you that the PR process is broken (buy me a drink sometime, and I’ll give you my rant). But could AI actually make things better? Honeyjar , which will be attending this week’s TechCrunch Disrupt as part of the Startup Battlefield 200 , wants to use AI to make the expertise and judgment of the best PR pros available to everyone, including founders who have no idea where to start. The startup’s founders, CEO Michelle Masek and CCO Nadia Jamshidi, certainly fit the bill when it comes to PR expertise. They’ve both spent decades in the field, doing in-house communications and working at agencies. Masek recently served as senior vice president of marketing and communications for Ev Williams’ venture firm, Obvious Ventures . As Masek described the challenges involved in “helping with the why and when of comms and marketing for 110 portfolio companies” (the startups her firm had invested in), I flashed back to my own brief stint leading marketing at an early-stage VC firm , where founders were constantly asking for help getting into TechCrunch. So I wasn’t surprised that Masek found herself asking, “Is there a way to scale the senior-level expertise into AI [in a way] that actually helps users do the work of comms in the proactive and skilled way that we do?” Honeyjar is her answer to that question. It automates processes like writing announcements, finding the best journalists to pitch, and identifying the most promising speaking opportunities. But Jamshidi told me in a follow-up email that Honeyjar’s vision goes beyond getting press coverage and beyond specific AI tools. “Honeyjar can find reporters, build media lists, scan news and social, track coverage, and surface opportunities,” she said. “Those capabilities are important, but they’re just one piece of what we’re building. The bigger idea is bringing the whole communications workflow together: signals, context, strategy, judgment, timing, and execution.” And it’s not just for founders. Masek said she’s come to realize there are “millions and millions of unassigned communicators responsible for the work of comms.” “They don’t have the title of comms, but they’re marketers, investors, authors, creators, school superintendents, sports team leaders,” she added. “It’s incredibly horizontal, this need to nail strategic communications. It’s always passed around, but the problems are very often not solved.” Nor is Honeyjar trying to replace PR professionals. Masek said she and Jamshidi built the tool they wanted to use themselves. She argued that Honeyjar can make PR firms and in-house comms teams more effective, while allowing individual PR practitioners to “take on that third client without any scaling cost.” When Honeyjar opened its waitlist, it received 10,000 signups in the first 24 hours, said Masek. Beta testers include Nextdoor, tech startup Coco Robotics, investor Bloomberg Beta, and agencies Mission North and Full Picture. That sounds promising for companies looking to get more attention, but it could be a nightmare for journalists. We receive more pitches than we can respond to, many of them already written by AI chatbots. When I raised my fears about getting inundated with even more PR slop, Masek noted that while Honeyjar can draft a pitch email or a social media post in the customer’s voice, the customer actually has to hit send or publish. “We never want a world where the human is removed from the loop,” she said. And that’s also where judgment is key. Masek said she and Jamshidi tried to “infuse and encode Honeyjar with our wisdom.” Through a broader initiative called the Comms Lab, they’re now training the product on the judgment of other PR pros as well. “For us, judgment is knowing what to do, what not to do, when to act, and how to adapt to the situation,” Jamshidi added. “That comes from understanding a company’s goals and priorities, what’s happening inside and outside the organization, and knowing what to say, to whom, where, and when.” In some cases, Masek said Honeyjar might even tell a founder that they’re simply not ready for coverage. “We hear from reporters all the time who want better pitches, who want to hear from experts directly,” she said. “We actually see a future where there are more credible pitches in your inbox from sources who you actually want to hear from.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: This AI startup says it can generate permit-ready blueprints in minutes
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Nearly two decades ago, a young college student wrote his final thesis about software capable of generating design documents for school buildings. Al Dram was studying architecture — following in the footsteps of his parents and grandfather — but it was technology that really intrigued him. There was just one problem: The technology his idea required didn’t exist yet. “Then ChatGPT came along,” said Dram, recalling when OpenAI released the generative AI chatbot that uses large language models (LLMs) in November 2022. His old idea suddenly seemed a lot more possible. Within six months, he launched the concept of Blueprints AI, a startup that uses AI to produce code-compliant and permit-ready architectural construction blueprints in minutes from a 2D sketch or PDF. Blueprints AI , which Dram officially incorporated in 2025 in Santa Monica with co-founder Coco Cao, was selected for the 2026 Startup Battlefield 200 , a cohort of promising early-stage startups that have earned a spot to exhibit at this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt , taking place this week from October 13 to 15 in San Francisco. During that 20-year lead-up to Blueprints AI, Dram earned his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in architecture from the University of Tehran and completed two years of PhD coursework on digital design at the European Graduate School in Switzerland. He moved to the United States and opened an architecture firm in 2018 called Drams Design-Build. Then, after obtaining a general contractor’s license, he added a construction business in 2021. Dram should have been satisfied. He wasn’t. “I was saying, okay, maybe I can build new projects that change people’s life in that area, but it wouldn’t be a big impact,” he said. “What makes me very excited about technology is the impact, the hours saved, the energy saved of people doing the same thing over and over and over.” Blueprints AI will unveil a more capable second-generation version of its software at Disrupt. Dram and Cao say it will make a big impact because it takes over the repetitive drafting work that fills most of an architect’s day. “It will make better spaces for people because now architects have the time to design,” said Dram. He said architects spend about 80% of their time on drafting and only 20% on design. “I want to flip that to be 20-80.” Dram and Cao met at an AI conference several years ago and combined their skills to build the company. Cao, a data scientist from Hong Kong, handles sales and go-to-market strategy as chief commercial officer. The pair trained their models using eight years of approved drawing sets from Dram’s design and construction firm, which is still in business. Its first-generation software produces architectural construction documents and costs between $3,200 and $8,500 a month, depending on the plan. Custom pricing for enterprises is also available. The startup’s second-generation software will deliver a considerable upgrade. Customers can start with a description or sketch of a project and create blueprints for every aspect of a building at once, including architecture, structural, mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and interior design. Version 2 allows users to design and make changes to the project, an upgrade over the first iteration. Importantly, one design change updates the entire project and is checked against local building codes. Early customers are already using the second version, and Dram said it will become publicly available this week. The startup is already working on a third version of its software that will add in structural analysis and electrical panel design. The technology doesn’t replace licensed architects, according to the co-founders. Licensed professionals still review the documents and affix their seal before submitting them for permits. The judgment stays human, they say. Blueprints AI is targeting two groups with its new software. Professional architecture, engineering, and design firms make up one group, while developers and real estate owners make up another. The startup offers its software as a subscription and may add a one-time flat-fee option for those who just want it for a single project. To learn more about Blueprints, catch hundreds of other startups, and learn from headliners like RJ Scaringe of Rivian and Amjad Masad of Replit, join us at TechCrunch Disrupt , kicking off Tuesday in downtown San Francisco. events.title: Britain faces looming energy crisis as gas reserves dwindle
events.summary: Britain faces a deepening energy crisis as a result of dwindling reserves and the possible closure of its largest storage site. With a 150 per cent surge in European gas prices before the seasonal dip in temperatures, the prospect of another inflationary shock is casting a shadow over the October 28 Budget. The prospect of losing Rough, which accounts for about half of Britain's gas storage capacity, threatens to further weaken the country's ability to withstand supply disruptions as Europe heads into winter with depleted reserves. Underground gas storage in Britain was only 48 per cent full at the start of October, compared with 94 per cent in Portugal and 99 per cent in Poland, according to figures reported alongside the latest winter outlook from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas. Britain has historically relied on imported gas rather than extensive domestic storage. In 2024, its storage capacity amounted to only 5 per cent of annual gas demand, compared with an EU average of 29 per cent, according to government figures. Its current capacity equals about seven days of average winter demand. The problem of limited UK reserves is compounded by uncertainty over the future of Rough, which could close next year unless the government backs a £2 billion redevelopment proposed by its owner, Centrica. Chris O'Shea, chief executive of Centrica, which also owns British Gas, stepped up pressure on the government on Tuesday, warning that the site, which accounts for about half of Britain's gas storage capacity, would close at the end of the first quarter without a plan to support investment. "The commercial decision will be that this facility will close at the end of the first quarter," Mr O'Shea told the BBC, rejecting the government's position that Rough's future was a commercial matter for the company. He said Centrica was seeking a regulatory framework similar to those available to other critical infrastructure operators, providing more predictable returns in exchange for lower investment risk. Mr O'Shea described Rough as "the biggest battery in the UK", saying the proposed investment could create up to 5,000 jobs while safeguarding almost 1,000 existing positions. The company has also offered to make the site available as a temporary strategic gas reserve this winter but has yet to receive a response from the government, he said. "Our system is not resilient. Without energy security, we have no national security," Mr O'Shea said, pointing to increasingly frequent electricity supply margin notices. Britain’s grid operator sought emergency assistance from France on Monday, requesting as much as 1,200 megawatts of additional electricity through an undersea interconnector to help maintain the security of the power system. Britain will probably not run short of gas this winter, but its limited reserves leave it increasingly exposed to global supply disruptions and competition for liquefied natural gas, according to Neil Quilliam, associate fellow for the Middle East and North Africa at Chatham House. “The greater risk is not a physical shortage of gas, but a period of tight supply, higher prices and increased competition for LNG cargoes if winter is unusually cold or if there are disruptions to Norwegian supplies or global gas markets,” he said. Britain still benefits from North Sea production, Norwegian imports, LNG terminals and interconnectors with Europe, which should provide sufficient supplies under normal conditions, he said. However, “the margin for error is becoming uncomfortably small”. European gas storage is expected to be just 75 to 78 per cent full by November 1, about 10 percentage points below the five-year average, as the Iran war continues to disrupt liquefied natural gas exports from the Gulf. The supply constraints could persist into next year even if the Iran war ends, with analysts warning that competition for alternative LNG cargoes and the need to replenish depleted reserves could keep prices high. Even with average winter weather, north-west European reserves could fall to about 20 per cent by early April, according to the London Stock Exchange Group. “It’s not just this coming winter that we are tight, but we risk being tight the next summer,” Yuriy Onyshkiv, an analyst at LSEG, told Reuters. Entsog warned last week that strong LNG deliveries would be needed throughout the winter to maintain European storage levels. EU gas storage was 72 per cent full at the start of October, compared with about 83 per cent a year earlier. Entsog’s central scenario has EU inventories falling to about 30 per cent by the end of March. In its worst case – a severe winter combined with tight LNG supply and a halt to Russian pipeline flows – stocks would drop to 11 per cent, the level of the bloc’s remaining strategic reserves. A further challenge comes on January 1, when an exemption allowing imports of diesel and jet fuel refined from Russian crude in third countries is due to expire. In the same month, the EU’s full ban on Russian LNG imports takes effect, which is expected to tighten European gas supply further. Consultancy Cornwall Insight forecasts a 16 per cent increase in Britain’s annual household energy price cap to £1,999 in January, after a 4 per cent rise this month that took bills to a three-year high. The outlook adds to pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham ’s government before the budget, with limited fiscal room expected to constrain further support for consumers.

events.title: HSBC moves to Wall Street bonus model, cuts fixed-pay deals
events.summary: The London-headquartered bank will switch to the new pay system at the start of 2028, according to a memo seen by Bloomberg News. LONDON – HSBC Holdings will phase out fixed-pay allowances for its senior staff and instead hand out a greater proportion of its compensation in the form of bonuses, becoming the latest British lender to switch to Wall Street-style remuneration to better align with performance. The approach “strengthens our ability to pay for performance, better differentiate, attract the best talent, and recognise” top performers, a spokesman for HSBC said in a statement. HSBC’s shift follows a similar update by Barclays, which said in July it would switch more of its employees’ pay toward bonuses after Britain changed its rules around compensation in 2025 to allow for higher variable pay in an effort to boost domestic competitiveness. Wall Street bankers have typically received the bulk of their pay through bonuses tied to performance, rather than fixed salaries. Fixed pay allowances were introduced more than a decade ago at major British banks to provide a way of topping the base salary of senior staff after the introduction of European Union rules capping the compensation of financiers. At HSBC, those allowances have taken the form of share awards in immediately vested stock, though these have been subject to a retention period to ensure alignment between an executive’s interests and those of the bank. These payouts are non-pensionable and have been capped at a maximum of 150% of an individual’s base salary under the terms of HSBC’s fixed-pay structure. In its most recent annual report, HSBC said fixed pay remained the largest part of its bankers’ compensation. The UK rule changes have now lessened the need for these fixed-pay allowances. The lender spent US$3.93 billion (S$5.03 billion) in 2025 on variable pay, up 10% from the previous year, according to the annual report. Gross compensation and benefits stood at US$21.5 billion in 2025. The planned compensation overhaul is part of a broader restructuring HSBC has seen since Georges Elhedery took over as chief executive officer in September 2024 . His shake-up of the lender has resulted in the sale, closing or merger of several businesses and hundreds of job cuts. The CEO has also led a cost-cutting programme that has included the paring back of long-time benefits enjoyed by some of the company’s staff such as education allowances and contributions to private club memberships for employees of its Hong Kong-based business. In the Asian hub, the lender ended a long-standing education subsidy covering 95% of school fees for the children of new hires and senior staff relocating to the city. Existing band-three employees and managing directors who already receive the benefit will retain it, Bloomberg News reported in September. It is also cutting a perk worth up to HK$200,000 (S$32,645) that subsidised some private club access for its bankers in the city. The share price of HSBC has more than doubled since Elhedery became CEO. BLOOMBERG
