Google’s Fitbit lineup expanded on Monday with the introduction of the Fitbit Edge, a new wearable that’s positioned between the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch. Priced at $179.99, it combines the Fitbit Air’s slim band with an OLED display for checking map directions, notifications, weather, and music controls. Like the Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air, the Edge works with Google Health Coach, powered by Gemini. (You’ll need a Google Health Premium subscription to use it.) The coach can use your fitness, health, and medical information to put together weekly routines and workout plans, then adjust them around your schedule. It also comes with Google’s Health Guardian feature, which is designed to spot notable changes in health measurements over time, including indicators related to blood pressure and insulin resistance. (The company announced these features at the Pixel Watch 5 launch in August.) Google says the Fitbit Edge can automatically recognize and log up to 100 activities, including runs, bike rides, and walks. The company explains it uses context from your movement to work out what you’re doing and add it to your weekly goals. Plus, the device supports more than 50 exercise modes and can offer on-screen prompts during workouts, such as a nudge to push harder or take a breather. The Fitbit Edge’s built-in GPS is 40% more accurate than the previous generation, the company claims, which should make it easier to track outdoor runs. Google says sleep-stage detection is also 15% more accurate than on earlier generations, helping the device provide better sleep summaries and coaching tips. Meanwhile, the battery is rated for up to seven days on a charge, and the wearable is water-resistant to 50 meters. The Fitbit Edge is available to preorder through the Google Store, with store availability set for October 27. Color choices include Obsidian, Fog, Olive, and Canyon. events.title: AI minister warns 'likely' UK's cyber defences will be breached
events.summary: The UK's AI minister has warned it is "likely, if not inevitable" the country's cyber defences will at some point be breached. Speaking at a press conference, Kanishka Narayan pointed to an incident of a rogue OpenAI agent hacking an Australian government website in June. He said while no medical records are known to have been accessed in the attack, the incident should still "concern us". Narayan said the government plans to put advanced AI to work to combat the threat, as he set out how the government plans to prepare for any serious future incidents. The minister said the move would build on two existing pilots which have helped identify and fix over 1,000 vulnerabilities across government systems. He said his message to the largest companies behind the world's most powerful AI systems was: "Listen when your scientists warn of serious dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviour. And if you cannot adequately control the risks, do not release the system." In his speech, Narayan also confirmed scientists at the UK's AI watchdog, the AI Security Institute (AISI), were conducting "rigorous evaluations" of the latest generation of advanced AI models to "identify risks early" and "to test robust safeguards to help keep people safe". AISI began evaluating risks of the latest frontier AI models, prior to their public release, shortly after it was established in November 2023. But it was reported in September , external that the White House had asked some leading US labs not to share their models with the research organisation until its own tests were completed. The move was viewed at the time as a blow to AISI - which has been championed by the UK government and its partners for advancing open, constructive and collaborative AI testing. Microsoft president Brad Smith recently told the BBC the institute had helped cement the UK as the country best-placed to drive forward global regulation. On Monday, Narayan said that in the last few weeks, the government had worked with the US "to retain access for Britain's AISI to the most powerful AI models before they are released". He also said the UK would also look into creating stronger protections through the Cyber Security and Resilience bill, particularly at how serious AI incidents can be identified and reported. Nuala Polo, UK Public Policy Lead at the Ada Lovelace Institute, said the announcement committed the government to "very little". "Stronger protections will be 'considered', strengthening the Cyber Bill 'explored' and near-miss reporting 'looked at', with the detail to come later," she said. "There is no new regulatory power, no timetable and no obligation on AI developers." The announcement follows a series of incidents involving AI agents across major firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic acting outside human control and hacking into external systems. On 9 September, Evan Hubinger, a top safety researcher at Anthropic, warned in a post on X that AI is advancing so quickly he believed there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade. The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown . However, there are currently no global safety rules in place to regulate the companies and their technology. President Trump has called for the sector to regulate itself so that US firms do not lose out to Chinese rivals. Speaking to the BBC following the announcement, Narayan said the UK needed "to be confident... as a country" when questioned as to how the government can make foreign AI firms abide by UK rules. "We have the capability, we have the trust, and we have a government that is right on the side of the British public in making sure we don't just have laws but the ability to enforce those laws," he said. "What we are focused on is delivering the right outcome for the British public, where the law was the answer." On the question of whether the UK should have its own sovereign AI frontier model, the minister said he was "focused" on securing British sovereignty, which meant "placing the right set of investments". "It's British chips being made here. It's British models outside of just language, looking at things like drug discovery, materials discovery, computer vision and its areas of adoption, including AI, security and cyber-security," he said. events.title: OCP Global Summit: Amid Ecosystem Adoption, NVIDIA Opens Vera Rubin Architecture to Help Scale AI Factories Worldwide
events.summary: As AI factories grow from megawatts to gigawatts, building them takes more than advanced computing. Open standards are helping the industry scale AI infrastructure faster, more efficiently and more reliably. At the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, taking place in the San Jose McEnery Convention Center, NVIDIA announced new partnerships and contributions aimed at creating a common foundation for next-generation AI infrastructure. NVIDIA contributed key NVIDIA Vera Rubin rack and compute tray designs to OCP through the open NVIDIA MGX architecture, giving system builders a common foundation for developing next-generation AI factory infrastructure. Together, these efforts span the AI factory itself, the utility grid that powers it and the rack-scale architecture at the heart of modern accelerated computing. NVIDIA and Partners Announce Open Architecture Advances At the OCP event, NVIDIA and partners made a handful of announcements: NVIDIA and hyperscalers published open standards for next-generation AI factories, including AI factory design standards and grid resilience. NVIDIA launched new open source software components for NVIDIA DSX AI Factory. Meta and NVIDIA advanced open AI networking with NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet SuperNIC and Spectrum-6 innovations. Visionbay introduced an 800V DC AI factory design for the Vera Rubin era. NVIDIA and Cisco announced the Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP) standard, the industry’s first module ​for 400Gb/s-based networking fabrics. NVIDIA and Google announced Falcon Transport support on future NVIDIA ConnectX-10 SuperNICs and BlueField DPUs. Before a packed audience, Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA, discussed how open infrastructure is becoming a critical ingredient for scaling AI factories worldwide. The news at OCP spotlights how NVIDIA’s extreme codesign combined with open standards is accelerating deployment, improving power efficiency and driving tokens-per-watt performance. Vera Rubin AI Factories Advance With MGX Rack Contributions at OCP 🔗 NVIDIA joined industry leaders in contributing to the third-generation MGX AI data center reference design through OCP’s Open DC Initiative. Combined with open liquid-cooling technologies such as MQD and MQDB, the effort helps turn proven AI factory designs into industry standards that others can adopt, manufacture and scale. For NVIDIA Vera Rubin AI factories, the updated MGX 1.2 specification extends the open architecture for AI factories with rack-scale blind-mate liquid cooling, interoperable rack-scale interconnect infrastructure and a liquid-cooled 5,000A busbar designed for higher-power AI systems. It also adds native 19-inch equipment support and higher-density rack designs. MGX 1.2 further expands modularity with configurable I/O bays, fanless liquid-cooled compute trays, standardized power and cooling interfaces, and a common infrastructure that helps ecosystem partners build interoperable accelerated computing platforms. It improves assembly, test and service times to streamline manufacturing and field service to enable faster and more efficient infrastructure buildout. The architecture supports rack deployments up to 250kW while simplifying serviceability, deployment and infrastructure reuse. The Vera CPU rack design specification extends the NVIDIA MGX open architecture beyond accelerated computing, providing a purpose-built platform for the growing agentic AI era. While Vera Rubin NVL72 serves as the foundation for large-scale training and inference, the NVIDIA Vera CPU rack is designed to support tool calling, orchestration and sandboxed execution, helping AI agents interact with applications, data and services in real time. Built on the third-generation NVIDIA MGX rack architecture, the Vera CPU rack shares the same rack-scale design principles that unite compute, networking, power and cooling into a common modular platform. This approach enables partners to deploy specialized infrastructure while benefiting from a shared ecosystem, simplified integration and a consistent foundation for next-generation AI factories. NVIDIA Launches New Open Source Software Components for DSX AI Factory 🔗 NVIDIA DSX AI factory platform applies extreme codesign to unify computing, networking, power, cooling, facilities and software, helping AI factories operate as a single optimized system, maximizing AI output within available infrastructure constraints. At the center of this unified system is DSX OS, the open operating layer that turns the DSX architecture into coordinated, repeatable operations at scale. At OCP, NVIDIA expanded DSX OS with open source components for configuring networks, validating clusters, managing racks and provisioning bare metal: NVIDIA Config Manager : Automates switch configurations at scale, allowing customers to deploy, validate and maintain consistent AI factory network fabrics with minimal to zero manual intervention/ NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine : Helps eliminate costly job crashes by stress-testing GPU clusters with real workload simulations to guarantee hardware health before training begins NVIDIA Rack Management Service : Offers a rack hardware abstraction and operations solutions that treats racks as first-class units for improved AI factory scale firmware management. Cluster API Provider for NVIDIA Infrastructure Controller : Accelerates bare-metal deployment and tenant onboarding, turning raw AI hardware into production-ready clusters in hours instead of days. Developed from NVIDIA’s experience running NVIDIA DGX Cloud, these open source components enable cloud providers and software partners to integrate AI factory capabilities directly into their multi-tenant platforms. Developers can visit the DSX AI Factory Github page to explore and contribute to both the new and existing open source software components from NVIDIA DSX AI Factory platform. NVIDIA and Hyperscalers Publish Open Standards for Next-Generation AI Factories 🔗 For AI infrastructure to scale globally, it needs more than advanced hardware — it needs a common foundation that the entire industry can build on. At OCP, NVIDIA joined AMD, Google and Meta t o publish a new open specification that establishes that foundation. The Open Data Center Specification v0.7 defines a unified blueprint for next-generation AI factory facility design — from power architecture to cooling infrastructure to physical layout. The OCP Grid Resilience Specification , published by Google , Meta, Microsoft and NVIDIA, establishes how large-scale AI infrastructure should behave during utility grid disturbances: staying connected, responding automatically and restoring to near-full load within less than two seconds. With these standards now open, manufacturers around the world have a common target to build for.

events.title: NVIDIA and Cisco Introduce New Pluggable Optics Form Factor to Scale AI Factories
events.summary: Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP) is designed to be the first module to support 400Gb/s-per-lane electrical signals, enabling capacity up to 12.8Tb/s so AI factory builders can scale Ethernet AI fabrics, while extending a proven deployment model across multiple generations of data center networks. USFP delivers 4x the bandwidth density and 1.3x the power efficiency of 200Gb/s-per-lane optics so AI factories can connect more computing systems without adding network tiers, while using less power to move each bit of data. NVIDIA and Cisco are working with TE Connectivity and Amphenol to build a multi-source hardware ecosystem around USFP. NVIDIA and Cisco today announced plans for Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP), a new high-density 400Gb/s-per-lane optical module designed to equip the hardware ecosystem for the next generation of AI factories using pluggable transceivers. As AI models grow and inference demand expands, AI factories must connect more computing systems while managing network complexity, power and costs. Moving more data per watt and per switch helps operators make better use of their infrastructure investments. Scaling AI factories requires more bandwidth per connection and more connections per switch. When a switch reaches its capacity, further network expansion can require additional switch layers and optical links, increasing latency, power consumption and costs. USFP is designed to enable AI factory builders to scale from 200 Gb/s per lane to 400Gb/s-per-lane Ethernet AI fabrics, while extending a deployment model proven at scale across multiple generations of data center networks. With USFP, customers can embrace next-generation optical technology and meet the performance demand of AI workloads without overhauling their data center infrastructure. The first planned USFP-based transceivers will pack 16 full-duplex lanes in an octal small form factor (OSFP)-sized footprint supporting both switches and SuperNICs, with the ability to expand to 32 and more lanes in the future. By doubling both the lane count and bandwidth per lane, USFP enables AI fabrics to connect more 1.6Tb/s endpoints without adding network tiers. Customers will be able to achieve 12.8Tb/s of overall capacity with USFP. Comparable with an OSFP-sized module, it delivers 4x the bandwidth and front-panel bandwidth density, with approximately 1.3x the power efficiency, versus 200Gb/s-per-lane pluggable modules. This means AI builders can increase their compute scale within the same network footprint, while decreasing networking’s share of the overall AI factory power budget. “Building the world’s largest AI factories starts with rethinking the smallest of connections,” said Gilad Shainer, senior vice president NVIDIA. “With USFP, NVIDIA and Cisco are building an ecosystem to reinvent pluggable optics — connecting more computing with greater efficiency to power the next generation of AI factories.” “AI builders need an interconnect architecture that can scale performance without locking them into a more complex operating model,” said Bill Gartner, senior vice president and general manager of optical systems and optics at Cisco. “Cisco and NVIDIA recognized that scaling pluggable optics to 400Gb/s per lane would require more than another incremental extension of today’s module designs. Through our collaboration, USFP is designed to deliver a new level of bandwidth density while preserving the serviceability, deployment flexibility and operational simplicity of pluggable optics. By taking a full-stack approach — from silicon and systems to optics and the network operating system — we can optimize every layer to deliver the performance and scale the next generation of AI networks will require.” More AI Infrastructure From Every Switch Designed for electrical signals of 400Gb/s per lane, USFP uses a new two-dimensional array connector with a two-step insertion design that engages high-speed contacts after the module is inserted, reducing contact wear, improving signal integrity and making insertion force more predictable. The connector technology allows for further scaling of lane count to 32 full duplex lanes and more in the future. Because the connector is designed for 400Gb/s performance, it also offers improved performance at 200Gb/s per lane. USFP supports power dissipation of up to 100 watts without needing a separate, dedicated embedded cooling circuit within the transceiver, reducing switch design complexity and improving reliability. Together, these capabilities enable higher-bandwidth fabrics while preserving the mature deployment, serviceability and manufacturability of existing pluggable transceivers. All USFP configurations support optical designs that reduce latency and power consumption by simplifying signal processing. Support for a broad range of optical technologies and connection distances gives system designers the flexibility to meet unique AI factory deployment needs. A Hardware Ecosystem for Next-Generation AI Factories NVIDIA and Cisco are collaborating with TE Connectivity and Amphenol to build USFP cages, connectors and modules, with additional partners expected to join. The shared form factor gives suppliers a common foundation for developing high-density pluggable infrastructure for 400Gb/s-per-lane fabrics to build a robust ecosystem for AI factory builders. The collaboration builds on NVIDIA and Cisco’s existing work to ensure NVIDIA Spectrum-X™ Ethernet networking and Cisco Silicon One-based Ethernet networks work together seamlessly, simplifying AI infrastructure deployment for enterprises, neoclouds and sovereign clouds. NVIDIA and Cisco plan to create an open industry specification for USFP through an upcoming community-led multi-source project. events.title: Global smartphone shipments record worst third quarter in 14 years amid memory shortage
events.summary: Apple’s market share reached 22%, crossing 20% for the first time in a third quarter, despite a year-on-year decline in shipments. Global smartphone shipments fell 20% on-year to their lowest third-quarter level since 2012, as soaring memory chip costs and supply shortages pressured manufacturers and pushed up prices, preliminary estimates from Counterpoint Research showed on Oct 12. Rising prices for memory components as AI infrastructure projects corner supplies have driven up production costs and prompted manufacturers to raise retail prices, cut shipments and prioritise profitability over volumes. “Consumers are holding on to their devices longer than estimated, increasingly considering refurbished devices and prioritising higher-value devices,” said Counterpoint senior analyst Shilpi Jain. Samsung retained its top position with a 23% market share, helped by demand for its Galaxy Z Fold8 series and stable component supplies for its mid-range devices. Shipments fell 3% from a year earlier during the quarter Apple’s market share reached 22%, crossing 20% for the first time in a third quarter, despite a year-on-year decline in shipments The absence of a base iPhone 18 model resulted in a smaller launch-month channel fill than the full iPhone 17 line-up a year earlier, Counterpoint said OPPO and vivo recorded shipment declines of more than 20%. Xiaomi saw a more than 30% fall, reducing its market share to 10% as the company cut exposure to lower-priced devices and some overseas markets to protect margins. “The outlook for the remainder of 2026 remains challenging,” Counterpoint said. “Production cuts, tighter portfolios, and greater focus on premium devices are likely to continue, while price-sensitive segments face further pressure from higher device prices and limited availability of components.” REUTERS

events.title: Nobel Prize for economics awarded to Hall and Woodford for work on ‘smoothing’ crises
events.summary: US economists developed models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their economies Two US economists have won the 2026 Nobel economics prize for their work developing models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their countries, avoiding long recessions and runaway inflation. Robert Hall of Stanford University, California, and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, New York, were recognised for developing the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation” , giving policymakers better tools to smooth out the peaks and troughs of their economies. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said it was recognising the pair for generating “a paradigm shift in stabilisation policy”, awarding them the prize worth a combined $1.2m (£900,000). “New Keynesian models, a result of their research, allow us to explain and quantify how stabilisation policy affects business cycles and are now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world,” the academy said. These models improved on John Maynard Keynes’s stabilisation models, which struggled to handle the impact of the oil shock in the 1970s, when countries suffered high inflation, weak growth and high unemployment at the same time. Hall and Woodford demonstrated how traditional models could be reconstructed, based on how individual households and businesses collectively affect an economy through their actions. Hall’s work was based on forward-looking consumer behaviour rather than the more mechanical rules of thumb used by Keynes, which linked key variables such as inflation, unemployment and gross domestic product (GDP). Woodford built on this work to create the New Keynesian model, a full macroeconomic stabilisation framework that is the main tool for policymakers now. This model was used after the 2008 financial crisis by policymakers as they steered the global economy away from the risk of a second great depression. “The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” John Hassler, the chair of the committee for the economics prize, said. Hall and Woodford’s work also led to the development of forward guidance, where central bankers communicate where they expect interest rates to be in the future. That became an important tool after the 2008 financial crisis, and the Covid pandemic, when interest rates were cut to record lows. Forward guidance has had its critics, though – the current chair of the US Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, has argued it should only have a “limited and circumscribed” role in normal times, to avoid “creating ambiguity in the name of clarity”. And in 2014, the then Bank of England governor, Mark Carney, was labelled an “unreliable boyfriend” for dropping hints over interest rate rises that never came to pass. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Woodford said he was “elated”. “It’s a tremendous honour. It’s a surprise but I’m feeling very good about it,” he told reporters in Stockholm by phone after receiving the news. The Columbia University president, Jennifer L Mnookin, said: “I offer my deepest congratulations to Michael Woodford on this tremendous honour. “What a tribute to his groundbreaking work alongside Robert E Hall that has fundamentally reshaped the theoretical foundations of stabilisation policy and provided us with the tools to navigate economic upturns and downturns more effectively.” Hall is also known for coining the idea that US economists can be divided into freshwater and saltwater varieties. The fresh water group, who tend to be based at inland universities located near the Great Lakes, such as the University of Chicago, believe in free markets, neoclassical price theory, rational expectations and monetarism. Salt water economists, though, cluster at coastal universities, such as Harvard, MIT, UC Berkeley, Yale, Princeton, UCLA and Columbia. They tend to be Keynesians and New Keynesians, believing that governments and central banks can affect demand in their economies. The economics Nobel prize is not one of the five created by Alfred Nobel. Instead, it was invented by Sweden’s central bank, and is known as the Sveriges Riksbank prize in economic sciences in memory of Alfred Nobel.

events.title: Smart ring maker Ultrahuman to roll out biological-age model across UAE
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Ultrahuman , a Bengaluru-based health tech startup best known for its smart rings, has partnered with Abu Dhabi health authorities to develop a biological-age model that it says will eventually be made available to people across the United Arab Emirates. On Monday, Ultrahuman announced that it had signed a two-year memorandum of understanding with the Abu Dhabi Public Health Center (ADPHC) to develop and validate the model, which will combine clinical biomarkers with data from wearable devices. The partnership aims to use these signals to estimate how quickly an individual is aging and identify factors — including sleep, activity, cardiovascular health, and metabolism — that may be accelerating or slowing that process. The partnership marks Ultrahuman’s latest effort to go beyond selling wearable hardware and deploy its health algorithms at a much larger scale. The startup increasingly sees itself as a health-data company, with its smart ring serving as one way to collect information that can underpin algorithms spanning aging, longevity, and other areas of health, CEO Mohit Kumar said in an interview. “If you look at Ultrahuman as a company, we obviously have the Ultrahuman Ring, which is a way to acquire data from the human body,” Kumar told TechCrunch. “But truly, what we care about is not just the form factor, the ring, but what do we do with this data?” Working with a government gives Ultrahuman the opportunity to apply its algorithms to a far broader population than its own customer base, Kumar said. The startup has sold around 800,000 smart rings globally so far. The Abu Dhabi partnership is Ultrahuman’s first step toward deploying a health algorithm at a national scale, with the health age model eventually intended to be available to people across the UAE, according to the company. Even though Ultrahuman is known for its smart rings, Kumar said the biological-age model is being designed to be wearable-agnostic, allowing data from rings, wrist-worn devices, straps, and patches to feed into the system alongside clinical biomarkers. Individuals will eventually be able to access their health age through government digital-health platforms including TAMM and Sahatna, the startup said. Ultrahuman and ADPHC will spend the next two years working on research and clinical validation of the model. Kumar told TechCrunch that the broader rollout will happen in phases, but did not provide a timeline. The UAE is already among Ultrahuman’s 10 largest markets and accounts for about 4% to 5% of its overall revenue, Kumar said. The startup has operated in the market for nearly five years and sees about 25% higher retention there compared with its other markets, he noted. Ultrahuman’s existing customer base gives it a narrower view of the population than a government health system. Its typical users are between 25 and 43 years old, Kumar said, while deploying the model across the UAE would expose it to a much broader range of age groups. The underlying biological-age model was developed using Ultrahuman’s existing data, combining users’ chronological ages with wearable signals and, for some users, blood-test markers, Kumar told TechCrunch. That allows the startup to track how health markers typically change with age and identify deviations from those patterns. Kumar stressed the model will not be trained on data from the UAE. “We will deploy an algorithm on the UAE data,” he said, adding that Ultrahuman will not have access to personally identifiable information through the program. Ultrahuman is not the only smart-ring maker working with Abu Dhabi on preventive health. In May, the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi announced a partnership with Ultrahuman arch-rival Oura to combine the company’s wearable data with the emirate’s longitudinal health data, initially focusing on women’s health and cardiometabolic risk. Kumar told TechCrunch that Ultrahuman is not aware of another company working with Abu Dhabi authorities on the health age model specifically. While he acknowledged that the government works with multiple health-tech companies, he declined to comment on the scope of Oura’s work with Abu Dhabi. The parallel partnerships come as Ultrahuman and Oura compete in the smart-ring market while looking to push their businesses beyond wearable hardware and deeper into preventive health. The work with the Abu Dhabi authorities also comes as Ultrahuman is looking to build a smart ring that can run software on the device and even power everything from AI interactions to games . Text of this article October 12, 2026 UPDATE App Store Indie Games Week kicks off today Seven acclaimed indie games, including Sifu, Vampire Crawlers, and No Man’s Sky, make their App Store debut Today, Indie Games Week lights up the App Store with a celebration of the incredible catalog of imaginative games made by independent teams with big dreams. Players worldwide can jump into their next adventure with seven highly acclaimed indie games, available for download or pre-order on iPhone and iPad. All week, the App Store will spotlight these indie gems with daily features and curated collections. “Indie games are constantly pushing the boundaries of creativity to deliver unique gameplay experiences to Apple users, and we wanted to take a moment to celebrate these games and the teams that take creative risks to push gaming forward,” said Carson Oliver, Apple’s head of App Store Worldwide. “Whether from a solo developer or a growing studio, the App Store gives bold ideas a global stage — turning daring visions into worldwide hits. We’re thrilled with the incredible games launching on the App Store this week and amazed by their breathtaking artistry, brilliant design, and deeply moving stories.” There are whole new worlds to discover during Indie Games Week, from building empires, to brawling through cinematic combat, to getting lost in another universe entirely. With the critically acclaimed Sifu , Indie Games Week puts the art of combat front and center. This stylish third-person brawler follows a young kung fu student on a relentless path of revenge. Battles are ferocious and unforgiving, with enemies attacking simultaneously, forcing players to parry strikes, chain combos, and weaponize everything around them. Sifu arrives fully adapted for iPhone and iPad, with custom-tuned touch controls, a reworked camera system, and full controller support. For players looking for quick bursts of strategy mixed with dark humor, Vampire Crawlers is an invitation to rough up skeletons, bats, and other nefarious creeps in a gothic card battler. The spin-off of the smash hit Vampire Survivors cleverly trades dodging bullets for tactical deck building. Players conquer chaotic dungeon runs by discovering game-changing card combos, uncovering secret relics, and mastering the luck of the draw. After celebrating a decade of continuous evolution, Hello Games’ groundbreaking space odyssey No Man’s Sky makes its mobile debut on iPhone and iPad on October 28. Set in an infinite, procedurally generated universe rendered entirely at runtime, No Man’s Sky lets players explore, trade, fight, and survive across an interconnected galaxy — all in the palm of their hands. events.title: Revealed: Nigel Farage adviser had unpublicised role at polling firm
events.summary: Exclusive: Chris Bruni-Lowe used Redfield & Wilton Strategies role to develop potential campaign tactics, sources say A close adviser to Nigel Farage had an influential role at a national polling company despite not being publicly associated with the firm, the Guardian can reveal. Chris Bruni-Lowe, Farage’s private pollster for many years, played an important role in the operations of Redfield & Wilton Strategies and used it to develop potential campaign strategies, according to several sources who have worked there. The firm, founded in 2020, is owned by Bruno Rodrigues, a lawyer. Its main public face was Philip van Scheltinga, a Harvard graduate. As the Covid pandemic grew and the UK entered lockdown, the company’s polls received increasing coverage, even while the source of the firm’s polling expertise was unclear. Former employees have now revealed the important role of Bruni-Lowe, who sometimes went by the name “Chris Redfield”, under which quotes were published by the Washington Post newspaper. As well as ordering UK and US voter intention polls, sources said Bruni-Lowe directed research on issues such as council spending, and appeared “obsessed” with producing a dossier which he suggested could be sold to political parties. Bruni-Lowe’s role at the company will amplify questions about transparency in the polling industry, given his longstanding association with Farage at a time of intense scrutiny over the party’s use of polls to shape its political narrative. The rules of the British Polling Council do not require pollsters to state any political affiliations, but they have strict guidelines on how they must declare who has commissioned and paid for any polling. In a statement, Rodrigues, the company’s sole director, said there had never been “an institutional, polling, research, commissioning or financial relationship” between Redfield & Wilton and Reform UK or Farage. He said Bruni-Lowe had worked as a “consultant” from mid-2020 until late 2022, and returned “voluntarily” in the summer of 2025 to train interns. Rodrigues added that Bruni-Lowe was “an important and highly valued member” of the team. Sources said Bruni-Lowe, who some employees said had been known as “Chris Redfield”, was heavily involved in the company’s polling operations. Rodrigues said the surname Redfield was used as an email account convention within the organisation, citing other examples of “Philip Redfield” and “Bruno Redfield”. He said: “It was not a device created specifically for Chris and it did not conceal his identity from people working within the company.” Nonetheless, the situation was confusing enough that at least one newspaper, the Washington Post, attributed quotes to that name, while notes taken by one former employee during an oral induction in the summer of 2021, and seen by the Guardian, described “boss – Chris Redfield is COO essentially”. Rodrigues said: “He was never presented to staff as the company’s chief operating officer and staff were never instructed to treat him as such.” He added that Van Scheltinga, as director of research, led the “day-to-day operation”. The Guardian can also reveal that Dan Jukes, then a senior adviser to Farage, sought to promote Redfield & Wilton’s work in 2020, looking to place exclusive polls in publications including the Guardian, which turned down the offer. Jukes stepped down as Farage’s chief of staff recently over a scandal in which undercover reporters posed as potential overseas donors to Reform UK. Footage published by Channel 4 News showed the co-founder of polling firm JL Partners, James Johnson, apparently acknowledging that Jukes had commissioned polling funded by an overseas donor. The polling had appeared in newspapers without any reference to the party, with JL Partners acknowledging “weaknesses” in its procedures. Jukes denies wrongdoing and Reform UK has said the party itself did not commission the work. On Wednesday, Reform announced that an internal inquiry had cleared the officials of breaking the law . The matter remains under police investigation. Redfield & Wilton started producing polls in 2020 with little information about the people behind the company. During its publicly active years before it became less visible in late 2024, its voter intention polls frequently appeared in politically influential newsletters from Politico, the Times, and the New Statesman. Bruni-Lowe ran Farage’s 2015 election campaign, helped test messaging for the formation of the Brexit party and advised on the 2019 local elections campaign, as well as having produced private polling for Farage since at least 2014, apart from during a brief period of working for Rishi Sunak before the 2024 election. In his book on political strategy, he writes of having worked for “organisations and candidates of all political persuasions”.

events.title: Why are the Houthis attacking Saudi airports and how are the missiles getting through?
events.summary: Attacks by Iran-backed group come amid counteroffensive by Yemeni government supported by Riyadh On Saturday, a missile strike by the Houthis in Yemen hit Riyadh’s international airport , killing 13 people and wounding hundreds. On Sunday, another attack ‌killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others. CCTV footage showed people cowering at the moment of impact of Saturday’s attack. Footage filmed in the aftermath of showed damage inside one of the terminal buildings at the airport, which is located about 22 miles north of the Saudi Arabian capital. The attacks by the Houthis, an Iran-backed group, were the biggest escalation yet in their campaign ⁠against Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in recent weeks. Though the violence might appear at first sight to be restricted to the Arabian peninsula, it could have global consequences , pushing up fuel prices and so international inflation. The Houthis’ timing is partly opportunistic but also rooted in the dynamics of the conflicts across the Gulf. The Houthis initially stayed on the sidelines of the conflict launched by the US and Israel against Iran earlier this year. But last month, the Islamist militia movement seized control of key territory and gained virtual control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, which dominates the Red Sea, a critical shipping route for oil and gas exports from the region. The Yemeni government forces and local allies began a major counteroffensive last week to drive back the Houthis from the Bab al-Mandab and also hit other Houthi positions . Saudi Arabia is in the Houthis’ crosshairs because it supports Yemen’s UN-backed government and its forces. Their attacks on high-profile targets in the kingdom such as oil infrastructure and the capital’s airport – key symbols of its international integration and economic future – makes painfully obvious the costs of Riyadh’s strategic choices. Such attacks also benefit Iran, which has long supported the Houthis as part of its “axis of resistance”, a coalition of Islamist hardline movements that allows Tehran to project power and influence round the region. The new threat from the Houthis to the Red Sea and to Saudi Arabia highlights again the massive leverage Tehran and its allies can exert on global oil and gas supplies, countering recent US pressure in bold move on the conflict’s chessboard. How is this new territory for Saudi Arabia? The recent attacks on Saudi Arabia have been the deadliest to hit the kingdom in a decade. They also marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi civil aviation in years, forcing airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services. Businesses in Riyadh’s financial hub have told employees to work remotely, authorities in Riyadh have asked schools to switch to online classes this week, and top energy executives were ⁠dropped from the schedule of a high-profile conference this week in the capital. Though Saudi Arabia has intervened indirectly in conflicts around the Middle East and beyond for decades, violence has rarely struck the kingdom itself. In recent months, the country has found itself on a frontline, something its rulers have long sought to avoid. Why couldn’t Riyadh stop the missiles? Saudi Arabia has invested enormous sums in its military – the kingdom is the world’s eighth biggest spender on weapons – but Houthi attacks are very hard to stop. “Saudi air defences have been able to intercept some Houthi missile and drone attacks, but Saudi Arabia is so large that it’s simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves,” said Thomas Juneau, a security analyst at the University of Ottawa. Other analysts point out that even the vaunted Israeli air defence systems failed to stop a ballistic missile narrowly missing Ben Gurion international airport last year. Reprisals against the Houthis and efforts to pre-emptively destroy the movement’s offensive capabilities are not easy either. The US bombardment in 2025 showed how hard it is to destroy the militia’s capabilities, which have been much enhanced over recent years, in part through Iranian advice and investment. The Houthis say their actions were “guided by reciprocity” – suggesting they are responding to ongoing Saudi strikes on the territory they control in Yemen – but show no sign of stopping their attacks. “Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing,” official statements carried by the Houthi-run al-Masirah television channel said. It seems unlikely Saudi Arabia will halt its counterstrikes, and equally unlikely the kingdom will be able to find a way to block all incoming Houthi missiles, though it may improve its intelligence gathering and early warning to allow better defence of specific high-value targets. Nor is there any imminent prospect of an end to the hostilities between Iran and the US that are a major factor in the surge of the recent violence in Yemen.

events.title: OPay readies $4B New York IPO
events.summary: The News OPay, the Lagos-based fintech firm backed by Softbank and Chinese billionaire Zhou Yahui, more than doubled its revenue in the first half of 2026 as lending overtook payments as its top source of income, according to a filing ahead of a planned New York listing likely set for next month. The company has applied to trade under the ticker OPAY, with a potential Nigerian secondary listing to follow. The filing lays out a business growing rapidly after jumping 137% to $467 million in revenue in the first half of 2026 while net income rocketed by over 300% to $91 million. OPay launched in Nigeria as a payments company in 2018 backed by Chinese investors and later funded by venture investors led by Softbank. OPay hadn’t disclosed an IPO price range or a listing date as Semafor was going to press but based on the normal sequence of filings and roadshows, investors will be expecting pricing to be revealed in mid-November. Previous reports have put the initial valuation estimates around $4 billion. The fintech firm also outlined plans for a secondary listing on the Nigeria Stock Exchange after the NYSE debut to give local investors an opportunity to buy into a business that drives nearly nine-tenths of its revenue from Nigeria. But the F-1 filing warned investors that shares traded in Lagos may not be exchangeable for the New York-listed American depositary shares, potentially limiting liquidity and allowing prices to diverge. Know More A key part of the IPO is a broader strategic relationship with Standard Bank Group, Africa’s largest lender by assets. Its subsidiary, Stanbic Africa Holdings, has agreed to invest up to $200 million, subject to a formula that caps its stake at 4.99% of OPay after the offering. Standard Bank’s Africa head Lungisa Fuzile is expected to join OPay’s board following the IPO. The two companies have also signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding to explore partnerships spanning payments, merchant acquisition, lending, remittances and the distribution of selected banking and financial products. OPay suggested in the filings that it will use Standard Bank’s infrastructure, regulatory expertise and presence to expand across Africa. Step Back OPay took off in 2019 in Nigeria with ambitions to be a super app that offered various features, including motorcycle taxi bookings, food deliveries, and quick loans. But it narrowed its focus to financial services in recent years and raised $570 million in venture funds between 2018 and 2021. A handful of African tech companies have successfully listed in the US, notably e-commerce platform Jumia and telecom towers provider IHS but have had mixed performances. An OPay listing in the US would be the first by a fintech company with a mostly Nigerian customer base.

events.title: Ecobank agrees to join Chinese payment platform
events.summary: Ecobank agreed a partnership with China’s payment system to enable transaction settlements in the yuan currency. The Togo-based bank, which operates in 34 African countries — more than any other continental lender — will sign an agreement this month to join the China Interbank Payments System (CIPS). South Africa’s Standard Bank and the African Export Import Bank have taken the same step in the last year. The move follows increasing demand from businesses on the continent to transact and settle deals using China’s currency. An 18% rise in China-Africa trade last year — marked by a surge in the continent’s imports of Chinese solar power equipment — underscored the growing commercial relationship between both parties, highlighting the appeal of financial systems that make transactions easier to complete. China this year removed tariffs for imports from all African countries except Eswatini. Its move to increase bank integrations with its payments system furthers a push led by the BRICS bloc against the US dollar’s dominance in international trade. — Alexander Onukwue

events.title: Time to tell US raider Saba Capital to get lost – again | Nils Pratley
events.summary: Time to tell US raider Saba Capital to get lost – again Boaz Weinstein’s hedge fund is waging an aggressive campaign against the FTSE 250’s Baillie Gifford US Growth Trust H ere we go again: another episode in the Saba saga , the story of a New York hedge fund causing havoc in the UK investment trust sector by taking big stakes in funds and then demanding change, often in only vague terms. The best that can be said about Saba Capital (and it’s not much) is that its belligerent boss, Boaz Weinstein, has disturbed the complacency that used to infect corners of the UK investment trust world, meaning companies that invest in other companies. It is now harder for a board to do nothing if the share price sits at a wide discount to the value of the underlying assets for long periods. Too often, though, Saba’s assaults look self-interested, short-termist or damaging for UK investors. The attack on Baillie Gifford US Growth Trust, a FTSE 250 constituent usually known by its USA ticker, is all three. Regular shareholders in USA have roundly told Saba to get lost twice in the past 18 months but they will have to do so again if they value what they own, which they should. The US raider, sitting on a near-30% stake, wants to install three of its nominees on the board via a vote at next week’s annual meeting . On a long view, USA’s performance has been excellent: an annualised return of 16.7% since launch in 2018, beating the S&P 500 over the period and within the top 10% of all UK investment companies. The only reason an opening, of a sort, has appeared for Saba is because the 16.7%-a-year returns haven’t happened in a straight line. The pop in AI valuations in late-2022 means USA’s five-year statistics are less impressive. But volatility is what investors accept when they buy into a strategy of backing high-growth US companies for the long-term. The portfolio is stuffed with stakes in big names in the AI world – Anthropic, Databricks, OpenAI, SpaceX and Stripe – that were acquired when the companies were smaller and sometimes still privately owned. A little bit of biodiversity in the UK investment landscape will be lost if USA falls under Saba’s control. What would a Saba-dominated board do? It’s hard to say definitively because this is all Saba says: “If our nominees are elected, we would urge them to offer all USA shareholders a 100% cash exit at or near NAV [net asset value] – providing a long-overdue liquidity event.” The absurdity of that proposal lies in the fact that the board of USA says it has already offered Saba what it supposedly wants – a chance to get out at a price nearly equivalent to the value of the assets. But the US hedge fund declined. The suspicion is that Saba’s nominees could try to appoint Saba itself as manager, or wrap USA into a Saba-managed vehicle. And, note, Saba’s main funds in the US now trade on far wider discounts to asset value than USA’s relatively modest 3%. Since Saba hasn’t spelled out much, all one can say is that its nominees cannot possibly be regarded as independent. One is a Saba employee; the other two are serial picks in Weinstein’s various campaigns. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Here is broker Investec’s assessment: “Saba offers no credible plan. Shareholders are being asked to give its nominees potential board control on the strength of a conditional, non-binding liquidity proposal, with no roadmap for the future manager, strategy or governance: vote first, then find out later what you’ve voted for.” The choice, then, is between a known strategy that has been successful, with a few bumps, or a mystery ride under Saba’s tame directors. The analysis should not be hard: shareholders should stick with the existing board. Independence matters. Here’s the tricky bit, however. Saba’s near-30% holding, plus 7.7% in the hands of assumed sympathiser Sessa Capital, means USA shareholders need to act. “Not voting is a vote for Saba,” says broker Panmure Liberum. “Support the board, or suffer the consequences,” warns Investec. Sound advice. The annual meeting is on 23 October but, for anybody holding via an investment platform, the effective voting deadline can be as soon as this Wednesday. Those platforms – looking at Hargreaves Lansdown, AJ Bell and Interactive Investor – should be warning clients of deadlines right now. Preferably in red for danger.

events.title: Americans Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford win Nobel memorial prize in economics
events.summary: STOCKHOLM -- American economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel Memorial Prize in economics Monday for their work on models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks, such as energy crises and inflation. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, noting that their work created the theoretical foundation to better understand how consumers decide whether to save or spend, insights that make it easier for policymakers worldwide to stabilize economies after fluctuations. “The laureates’ research has made it possible to manage major macroeconomic crises far more effectively than before,” the Nobel committee wrote. “It has been hugely beneficial during the pandemic and the energy crises of recent years." Hall is affiliated with Stanford University in California, and Woodford with Columbia University in New York. Woodford spoke to the committee by phone from New York: “It’s a tremendous honor. It’s a surprise." For decades, governments responded to economic shocks by following the Depression-era prescriptions of the British economist John Maynard Keynes: Intervene in the economy by lowering taxes and hiking government spending, thereby encouraging consumers and businesses to spend and invest and help restart growth. “This is the Keynesian recipe and it worked well — until it didn’t,’’ said Timo Boppart of the Nobel economics committee. Policymakers had thought economic management involved simple trade-offs — unemployment, for instance, would stay low at a time of high inflation and rise when inflation fell. But the “ stagflation ’’ of the 1970s — when the world economy experienced simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment — proved the formula was simplistic. Some economists argued that government attempts to intervene in the economy were doomed to fail. But Hall and Woodford, in separate contributions, set about improving the Keynesian model to take into account how consumers and businesses actually make decisions about whether to invest and spend. “Economic outcomes are the result of millions of decisions made at the microlevel by households and businesses,’’ the Nobel committee wrote. “Using models based upon this approach, rather than simply studying the economy from a macro perspective, like a bird’s eye view," Hall and Woodford’s research "generated a paradigm shift in the theory of stabilization policy.’’ Hall studied the way that consumer decisions about whether and how much to spend depend on what they expect their future income to be. “If they are optimistic, they will consume more than if they are pessimistic,’’ the committee wrote. But consumer expectations can change unexpectedly as new information about the economy comes in. And some households are so poor they can’t borrow or tap savings in response to economic changes. In a 1982 paper with the economist Fredric Mishkin, Hall found that around 80% of households made spending decisions based on their expectations for the future “while the rest lived hand to mouth,’’ the committee wrote. “The prize is for research that pushes our understanding of macroeconomics from the bottom up, from families and firms making decisions over time, while looking ahead,” Ivan Werning, an economist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said in an email. 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police Collin Gosselin says life on TV with mom Kate Gosselin was ‘a lie’ Hasan execution will be live-streamed, Pentagon official says Woodford’s research established that businesses make decisions about prices based on where they think interest rates will go in the future. “If the business believes that its competitors’ prices and its own costs will increase, it is best to set a higher price than it would with the opposite expectation,” the Nobel committee wrote. “Businesses’ decisions are thus also governed by their expectations.’’ Therefore, central banks such as the U.S. Federal Reserve, which set short-term interest rates, should provide “clear and credible communication about how they reason and what they plan to do.’’ Central banks have responded to this insight by working harder to explain what they are doing. During the phone call broadcast at a news conference, Woodford said his work has stressed “the understanding of the people who are in the markets and making decisions about spending.” The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. The central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel Prizes. Nobel purists stress that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel Prize, but it is always presented together with the others on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Nobel’s death in 1896. Nobel honors were announced last week in medicine , physics , chemistry , literature and peace.

events.title: First Utility-Scale Enhanced Geothermal Plant Goes Live
events.summary: This article was originally published by Canary Media . The geothermal startup Fervo Energy is now selling power to the grid from its Cape Station project in Utah — marking the first time a utility-scale, next-generation geothermal facility has achieved such a feat worldwide. The Houston-based firm turned on an initial 33-megawatt unit late last week and has been testing and ramping up output since then. On Thursday, Fervo will officially begin commercial operations, supplying carbon-free electricity to Shell Energy, a retail power provider in California. Cape Station, a $2 billion project that will eventually be 500 MW, is unique among the world’s commercial geothermal plants. While other facilities draw on naturally occurring hot water and steam, Fervo has engineered its own geothermal resource deep underground. The startup uses drilling techniques from the oil and gas industry to create reservoirs in hot, dry rocks that generate steam to produce electricity. “Traditional geothermal would have never been done in southern Utah,” sa ys Dawn Owens , Fervo’s senior vice president and head of development and commercial markets. With the first unit online, Fervo sa ys it is working to commission two more 33-MW power blocks by 1 Jan uary , 2027. The project’s remaining 400 MW — which is supported by a new agreement with Google — is under construction and slated to come online in 2028. Fervo’s Next-Generation Geothermal Journey Fervo already operates a 3.5-MW commercial pilot plant in Nevada, which went online in late 2023. Owens sa ys the pilot, called Project Red, was important for demonstrating the technology itself. But firing up Cape Station proves that Fervo’s approach can achieve utility scale and export power to wider markets. “This is massive for both Fervo and the geothermal industry at large,” she sa ys . Fervo , which went public in May, is leading the fast-growing movement to develop clean, always-on geothermal power to meet soaring demand from data centers and balance growing supplies of intermittent solar and wind energy. Next-generation geothermal firms have raised billions of dollars in private capital in recent years to develop and deploy technologies that can harness energy in harsh, deep environments. Drilling continues at Fervo Energy’s Cape Station geothermal plant in Beaver County, Utah, where the company plans to ramp up production to 500 MW. Fervo Energy Today, geothermal represents just 0.4 percent of total U.S. electricity generation every year. Expanding geothermal’s share of the mix will require not just building more projects like Cape Station but also tackling high upfront drilling costs and other economic and regulatory barriers — all while working to limit potential impacts on communities and the environment, experts say. “ Fervo’s first power achievement shows investors the size and scale of the opportunity to fuel many more such milestones across developers and sites in the future,” sa ys Mitchell Smith , who serves as grid lead for the Mountain West Geothermal Consortium. The bipartisan initiative is calling for increased public and private financing “ to help bring more projects online responsibly and at the speed of demand,” he added. Enhanced Geothermal Energy Gets Cheaper Fervo has declined to disclose the terms of its power purchase agreements for in-progress and future development, which together represent about 1,000 MW, or enough to power roughly 1 million U.S. homes every year. Phase 1 of Cape Station is set to deliver power at $7,000 per kilowatt, while Phase 2 should come at $5,500 per k ilowatt , the company previously told Canary Media. (By comparison, the average cost to build a natural gas–fired power plant was $2,157 per k ilowatt in 2025.) Along with slashing drilling costs, enhanced geothermal projects could improve their economics by delivering power when it’s most valuable to utilities, according to researchers . While geothermal plants traditionally provide around-the-clock, baseload power, next-generation facilities might operate flexibly during certain periods — like in the evening, when solar output declines — to reduce overall grid costs. Geothermal plants could also operate “ behind the meter” to directly power data centers, so that the costs of adding new electricity capacity aren’t passed on to utility customers, Owens sa ys . “We’ve been saying all along that our technology makes geothermal more scalable and affordable in more places,” she sa ys . On Cape Station’s powering-up, she add s , “ That’s just something no next-generation geothermal company has ever been able to do before.”

events.title: Former Plaud exec raises $26M for AI app that listens to you in the background
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. One of the core promises of AI is that the more it knows about a person, the better it will be able to assist them with tasks and make appropriate suggestions, which, if you’ll believe the tech companies, requires apps and devices to listen, watch, or record users’ activity all the time and gather all possible context. There’s obviously privacy and data security concerns with anything that’s collecting data about you continuously. But startups are building such apps undeterred anyway, arming themselves with the belief that the market for personalized assistance is big enough to swallow such concerns. Former Plaud exec Peter Mo is building Ambi to do something similar. The app aims to provide real-time intelligence and insights to people by listening to them all the time. The company said on Monday that it has raised $26 million across multiple funding rounds led by Luminous Ventures, which has backed companies like Meituan and Unitree Robotics, and original design manufacturer (ODM) Huaqin. Ambi is also releasing apps for iPhones, Macs, and Apple Watch. These apps act like meeting notetakers, but users can choose to have them listening so they can capture context all day. Meeting notetaking companies have been working to automate tasks that follow once calls are done, based on the summaries and action items they gather during the conversation, and using multitudes of connectors to software systems. Ambi wants to take this a step further by having its agent start the work during the meeting itself. The company’s promise is that its AI agent can proactively give you suggestions or surface relevant knowledge while you are in a meeting, based on your calendar, meetings, knowledge base, and web data. Users can also start a task on one device and continue it on another. “The way we interact with intelligence is limited. Often the intelligence is trapped on the screen, and if you use hardware like Plaud, you need to wait for recording to transfer to the phone, upload to the cloud, and get intelligence after processing. That’s why we are building Ambi to use AI anytime and anywhere,” Mo, the company’s co-founder and CEO, told TechCrunch. The company has ambitions to capture more information. Its upcoming desktop app will be able to look at the work that users do and store important parts in its memory to give more personalized suggestions. Apps like Littlebird or Minimi already do something similar. The startup is also planning to launch its own hardware device, which will have a screen, a speaker, a camera, and microphones to capture context and display information. Ambi’s launch comes amidst growing concerns around AI devices that don’t have enough indicators to suggest they are capturing data on people around the user. It is not clear if Ambi’s apps or its upcoming device will have enough indicators to alert third parties that their conversations are being recorded if the user doesn’t disclose their use of Ambi’s tech. Some meeting notetakers have even been sued because their tech recorded people’s conversations and data without their consent. Plus, the recent release of Apple’s Audio Intelligence feature, which transcribes speech continuously, has raised privacy concerns . Mo said that users can turn off ambient data capture on Ambi’s apps and devices at any time, and the feature is off by default. The startup said it doesn’t store any recordings of users and encrypts the data, but it didn’t specify what kind of encryption it uses. Despite these measures, the onus of declaring ambient capture is still on the users. He classified this as an industry-wide problem. “We have to inform our users that they have to tell others about ambient capture. We, as an industry, haven’t solved this problem [of disclosure]. We have tried to put the information about disclosure in every place possible, but if users try to hide the capture, we can’t just solve the problem,” he said. Ambi currently has over 50 staff across offices in San Francisco, Beijing, Shanghai, and Shenzhen. The $385 billion Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund is looking to boost investments in China, India, Japan, and South Korea , with plans to deploy about 10% of its assets each year globally, Chief Financial Officer Carlos Obeid said at the Milken Institute Asia Summit in Singapore last week. The energy transition, technology, the restructuring of global supply chains, and evolving consumer behavior are Mubadala’s four focus areas, he added. Last month, the world’s most active sovereign wealth fund bought a minority stake in Luckin Coffee, which may bring the Chinese chain to Abu Dhabi. events.title: Turmoil within Dolly Parton’s estate underscores the precariousness of family businesses after founders die
events.summary: Dolly Parton waves to her fans at Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tenn., in March 2024. Amy Harris/Invision via AP Dolly Parton’s nephew Bryan Seaver announced the legendary singer’s death on Aug. 25, 2026, in a prerecorded video. Seaver, the son of one of Parton’s 11 siblings , had been her head of security for many years. But Seaver is currently embroiled in a messy dispute with She’s Alive LLC, the company Parton established to manage her business assets after her death . This unusually acrimonious fight highlights some of the business succession problems that can arise when the founder of a company dies but wants its other leaders to keep it going. Parton, a legendary American singer, actress, entrepreneur and philanthropist, left behind an estimated US$450 million estate . She’s Alive LLC terminated Seaver’s involvement with the business, and a court has issued a restraining order against him. Seaver is accused of engaging in “ an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats” against Parton’s estate . He denies the allegations. As professors who research and teach topics related to inheritance law, we are fascinated by the Parton case. It illustrates some of the pitfalls of planning for the transition of a privately held business after the founder’s death – a concern for celebrity and noncelebrity estates alike. Following Dolly Parton’s death, there has been turmoil in her management involving her nephew Bryan Seaver. Managing celebrity estates after death Celebrity estates, like Parton’s, are distinct because they often contain valuable intellectual property. This includes copyrights, which protect creative works , such as songs and recordings, including Parton’s catalog of hits. Another valuable asset in these estates are publicity rights , which protect the use of the celebrity’s name or likeness, such as the use of Parton’s face on a T-shirt sold for profit. These rights can be enormously valuable long after the celebrity has died. Without careful planning beforehand and appropriate management after death, the estate may never get the full value of these property interests. Prince, for example, died in 2016 without a will or any formal estate plan. The twice-divorced Minneapolis pop star had no surviving children. His estate passed to his siblings, who were his sole heirs . It took more than six years to administer his complicated $156 million estate , which concluded with the heirs establishing corporate entities to manage his intellectual property rights. One of those entities, Prince Legacy LLC, recently became embroiled in litigation when some of Prince’s heirs sought to fire the managers who had been hired to manage their share of the intellectual property rights. Marilyn Monroe, who died in 1962, also without any children, left behind a professionally drafted will under which her longtime acting coach, Lee Strasberg (and his then-wife) inherited most of her publicity rights. But Strasberg remarried, and his widow – a woman whom Monroe never met – hired various professional managers, including a company known as CMG Worldwide , which specializes in the management, marketing and promotion of publicity rights associated with dead celebrities. Because of the successful management of her estate’s publicity rights, Monroe became known as one of the highest-paid dead celebrities – with large sums enriching a woman she’d never met. Marilyn Monroe’s will is seen on display at Julien’s Auctions in Beverly Hills, Calif., in 2012. Joe Klamar/AFP via Getty Images Should a founder’s relatives remain in charge? Many much-less famous family businesses face similar questions about how to keep their profits and revenue flowing and who should manage the company after the founder of a family business dies. A continuation of business operations may have many benefits for a deceased founder’s family. The founder may have relayed their succession plans to them. Relatives often have institutional knowledge and loyalties that can enhance the value of the business and make it last longer. Studies have not conclusively shown, however, whether continuing a business within the family is clearly better or worse for its bottom line than having outsiders manage it. As one study found, family managers often have a “ sense of kinship obligation ” and enjoy “personal and social fulfillment” from working together in the business. That, in turn, creates incentives to manage the firm carefully with an eye toward long-term survival. By contrast, another study of small and medium-size businesses after the sudden death of a CEO-owner found that, in the short run, nonfamily successors are better equipped to run the company . Relatives, by contrast, may be hampered by grief and the emotional impact of the death. But the study also found that in the long run, family members may be more successful in managing the business because they “are likely to view the firm’s survival as a way to stay connected with the deceased family member and keep their memory alive. In turn, this is expected to inspire great stewardship towards the firm.” Other studies, however, have found that maintaining family control over the management of a company after its founder’s death can hurt its performance. Restricting the pool of potential managers to relatives excludes better-qualified candidates who can bring expertise and experience that members of the family lack. Research has shown that hiring pros tends to be best for the business . Death can be bad for business When the owner of a privately held business dies, their assets, including real property, intellectual property and investments, will pass to others according to the estate plan, if the owner created one. But in many cases, the true value of a business is more than just the sum of all its assets. Some of the value may reside in the owner’s talent, knowledge and business acumen. In some cases, the owner maintained personal relationships with employees or customers that may have played a key operational role. In others, the owner may have relied upon unique personal qualities to achieve success in business. Parton herself, for example, was likely the most significant driver of value for her business because of her creativity and star power. According to a 2022 study by economists who studied what happened to startups following the death of nearly 1,500 business founders, growth and profitability fell after the founder’s death. Smaller companies are at risk of having to close altogether. The study found that the negative effects on business continuity “appear to be driven by entrepreneur specialness rather than leadership transition,” which suggests that the founder’s unique contributions to the business can be difficult to replicate after death even with excellent transition planning. events.title: Business faces a more interventionist Washington post-midterms
events.summary: Both parties will be pressured to intervene more in markets after the midterms as economic frustration animates the new Congress, according to an FGS Global sketch of 2027 Washington scenarios, shared first with Axios. Why it matters: In a Trump-dominated Washington, Congress ceded much of its power and relevance. That'll change three weeks from Tuesday if Democrats win the House, as expected, and perhaps the Senate in the midterms. The new analysis by FGS , a worldwide strategic leadership advisory with huge clients, is a sequel to a popular FGS report that Jim VandeHei and I used as the basis for a series of popular "Behind the Curtain" columns before the 2024 elections. FGS bills "Alternative Futures: Beyond November" as a framework for processing the epic battles ahead: how power will get used, how both parties will evolve, and how business leaders can navigate the uncertainty. "The 2026 midterms will begin — not end — a 27-month period of unusually high strategic uncertainty," the report says. Zoom in: Michael Feldman — FGS partner and co-chairman, North America — tells me that for Republicans, "intervention may mean tariffs, industrial policy, domestic manufacturing incentives, and other measures aimed at strengthening U.S. production capacity, economic security, and competitiveness." "For Democrats, intervention may mean affordability policies, labor protections, antitrust enforcement, plus regulation designed to reduce costs, curb concentrated corporate power and address inequality." "Everyone is focused on who controls Congress," Feldman added. "We think the more important question for business is what happens next. The midterms are the beginning, not the end, of a period of significant political and policy uncertainty." Left: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) campaigns in Linden, N.J., last year. Right: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) campaigns in Davenport, Iowa, last week. Photos: Getty Images Zoom out: Three structural shifts will drive the post-midterm operating environment for businesses of all sizes, FGS warns. " Voter dissatisfaction may be the most important force pushing both parties away from established policy orthodoxies. A frustrated electorate could push both parties toward more populist, interventionist and less predictable approaches to business." "Technological disruption could reshape the political agenda as profoundly as traditional partisan conflict. AI and related technologies are becoming a political variable — not merely a sector-specific policy issue." "Generational turnover will weaken established political assumptions even where ideology remains unchanged. The next generation of leaders may inherit existing parties without inheriting their relationships, orthodoxies or governing style." The bottom line: "Divided government does not necessarily mean lower political/legislative risk," FGS writes. "It may mean that policy/political conflict moves in less predictable ways." events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp. A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining. That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will. Find out what stands in the way of a city on the moon . —Robin George Andrews This story is from the next issue of our print magazine. Brimstone is a code-switching climate tech company for these polarized political times. The US startup is part green cement company, part critical mineral producer. During the Biden administration, its primary pitch was cement that generates about 60% fewer greenhouse-gas emissions. It achieves this by switching to silicate rocks instead of standard limestone, which releases carbon dioxide when heated. Under the Trump administration, however, the company is emphasizing another benefit of its process: the ability to extract valuable materials from those same rocks.
