events.title: Healey faces £35bn Budget challenge to meet spending pledges, says think tank
events.summary: Chancellor John Healey faces having to find £35bn to avoid cuts to public spending while meeting defence promises in his first Budget, an influential think tank has warned. The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said that if the government wants to raise defence spending to 3% of national income by 2030 and lift health spending without squeezing other departments, it will need a "top-up" of billions of pounds. Higher inflation, caused by the Iran war, could eat into what the government hoped to spend on public services, meaning Healey will have to choose between spending cuts, tax rises, or a mixture of both, the IFS said. The government is under growing pressure to show financial markets that it has a tight grip on finances as the cost of borrowing rises. The IFS said that Healey must set out "credible" spending plans in the Budget, which will take place on 28 October. "A 'steady-as-she-goes' Budget is not an option available to the chancellor," said IFS director Helen Miller. "Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments' spending plans off course. "Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the Budget a work of fiction," she added. Speaking ahead of the annual International Monetary Fund meeting this week, Healey said: "The consequences of conflict in the Middle East and Europe are hitting countries worldwide, leading to higher prices at the pumps and more expensive mortgages at home. "But Britain and our allies can face up to these challenges together." He said his Budget "will build on this approach with fiscal discipline helping to deliver economic resilience" and give people "breathing space". Miller told the BBC's Today programme that Healey had inherited spending plans for government departments where spending growth would slow in the coming years. "[It] already looked likely that he would have to make spending cuts just to live within those," she said. "Now, along comes the Middle East war, inflation goes up and those spending plans look very tight indeed." Added to that, the chancellor has said he wants to get defence spending up to 3% of national income. Under Keir Starmer's leadership, Healey resigned as defence secretary in June in a battle with the Treasury over military spending. Miller said: "You put all that together, if he wanted to do all of that within current spending plans he's looking at having to cut some other services by something like £35bn." She said the government would have a "tough time" if it wanted to raise taxes to stop cuts to departments and fund defence spending. Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced billions of pounds in tax rises. Meanwhile, Labour pledged in its manifesto "not increase taxes on working people", ruling out rises to National Insurance, income tax or VAT. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will stick to that promise. Miller said: "You'd really have to be scaping around and doing lots of small things to get up to big sums." The chancellor does not have to address spending totals in this Budget, and may choose to leave such decisions until future events - for example, next year's Spring Statement or Spending Review - by which time the outlook for the economy could look very different. But the IFS warned not addressing it would cast doubt on the credibility of the government's plans. Previous chancellors have relied on a similar strategy of pencilling in unrealistic future spending plans to ensure that they meet the fiscal rules on the day - only to change the plans further down the line. Miller said Healey's focus on fiscal discipline was a "good first start but what he needs to do is not just say he's going to cut borrowing in coming years but actually deliver on those plans." The US-Israel war against Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine have together helped drive up energy prices around the world. These higher costs have been passed to customers via higher prices on shelves and at the pumps. The wars have also contributed to a rise in the cost of UK government debt interest payments, adding to the pressure on Healey. Although higher inflation will boost tax revenues, it will also eat into the value of departments' cash budgets, the IFS said. Like other analysts, the IFS thinks recent turbulence on bond markets and higher inflation will add around £10bn to forecasts for the government's borrowing costs in 2029-30. However, it still expects the government to meet its self-imposed fiscal rules - that it will only borrow for investment projects by the financial year 2029-30 and also be reducing debt as a percentage of GDP - not least as inflation pushes up tax revenues. But it expects those rules to be met by a smaller buffer - known as "headroom" - of around £20bn. That is less than the £24bn buffer predicted at the time of the Spring Statement by the official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).

events.title: Saudi Arabia says oil supply to continue to flow despite Riyadh attacks
events.summary: Saudi Arabia sought to reassure the world’s energy industry that escalating attacks on the kingdom would not disrupt its role as a major oil supplier. “The word ‘fear’ in the Saudi dictionary does not exist,” Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said on Monday at the opening of the WPC Energy Congress . “We, as Saudis, are fearless, combatant and determined people.” The remarks came after King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was struck four times in five days, emphasising the growing security risks facing the world’s biggest crude exporter amid the Iran war. A missile attack on the airport on Saturday killed 12 people and injured 309, Saudi authorities said. Another projectile struck the airport on Sunday evening, killing one person and injuring 11. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen blamed the Iran-backed Houthi rebels for Saturday’s attack. But Riyadh is to press ahead with a week of high-level energy meetings, including Sunday’s International Energy Forum ministerial talks and the WPC congress, which the kingdom is hosting for the first time. “Riyadh is the capital of energy security and your presence here today proves that,” Prince Abdulaziz told delegates. “Our gathering today does not mean that risks have disappeared.” The attacks have sharpened focus on Saudi Arabia’s ability to keep oil flowing during periods of conflict, particularly as threats mount around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab Al Mandeb strait, two of the world’s most important energy chokepoints. Prince Abdulaziz said Saudi Arabia’s ability to withstand disruption was the result of decades of investment in storage, redundancy and alternative export routes. “Resilience is built before a crisis begins,” he added. He referred to the kingdom’s East-West pipeline , which carries crude from eastern oilfields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, allowing exports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. The flow was halted after Houthi attacks in September, before recovering to about 5.8 million barrels per day by October 6, compared with capacity of about seven million bpd. The disruption showed the importance of restoring operations quickly, Prince Abdulaziz said. Resilience depends not only on infrastructure but also on domestic expertise, he added. “Pipelines do not repair themselves. Our systems do not restore themselves. Facilities do not restart themselves. People do,” he said. At Sunday’s IEF meeting, he pledged that Saudi Arabia would continue to supply domestic and international customers “regardless of circumstances”. The gathering took place against an increasingly volatile market backdrop. Brent crude hovered at about $104 a barrel on Monday as the Riyadh attacks and strikes on two tankers near the Strait of Hormuz and Oman added to geopolitical risks. “The events of recent weeks are serious,” Prince Abdulaziz said. “Our response must be equally serious.”

events.title: Oman aims to launch new international financial centre by 2027
events.summary: Oman plans to launch full licensing at its new international financial centre by 2027 and is to begin registering companies later this year. IFC Oman, the plans for which were first revealed in January, is currently working on its legal framework, rule book and registry system, it said in a statement on Monday. A package of laws for business registration and licensing, financial services regulation and an independent dispute resolution framework are to be issued shortly, the financial centre said. They will provide the legal basis for IFC Oman’s authorities to adopt an initial package of regulations and rules. A registry system, which will enable businesses to submit their applications online, is to move into the testing phase soon, the statement added. “IFC Oman is accelerating towards opening its doors, with its legal, regulatory and digital infrastructure moving into place," said Mahmood Al Aweini, chairman of the IFC Oman Authority Board. "The centre will offer global businesses and investors a stable and competitive place to do business." IFC Oman will join other existing financial centres in the Gulf, including Abu Dhabi's international financial centre ADGM, the Dubai International Financial Centre and the King Abdullah Financial District in Riyadh, as well as the Qatar Financial Centre. The financial centre has started boosting its international outreach to engage prospective businesses, investors and professional services firms around the world, the statement said. Oman has been taking steps to diversify its economy away from oil , with investments in sectors such as logistics, manufacturing and property helping to expand its non-oil economic base. Under its economic and social reforms programme, Oman aims to reduce its dependence on oil income from about 30 per cent to 16 per cent by 2030 and 8.4 per cent by 2040. The sultanate has also announced the introduction of personal income tax starting in 2028, with a 5 per cent rate of tax on annual income exceeding 42,000 Omani rials ($109,134). Muscat also unveiled a golden visa programme in August to attract more foreign investment into the country. It also has plans to build a new economic area centred on developing its artificial intelligence capabilities, as it aims to accelerate its technology sector to strengthen its economy. Last month, S&P Global Ratings boosted the economic growth forecast for Oman to 3.5 per cent on the back of favourable trade logistics amid the Iran war. The outlook is more than double the previous 1.6 per cent real GDP growth estimate for the sultanate. It is also higher than the 2.3 per cent growth posted by Oman last year.

events.title: 'I just live on noodles': Report reveals scale of NT cost-of-living crisis
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Territorians 'in crisis' as report shines light on skyrocketing cost of living over past decade Four generations of Shirley Napurrula Miller's family in Central Australia are supporting each other to try to make ends meet. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) New data has revealed the rising cost of essentials is making it harder for people to meet their basic needs in the Northern Territory compared to a decade ago. The report by the NT Council of Social Service examines the changes in the cost of living between 2016 and 2026 across key spending areas of housing, utilities, transport and food. The community sector peak body is recommending federal government welfare payments be increased along with the remote area allowance for people in isolated areas. For an Alice Springs grandmother who receives a disability pension, the struggle to afford groceries between pay cheques is constant, with the cost of food "too high". Shirley Napurrula Miller is among the nearly 50 per cent of the Northern Territory's population who experienced food insecurity because of rising prices in 2025, according to a new report. "Sometimes I can't buy groceries, or meat, or anything," she said. Shirley Napurrula Miller says she struggles to afford the basics for herself and her family. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) The report by the NT Council of Social Service (NTCOSS), released today, examines changes in the cost of living between 2016 and 2026 across key spending areas of housing, utilities, transport and food. It shows every day, across all spending areas, many Territorians are having to make impossible money decisions and weigh up what they must prioritise to live. Hunger relief charity Foodbank Australia estimates that 46 per cent of NT households experienced food insecurity in 2025, above the national average of 33 per cent, according to the NTCOSS report. The report found that while incomes have increased in real terms in the past 10 years, the cost of essentials has too. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) In remote areas, the cost of food is even more prohibitive than in urban centres such as Darwin and Alice Springs, where prices have also risen substantially. "In 2023, the average cost of a healthy food basket was 40 per cent more in remote stores than in a supermarket," the report states. The 10-year comparison report found that while incomes have increased in real terms, the cost of essentials has too, making it harder for everyone — especially those on low incomes — to meet basic needs. Power costs have risen 18 per cent and those on prepaid plans, predominantly First Nations people in urban and remote public housing, are having their electricity cut off more frequently, with 2,284 more disconnections per month on average last year than in 2019-2020. The report found there were 103,648 involuntary self-disconnections in major centres in the NT last year. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) Further compounding cost pressures for those already on the poverty line, the report states the prepaid electricity price is higher than for standard postpaid billing to account for customers not paying a fixed daily charge. According to the report, there were 103,648 involuntary self-disconnections in major centres in the NT last year. "Affordability challenges are a key driver of such disconnections," the report states. Ms Miller said she had faced disconnection many times and Aboriginal families often lent on each other to share their limited incomes and keep the power on, particularly in the heat over summer. Linda Lechleitner says her electricity bill alone is more than her Centrelink payment. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) Her daughter, Linda Lechleitner, who lives between Alice Springs and a remote Aboriginal homeland near the community of Papunya, about a 3-hour drive away, said she worried about electricity costs amid a heating climate. "It's more than the government payment that they give you, the Centrelink payment doesn't carry people through fortnightly," she said. "Every little dollar counts … it's not carrying through to the next fortnight or the next week, they're having to borrow money from family and then pay that back. The report reveals rents have skyrocketed 55 per cent over the past decade. Meanwhile, the NT's social housing stock only increased by 4 per cent between 2017 and 2025, while social housing applications increased by 37 per cent over the same period. The report shows transport costs have also shot up, with an 80-litre tank of diesel now costing $28 more in Darwin and an extra $88 in Alice Springs.

events.title: AI investment boom offsets energy shock to keep global growth at 3%, IMF chief says
events.summary: Strong investment ⁠in AI infrastructure is keeping global growth at about 3 per cent, yielding major ​benefits for many Asian economies that supply the hardware, such as Thailand, International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva said on Monday. The artificial ⁠intelligence investment boom was already delivering a “demand shock, an investment shock” that could boost growth in advanced Asian economies by a half to one full percentage point, and emerging Asian economies by 0.2 to 0.8 percentage point, she said. “AI, love it, hate it. It's already here,” Ms Georgieva said. “That ⁠shift into higher gear is what is keeping the world economy growing at around 3 per cent, despite the fact we are ​being dragged down ⁠by the energy supply shock,” she told ‌hundreds of participants on the first day of a week-long series of meetings of the IMF and World Bank in the ​Thai capital. The IMF in July forecast global growth at 3 per cent in 2026. It will release an updated outlook on Tuesday. About 18,000 people are expected to attend the meetings this week, including finance officials from the IMF's 191 members. Several ministers will skip the meeting to focus on domestic priorities, including US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Spanish Finance Minister Arcadi Espana, sources said. Profound consequences Ms Georgieva said AI amounted to a “slow-moving tsunami” that would have profound consequences for jobs, growth, education and even how governments generate revenue through taxation, given the expected shift from labour to capital. The IMF estimates that AI could lead to 40 per cent of jobs being augmented, downgraded or eliminated, over time, she said. An initial study showed that 10 per cent of jobs in the US already required AI skills. While routine, repetitive jobs were shrinking, low-paying jobs were increasing in two lower-paying sectors, construction and data centres. “It is a transformative technology . It so completely changes how we work, how we live,” she said, noting that an AI assistant now gave her a ​30-second message about her schedule each day. The US, China and India are the most important ‌producers in the AI supply chain, but many of ⁠the firms building the needed infrastructure are in Asia , Ms Georgieva ​said, referring to Thailand, host of this year's annual meetings. Impact on entry-level jobs World Bank President Ajay Banga, who ​has made jobs ‌a central focus of his presidency, said the development bank was focused on leveraging “small AI”, which is not dependent on large language models, to generate ⁠enormous productivity gains for farmers, healthcare systems, educators and others in emerging markets. Singapore's President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, speaking at the same event, ⁠said governments should address how AI was reducing job opportunities for graduates. “There is a particular problem that we have to address very soon … and that is that, the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand,” he said. Mr Shanmugaratnam said the world should also guard against AI resulting in a “new divergence” in growth and job creation between ​developing and advanced economies. “AI is going to widen the divergence if we are too passive about it,” he said. “So we've got to do everything we can to first use AI to create good jobs and to create jobs that can be done well by human beings, can allow them to ride up a career ladder despite AI.”

events.title: Brake-pedal failures in luxury EV put Chinese cars’ quality in regulatory spotlight
events.summary: Viral video of broken brackets in test of car from Huawei-backed brand prompts ministry action to step up policing of quality A safety failure spotted in tests of a Chinese electric vehicle (EV) made by a Huawei Technologies-backed luxury brand has raised doubts about the cars many consumers view as a source of national pride, and prompted regulators to step up policing of quality and reliability. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, along with three other ministry-level departments, published draft rules on Saturday that would govern testing of new car models. The move came after a video released on Thursday on ByteDance-owned car-information platform Dongchedi showed that brake-pedal brackets snapped on all three Maextro V800 EVs used in a test of emergency braking from 100km/h. “A car’s brake pedal should absolutely never fail while driving,” Communist Party mouthpiece People’s Daily said in a commentary on Sunday.

events.title: Beijing police detain Yiren Digital chairman after massive product defaults
events.summary: Authorities launch a criminal investigation into firm after defaults Police in China have detained a controller of Yiren Digital, a US-listed Chinese digital lender, after two related investment platforms failed to repay mainland investors for over four months. The Beijing Municipal Public Security Bureau said that it had recently launched an official criminal investigation into relevant companies associated with CreditEase over suspected illegal activities and had arrested controllers, including a 53-year-old male with the surname Tang and a 51-year-old female surnamed Zhao, according to a notice on Monday. In 2015, Yiren went public on the New York Stock Exchange as a consumer loan arm of CreditEase, which was established in 2006. Tang Ning is the founder and controlling shareholder of both CreditEase and Yiren. The notice came one day after CreditEase announced “a material default” on fixed-income-like products on two of its asset management platforms, after deciding to fully suspend repayments on the products on May 22. The firm attributed the decision to the scale-down and underperformance of inclusive finance and wealth management businesses.

events.title: Startup Funding: Q3 2026
events.summary: AI dominated funding in the third quarter of 2026, with two inference companies each announcing $1 billion in funding. But with the data center buildout driving insatiable demand for memory, investors also rewarded startups with alternatives to costly, capacity-limited HBM. Some are building on commodity DRAM or holding models in on-chip SRAM, while others stack memory directly onto compute. Data movement at all levels of the stack remains a critical bottleneck, too. Interconnect technologies, networking chips, and photonics were the most active areas of the quarter, with startups tackling the problem with diverse approaches ranging from manufacturing-ready co-packaged optics, millimeter-wave RF signals over plastic waveguides, and ferroelectric glass modulators to optical couplers printed directly onto chips and coherent DSPs designed specifically for AI optics. Nearly $7.5 billion of the quarter’s total was directed to just 22 startups that raised $100 million or more, including eight that saw investors return within roughly a year, some more than doubling the previous round. Plus, agentic EDA and AI-generated analog layout, small chip fabs, diamond-based defect inspection, large-area nanoimprint lithography, and memory-safe microcontrollers feature in this look at 80 companies that collectively raised over $8.5 billion in Q3 2026. Summary table Chips AI hardware EDA Manufacturing & equipment Test, measurement & inspection Memory & storage Photonics & optics Previous reports Chips Xsight Labs raised over $300.0M in funding led by Fidelity Management & Research Company with participation from Aliya Capital Partners , Atreides Management , Artisan Partners , Battery Ventures , Diagonal Capital , Intel Capital , Key1 Capital , Maverick Capital , Sienna Venture Capital , T. Rowe Price , Union Group , and Valor Equity Partners . Xsight Labs designs fully programmable data processing units (DPUs) and Ethernet switches for hyperscale, edge, and AI data center networks. Built on open standards, its DPU runs native Linux, DPDK, and SONiC and uses 64 Arm Neoverse N2 cores that sit directly in the data path to process millions of connections per second at full 800 Gbps line rate. The company’s 12.8 Tbps Ethernet switch operates at deterministic, sub-700ns latency under 200W. Funds will be used to accelerate the company’s roadmap, add support for emerging Ultra Ethernet Consortium standards, hire, and scale manufacturing. Founded in 2017, it is based in Tel Aviv, Israel. Celero Communications raised $275.0M in Series C funding led by Atreides Management , Valor Equity Partners , and CapitalG , with participation from Sutter Hill Ventures and Maverick Silicon . Celero develops coherent DSPs for AI optical interconnects. Rather than adapting a long-haul coherent design, the company built a DSP architecture optimized for low power and low latency, paired with new analog circuitry connecting the DSP to the optical system that it says is designed to scale to higher bandwidth over multiple generations. The architecture targets scale-up, scale-out, and scale-across connectivity from 1.6T to next-gen 3.2T. Celero has validated 2nm coherent DSP silicon, including the DSP processing and analog technology. Funds will go to accelerating the product roadmap, R&D, and production readiness. Founded in 2024, it is based in Irvine, California, USA, and has raised $415M to date. Cornelis raised $205.0M in funding . Cornelis builds scale-out networking for AI and HPC, spanning SuperNICs, switches, and open-source software built around its own switch silicon. Its 400 Gb/s system uses credit-based flow control and fine-grained adaptive routing, which the company says makes the fabric lossless and congestion-free. The company is sampling an 800G SuperNIC that supports Omni-Path, RoCEv2, and Ultra Ethernet concurrently. Cornelis is extending into scale-up networking with programmable in-fabric compute built on UALink and ESUN, an approach it says lets the network offload collective operations. Funds will be used to scale production. Founded in 2020 as a spin-out of Intel’s high-performance interconnect business, it is based in Wayne, Pennsylvania, USA. The company is looking to cut $129 million from the business and spend about $100 million on new water infrastructure. The company says it will make changes to strengthen its long-term viability. Job losses are likely at South 32's manganese mine on Groote Eylandt in the Northern Territory as the operation battles years of flooding impacts and skyrocketing production costs. The Groote Eylandt Mining Company (GEMCO) mine has begun consultations with staff. The ABC understands it needs to cut $129 million from the business in response to costs increasing by more than 80 per cent in recent years. The island and mine site were hit hard by Tropical Cyclone Megan in March 2024, but it is understood multiple wet seasons and persistent seepage of groundwater into the pits are also responsible. Mining pits on Groote Eylandt filled with water after Cyclone Megan in 2024. ( Supplied ) A South32 spokesperson said in a statement the company would make changes to strengthen its long-term viability and was speaking to workers. "GEMCO has completed an internal review in response to a more challenging operating environment and increased cost pressures, and has begun implementing changes designed to strengthen the long-term sustainability of the business," the spokesperson said. "The review forms part of a program focused on improving structures, systems and processes and ensuring GEMCO is well positioned to operate successfully into the future. As part of this work, GEMCO has reviewed its workforce requirements and commenced consultation with employees and contractors who will potentially be impacted. Officials from two separate unions representing workers at GEMCO told the ABC they believed office staff would likely be the target of redundancies . A spokesperson for the NT branch of the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union said it was closely monitoring the situation to see if blue-collar workers were affected. Union officials were told South 32 management would provide staff with more information about the redundancies by the end of the week. According to GEMCO's enterprise bargaining agreement, the company must consult with workers before making any significant organisational changes. The bargaining agreement is due to expire at the end of 2027. The MV Anikitos was loaded with 41,000 tonnes of manganese ore when it crashed into a loading wharf on Groote Eylandt. ( Supplied ) The island's wharf was destroyed in 2024 when Tropical Cyclone Megan pushed a loaded bulk carrier into the structure during high tides . Experts say more investment is required to ensure EV charging infrastructure keeps up with vehicle sales. Residents have until next Monday to object to the company's plans. On a long stretch of highway roughly halfway between Melbourne and Adelaide is a farming town hoping to cement its reputation as an electric vehicle (EV) charging must-see. The western Victorian farming town of Kaniva, with a population of roughly 800 people, already has 10 Tesla Superchargers behind its quaint country pub. The global tech giant has submitted plans to the local council to install another eight, and publican Bob Cane couldn't be happier. Kaniva is home to 10 EV charging sites, with plans to install another eight. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) "It's about bringing people to Kaniva, connecting them with a classic, quintessential Australian classic town," Mr Cane said. Painted sheep have adorned the streets of Kaniva since 2012. ( ABC News: Martin Boulton ) Kaniva currently markets itself as the first and last highway town in Victoria, the gateway to the Wimmera Mallee Silo Art Trail and the "home of Sheep Art". Mr Cane said the chargers were invigorating the town and adding another string to its economy. "When they plug in their car, what are they going to do? [They will] go for a walk into town, get a coffee, grab a hamburger," he said. Bob Cane is hoping the new Supercharger stations will be up and running before Christmas. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) The Windmill Cafe owner Jemma Hill said the chargers had been a boon for the town. "They [travellers] stop, they come over, they grab their lunch and their coffee, they come into town," she said. "It's creating extra foot traffic within the town, which is fantastic, makes it feel very alive." Jemma Hill says the current EV chargers have helped her business. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) The existing chargers are a lifesaver for some travellers already tackling the trek between Melbourne and Adelaide. "We do this trip a few times a year … If we didn't have this, we couldn't get [to Melbourne]," Tom Beresford said. Kaniva is home to about 800 people. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) West Wimmera Shire Council deputy mayor Helen Hobbs said the site, which has been open for about nine months, had already made a difference in the town. "That has actually given people like the bakery confidence to invest," Cr Hobbs said. "To have a brand new bakery with seating for 100 people, it's beyond anything I could have imagined." Helen Hobbs says the EV chargers have brought outside investment into the town. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) EV sales doubled in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, according to the Electric Vehicle Council of Australia. The council's Aman Gaur attributed the jump to cheaper EVs, rising fuel costs and improved charging networks. "We're now up to 4,200 charging locations across Australia and over 11,000 connectors," Mr Gaur said. "Charging stations have definitely been increasing in Victoria and the number of connectors has also been following suit." Ampol this month paid $225 million to buy Evie, one of the country's largest charging networks. Milad Haghani says if EV demand continues to grow at the same pace, charging infrastructure will have to catch up. ( ABC News: Patrick Stone ) University of Melbourne associate professor of urban resilience and mobility Milad Haghani said charging infrastructure would have a serious job keeping up if the EV sales boom continued. "It's hard to predict whether or not the spike in demand that we have observed this year is going to be sustainable," he said. Public chargers have rarely had queues, he said, but that could change as more people buy EVs. events.title: UAE Property: 'Can my tenant legally list my apartment as a holiday rental without my consent?'
events.summary: Question: I own an apartment in Dubai Marina, which I've rented to the same tenant for two years. A neighbour recently contacted me because different people appear to be entering the apartment every few days with suitcases. I checked one of the holiday rental websites and, to my surprise, found what appears to be my apartment being advertised for short-term stays . I never agreed to this and my tenancy contract says the property is for residential use by the tenant. The tenant is paying the rent on time, so financially, I haven't lost anything, but I'm uncomfortable with strangers continually using a property I'm responsible for. Can a tenant legally do this without my permission, and could I as the owner face problems if something happens? Ahmed, Abu Dhabi Answer: I wouldn't ignore this simply because the rent continues to arrive on time. There's an important distinction between a tenant occasionally having friends or family stay and somebody commercially offering another person's property as short-term accommodation. Dubai's holiday-home sector is regulated, and properties being used for this purpose need to comply with the relevant licensing and registration requirements. Separately, your tenancy agreement determines what your tenant is permitted to do with the apartment. Subletting in Dubai is not illegal; however, the landlord must be informed and agree to the subleasing. Since you were not informed, his actions are illegal and he cannot simply decide to turn your property into his own short-term rental business. Before taking any action I suggest you document what you've discovered. Save screenshots of the advertisement, including photographs that clearly identify your apartment and keep any messages from neighbours or building management. I would then write to the tenant and ask for an explanation rather than immediately making accusations. I'd also establish whether the apartment has actually been registered as a holiday home and, if so, how this was done without your knowledge. There's another practical concern: short-term occupation can mean considerably more wear and tear than a conventional tenancy, as well as possible issues with access cards, building security and insurance. For landlords, this is a useful reminder that receiving the rent doesn't necessarily mean everything is fine with the property. Sensible asset management means knowing how your investment is actually being used. Q: My former partner and I bought a villa in Dubai several years ago in both our names. We have now separated. I want to sell the property so we can both move on financially, but my ex refuses. He says that because he owns half of the villa I cannot force him to sell his share. Neither of us can realistically afford to buy the other person out, and there is still a mortgage on the property. What happens when two people jointly own a Dubai property but one wants to sell and the other simply refuses? Are we effectively stuck owning it together indefinitely? Emma, Dubai A: This is unfortunately one of the complications of joint property ownership that people rarely think about when they're happily buying together. You cannot ordinarily sell your former partner's ownership interest simply because you want the whole property sold. Equally, however, joint ownership doesn't necessarily mean two people must remain financially tied together indefinitely. The first thing I'd establish is exactly how ownership is recorded on the title deed and the respective ownership percentages. Then have the property independently valued. Once you know the realistic selling price, deduct the outstanding mortgage and likely selling costs so both parties can see what equity would actually be available. Sometimes having a real number on the table makes negotiations considerably easier. Possible solutions include one party refinancing and purchasing the other's interest, an agreed sale on the open market or another mutually acceptable transfer arrangement, subject of course to the lender and Dubai Land Department requirements. I'd also check who has been paying the mortgage , service charges and other property expenses since the separation because those contributions may need to be considered when the financial position is ultimately resolved. If agreement genuinely cannot be reached, this moves beyond estate agency advice. You should speak to a Dubai lawyer experienced in property and co-ownership disputes about the legal mechanisms available to bring the joint ownership to an end. The wider lesson for unmarried couples, friends and relatives buying together is simple: discuss the break-up before the purchase. A written co-ownership agreement setting out what happens if one person wants to sell can prevent an enormous amount of difficulty later. events.title: The extra stripe that's landed Australian retailer White Fox in court
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Adidas sues White Fox Boutique over its trademark three-stripe design A pair of Adidas shorts with its trademark three-stripe design next to White Fox Boutique shorts with four stripes. ( Supplied ) German sportswear brand Adidas has accused Australian fashion retailer White Fox Boutique of infringing its trademark three-stripe design with garments featuring four stripes. Legal experts say the case could test the trademark registration. The matter is set down for hearing in early 2027. When is a stripe not a stripe? According to sportswear brand Adidas, when it is part of its trademark. The global sportswear giant is suing Australian online fashion retailer White Fox Boutique for selling items allegedly "deceptively similar" to its three-stripe logo, in a case experts say could test the trademark's registration. The German-based brand has filed a trademark infringement claim against the Sydney-based company, popular with teenagers, in the Federal Court of Australia. According to court documents, Adidas accuses White Fox of replicating its trademark across multiple clothing items and advertising content that feature four parallel stripes of equal width in a colour contrasting with the colour of the clothing. Adidas claims this design is "deceptively similar" to its three-stripe trademark, which it has used in Australia for more than 65 years and globally for more than 75 years. White Fox is defending the case, which will play out in court hearings next year. A White Fox Boutique advertisement seen on the back of a bus. ( Supplied ) According to the documents, White Fox Boutique has promoted and supplied clothing with four parallel stripes on it since March this year, including advertisements on buses, bus stops and on social media. Adidas said it asked White Fox to remove the garments from sale in March and to stop using the four-stripe design, which White Fox declined to do. Adidas further claimed White Fox used genuine Adidas shoes, in the same colours as its clothing, in some promotional material, which it said took advantage of the brand's reputation and may lead consumers to draw an association between the two companies. An Instagram post advertising a White Fox Boutique outfit paired with genuine Adidas shoes. ( Supplied ) It alleges White Fox's actions are likely to cause damage to its reputation. In court on Friday, White Fox's barrister Ed Heerey KC said the online fashion retailer would argue the four stripes emblazoned on the label's clothing were simply decorative rather than a trademark. He highlighted similar items bearing the four stripes from other brands, including fast-fashion labels Princess Polly, Glassons and Shein. Intellectual property law expert Muhammad Abbas said this case was not just about a fourth stripe. "Adding a stripe is neither a complete answer to a trademark claim nor automatically an infringement," Dr Abbas, a Queensland University of Technology lecturer, said. He explained a 2023 High Court decision considered the impression a notional buyer, "allowing for imperfect recollection", would have of the registered trademark, compared to the impression created by the sign used. The three-stripe design dates back to the brand's foundation in 1949, but was not trademarked until 1952 after Adidas discovered a Finnish brand Karhu had trademarked the same logo. Founder Adolf Dassler struck a deal and traded two bottles of whiskey and the equivalent of 1,600 euros ($AUD2,500) for the logo, which it has extensively protected ever since. In 2013, it successfully sued Pacific Brands over its use of a four-stripe design on some of its Dunlop and Grosby shoe designs, with the court ruling that three of the 12 designs in question were "deceptively similar". However, University of Technology Sydney School of Law senior lecturer Sarah Hook said challenges overseas had led to Adidas losing its trademark registration in some jurisdictions. In the US, Adidas unsuccessfully took high-end designer Thom Browne to court over a four-stripe design. Thom Browne wore socks with the four-stripe design to court in New York. ( Reuters: Eduardo Munoz ) Thom Browne then challenged the trademark registration in the UK, and the High Court ultimately ruled the trademark was invalid. Fashion designer Thom Browne emerges from a New York courthouse victorious over sportswear giant Adidas. University of Melbourne intellectual property law studies director Benjamin Hopper said distinctiveness was a core doctrine of trademark law, meaning it had to be distinguishable from other goods or services from other traders in the same marketplace.

events.title: Judge halts Trump administration's taxpayer-funded ads
events.summary: A federal judge on Sunday ordered the Trump administration to immediately halt taxpayer-funded ads featuring President Trump. Why it matters: The ruling temporarily blocks the ads weeks before November's midterm elections as multiple lawsuits challenging the Trump administration's use of taxpayer money play out in court. Sunday's ruling stems from a suit filed in the Southern District of New York by Washington, D.C.-based watchdog Common Cause, non-profit Democracy Forward and other plaintiffs. A similar lawsuit , filed by the Democratic National Committee, was filed in D.C. federal court earlier this month. The big picture: The Trump administration maintains that the ads are public service announcements and that previous Republican and Democratic administrations have used taxpayer-funded advertising to promote government policies. Trump pledged to pay for the ads himself after both lawsuits were filed, though the White House told Axios there were no plans to reimburse the government for millions already spent on the ads. Driving the news: The plaintiffs in the New York lawsuit allege that the Trump administration exceeded congressional authorization and violated restrictions on publicity and propaganda. In a brief order , U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon found that a motion filed by the coalition was "not moot." She found they had "demonstrated that they are likely to succeed on the merits, will suffer irreparable harm in the absence of an injunction, the balance of the equities tips in their favor, and an injunction serves the public interest," according to the order. The suit names the Department of Homeland Security, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought, and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles as defendants. What they're saying: The coalition said in a statement emailed by Democracy Forward it was "pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda." The statement added, "There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda." The White House referred Axios to Trump's Truth Social post last week last week, in which he described the ads as a "positive promotion" for the U.S. Representatives for the DHS did not immediately respond to Axios' Sunday evening request for comment. What's next: A hearing is scheduled for Tuesday to discuss next steps in the case. Editor's note: This story was updated with a statement from the plaintiffs and the White House's response to a request for comment.

events.title: Fox stays positive on data centers even as public backlash grows
events.summary: The News Despite increasingly critical media coverage of AI and the spread of data centers across the US, one news network has been painting a more positive picture. More than half of the references to data centers on Fox News over the last two years would have left viewers with a favorable impression, compared to less than 10% on CNN and 5% on MS NOW, according to a new Semafor analysis of mentions of data centers on each network. The mentions were pulled from closed captions preserved by the Internet Archive, which keeps a digital, searchable library of recorded TV news. A pair of AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI scored each reference on its content, with the network’s name removed. Mentions of data centers have, predictably, shot up across all three networks in recent months as political backlash against AI swells and the data centers themselves have become a salient issue ahead of the midterms. But Fox’s opinion and morning shows, including, , and leaned on the promise of AI, economic investment and the race with China, skewing Fox’s coverage more favorably, the analysis showed. The network’s news shows were more measured. In an Aug. 23 monologue that at one point featured a chyron reading “The case for data centers,” Fox host Brian Kilmeade acknowledged “real concerns,” but argued that “saying no to data centers nationwide also means saying no to the tax dollars that can flow into a community. … If Americans don’t build the infrastructure to meet the demand, somebody else will.” On CNN and MS NOW, the criticism focused as much on the facilities’ political toxicity as on harms like power bills or water use, casting them as unpopular with voters and a liability for politicians who back them heading into the midterms. Data centers “are driving up energy costs, sucking up water supplies, wiping out rather than creating jobs,” MS NOW’s Katy Tur said in May. “Politicians beware.” Polling shows that across demographic groups, Americans hold increasingly negative views of data centers: More than half of Americans say data centers are mostly bad for the environment , Pew Research Center found last month, compared with 39% in January. Fox News did not comment for this story. Max’s view The pro-data center programming on Fox News comes as the right tries to define its positions in an AI-fueled, post-Donald Trump future. Fox’s favorable data center coverage mirrors Trump’s position on their growth and the need for AI companies to help fuel the US economy. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in August. “If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame.” But anger about data centers and the rapid advancement of AI represents a faultline within the MAGA coalition that swept Trump back into office. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., have questioned some data centers in their states, while Texas Gov. Greg Abbott seems to have flipped from supporting data centers to looking to slow their growth in his state amid a tougher-than-expected reelection campaign. Some on the right I have talked to in the last several months worry that Fox News, which Trump watches religiously, and other pro-data center voices are encouraging the president to take positions that are broadly unpopular with his rural and suburban base. “The Big Tech oligarchs, the guys driving AI, did a terrible job,” Steve Bannon, a staunchly anti-AI Trump ally, told the Daily Signal in September. “They came in to try to muscle local communities, and particularly since President Trump’s strongest base is in exurban and rural communities, that’s where they were really the ugliest, and they haven’t made their case, and they particularly haven’t made their case at the local level about the economics of this, and the energy of this, and the water of this, and the manifestation of what these things are going to be used for.” Room for Disagreement Not all of Fox’s data center coverage has been rosy; its tenor grew slightly less favorable in 2026 compared to last year. “It’s taxing our system way too much on water, agriculture land, or electricity. events.title: Hack reveals Netanyahu campaign's media ties
events.summary: The News Hacked messages from an adviser to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu are providing a glimpse of his aides’ close ties to the media. The incumbent prime minister’s reelection campaign has been repeatedly rocked by hacked and leaked documents, part of broad attempts to destabilize a wildly divisive leader both inside and outside his country ahead of Oct. 27 elections. The latest breach comes from the WhatsApp account of Netanyahu aide Jonatan Urich, who appears to have exposed sensitive information through a vibe-coded media-monitoring app. Haaretz reported Sunday that it had “verified” the leak. The messages include conversations between Urich and Amit Segal, a central media figure who is chief political analyst for Channel 12 News, the country’s leading broadcaster, and host of the program , an analogue of the US show of that name. In the exchanges, Segal offers advice about the campaign’s videos and its messaging: Netanyahu’s management of the aftermath of the October 7 attack is his core political advantage, he suggests. Segal mentions he offered the same advice to Netanyahu’s campaign spokeswoman. In another message, Urich shares a speech Netanyahu is planning to give. Segal declined to discuss the messages on the record. Urich, who is also enmeshed in a scandal over payments from Qatar, didn’t respond to an inquiry, but in a lawyers’ statement posted to X confirmed that he had been hacked and threatened legal consequences against anyone who published the content of the leaks. Israel’s Privacy Protection Law prohibits republishing content obtained through illegal means. Ben’s view Hacks and leaks are challenging to cover. The most important story in most hacks — including this one — is the hack itself; this is part of the broad internationalization of the Israeli political campaign, in which actors across the region and in the US line up for and, mostly against, the leader who led his country’s response to the October 7 attacks. But Israeli commentators also professed shock, if not surprise, Sunday at how closely aligned the journalist and spin doctor appeared to be. Segal is a center-right figure broadly aligned with Netanyahu — but he’s also a top journalist who appears on international platforms, like the American political figure Dan Senor’s widely-followed podcast, as an independent analyst. One Israeli journalist compared Segal’s role in Israel to that of Fox News host Bret Baier, who maintains journalistic independence despite working for a right-wing platform. The messages put a dent in Segal’s version of that image, and offer a glimpse at parts of an Israeli media that has grown very close to its prime minister. Room for Disagreement Segal addressed the controversy on News 12, describing the messages as part of a “very delicate tango between the journalist and the subject of their coverage.” He added that “any people I’ve covered over the years gave me drafts of speeches, saying, ‘This will be our campaign, what are your thoughts?’” Notable The region’s politics have been buffeted — and illuminated — repeatedly by aggressive cyber campaigns for years. Semafor reported in 2023 on extensive, leaked Iranian government communications that revealed Iranian attempts to influence US politics.

events.title: ABC News offers contradictory explanation for vanishing Anduril story
events.summary: The News When ABC News removed a story about Donald Trump’s sons from its website without explanation on Thursday, an unnamed company source told media reporters the article had been published “prematurely.” Nathan Lee, the investigative reporter who wrote the original piece , used the same language in emails to Powerus and Anduril, two of the companies at the center of the piece. But emails between ABC News and its subjects, provided to Semafor, show the network seeking to downplay its errors by misrepresenting its own processes. On Oct. 7, ABC News published an investigation into a new $6.6 billion deal between defense contractor Anduril and the US Navy to build a new high-tech submarine shipyard in Maryland. The piece largely focused on the financial ties between President Donald Trump’s son and defense companies, noting that Donald Trump Jr. is a partner at investment firm 1789 Capital, which “claimed a major stake in Anduril in June 2025 from a $2.5 billion investment into the company.” After the piece was published, a spokesperson for Anduril reached out to Lee with several urgent requests for correction. The company — which had not responded to ABC News’ inquiries prior to its publication, according to an Anduril source — wanted the network to clarify connections between Anduril and 1789, noting that the firm had invested $50 million in Anduril’s latest round, a small percentage of the $2.5 billion total. “Today, 1789 owns approximately 0.13% of Anduril and has no major investor rights. Any suggestion that 1789 financed the round or holds significant ownership, governance position or ‘major stake’ in Anduril is inaccurate,” Anduril’s spokesperson wrote to Lee, according to emails obtained by Semafor. After the story was published on Wednesday, Lee told Anduril that the network was slightly tweaking the language in its piece, but it was otherwise standing by its story. “I have spoken to my editors and we have updated the story for accuracy,” Lee said in a note. “We had pulled the ‘major stake’ language from previous reporting. 1789 Capital did claim a stake from the $2.5 billion investment your company received, so we are standing by our language to that extent.” Anduril’s PR team was not satisfied, and continued to press the network to clarify its story, saying that the piece misstated 1789 Capital’s investment in Anduril’s fundraising round. “It’s still not clear. I read your text and it reads as if they invested the full $2.5b. Would be much more accurate to list their actual investment of $50m and even more accurate to share that they own less than a percentage point in Anduril,” a spokesperson wrote. In another email later Wednesday afternoon, Lee said ABC News’ editors had reviewed the language and were standing by the piece. “Apologies, but my editors said we are standing by the language. I’ll make sure to reach out to both of you directly for any future stories,” Lee said. But by Thursday, the network had changed its mind. The network removed the piece without explanation, and Peter Charalambous, an ABC News producer in New York, reached out to Anduril and Powerus, a drone contractor mentioned in the story, saying the story had been “published prematurely and removed from our website.” On Friday evening, ABC News republished a new version of the story re-reported by Charalambous, now without a byline . An editor’s note did not include language that the initial piece was published early. “Editor’s Note: CORRECTION: A version of this story published on Oct. 7 contained errors in the description of certain company investments, government contracts and event chronologies. After subsequent reporting, this version contains corrected information and additional context regarding some of those investments, contracts and events.” A network source told Semafor: “We always review every situation in a thorough and thoughtful manner and will not be providing further comment at this time.” The source also noted that it was extremely rare for ABC News to remove a story. Status reported Sunday that the article was mentioned during the network’s regular 9 am editorial call the day it was published, “suggesting at least some staffers were aware of its publication,” and it “circulated it through its usual email distribution without raising any immediate alarms.” Max’s view ABC News’ suggestion that its initial story was published prematurely is familiar spin to anyone who has dealt with crisis PR. It minimized the company’s mistakes and made the situation seem like an accident. But at a time when distrust in the news media continues to rise, deflections like this can damage the credibility of mainstream, nonpartisan American journalism. Tellingly, the network seemed to know the difference in its official response, acknowledging that the original piece contained errors. Brett Velicovich, co-founder of Powerus, another company mentioned in ABC News’ initial piece, complained that the network’s handling of the story reinforced his frustration with much of the media coverage of his company and the president’s administration. “It’s destroying the integrity of what reporting is all about,” Velicovich said. “The damage is already done.” The Trump family’s mix of business and governing, unprecedented in recent history, is an important reporting target, as journalists attempt to understand how companies and countries are attempting to influence policy by investing in Trump businesses or bringing the Trumps on as partners themselves. But ABC News’ decision to remove its story without explanation while misleadingly telegraphing that it was simply published on accident gave the president’s son and many on the right another opening to criticize mainstream news outlets. If more and more people continue to believe that news organizations are willing to mislead or fail to take full accountability for mistakes, will they listen when outlets have legitimate stories? Room for Disagreement Remove the numbers, and the most basic version of the story — the Pentagon is paying very large sums to a defense contractor in which the president’s sons have invested, and whose co-founder, Palmer Luckey, is a high-dollar Trump donor — is correct . It also follows a pattern congressional Democrats have promised to investigate should they retake power after the midterms.

events.title: Six senators call for Trump administration to 'immediately reverse course' on Russian diesel plan
events.summary: A bipartisan group of six senators are calling on President Donald Trump’s administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices WASHINGTON -- A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump's administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices. Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote. Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute. “The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” they wrote. The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut. Tillis, in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” said there's a legitimate case for saying the president is not following the law if the administration goes through with its diesel purchase plan. “We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied,” Tillis said. Trump's announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. The congressional effort was aimed at cutting the flow of money Russia receives from oil and gas sales to finance its war against Ukraine. The lawmakers also noted that Congress explicitly banned Russia energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war. “Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies,” the six lawmakers wrote in their statement. “President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law.” Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Trump is focused on reducing the cost of energy when asked whether the president's action would be in violation of U.S. law. Energy experts say the Russia deal is unlikely to make a dent in high prices at the pump. events.title: Buttigieg gambles on a different path for 2028
events.summary: Pete Buttigieg has been able to campaign for Democrats across the country more than many of his potential 2028 rivals this past year. One reason: He doesn't have a job. That's by choice. Buttigieg said no when top Democrats urged him to run for governor or the U.S. Senate in Michigan this year. Why it matters: That decision is a gamble for Buttigieg's presidential ambitions. He's been able to build a national network over the last two years but hasn't added to his relatively thin resume as a former mayor of South Bend, Ind., and Joe Biden's transportation secretary . Buttigieg, 44, became a national political figure without following the typical path. He ran for president in 2020 as a small-town mayor and won the Iowa caucus by offering an optimistic vision and impressing voters with his communication skills — including in hostile environments. Driving the news: In early 2025, Democratic lawmakers and strategists including New York Sen. Chuck Schumer and former Michigan Sen. Debbie Stabenow urged Buttigieg — who had moved to Michigan — to run for office in his new state. Winning such an office, they argued, would help Buttigieg build his resume for a future White House run and give him a chance to distance himself from the unpopular Biden administration. Buttigieg passed, citing both a desire to stay home more with his husband and young twins, and figuring that he could still get his message out without being in the Senate. Instead, he set about building a larger national network among Democrats — particularly with Black voters in the South, where he had struggled in the 2020 Democratic primary. Buttigieg has traveled to 37 states since he left the Biden administration, Politico reported last week. Democratic candidates in vital swing districts and states have welcomed him to campaign for them this year while resisting offers from other potential presidential candidates such as former Vice President Kamala Harris , New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and California Gov. Gavin Newsom. In Buttigieg, many Democrats see a surrogate who can draw attention and crowds without the degree of negative attention that other prominent Democrats attract. Buttigieg also will campaign in key races in the final weeks before the Nov. 3 election. He's scheduled to be in Michigan and Virginia — which happen to hold early contests in the 2028 presidential primary. Between the lines: Buttigieg has tried to position himself as a candidate of the next generation who also has enough experience in the executive branch to be able to deliver. He's betting that the traditional ladder of running for president — becoming a senator, governor, or vice president first — no longer applies, especially after the Trump era. What they're saying: Buttigieg "knows what no one else on the Democratic side does, which is what it's actually like to run for this office — the pacing, the pressures and imperatives," David Axelrod, a former senior aide to President Obama and an outside adviser to Buttigieg in the past, told Axios. "At a time when the party and country will be searching for youth and forward-looking vision, he has the capacity to articulate one in a powerful way," Axelrod added. Axelrod said that if Buttigieg runs, "it will be because he feels the timing is right for someone like him, and the big mission is more compelling than the statewide races on which he took a pass." A Buttigieg spokesperson said that "when Pete decided not to run for office in Michigan, he promised he would still get to work to help candidates everywhere. He's been doing just that."

events.title: Trump bears down on Zelensky as Russia keeps up attacks on Ukraine
events.summary: President Trump's announcement Sunday about an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine referred to a potential deal that includes each side stopping attacks on oil refineries — and he expects Volodymyr Zelensky to abide by it, a White House official said. The official said if attacks on oil refineries cease, a deal to stop hitting power plants and energy grids could come next. Why it matters: Trump appears to be singlehandedly trying to will a partial ceasefire into existence. But for now Russia hasn't accepted any kind of ceasefire — and Ukraine wants one that forbids attacks on power plants. Reality check: The "refinery for refinery" proposal, as the official dubbed it, is lopsided. A Ukrainian official told Axios that the country has a single oil refinery which the Russians have attacked multiple times and isn't fully functional. Russia, by contrast, has a vast network of refineries. "We import diesel and gas. What we need is for the Russians to stop attacking our electricity grid," the Ukrainian official said. "The Russians are thinking about" it, the White House official said. "We will know soon if they are ready." Case in point: Hours after Trump's announcement, Russia conducted strikes on power plants in Ukraine, according to Ukrainian media. What he said: Trump's Truth Social post sounded at first like a major breakthrough. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" he wrote. It appears much more tenuous than that. Zelensky said the announced ceasefire "was news for me." State of play: After reaching a deal with Russia Friday to lift diesel sanctions, Trump remains focused on stopping Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. He believes the strikes are driving up U.S. gas prices. White House officials warn that Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries are hurting Zelensky's relationship with Trump more than they're damaging Russia. "Trump is really mad. He feels Zelensky is taking the U.S. for granted," the White House official said. Zoom in: Amid the crisis with Ukraine, presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have put their planned trip to Moscow on hold, at least until they get clarity on whether Ukraine and the Europeans are ready to agree to a new unified proposal for Putin. A Ukrainian official told Axios on Friday that during a meeting with U.S. negotiators in Miami on Friday, Witkoff and Kushner threatened that Trump could stop sharing U.S. intelligence if it continued to ignore his requests. A U.S. official denied that, saying Witkoff and Kushner told the Ukrainians that the U.S. was a strong partner, providing munitions and intelligence. Ukraine therefore shouldn't take actions that hurt American consumers, the two said. On Sunday, the Financial Times reported that the U.S. told European countries it might stop selling weapons to Ukraine through NATO if Ukraine continues to strike Russian refineries.

events.title: Trump sticks with tariffs even as US voters turn against them before the midterms
events.summary: President Donald Trump shows no signs of budging from a trade policy that many Americans don't like as the midterm elections loom NEW YORK -- Maybe President Donald Trump really does believe that “tariff” is the most beautiful word in the dictionary . Despite higher prices, criticism from trade experts and displeasure among voters, Trump holds fast to his belief that imposing the highest import duties on U.S. trading partners since the Great Depression is a winner . A recent poll suggests that is a big gamble with less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterms. Most U.S. adults disapprove of his trade policies, with more than 64% saying he has gone too far with his latest tariffs, compared with 58% in January. A look at the political, legal and economic challenges to the Republican president's approach to trade. The United States has set taxes on imports from most countries in the low double digits, although the rates have gone up and down because of legal setbacks as well as Trump's habit of changing them seemingly on a whim . In the biggest round last year, Trump levied what he called “reciprocal” tariffs and other duties on dozens of countries. He cited a 1977 law that he said allowed him to act without congressional approval in an economic emergency. After the Supreme Court struck that down in February, Trump turned to an array of other trade laws to accomplish his goals. The primary one he is using now, Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 , allows him to impose tariffs on countries that he believes are engaging in unfair trade practices, such as not adequately enforcing a ban on forced labor. The new duties range from 10% to 12.5% on imports from 60 economies, including big U.S. trading partners such as the European Union, India, Japan, Canada and Mexico. Trump is taking a sledgehammer to a relatively open global trading system that many mainstream economists think has benefited the U.S. enormously. It has helped boost growth, keep prices low and make U.S. businesses more competitive and often dominant in global industries. The U.S. is the second-largest exporter in the world, after China. It exported $3.4 trillion in goods and services last year, far ahead of third place Germany’s $2.3 trillion. Although Trump claims foreign exporters are paying tariffs, it is mostly Americans who are footing the bill. Studies, including ones from New York Fed and Harvard , have shown that overseas companies have largely not lowered their prices to offset the tariffs that U.S. businesses pay at the border. Those businesses are absorbing the added costs or passing them along to consumers through higher prices. 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police Collin Gosselin says life on TV with mom Kate Gosselin was ‘a lie’ Hasan execution will be live-streamed, Pentagon official says The White House responds that the factory boom is already underway and points to statistics showing that manufacturing jobs, after falling last year, are on the upswing and work in certain nonresidential construction trades is rising, too. “Factory construction jobs of today mean more manufacturing jobs down the road once those factories come online,” said White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers. In the four years after China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001, nearly 3 million U.S. manufacturing jobs were lost, accelerating a shift away from factory work. Even global trade enthusiasts recognize the damage. Many U.S. companies struggled to compete with an influx of discounted products from China, which has suppressed consumption to encourage exports It also is true that some countries have higher tariffs than the U.S., manipulate their currencies lower to ensure to make their exports to the U.S. cheaper and help industries with subsidies. But tariffs among U.S. major trading partners are low, often comparable to U.S. rates and sometimes lower. Before the trade war, the U.S. rate averaged 1.47% for goods from the European Union, slightly above the average 1.35% imposed by the EU on American products , according to the Brussels think tank Bruegel. Europeans are big buyers of what America wants to sell. About 30% of European imports are from U.S.-owned companies, according to the European Central Bank. The relationship with Canada, America's big trading partner to the north, was also similar before trade talks broke down this summer. Canada's effective tariff rate on U.S. imports was about 2.4%, less than half the 5% that the U.S. had on Canadian imports, according to calculations by Oxford Economics. Now the countries are mired in a tit-for-tat dispute, with both countries escalating tariffs on each other. events.title: Trump claims Russia and Ukraine agree to energy ceasefire
events.summary: President Trump claimed Sunday that Russia and Ukraine agreed to an " energy ceasefire " and will halt attacks on each other's energy facilities. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky tells Axios the announcement "was news for me. But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire, Ukraine will agree." Why it matters: An " energy ceasefire" would be a dramatic diplomatic breakthrough ahead of the winter. It remains unclear if Russia indeed agreed to stop the strikes. Trump made a similar announcement last month, but neither party confirmed that there was a deal. Both Russia and Ukraine continued attacking energy infrastructure. What they're saying: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump wrote on Truth Social. In a short interview after Trump's announcement, Zelensky told Axios, "If President Trump negotiated it with Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready, and we will accept it." Catch up quick: The announcement follows days of escalating tensions between Trump and Zelensky over Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries. On Friday, Trump announced a deal to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports in an effort to lower soaring fuel prices, infuriating Ukraine. On Saturday, Trump called for Ukraine to replace Zelensky , accusing him of refusing opportunities to end the war. Zelensky responded Sunday on ABC's "This Week," saying Ukraine would hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire. He also said Ukraine was prepared to stop attacking Russian refineries if Moscow halted strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The big picture: The war with Iran has driven up global fuel prices, intensifying pressure on Trump to deliver relief for American consumers. "It's more difficult to stop Putin than to pressure others," Zelensky told ABC on Sunday. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.
